In accordance with these three operations, then, there are three different opinions. The first asserts that the universal is made through the abstraction of the agent intellect. It is followed by Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, toward the end; Soto, q. 3 on universals; Zumel, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, concl. 3. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, On the Soul 3, text 18, where, comparing the office of the agent intellect with corporeal light, he teaches that just as corporeal light by its material illumination makes colors actually visible, which in the darkness were only potentially visible, so the agent intellect, through the action by which it produces the intelligible species in the possible intellect, makes the nature actually intelligible. From which they gather as follows. The object of the possible intellect is the universal; but through the agent intellect the nature becomes actually intelligible, while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore it becomes actually universal.

Then by a twofold argument. The first is taken from the definition of the universal, which is one in many; but the nature through the abstraction of the agent intellect is one in many; therefore it is universal. The minor is proved: because in the intelligible species it is represented without the conditions; therefore, as so represented, it is one, since it is many on the part of the thing only through the conditions; and it is also in the many from which it is abstracted; therefore it is universal.

Second, for the nature to be one by universal unity expresses two things: one as foundation, namely the formal unity by which it is one in itself; and the other as it were as the formal element, namely the lack of the division which it has on the part of the thing through the individual differences; but represented in the intelligible species it is formally one, and it lacks division, since it is represented without the conditions; therefore it is one by universal unity; and it has the aptitude of being predicated of many, because, represented without the conditions, it is not determined to any individual, but is indifferent to all; therefore it is universal.

The second opinion holds that through the abstraction of the agent intellect the nature is not yet universal, but that the abstraction of the possible intellect is required, through which the nature is cognized without the conditions, and that through it it becomes universal. This is the opinion of Durandus in 1, d. 2, q. 5, ad 2, and in 2, d. 3, q. 7, no. 12, and of Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on universals. There is a single argument for this opinion. The nature is not universal on the part of the thing; therefore its universality is not real, but must be attributed by the intellect; but the intellect can attribute nothing to the nature unless it cognizes it; therefore, since the agent intellect does not cognize, it cannot attribute universality to it; but when it is first cognized by the intellect, it is denominated universal.

61 The third opinion teaches that neither the one nor the other abstraction suffices for the nature to become universal, but that it is necessary that it be compared to the individuals; and since this is done through the second operation of the possible intellect, which is called comparison, that the universal is made through this. It is followed by Soncinas, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 2, and Metaph. 10, q. 15; Niphus, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 1; Deza of Seville in 1, d., q. 1, a. 4, ad 1; Canar., 1 part, q. 28, a. 1, fol. 2. It is proved first: because the intellect cannot attribute to the nature the denomination of universal unless it cognizes it as universal. The universal expresses a respect to many, as is gathered from its definition, in which it is said to be one in many; therefore the nature is not cognized as universal unless it is cognized through its respect to many; but it cannot be cognized through its respect to many unless they are cognized, because a respect is not cognizable unless its term is cognized. But through the abstraction of the agent intellect it is in no way cognized, and through the abstraction of the possible intellect it is cognized without the individuals being cognized; therefore it is not cognized as universal, nor can such a denomination be attributed to it, except through comparison alone, through which it is cognized in order to many.

Second, universality is a relation of one to many, not real, since it does not belong to the nature on the part of the thing; therefore of reason; but a relation of reason cannot be made except through comparative cognition; therefore the universal is made through this alone. The minor is proved: because a relation is a comparison between two extremes; therefore it cannot be made except by the intellect cognizing and comparing both; therefore it becomes universal through comparison alone.

62 Besides these three different opinions, I find a fourth, through which certain moderns seem to bring the second and third into agreement, by this distinction. The universal can be taken in two ways. First, after the manner of an absolute, not expressing a respect to another but able to found such a respect, as white or quantity, which are absolute and can found a relation of similarity or equality. In another way, as a relative. For they think that universality can be understood in both ways, namely as a relative form, and also as an absolute one, upon which, however, there follows a certain respect through which it is explained: for the unity by which something is common, and the aptitude of being predicated of many, are absolute forms, just as numerical unity and the aptitude for laughing, which we nevertheless explain through a respect to the act of laughing and to the object. And they illustrate this by the example of the Platonic universal, separated from singulars: which would truly be a substance, since it would exist per se, and therefore its universality would be an absolute form, because substance is an absolute thing, not expressing a respect

essential to another, and yet it would be explained by us through a respect to the many by which it would be participated; therefore the universal made by the intellect can also be taken after the manner of an absolute. In another way it is taken as a relative, essentially regarding the individuals. The universal taken in the first way, then, they say is made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, because it has unity with the aptitude of regarding the many from which it has been abstracted. But if it is taken in the second way, it is not made except through comparison: because a relative cannot be cognized except through comparison to its term; and therefore neither can the universal as a relative, except through comparison to the many. And they affirm that the second opinion is to be understood of the universal as absolute, and that so understood it is true; but the third, of the universal as relative.

63 In order to propose our view, certain things must be noted. First, that universal is a concrete name, having a material significate, which is the nature, and a formal one, which is universality, from which it is denominated. Now a concrete is twofold, absolute and relative, just as the denominating form is also absolute or relative. An absolute concrete is white; a relative one, similar, or father. And this is the difference between the one and the other, that the absolute concrete has for its material significate only the bare subject, as white the bare body. But the relative concrete has not the bare subject, but something else by reason of which it is made the proximate foundation of the relation: as similar, besides white, must have some unity or commensuration with another, by reason of which it is capable of the relation, namely unity in whiteness and commensuration in the same grade of it. For in order that some things may properly be called similar, they must agree in whiteness, and also in its grade, so that it is in both as three, or as four.

Second, it should be noted that there are three foundations of a relation: the Most Remote, the Remote, and the Proximate; as in similarity, the most remote foundation is the body; the remote is the white; but the proximate is the white having unity and commensuration with another. And the foundation is called most remote and remote because the relation does not follow upon them: for the body, unless it has whiteness or some other quality, will not be called similar; nor even if it has whiteness, until it has unity and commensuration with another. But then it will be called the proximate foundation, because, once it is posited, the relation follows at once and necessarily. So, then, must it be understood of the universal, if it is a relative. For the most remote foundation of the relation of universality will be the nature on

the part of the thing, through the formal unity by which it is formally one in itself. The remote foundation, however, is the nature while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions, or while it is cognized without them through the first cognition of the intellect, if the relation of universality, from which it is denominated, does not follow at once. And finally it will be the proximate foundation while it is compared to the inferiors, because the relation of universality to them follows at once.

These things being supposed, our view is contained in these conclusions. First: The universal is not an absolute name but a relative one. This is against the last opinion, and it is proved by a twofold argument. First: A concrete name is absolute if the form signified by it is absolute, and relative if it is relative; but the form of universality is not absolute but relative; therefore the name universal will not be absolute but relative. The minor is proved from the definition of the universal: One in many, and apt to be predicated of many. In which the universal is explained through a relation to many; and not only is it explained so, but universality is a relation, not an absolute form, as the last opinion asserts: which I prove thus. Universality is not a form belonging to the nature of itself or essentially, nor on the part of the thing, but through the intellect, as the same opinion grants; therefore it is not a substantial form but an accidental one; it is not a real accident, but one of reason; but every accident of reason which the intellect attributes to things is a relation of reason: for it does not attribute to them an absolute accident of reason after the manner of quality, or quantity, or of another category, having its foundation in those same things understood by it, as will be proved; therefore universality is a relation of reason and not an absolute form. Second: The nature is not called universal solely from the fact that it is one or common in itself, but because it is one of many and common to many, or one in which many agree: as Porphyry taught in the chapter on species, saying: By participation in the species many men are one man. Therefore through universality it is essentially ordered to the inferiors, of which it is the one nature; and therefore universality is a relation and not an absolute form, and universal is a relative name, not an absolute one. Understanding which, Porphyry taught that the predicable names (which are certain universals) are to be defined through their inferiors, as genus, that it is predicable of several things differing in species, and so of the rest.

65 Second conclusion: Through the operation of the agent intellect the universal is given only as in its remote foundation, or in remote potency; not as in its proximate foundation, nor actually and formally universal. This follows from the preceding and from the doctrine noted, and it is proved by this argument. The univer-

Et probatur primò : Nihil denominatur actu & formalitertale,nifi à forma propria: fed propria forma vniuerfalis eftvniuerfalitas : quæ eft relatio rationis ad indi-uidua:ergo non denominatur natura actu, & formaliter vni-uerfalis,nifi à relatione rationis ad indiuidua : naturam autem cognitamperprimam operationem intellectus,non conſequi-turtalisrelatio rationis: ergo non eitper illam actu, & for-maliter vniuerfalis. sal is a relative; therefore the nature is not called actually and formally universal unless it is denominated from universality, which is a relation; but through the operation of the agent intellect it only has being represented in the intelligible species, the singulars not being represented; therefore it neither regards them nor can it be denominated from universality, which is a respect to them: and this is not to be actually and formally universal. Therefore it can only be universal in potency, or in its foundation, not the proximate one, because the relation follows at once upon the proximate foundation, and yet the relation to the individuals does not follow upon the nature so represented until it is understood in order to them; but in potency and in its remote foundation, although less remote than while it is outside its causes.

66 Third conclusion: The universal actually and formally, or in proximate potency, is not made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, which is called abstraction. This is against the last opinion. And it is proved first: Nothing is denominated actually and formally such except from its proper form; but the proper form of the universal is universality, which is a relation of reason to the individuals; therefore the nature is not denominated actually and formally universal except from a relation of reason to the individuals; but no such relation of reason follows upon the nature cognized through the first operation of the intellect; therefore through it it is not actually and formally universal. The minor is proved: Through that cognition it is not cognized in order to the individuals; indeed, the individuals are not even cognized; therefore neither is the relation of reason of the nature to them cognized; but a relation of reason has no other being than to be actually cognized; therefore, if it is not cognized through that cognition, it does not exist, nor does it denominate the nature actually and formally universal.

Second, the nature through the first cognition has nothing other than to be cognized as represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore only a new real extrinsic denomination follows upon it through that cognition, that of being cognized without the conditions: which it is certain is not the denomination of the universal; for this is neither real nor merely an extrinsic denomination, but one of reason, having the mode and likeness of an inherent form, like the denomination of predicate or subject. Therefore through such a cognition the nature will only be universal in potency, not proximate but remote, in the same way as through the operation of the agent intellect already explained.

67 Last conclusion: The nature becomes universal, not only in proximate potency but actually and formally, through the cognition of the intellect

> lectus,quæ dicitur comparatio. Hæc probatur primò , ex tri-buspræcedentibus: quia fi non fit per operationemintellectus agentis , nec per primam cognitionem intellectus poffibilis, non reſtat alia operatioper quam fieri poflit, præter compara-tionem . Sedprobatur ſecundò quòd per çam fiat:quia vniuerfalitas eſt relatio rationis naturæ ad indiuidua : & relatio eſt compa-ratio duoram extremoruin: ergo relatio rationisnaturæ ad indiuidua, eſt comparatio naturæ ad illa : quare fietper com-parationem vniuerfalitas,& vniuerſale formaliter. 68 Sed, vt cocluſiones iſtæ melius intelligantur,&ex eis co-gnofcamus aliquo modo fieri vniuerfalem, pertres illas ope-rationes intellectus agentis, & poffibilis , notanda eſt illa di-ſtinctio vniuerfalis, fatis manifeſta in ſchola Dialecticorum : Vniuerfaleduplex eſt, Logicum &Metaphyficum .Vniuerfale Metaphyficum, eſt natura realis in communi ſumpta,hoceſt fine conditionibus indiuiduantibus , &non vt denominataà ſecunda intentione, aut relatione vniuerfalitatis . Et vocatur vniuerfale Metaphyſicum :quia folùm fumitur ſecundùm ef-fentiam realem ,quaſi abſtractam àmaterialibus conditioni-bus,qui eſtproprius modus, ſecundumquemres confideran-tur inMetaphyfica : &vocari etiampoteſt Vniuerſale funda-mentaliter,atque etiam Vniuerfale inpotentia,ſa tem remo-ta,vtexplicatum eft. Aliud eft Vniuerfale Logicum , nempe natura denominata àſecunda intentione, aut relatione vni-uerfalitatis,quæ etiamdicitur Vniuerfale in potentia proxima, actu & formaliter:quia dum actu denominatur natura à rela-tione, proximè dicitur eandem relationem fundare : & voca-tur vniuerfale Logicum,quia ſecunda intentio ,aut relatio v-niuerfalitatis,propriè pertinetad confiderationem Logicam. Hacdistinctione ſuppoſita dicimus,vniuerfale Metaphyficum fieri per operationemintellectus agentis, cum repræfentetur natura inſpecieintelligibili peream producta, fine conditio-nibus : quod eſt effe vniuerfale Metaphyficum. Perprimam verò cognitionem intellectus poffibilis , fit idem vniuerfale Metaphyficum, vel potiùs iam factumper intellectum agen-tem cognofcitur:fed vniuerfale Logicum, fitper ſolam com. parationem. 69 Adargumenta aliarū opinionum refpondendum eft,&ad testimonium Ariſto pro prima opinione duobus modus. Pri-mò,fenfum eius efle:quòdlumen facit colores actu viſibiles: non quia ipſiactu viſibiles non effent in tenebris : fed quia viderinonpoterant permedium obfcurum: illud verò illu-

which is called comparison. This is proved first from the three preceding: because, if it is not made through the operation of the agent intellect, nor through the first cognition of the possible intellect, there remains no other operation through which it can be made besides comparison.

But it is proved second that it is made through it: because universality is a relation of reason of the nature to the individuals, and a relation is a comparison of two extremes; therefore the relation of reason of the nature to the individuals is a comparison of the nature to them: wherefore universality, and the universal formally, will be made through comparison.

68 But in order that these conclusions may be better understood, and that from them we may come to know how the universal is in some way made through those three operations of the agent and the possible intellect, that distinction of the universal, sufficiently well known in the school of the Dialecticians, should be noted. The universal is twofold, Logical and Metaphysical. The Metaphysical universal is the real nature taken in common, that is, without the individuating conditions, and not as denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality. And it is called the Metaphysical universal because it is taken only according to its real essence, as it were abstracted from material conditions, which is the proper mode according to which things are considered in Metaphysics; and it can also be called the universal fundamentally, and also the universal in potency, at least remote, as has been explained. The other is the Logical universal, namely the nature denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality, which is also called the universal in proximate potency, actually and formally; because while the nature is actually denominated by the relation, it is said proximately to found that same relation; and it is called the Logical universal because second intention, or the relation of universality, properly pertains to logical consideration. This distinction supposed, we say that the Metaphysical universal is made through the operation of the agent intellect, since the nature is represented without the conditions in the intelligible species produced by it: which is to be the Metaphysical universal. But through the first cognition of the possible intellect the same Metaphysical universal is made, or rather, already made by the agent intellect, it is cognized; but the Logical universal is made through comparison alone.

69 The arguments of the other opinions must be answered, and the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion in two ways. First, that its sense is that light makes colors actually visible not because they were not actually visible in the darkness, but because they could not be seen through an obscure medium; but that light, illuminating

Simplex comparatio eft,perquam intellectus vnum inalte-ro,vel in ordine ad alterum cognofcit fine compofitione , ve dam fimplici cognitione cognofcimus patrem in ordine ad

it, makes them actually seen. Or second, I reply by granting that light makes colors actually visible, since in the darkness they were only potentially visible; and so the agent intellect, as a kind of spiritual light, makes the nature actually intelligible: from which it does not follow that it makes it actually universal, because for it to be actually intelligible it suffices that it be universal in potency, which it has while it is represented through the intelligible species without the conditions, etc.

To the first argument of the same opinion, granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: for the nature is one in two ways. First, by negative unity, and this it has as represented in the intelligible species, because it is represented without the individuating conditions; but through this unity it is only the Metaphysical universal, or the universal in potency. In another way it is one positively, which it does not have except while it is compared to the individuals; and because this is required for it to be actually and formally universal, it is not universal in this way except through comparison.

To the second the reply is by the same distinction: because the nature represented in the intelligible species has the negative unity of the Metaphysical universal, and in potency, not that of the Logical universal, except through comparison.

To the argument of the second opinion, I grant that the nature is not universal on the part of the thing, but becomes universal through the cognition of the intellect; I deny, however, that through the first cognition of the intellect the form of universality is attributed to it: rather, it is attributed to it only through comparison.

To the third opinion it must be denied that the universal can be divided into absolute and relative, because by its proper nature and essence it is relative, as we have proved. It is false, therefore, that an absolute universal is given, and no less false that this absolute universal is made through the first cognition of the intellect.

## QUESTION VI

Whether the Logical universal is made through a simple comparison of the nature with the individuals, or only through the composite comparison which is called actual predication. 70

That the title of the question may be explained, it should be noted that almost all posit a twofold comparison of the intellect, one Simple, the other Composite.

Simple comparison is that through which the intellect cognizes one thing in another, or in order to another, without composition: as when by a simple cognition we cognize a father in order to

[p. 58]

the son, without affirming that he has a son; or whiteness in a wall, without affirming that it is in it. The other is the comparison through which the intellect cognizes two extremes and attributes one to the other, affirming that it is in it; and therefore this comparison is called actual predication. We ask, therefore, whether, supposing that the universal is made through comparison, as we proved in the preceding question, it is made through simple or through composite comparison. And there are two opinions. The first does not admit simple comparison, but only composite, and asserts that the universal is made through it; and since this comparison is the actual predication of one thing of another, it teaches that it is made through actual predication, and that before it the universal is not given actually and formally, but that actual predication is the universality from which the nature is denominated universal; and so it does not admit an aptitude or potency of being predicated in the nature, but holds that it is the same for it to be universal and for it to be an actual predicate. This opinion is followed by certain moderns, and they prove it by this argument.

71 The intellect cannot compare the nature to the individuals unless it cognizes that it is in them; but it cannot cognize that it is in them except by judging that it belongs to them. But to judge that it is in them and belongs to them is to predicate it of the individuals; therefore there is no simple comparison of the nature to the individuals, but only composite, which is actual predication: wherefore, if it is true that the universal is made through comparison, it necessarily follows that it is made through actual predication, so that it is not given before it.

72 This opinion is, in the first place, against Aristotle and St. Thomas, which is proved by a single testimony of each. For Aristotle, treating of the universal in On Interpretation 1, ch. 5, defines it in these words: And I call universal that which is apt to be predicated of several. From which it is evidently gathered that the nature is universal through the aptitude of being predicated of the individuals; but the aptitude of being predicated, since it is a potency, is prior to actual predication, which is the act of that same potency; therefore the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, according to the mind of Aristotle. Wherefore it does not become universal through composite comparison, which is actual predication, but through another, prior comparison, which is called simple.

And St. Thomas, in the same place, explaining the same definition of Aristotle, says: He defined the universal well through the aptitude of being predicated and not through actual predication, because there are some natures, such as the Sun and the Moon, which are not actually predicated of many, since they have only one individual, and yet they are truly universal through the aptitude and potency of being predicated of many. St. Thomas therefore posits the aptitude of being predicated in the universal nature, and asserts that through it

[p. 59]

Quòd verò conſequens fitfalfum,probo,quia hæc eſt prædicatio generis , Homo eſt animal: ergo eſt prædicatio fuperioris,quia genus fuperius eft ſpecie:fedprædicatum fuperius eftvniuerfale, ergo eſt prædi- catiovniuerfalis,& tamen defolovno : ergo vniuerfalis crit natura,dum de vno inferiori prædicatur, quia prædicabilis eft demultis : quare non per actualemprædicationem, fed per prædicabilitatem,vt omnes aſſerunt. 73 Communis ergo fententiaArift. it is universal, with Aristotle. Therefore the opinion which takes away the aptitude, and affirms that the universal is made only through actual predication, is expressly against Aristotle and St. Thomas.

Next, it is against reason, which I prove thus. If the nature is universal through actual predication, it follows that it is not universal unless it is predicated of many at once, so that we say that Peter and John are men, not man, and that man and horse are animals; and not while it is predicated of single ones: wherefore neither will there be a universal predication when the species is predicated of the individual, or the genus of the species, as in these predications: Peter is a man, and Man is an animal; but the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also. That the nature is universal through actual predication, the consequence is proved: because universality is actual predication; but universality is the respect of the nature to many; therefore the nature is not universal except actually, while it is predicated of many, and not of one only. But that the consequent is false I prove: because this is a predication of the genus, Man is an animal; therefore it is a predication of a superior, because the genus is superior to the species; but a superior predicate is universal; therefore it is a universal predication, and yet of one alone; therefore the nature will be universal while it is predicated of one inferior, because it is predicable of many: wherefore not through actual predication, but through predicability, as all assert.

73 The common opinion, therefore, of Aristotle, St. Thomas and all, is true and to be held: That the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, through the potency of being predicated of many; and that it becomes universal through the simple comparison of the intellect, through which it is cognized in order to the individuals, and not through the composite comparison, which is actual predication. Which I prove by this argument. The intellect can cognize one thing in another, or in order to another, without affirmation and negation and without actual predication; therefore it can cognize the nature in order to the individuals through simple comparison, without actually predicating it of them; but, cognized in order to the individuals, it is cognized as universal; therefore it becomes universal through simple comparison, not through composite. The antecedent is proved in two ways: first in the intellect, then in the senses. In the intellect indeed: because through a simple cognition we cognize a father ordered to his son, and two walls similar in whiteness, both being cognized at once; and in such a cognition we neither compose nor judge anything; therefore without composition and judgment we can compare one thing with another. Then in the senses, of which it is most certain that they do not judge, nor compose or divide; and it is no less

[p. 60]

> certum , quòd cognofcant youmin ordine ad alterum , vel comparando ad alterum : ergo idem poterit intellectus facere per fimplicem comparationemnaturead indiuidua.Probatur minor : Senfus communis , cognofcit ſenſibile vnius fenfus externi,vt viſus,noneſſe ſenſibile alteriusfenfus,nempe au-dicus : quod non potest vllo modo fieri fine comparationev. nius cumaltero:& ouis cognofcitlupum vtinimicum & ideo fugitab illo,& agnum vt amicum. a quo non fugit : & inter duosagnos,cognofcit huncefle filium,& alium:non ergo co-gnofcit vnum in ordine ad alterum : & per comparationem cum co,fineformaliiudicio,& fine compofitione, aut actuali prædicatione; ergo meliùs poteritintellectus cognofcere na-turaminordinead indiuidua,& cam cum illis comparare , fi-ne compofitione, aut actuali prædicatione. Vnum formale,&expreffum,per quod intellectus iudicatvnum cons uenirealteri per modum attributionis:Alterum, quafi virtua-le,perquodnotitia fimplici cognofcitvnum inaltero , velin ordinead alterum:tanquam eiconueniensaut diſconueniés, fednonpermodum attributionis.Negamus igitur, quòd in-tellectus nonpoffit cognofcere naturam effeinmultis, nifi perexpreffum,&formale iudicium: & concedimus,quòd non poffitſine iudicio virtuali incluſo in, comparatione fimplici, quamideovocamus iudicium virtuale: quia cognofcere ve pum,percomparationemad alterum, fundamentum eft for-malis, & expreffi iudicii, per quod ci attribuitur.

certain that they cognize one thing in order to another, or by comparing it to another; therefore the intellect will be able to do the same through a simple comparison of the nature to the individuals. The minor is proved. The common sense cognizes that the sensible of one external sense, such as sight, is not the sensible of another sense, namely hearing: which cannot in any way be done without comparison of the one with the other. And the sheep cognizes the wolf as an enemy, and therefore flees from it, and the lamb as a friend, from which it does not flee; and between two lambs it cognizes that this one is its offspring, and the other another’s. Does it not, then, cognize one thing in order to another, and through comparison with it, without formal judgment and without composition or actual predication? Therefore the intellect will be all the better able to cognize the nature in order to the individuals and to compare it with them, without composition or actual predication.

For the solution of the argument of the other opinion it should be noted that one thing can be cognized in order to another, or compared to it, in two ways. First, by cognizing each extreme per se, as agreeing with the other, attributing the one to the other: and this cannot be done except through a formal and express judgment and composite comparison, which consists in the actual predication of one thing of another. Second, by not cognizing each extreme per se, nor attributing the one to the other, but only the one with an order to the other, as agreeing or disagreeing, but not after the manner of attribution, or by affirming anything about the agreement or disagreement: and this is done through simple comparison by the intellect, and also by the senses, as I have proved; and in this way the nature is compared to the individuals and becomes universal and predicable before it is actually predicated of them. To the form of the argument, then, the minor must be distinguished, namely that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in the individuals except by judging: for judgment is twofold. One formal and express, through which the intellect judges that one thing belongs to another after the manner of attribution; the other as it were virtual, through which by a simple cognition it cognizes one thing in another, or in order to another, as agreeing or disagreeing with it, but not after the manner of attribution. We deny, therefore, that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in many except through express and formal judgment; and we grant that it cannot do so without the virtual judgment included in simple comparison, which we therefore call virtual judgment, because to cognize one thing through comparison to another is the foundation of the formal and express judgment through which it is attributed to it.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the universal is univocal with respect to the predicables, and their true genus.

75

The title of the question presupposes what a univocal name is, and also what an analogous one is, which is known from the Summulae. It asks, however, in what manner the universal stands with respect to the predicables: as analogous, or rather as univocal, so that it is their genus.

The first opinion holds that it is analogous. Different authors defend it in different ways, but they agree in this, that it is said primarily of one, or of several, and secondarily of the rest. So teaches Albert the Great, tract. 2 on the Predicables, ch. 9, affirming that it belongs first to genus, then to species, and by reason of the latter to difference; but secondarily, and as it were per accidens, to property and accident, as to accidental predicates. And Canterus explains the analogy in almost the same way, ch. 4 of the Categories. The chief argument of this opinion is that real being is analogous to substance and accidents; but three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, are substances, while the other two, namely property and accident, are accidents; therefore the universal, which is said of all, since all the predicables are universals, cannot be univocal.

Secondly, it can be proved in this way. The universal and the predicable are convertible and stand as essence and proper attribute; but the predicable is analogous with respect to all; therefore the universal too will be analogous.

The minor is proved: predication is said analogically of predication per se and per accidens, since the former is such simply, the latter only in a qualified sense; therefore the predicable too will be analogous, since they stand as act and potency with respect to the predicable per se and per accidens; but three predicables, genus, species and difference, are predicated per se, since they are predicated essentially; and the two others are predicated per accidens, since they are predicated accidentally; therefore the predicable is analogous with respect to all.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is univocal with respect to the predicables, and their true genus, as animal is with respect to man and horse; and it is that of St. Thomas in the questions on universals, q. 2; Scotus, q. 8; Javelli, tract. 4 on the Predicables, ch. 1 and 6; Soto, q. 4 on universals, and the chapter on genus, the only one; and Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on universals; and it is now almost common, true, and to be held.

76 But in order that we may prove it effectively, it should be noted that the universal

since it is a concrete and accidental name, can be taken in two ways: Materially, for the subject or nature denominated; and Formally, for the universality that denominates it; just as white is taken for the body and for the whiteness. But further, the subject denominated is considered in two ways: according to its proper essence and nature, or inasmuch as it is denominated by universality; just as body is taken according as it is corporeal substance, or inasmuch as it is denominated by whiteness, in which way it is visible and is reduced to the category of quality. And of the natures that are denominated universal, if they are taken according to their proper essence or entity, some are substances and some accidents; indeed some are real accidents and some accidents of reason; and since nothing univocal can be common to substance and accidents, nor to real accidents and accidents of reason, neither can anything univocal be common to the diverse natures which are denominated universal, taken in this way. But if they are taken in the second way, they will be able to have a univocal ratio, if the form that denominates them is univocal. We can give an example in genus, which is the first of the five universals, and consider the universal natures which are denominated by the second intention of genus as by a form, such as substance, quantity and quality. First, indeed, according to their proper essences; and in this way they can have nothing univocal in common. Then, inasmuch as they are denominated genera; and since the ratio of genus is univocal, explained by Porphyry through one definition, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid, substance, quantity and quality agree univocally under the ratio of genus, because they are denominated by such a form in the same way, so that substance is not more, nor prior, predicable of many differing in species than quantity or quality, but altogether equally.

77 From this distinction an argument is gathered to prove our view, which is also the common one: The univocal is that which signifies many things under the same ratio; but universal signifies all universals or predicables under the same ratio; therefore it is univocal with respect to them. The minor is proved: that ratio is one and the same which is explained through one definition; but the ratio of the universal is explained by Aristotle through one definition, namely, that it is one in many, apt to be predicated of many; therefore it is one with respect to all universals, and under it they agree univocally.

To the first argument one must reply, from the doctrine delivered, by distinguishing the major in this way: if substance and accidents are taken according to their proper entity and essence, nothing

univocal can they have in common; but if they are taken as they are universals, they agree univocally, because they are denominated in the same way by universality; and therefore the universal is univocal with respect to them.

For the solution of the second, it should be noted that, just as animal signifies only the sentient nature, not the rational or the irrational, because the differences, as Porphyry teaches in the Predicables, are outside the signification of the genus, in the same way universal expresses only one in many, and apt to be predicated of many; but that it is predicated essentially or accidentally, per se or per accidens, is outside its signification, and belongs to the different universals not under the ratio of universals, or as they are signified by such a name, but according to other particular rationes not signified by the name universal. Hence, although those rationes are so related that one is prior to another, or one is such simply and another in a qualified sense, the common name by which they are signified does not on that account cease to be univocal.

Now, then, to the form of the argument the minor must be denied, namely that the predicable, or predication, is analogous with respect to the five predicables: for although some of them are predicated essentially, or per se, and others accidentally and per accidens, these particular rationes do not pertain to the signification of predicable, but only the potency of predicating in common; and since this is the same in all, all the predicables are signified univocally by the name predicable, common to all; nor is the univocation taken away by particular rationes not signified by the same name.

## QUESTION VIII

Whether the universal is the adequate object of the book of the Predicables, or rather the predicable. 79

The book of the Predicables is a certain part of the whole of Logic, and therefore some partial object ought to correspond to it, which is as it were a part of the total and adequate object of the same science; concerning which we inquire whether it is the universal or the predicable, since it is certain that nothing else besides these can be the object; and of them that one will be the object to which the general conditions of an object, delivered by us in the last proemial question, belong rather than to the other.

The first opinion defends that the predicable is the object rather than the universal. It is usually attributed to Scotus, and is defended by many moderns. And it has two arguments. The first: that is the object of any

part or science which contains all the things it treats of; but the universal does not contain all the things treated of in this book; therefore it is not its object. The minor is proved: Porphyry, in the chapter on species, treats of the individual, and also of the subjicible species, which are not universals: because the individual is not in many, nor does the subjicible species, inasmuch as it is such, regard individuals.

The second: that is the formal object of a science under whose formal ratio it considers all things; but all the things treated in this book are considered under the ratio of the predicable, and not under the ratio of the universal; therefore the universal is not the object, but the predicable. I prove the minor from the definitions of the predicables, which Porphyry delivers through the predicable, as the definition of genus, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid; and so of the others: whence he also calls this work the book of the Predicables.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is rather the object. St. Thomas holds it, q. 9, on the object of this book; Soto, q. 4 on universals; Toledo, q. 1; and it seems to us the more probable and to be held. For its explanation it should be noted, from the doctrine of St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 6, that the intellect attributes universality to the nature as the foundation of the other denominations: because the first thing it understands in it is being in many, and therefore it calls it universal; and because from the ratio of being in many there follows being able to be predicated of many, it immediately attributes to it the denomination of predicable; and then other special denominations, of genus and of species. From which it follows that, just as the first thing that is in a thing, as the foundation of the others, is its essence, so universality, which is the first denomination of the nature, is as it were its essence in the logical order, while predicability is an attribute common to all universals.

From this doctrine of St. Thomas, true and necessary, this argument is gathered to prove his view and ours: The universal and the predicable are considered per se in this book, and the former stands as essence, the latter as proper attribute; therefore the universal is the object rather than the predicable. The consequence is proved: because the office of a science is to prove attributes of the subject; but in this book it is proved of the universal that it is predicable, as the posterior of the prior, therefore as a proper attribute of the subject; which cannot belong to the predicable, since it has no attribute that can be proved of it; therefore neither can it be the object.

under the universal: not because they are formally universals, but because they are the terms of the relation of universality of the genus and of the species. For the genus is universal because it is in many species, of which it is apt to be predicated; and from this relation of the genus to the species there results in them another relation, of subjicibility, through which they are said to terminate it, as will be explained in the chapter on species. And for the same reason the individual is the term of the relation of the species, by which it is denominated universal and predicable, because it is in many individuals and is apt to be predicated of them; and therefore individuals and subjicible species are reduced to the genus and the species, and to their treatment.

To the second I reply by distinguishing the minor: for that the universal is considered by Porphyry in this book under the ratio of the predicable can be understood in two ways. First, so that predicability is the objective ratio which is considered; and in this sense it must be denied, because, since universality is the essential ratio and foundation of predicability and of the other denominations which the intellect attributes to the nature, it is the objective ratio under which all things are considered. In the second way it can be understood that all things are considered under the ratio of predicability as under a common attribute which is demonstrated of the five universals in this work; and in this sense the minor must be granted; but from this it is not rightly inferred that the predicable is the object, but only that it is an attribute which is demonstrated of the object. And it is demonstrated in this way: Whatever is one in many is predicable of many; but genus is in many species; therefore it is predicable of them; and so of the other predicables, which are defined by Porphyry through predicability as through a proper attribute more manifest to us; and therefore by definitions that are not quidditative but descriptive, as will be explained in the chapter on genus. And in the same way it must be understood that this work is called the Book of the Five Predicables, the denomination being taken from the common attribute, better known, which is demonstrated of them, rather than from the universal, which is its object.

## QUESTION IX

Whether the predicables are five, or more, or fewer.

82

Just as Aristotle invented the art of the categories in order to reduce the modes of being of all things to certain heads, so that we might easily recognize their nature once the category in which it is placed is known, so Porphyry invented the art of the predicables in order to reduce all predications

to certain heads, and so that we might easily know of what kind any predication whatever is, Essential or Accidental; and, if essential, generic or specific; and in the same way, if accidental, of a proper or of a common accident; from the knowledge of which we may know the natures of things. But in order that we may better understand this art of the predicables, it is necessary to know their determinate number; and therefore the last question on universals inquires about their number, whether they are five, so that they are neither more nor fewer. And although there are no differing opinions about the number, but all follow Porphyry, the author of this book, who posits only five,

we nevertheless propose certain arguments to the contrary, which seem to prove, on the one side, that they are fewer, and on the other, that they are more, so that from their solutions the truth may become manifest. That they are fewer than five, then, is proved by two arguments. First, predicables and predicates are distinguished only as potency and act: because the predicable is that which can be predicated of another, and the predicate that which is actually predicated; but the predicates are four, and not more, as Aristotle teaches in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, namely Genus, Definition, Property and Accident; therefore there will be only four predicables.

83 Second, Porphyry distinguishes two predicables, of genus and of difference, because genus is predicated in quid and difference in quale quid; but definition contains both; therefore it will suffice for two predicables. The consequence is proved: because definition is predicated of the same things of which genus and difference are predicated; and moreover it contains the mode of predicating of both, in quid and in quale quid, by way of one predicable. For if it is the definition of a subalternate species, as living sentient, it is predicated of many differing in species, namely of man and of lion, like a genus; but if it is of a lowest species, as rational animal, it will be predicated of many differing in number, as the difference is predicated of Peter and John; therefore two predicables, of genus and of difference, are not to be distinguished, but definition will suffice for both; and so they will be only four and not five.

The other part, however, that the predicables are more than five, can be proved. First, because Porphyry, in the chapter on genus, distinguishes the predicables by the things of which they are predicated, as genus from species: because the former is predicated of many differing in species, the latter of many differing in number; and so of the rest. But if they are distinguished in this way, it follows that at least seven must be posited, so that there are two predicables of difference and two others of property. The consequence is proved: because the subalternate difference,

[p. 67]

> Vécorporeum , prædicatur de pluribus differentibus ſpecie, nempede corpore viuente,&non viuente:fiverò fitinfima,ve rationale,ſolum de pluribus differentibus numero, nempe de Petro& Ioanne : ergo diſtincta efficientprædicabilia. Sed rationes iftæ inſufficientes mihividen-tur: ſufficiens verò per quam probatur efficaciterprædicabilia non effe plura,necpauciora, quàm quinque ex modo formali prædicandi ,autſehabendiin ordine ad fubiectum,ſumenda eft:quod ficprobatur.Modusprædicandi,quiex modote ha- Bendi prædicati adſubiectum fumitur, eſt formalis ratiopræ-dicationis : ergo eritetiam ratioformalis prædicabilium:fed eſſentialis diſtinctio rerum,fumiturex diuerfis rationibus for- malibus earum:ergo prædicabilia diſtinguidebentper diuer- fos modos prædicandi. Ea quæ conftituunt prædicabi lia, in primis debenteſſe vniuerfalia , quiaprædicabiletam-quam propria paflio vniuerfalis , cum co conuertitur : fed vniuerfale eſt ynum in multis: crgo nihil eritprædiccabile, Eij

as corporeal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of living and non-living body; but if it is a lowest one, as rational, it is predicated only of many differing in number, namely of Peter and John; therefore they will make distinct predicables. Property too, if it is subalternate, as sensible, which follows the nature of the subalternate species animal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of horse and lion; but if it is a lowest one, as risible, it is predicated only of things differing in number, as of Peter and John; therefore there will be seven predicables.

4 Second, the vague individual, as a certain man, is predicated of many differing in number, as of Peter and John; and yet it is not a species, because it is not predicated in quid. And actual existence too has the same character; therefore another predicable, distinct from species, must be posited for them. The minor is proved: because, just as a certain man does not express the essence or quiddity of individuals, but the common ratio of individual, which either is accidental or at least is outside their essence, so actual existence does not pertain to the essence of any creature, which easily loses it through corruption, or can lose it through annihilation. Wherefore it is not predicated in quid, since to be predicated in quid is the same as to predicate the quiddity or essence of a thing.

Yet the opinion of Porphyry, which is also the common one in the schools, is true. But the whole difficulty of it consists in assigning the reason by which it may be sufficiently proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five; and different reasons are assigned by different authors. For some distinguish the predicables by the things of which they are predicated; others by the things that can be known about a thing, which seem to be five. But these reasons seem to me insufficient: the sufficient one, by which it is effectively proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five, must be taken from the formal mode of predicating, or of standing in order to the subject; which is proved thus. The mode of predicating, which is taken from the mode in which the predicate stands to the subject, is the formal ratio of predication; therefore it will also be the formal ratio of the predicables; but the essential distinction of things is taken from their diverse formal rationes; therefore the predicables ought to be distinguished by the diverse modes of predicating.

By this discourse, then, it must be proved that they are neither more nor fewer than five. The things that constitute the predicables must, in the first place, be universals, because the predicable, as the proper attribute of the universal, is convertible with it; but the universal is one in many; therefore nothing will be predicable

Exquibus fequitur , quatuor tantum effe prædicata: quod ficprobatur. Species non eftprædicatum,fedfubiectum com-mane , in ordine ad quem fumitur diſtinctio prædicatorum: quodadeò verum eft,vtnonfit aliud fubiectum commune

unless it is one. And in order to be one, it must be simple, that is, not complex: because the complex is not one but many, as white man, or rational animal. Moreover, if it is one, it will be univocal, not equivocal or analogous. By the first condition, then, complex predicates, such as definition, are excluded from the ratio of the predicable; by the second, equivocal and analogous ones, as dog, being, accident, and the like. Next, that which is one, that is, incomplex and univocal, can stand in only five ways in order to the subject; therefore it can be predicated of it in only five ways; wherefore there will be only five predicables. The antecedent is proved: for it is predicated either essentially or accidentally; and if essentially, either by way of an actual whole, because it actually contains the whole essence of the subject, as man is predicated of Peter and John, and this is the predicable of species; or by way of a potential whole, which is truly the material part of the same species, and therefore contractible by differences as by forms, and this is genus; or by way of a formal, actual and contracting part, and this is difference. But if it is predicated accidentally, either by way of that which proceeds from the essence and is convertible with it, and this is property; or, if by way of an extrinsic or common accident, it is called the predicable of accident. And since no other modes of predicating besides these are possible, and all predications can be reduced to them, it follows that there are only five predicables, so that they are neither more nor fewer. For the solution of the first argument, the difference between predicable, predicate and category should be noted: namely, that a category is a certain essential ordering of the predicables, according to due subjection and predication, from the supreme genus down to the last species and the individual; as the category of substance is this ordering: substance, body, living, animal, man, Peter.

86 But Aristotle took the predicates, in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, in order to the dialectical or probable proposition from which a dialectical or probable syllogism is made; and because the syllogistic form requires propositions about a common subject (for from singular propositions only expository syllogisms are made, which have no mood or figure except in order to universal propositions), he therefore takes the ratio of predicates from their order to a common subject.

From which it follows that there are only four predicates, which is proved thus. Species is not a predicate but the common subject, in order to which the distinction of the predicates is taken; which is so true that there is no other common subject

[p. 69]

Numerus verò prædicamentorum , ex diuerfis modis eſſendi accipitur:quorumprimus eſt modus eflendiper fe. Modi verò eſſendi in alio , quiaccidentibus conueniunt, nouem funt: & ideo ſequitur decem effe prædicamenta , qua-tuorprædicata,&quinque prædicabilia. Etadformam argumenti,negandum eft antecedens, quòd prædicatum , & prædicabile ſolum diftinguantur tanquam actus,&potentia: nam fi prædicatum communiffimèaccipia-tur, non eſt actus prædicabilis , nec etiam fi accipiatur ſpeciali modo,pro prædicato topico,ſed ſolum ſe habet ad prædicabi le, ficut actus , ſiaccipiatur tali modo, nempe vtpetitnatura eiufdem prædicabilis. Secundum verò argumentumhuius partis,exdoctrina tradita ſolutum eft. Adprimum veròalterius partis reſpondeo, quòd Porphy- Bus nou diftinguitgenusab ſpecie per ea,de quibuspredicam sur, nifi adiuncto talimodo prædicandi, ex quo effentialisdi-tinctioprædicabiliumfumendaeft. ‫زند‬

besides it. This supposed, the predicate either is convertible with the species or is more universal. If it is convertible with it, either it is within its essence, and it will be a definition, as rational animal; or it follows naturally from it, and it will be a property, as risible with respect to man. But if it is more universal than the species, either it pertains to its quiddity, and it is a genus; or it is outside it, and it will be a common accident. Difference, however, Aristotle teaches is to be numbered with genus, in that ch. 3, in these words: Difference, since it is generic, is to be ranked with genus. And he is speaking of subalternate difference, because this is generic, since it is convertible with the genus, as corporeal with body; but if it is a lowest one, it is reduced to the definition. In distinguishing the predicates, however, nothing is said of the modes of predicating in quid or in quale quid, of genus and difference: because in order to the dialectical proposition and syllogism they make no distinction, since the mode of disputing probably is the same in those propositions in which the predicate is more universal than the subject and is within its essence, whether it is genus or difference. Nor are complex predicates different from incomplex ones, if they stand in the same way in order to the common subject: because one disputes in the same way about dialectical propositions made from either; and therefore definition is numbered among the predicates, though it is excluded from the predicables on account of its complexity.

87 The predicables, finally, are taken in order to the categories; and therefore definition is excluded, because a category is made of simple things alone, while genus, species and difference are placed in it. The number of the categories, however, is taken from the diverse modes of being, the first of which is the mode of being per se. But the modes of being in another, which belong to accidents, are nine; and therefore it follows that there are ten categories, four predicates, and five predicables.

And to the form of the argument, the antecedent must be denied, namely that predicate and predicable are distinguished only as act and potency: for if predicate is taken most commonly, it is not the act of the predicable; nor even if it is taken in a special way, for the topical predicate; but it stands to the predicable as act only if it is taken in such a way, namely as the nature of the same predicable requires. The second argument of this part, however, has been solved from the doctrine delivered.

To the first argument of the other part I reply that Porphyry does not distinguish genus from species by the things of which they are predicated, except with such a mode of predicating joined to them, from which the essential distinction of the predicables is to be taken.

To the second argument some reply that the vague individual is not predicated univocally of Peter and John, but equivocally: because, since such individuals exist through altogether diverse individual differences, they can have nothing in common except the name. I, however, hold it more probable that a common modal concept can be abstracted from the individual differences, because they all agree in this, that they are particular and substantial modes determining the species; whence the ratio of particular mode, considered in common, which the vague individual signifies, is univocal with respect to the individuals. Therefore I reply in another way, granting that the vague individual is not properly predicated in quid, as species is, but is predicated in a similar way, since it signifies a substantial mode; and by reason of this similarity it is reduced to the predicable of species: because, since it is not a predicate of the nature but of a mode of the same nature, a distinct predicable ought not to be posited for it, but it ought to be reduced to the predicable of the nature. And one must think in the same way of actual existence.

But two very brief doubts remain which pertain in some way to the number of the predicables, and therefore they are to be solved at the end of this question. The first is whether, supposing that the five predicables are universal species, the universal is their immediate genus or a remote one, so that between it and the predicables there is given another immediate genus, as living is called the remote genus of man and horse, because animal mediates between it and these species. To which I reply that it is not the immediate genus but a remote one, which is proved by this argument: from any essential agreement a concept common to the things that agree essentially can be abstracted; but the predicables agree essentially in some ratio inferior to the universal; therefore a concept of that ratio inferior to the universal can be given, which will be predicated of the same things differing in species; and therefore it will be their immediate genus, and the universal a remote one. The minor is proved, because three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, agree in an intrinsic or essential mode of predicating, and two others, namely property and accident, in an accidental mode of predicating; therefore essentially predicable will be common to the former, and accidental predicate will be common to the latter, and nearer than the universal; and each is predicated of several species, the former of three, the latter of two; therefore they will be nearer genera than the universal, and consequently the universal will not be their proximate genus, but a remote one.

The second doubt is whether the five predicables are species

[p. 71]

> cies fubalternæ,habentes fub ſealias ſpecies, ficutanimal, aut viuens,vel infimæ non habentes fub ſe alias ſpecies,fed folum indiuidua,vthomo,vel equus,& reliqux ſpecies infimæ alio- zum generum.Si enimdicatur eſſe ſpecies ſubalternas, ſequie turprædicabilia plura efle quam quinque:quia cum eis dele buntconnumerari fpecies,quas fub fe habent : fiverò fint in- fimæ, non erit maior numerus prædicabilium Refpondeo efle ſpeciesinfimas , quod ita probo : Prædicabilia diftinguantur ſpecie,perdiuerfos modosprædicandi,ſed iſtimodi nonfunt diuifibiles in alios;ergo prædicabilia nonhabent alias ſpecies. that are subalternate, having other species under them, as animal or living, or lowest ones, not having other species under them but only individuals, as man or horse, and the other lowest species of the other genera. For if they are said to be subalternate species, it follows that the predicables are more than five, because the species they have under them will have to be counted together with them; but if they are lowest, the number of the predicables will not be greater. I reply that they are lowest species, which I prove thus: the predicables are distinguished in species by the diverse modes of predicating; but these modes are not divisible into others; therefore the predicables do not have other species. The minor is proved: because the mode of predicating of genus is that it is predicated as the material part of the species and by way of a potential whole, contractible by differences; but it is impossible that there be a genus which is not predicated in the same way; therefore this mode is not divisible into others; and this is for genus to be a lowest species of the universal. And the same argument is made about the other predicables; wherefore none of them can be a subalternate species.

## TREATISE ON THE NATURE OF THE BEING OF REASON, AND OF SECOND INTENTIONS

even things are to be disputed in this order concerning the being of

S       reason. First, whether it exists. Second, what it is. Third, how manifold

it is. Fourth, whether it is made by the intellect or reason alone, or also by other powers. Fifth, whether by our intellect alone, or also by the angelic and divine. Sixth, to which science it pertains to treat of it. Last, in what manner it is reduced to the categorial order.

1

Some few, and without foundation, deny that there is a being of reason, as

Vallés, controversy 9, ad Tyron., and others; and therefore it is not to be called an opinion, nor to be held; but it is the common view of the whole school that there is a being of reason. But in order that we may understand it, it should be noted that the being of reason is twofold. The first, that which is made directly and per se by reason or the intellect, and inheres in it,

Quidfit Ens rationis. 2      Irca effentiam Entis rationis,eftprima opinio , aſſeren. Ctium tium: Qmnem denominationem extrinfecam eſſe Ens rationis,vt denominatio,àqua paties dicitur dexter:quia eſt à manu dextra hominis ,autlapis dicitur viſus, quia videtur à nobis.Quodprobantprimò,Quja Quia denominatio eft opus ra-tionis:ergonon datur ante operationem intellectus :ſedde-nominationes extrinfecæ nihilin rebus denominatis ponunt, præterdenominationem ipſam,quam intellectus efficit: ergo funtentia rationis. as in a subject; and this is the operation of the intellect itself, and therefore it is a real being, like the operation of sight; and it is called a being of reason only because it is made by reason. The other is the being of reason which is not made directly by the intellect, nor per se, but follows its operation as it were per accidens:

as, if the intellect composes this proposition, Man is an animal, the composition itself, which is a real operation of the intellect, is followed by the denomination of proposition, and of predicate and subject; and these denominations are nothing other than certain relations of reason, of the whole proposition compared to the predicate and the subject as to its parts, and of the same predicate and subject among themselves: for by the very fact that one is attributed to the other, the former is called the predicate and the latter the subject. And the first being of reason is not properly called such, since it is a real being; and therefore we do not treat of it, but only of the second, which is not in anything as in a subject, but only has being while it is known by the intellect; and therefore it is said only to be objectively in the intellect. Of this being of reason, then, is our conclusion, that it exists in the nature of things, which is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 3; bk. 4, 13 and 4; and bk. 6, text 8; in which places he teaches that the most universal being is divided into that which is in things, and that which is said to be not in things but only in the mind, which is only to be objectively in the intellect; and the whole school follows the same conclusion.

It is proved by reason, because the intellect composes a proposition out of two extremes which are not distinguished on the part of the thing, as out of man and

Peter; and out of Peter alone it makes an identical proposition, making him the predicate and the subject; but the distinction and attribution of one to the other is an ordering to it, and the ordering is a relation between them, not a real one, because on the part of the thing Peter is neither distinguished from himself nor ordered to himself; therefore it is a relation of reason, or a being of reason. It follows, then, that a being of reason is given and exists.

What the being of reason is. 2

Concerning the essence of the being of reason, the first opinion is that of those who assert that every extrinsic denomination is a being of reason: as the denomination by which a wall is called right, because it is at the right hand of a man, or a stone is called seen, because it is seen by us. Which they prove, first, because denomination is a work of reason; therefore it is not given before the operation of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations posit nothing in the things denominated besides the denomination itself, which the intellect effects; therefore they are beings of reason. The minor is proved, because the stone acquires nothing by being at my right, except the denomination

[p. 73]

> dextri, & fic de reliquis. Secundò,denominationes extrinfecæ funt relatiuæ, &non fiūtàrelationibus realibus:ergo à relationibus rationis, quod eſt eſſe Entia rationis.Maiorem ficprobo:Quia perdenomi-nationes extrinfecasreferuntur res denominatæ ad alias , vt paries dexter,ad hominem, ad cuius dexteram eſt : Minorem verò: quia pertales denominationes nullam relationem rea-lemacquiruntres denominate:vtparies exco quòdvideatur, nonacquirit relationem realemad hominem cum videntem. Vna, quæ fit ab aliqua forma reali,fiue inhereat in redenominata,quales funt denominationes intrinfeca:aut inaliaab eadiuerfa,vtdenominationes extrinfece: & iſte non funtopusrationis,nec ab intelle&u dependent, ficut nec de-pendet forma realis,à qua fiunt quia fidependerent:ficutnon denominaturparies viſus , ante operationem intellectus , ita nec denominaretur homo albus ab albedine, quodpatet effe falfuma.Alia eſtdenominatio,quæ non fità forma reali:ſed ſo-lúm tribuitur ab intellectu rebus intellectis. Vt denominatio fubiecti, autprædicati : &de hac denominatione verum eft, quod fit opus rationis, fieut forma à qua fit. Quæ eft relatio rationis,dicitur fieri ab intellectu. Secunda opinio afferit, Non omnes denominationes ex. trinfecas effeEntia rationis:fed eastantum, quas res cognita accipit ab actu intellectu: perquem cognofcitur, & à quo

of right; and so of the rest.

Second, extrinsic denominations are relative, and are not made by real relations; therefore by relations of reason, which is to be beings of reason. I prove the major thus: because through extrinsic denominations the things denominated are referred to others, as the wall that is right to the man at whose right it is. And the minor: because through such denominations the things denominated acquire no real relation, as the wall, from the fact that it is seen, does not acquire a real relation to the man seeing it.

But this opinion is false. It is proved by two arguments. First, the being of reason has no other being than to be known by the intellect, and therefore it is not given before the operation of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect; therefore they are not beings of reason. The minor is proved: God is called creator, and a wall that is seen by some animal is called seen, not only before they are known by the intellect, but even if there were no intellect in the nature of things; therefore extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect, and therefore they cannot be beings of reason.

Second: these denominations (although they are not made by any form inhering in the things denominated, and are therefore called extrinsic) are real; therefore they are not beings of reason. The consequence is evident, because the being of reason has nothing real, but only to be known by the intellect. The antecedent is proved, because God is really called creator, and the wall really seen. Therefore these denominations are real.

To the argument of this opinion, the antecedent must be distinguished, that denomination is a work of reason. For denomination is twofold. One, which is made by some real form, whether it inheres in the thing denominated, such as intrinsic denominations are, or in another thing diverse from it, as extrinsic denominations; and these are not a work of reason, nor do they depend on the intellect, just as the real form by which they are made does not depend on it; because if they did depend on it, just as the wall is not denominated seen before the operation of the intellect, so neither would a man be denominated white by whiteness, which is plainly false. The other is the denomination which is not made by a real form but is only attributed by the intellect to things understood, as the denomination of subject or of predicate; and of this denomination it is true that it is a work of reason, as is the form by which it is made, which is a relation of reason and is said to be made by the intellect.

The second opinion asserts that not all extrinsic denominations are beings of reason, but only those which things known receive from the act of the intellect by which they are known, and from which

[p. 74]

> minaturintellecta & cognita. Verbigratia, dum co- gnoſcit intellectus naturam humanam abſtractamab indiui- duis,&eam comparatcum eis,petit,vt ita cognita, denomi- pationem ſpeciei: &ideotalis denominatio cit Eps rationis habeus fundamentum in re.

they are denominated understood and known. And so that the sense of this opinion may be declared in one word, it asserts that the being of reason is that being-known which a thing acquires when it is known by the intellect, which is plainly an extrinsic denomination.

But this opinion is proved false by the same reasons by which the falsity of the other was proved: because the denomination of known (although it is extrinsic) is no less real than the denomination of seen in the wall, or the denomination of creator in God; therefore it cannot be a being of reason, because the being of reason has nothing real.

The common view is explained in two conclusions. The first: the being of reason is not something inhering in the things denominated, nor an extrinsic denomination from some real form existing in another, but solely a denomination which the intellect attributes to them. This is proved by this argument: to be a genus, or to be a species, does not belong to man or to animal on the part of the thing, but the intellect attributes these denominations to them through comparison to their inferiors; therefore they are neither something inhering, nor are they made by some real form existing in another. The consequence is proved, because that which inheres in something, or is made by a form inhering in another, belongs to it on the part of the thing.

Second conclusion: although the being of reason is not something inhering, and can therefore be called an extrinsic denomination, it nevertheless has a likeness to an inhering form, and on account of this likeness it can be called an intrinsic denomination. The first part of this conclusion follows evidently from the preceding conclusion, already proved; the second part, that it can be called an intrinsic denomination on account of the likeness, is proved because the denominations of genus, species, predicate and subject are like real denominations proceeding from inhering forms, such as the denominations of white and black; therefore, just as the latter are truly intrinsic denominations, so the former can be called intrinsic by likeness.

How manifold the being of reason is.

By the first division the being of reason is divided into that which has a foundation in the thing, and that which has no foundation but is truly impossible. The being of reason having a foundation is that denomination which is attributed by the intellect to things known by it in such a way that their nature, as known in such a way, requires that denomination. For example, when the intellect knows human nature abstracted from individuals and compares it with them, it requires, as so known, the denomination of species; and therefore such a denomination is a being of reason having a foundation in the thing.

[p. 75]

> Sed fundamentum hocduobus modis intelligitur à diuer-fismodernis. Primò,ita vt folùm conſiſtat in modo noftro in-telligendi,qui eaquæ verènonfunt diftincta, diftinguit, & ca quæ verènonfuntſeparata ab inferioribus,ſeparat,velabſtra-hit,nontamen inrebusipfis.
