Vt dum diftinguitin anima rationali,gradum vegetandi, fentiendi atque intelligendi, cùmtamenanimaipfa fitfimplex quædaın ſubſtantia. Secundò notandum eſt, in rebus ipfis cognitis dari etiam fundamentum,vt cognofcanturdiſtinctæ, aut vt eis attribua. turtalisdenominatio , quæ dicitur Ens rationis : vtin rebus compofitis ex materia,& forma, reperitur vnitasformalis, quam tribuit eiforma,& etiam vnitasnumerica, quæ ex hac materia,& formafumitur , aut fi ex fola formadiuerfa ratione acfumitur numerica : quia Formalis fumitur à forma , vt eft principium, & radixprædicatorum effentialium : Numerica verò ab eadem,vt eſtprincipalispars componens.Ex hoc ergo reperitur fundamentum innaturahumava, vtintelligiponit ineavnitasformalis ,non intellecta vnitate numerica : quod eſt abſtrahi ab indiuiduis , atque etiam , vt cum multis corum comparetur,& denominetur ſpecies,aut cum vnotantum,per modum attributionis,&denominetur prædicatum. Hisſuppoſitis,noſtra ſententia explicaturduabus conclufio-pibus. Prima eft: Ens rationisaliquando habetfundamentum, noſtro modo intelligendi imperfecto,fedin rebus nó folùm in noftro ipfis quæ ex propria naturahabent fundamentuin, vreistri buaturtalis de ominatio.Probatur nico argumento, exde- Etrinatradita no foluin noftromodo cognofcediimperfecto,

But this foundation is understood in two ways by different moderns. First, so that it consists only in our mode of understanding, which distinguishes things that are not truly distinct, and separates or abstracts things that are not truly separated from their inferiors, but not in the things themselves. By others, however, it is affirmed that beings of reason have a foundation not only in our mode of understanding but in the known things themselves.

But for the understanding of this it should be noted, first, that for producing beings of reason and attributing them to known things it is necessary that the things be known imperfectly, that is, through several concepts, although they could be known through one by an intellect that knows perfectly. For example, in order that the intellect may attribute to man the denomination of species, and of predicate of this proposition, Peter is a man, it must know it as it were abstracted, or separated and distinct from him, although on the part of the thing it is neither distinguished nor separated. But it does this without falsehood, because it does it without affirmation or negation, but only through knowing one thing without another; and this proceeds from an imperfect mode of knowing, because it knows not the whole at once but as it were by parts, or by diverse grades: as when it distinguishes in the rational soul the grade of vegetating, of sensing and of understanding, although the soul itself is a certain simple substance.

It should be noted, second, that in the known things themselves there is also given a foundation for their being known as distinct, or for such a denomination, which is called a being of reason, being attributed to them: as in things composed of matter and form there is found the formal unity which the form gives it, and also the numerical unity, which is taken from this matter and form, or, if from the form alone, it is taken as numerical under a different ratio: because the Formal unity is taken from the form as it is the principle and root of the essential predicates, but the Numerical unity from the same form as it is the principal component part. From this, then, there is found a foundation in human nature for the formal unity in it to be understood without the numerical unity being understood, which is to be abstracted from the individuals; and also for it to be compared with many of them and denominated species, or with only one, by way of attribution, and denominated predicate.

These things supposed, our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: the being of reason sometimes has a foundation not only in our imperfect mode of understanding, but in the things themselves, which from their own nature have a foundation for such a denomination being attributed to them. It is proved by a single argument from the doctrine delivered: not only in our imperfect mode of knowing,

[p. 76]

Entia rationis aliquando non habét fundamentumin rebus quibus attribuuntur,fed in aliis,aut in ſolo modo noſtrointelligendi imperfecto.In hac conclufione conueniuntomnes, &probatur duplici exemplo. Primò , in Deo , in quo diftinguimus iuftitiam à mifericordia : non pro-prerfundamentum in eis exiftens, fedin creaturis, in quibus virtutes iſtæ diftintæ funt. Secundò in propofitionibus , quæ dicunturIdenticæ, quia idem prædicatur deſe ipſo, vt inhac, Petrus eft Petrus:in qua intellectus diftinguit Petrum àfeipfo, cumfaciensquaſi duos: & tribuitillidenominationem prædi-cari, & fubiecti , cuius diſtinctionis nullum eft fundamentum in co,fedfolùm in modo cognofceadi imperfecto,qui diſtin-guit quafi induo extrema illud, quod in ſe necdistinctum eft , nechabet fundamentum,vt à ſeipſo distinguatur, Exhis conclufionibus ſequitur , diftinctionem rationisdu-plicem effe,vt yt communis confenfus ſcholæ afferit.Vna eft, que habet fundamentum inrebus ipfis , & hæc dicitur diſtinctio Rationis ratiocinatæ, quam ponimus inter vniuerfale , & fin-gularia,& interdiuerfos gradus vegetandi,ſentiendi , & intel-ligendi animæ rationalis:Alia eſt diſtinctio , non habens fun-damentum in re ipſa cognita,ſed in aliis , aut folum in noftro modo cognoſcendiimperfecto , vtea , quam ponimus inter Petrum, &feipfum, duim prædicaturin propofitione identica. Et hæc de Entibus rationis habentibus fundamétum in rebus . 8 Alia funtEntia rationis,quæ nullü habent fundamentum in rebus : fed ex quibufdam impoffibilibus ab intellectu con-junctis finguntur,vt Chimera,& Sphinx. Eximpoffibilibus

but in the things we conceive, there is sometimes given a foundation for one thing in them being able to be known without another; therefore there is given a foundation for denominations which are beings of reason being able to be attributed to them. The antecedent is proved. First: in human nature, in which there is given a foundation for knowing the formal unity without the numerical unity being known; therefore there is given a foundation for abstracting it from the individuals, and for comparing it with many by a simple comparison and attributing to it the denomination of species, or with only one by a composite comparison, by way of attribution, and attributing to it the denomination of predicate. Second: in the rational soul, in which there is given a foundation for distinguishing the vegetative, sensitive and rational grade; and this foundation is nothing other than its eminence or perfection, by reason of which, under the grade of a superior form not depending on matter, it contains the other grades which are found in diverse inferior forms.

7 Second conclusion: beings of reason sometimes have no foundation in the things to which they are attributed, but in other things, or in our imperfect mode of understanding alone. In this conclusion all agree, and it is proved by a twofold example. First, in God, in whom we distinguish justice from mercy, not on account of a foundation existing in them, but in creatures, in which these virtues are distinct. Second, in propositions which are called Identical, because the same thing is predicated of itself, as in this one, Peter is Peter, in which the intellect distinguishes Peter from himself, making him as it were two, and attributes to him the denomination of predicate and of subject; of which distinction there is no foundation in him, but only in the imperfect mode of knowing, which distinguishes as it were into two extremes that which in itself is neither distinct nor has a foundation for being distinguished from itself.

From these conclusions it follows that the distinction of reason is twofold, as the common consensus of the school asserts. One is that which has a foundation in the things themselves, and this is called the distinction of Reasoned Reason, which we posit between the universal and the singulars, and between the diverse grades of vegetating, sensing and understanding of the rational soul. The other is the distinction having no foundation in the known thing itself, but in other things, or only in our imperfect mode of knowing, as that which we posit between Peter and himself when he is predicated in an identical proposition. And so much concerning beings of reason having a foundation in things.

8 There are other beings of reason which have no foundation in things, but are feigned by the intellect out of certain impossible things joined together, as the Chimera and the Sphinx. Out of impossible

Phyſicorumde priuatione, quòd

joined together we say they are made: not because they are impossible in themselves, for this is necessary, but because, although they are possible, their conjunction is judged impossible. And in this way the Chimera is called impossible, because it is feigned as it were composed of things of different species, as of some part of a man and of another part of a lion or of some other animal. And beings of reason of this kind can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect, just as it can join things of different species in infinite ways.

9 The second division of the being of reason is as it were a subdivision of the first member. For the being of reason having a foundation in things is divided into three members, namely into Negation, Privation and Relation; which division Aristotle intimated in Metaph. bk. 4, text 2, and bk. 5, ch. 7, text 14, asserting that privation and negation are non-beings, so as to signify that they are not true real beings, but made by the intellect after their likeness. And in the second place he teaches that besides true beings there are certain others, true not so much according to entity as according to the truth of predication, affirmative as well as negative; which cannot be anything but beings of reason, which are called privations and negations. Of the relation of reason, however, he treated in ch. 15 of the same book, explaining the relations of the third kind, of the measurable and the measure, and teaching that the measure is referred to the measurable not by an intrinsic relation but by an extrinsic one, of the measurable to it; although it is certain that nothing can be ordered to another except by a relation existing in itself, which it is also certain that the measure does not have in itself, since it is rather an absolute thing. Aristotle therefore means it to be inferred that, through a relation made by the intellect, the same measure is ordered to the measurable as if it were ordered from its own nature. St. Thomas seems to gather the same division from these places: q. 21 On Truth, a. 1; d. 1, q. 2, a. 3; and d. 13, q. 1, a. 1; and it is also common in the school.

But concerning Negation and Privation two things are to be noted, so that their nature and distinction may be understood. The first is that both can be considered in two ways. First, according to themselves, or according to their essences, namely as they are negations of some real form; and in this signification they are called by Aristotle not real beings: because, since real being has being from some real form, negation or privation, which deny the real form, are consequently said to deny real being, and therefore not to be real beings, but rather non-beings, as Aristotle taught in Phys. 1 and 5. Which is to be understood of being simply; for negations of a real form are called real beings in a qualified sense, that is, not positive but negative ones. In this signification too Aristotle taught in Phys. 1, concerning privation, that

[p. 78]

> fitprincipium rei naturalis. Etde negationibus, docetD. Thơ. in opufculode Ente,& Effentia, quòdfintde effentia naturerea-lis. Vtde eſſentiahominis eſt eſſenon equum,aut nonhenni-bilem.Inhactandem fignificationeſumptæ, verum eft, & ne ceflarium , quòddentur ante operationem intellectus , & ab conondependeant. Exquibus intelligitur,quonam modo diftinguantur Priua-tio,&Negatio:diftinguuntur enim distinctione formali, quæ vocari ſolet Includentis, & incluſi : quia priuatio includit ne-gationem,& addit fupra illamordinemaddeterminatum fub-iectum,aptumhabere formam,quacaret, cùmtamennegatio

it is a principle of a natural thing. And of negations St. Thomas teaches, in the opusculum On Being and Essence, that they belong to the essence of a real nature: as it is of the essence of man to be not a horse, or not capable of neighing. Taken, finally, in this signification, it is true and necessary that they are given before the operation of the intellect and do not depend on it. This is proved evidently: because privation cannot be a principle of natural generation if it depends on the intellect, before whose operation it is certain that that same generation is given. Negation cannot belong to the essence of a real nature if it is not given before the operation of the intellect, taken in this way.

In another way Privation and Negation can be taken as they are attributed to things in a proposition; and in this way they are not taken according to the ratio of negation and privation, but after the likeness of a positive form, because what is attributed to another must be a positive form or have its likeness; and since they do not have of themselves to be taken by way of a positive form, but only from the intellect, therefore, taken in this way, they depend on it: they are not given before its operation, nor can they in any way be real beings, but they are beings of reason. Which we can explain by this example: when we say that a man is blind, we do not take blindness as a negation but as a privation of sight; because, taken in this way, it is not properly said to be in another, but rather to take away a form from it; therefore neither is it attributed to another in a proposition as it is a privation, but inasmuch as it is conceived after the likeness of a positive form; and since it has this from the intellect alone, it is also said necessarily to depend on it and not to be given before its operation; which are the proper conditions of a being of reason.

It should be noted, second, for understanding the distinction of privation from negation, that they agree in one thing and are distinguished in another. They agree in this, that each is a negation of a real form in a subject. But they differ, because Negation only denies the form of the subject, whether it is apt to have it or not; whereas Privation expresses the negation of a form not in any subject whatever, but in one apt to have it. Whence a stone is not called blind, even if it does not have sight, because it does not have the aptitude for having it; but a man or an animal is rightly so called, in which, if it is not present, there is nevertheless the aptitude for having sight.

From which it is understood in what manner Privation and Negation are distinguished: for they are distinguished by a formal distinction, which is usually called that of the Including and the included; because privation includes negation and adds over it an order to a determinate subject apt to have the form which it lacks, whereas negation

[p. 79]

> nondicatordinem, nifiadfubiectumnon habens,fiue aptum fithabere, fluenon. Exhis , quæ de diuerfitate Entium rationis dicta funt,fe-quiturnoneffeabſolutè afferendum,quòd ens rationis,fit Ens confictum ab intellectu,fed folum eſſeverahanclocutionem, deEnte rationisnonhabentefundamentum inrebus,quibus attribuitur: vt Chimæra aut Sphinge,non verò deiis,queha-bent fundamentum.Et huius ratio eſt manifeſta:quia fingere folumdicitur ille,quifinealiquofundamento loquitur :locu-tio verò aliquo modo fundata in veritate, autnatura rerum, nonproprièdicitur ficta: ſed proprièloquendum eft, dehis Entibus rationis, dicendum eſt,quòd facta fintab intellectu, præfuppofito fundamento in rebus. Et ratio huius eft, quiahæc Entiarationisfuntdenominationes quædam vel re-lationes,quas intellectus tribuitnaturis,iam cognitis àfe, per aliani cognitionem: vnde quafi per cognitionem reflexam fieridicuntur:fednulla alia potentia præter intellectum haber hanc virtutem reflexiuam, per quampoffit fumerepro obie- Eto rem,vt à ſe cognitam alia cognitione:ergo nec habet vir-tutem efficiendiEntia rationis. Maior eſt manifeſta ex his, quædiximusin quæſt.5.Vniuerfalium,de modo,quoVniuer-falefitab intellectu per fimplicem comparationem. Diximus enimCompararionem effe cognitionem,perquam intellectus quaſi reflectitur fupra naturam ium cognitam ,per ſimpli-cem abſtractionem :& naturam ita cognitam comparat ad

does not express an order except to a subject without it, whether it is apt to have it or not.

From what has been said about the diversity of beings of reason, it follows that it is not to be asserted absolutely that a being of reason is a being feigned by the intellect, but that this way of speaking is true only of the being of reason having no foundation in the things to which it is attributed, as the Chimera or the Sphinx, but not of those which have a foundation. And the reason for this is manifest: because only he is said to feign who speaks without any foundation; but speech in some way founded in the truth or nature of things is not properly called feigned; but, speaking properly of these beings of reason, it must be said that they are made by the intellect, a foundation in things being presupposed.

By what power and operation the being of reason is made.

To this doubt some reply that not only the intellect produces beings of reason, but also the interior senses, especially the imagination or phantasy, of which we know that it feigns a golden mountain, which, since it is not given in the nature of things, will be called a being feigned by the imagination, which is a being of reason.

We, however, assert that one must reply with a distinction: for beings of reason that are feigned, that is, that have no foundation in the thing, can be made not only by the intellect but also by the phantasy; but those which have a foundation, only by the intellect. And of the first it is plain that they are made by the phantasy, as it were composing some one thing not existing in the nature of things out of two truly existing ones: as out of the species of mountain and of gold it composes a golden mountain; which cannot be done by any other sense, nor by the will or appetite, because they do not have such a power of composing. But beings of reason which have a foundation in things cannot be made by any other power except by the intellect alone. And the reason for this is that these beings of reason are certain denominations or relations which the intellect attributes to natures already known by it, through another cognition; whence they are said to be made as it were by a reflex cognition; but no other power besides the intellect has this reflexive power, by which it can take as object a thing as known by itself through another cognition; therefore neither does it have the power of producing beings of reason. The major is manifest from what we said in q. 5 on Universals, about the mode in which the universal is made by the intellect through simple comparison. For we said that Comparison is a cognition by which the intellect as it were reflects upon the nature already known through simple abstraction, and compares the nature so known to

[p. 80]

> inferiora. Minorverò manifeſta eſt,quia reflexio hæcnon po-teſt conuenirevoluntati, quæ nihil cognoſet, ſed tendit in obiectum cognitum ab intellectu: nec minus poteſt tribui fenfibus , quorum cognitio imperfectiſſima eſt :& ideo non poffunt operari circarem, vt àſe iam cognitam: quamuis pof-fit contingere, quòdeandem rem cognitam,iterum cogno-ſcant,nontamencognitione reflexa,fed pluribus cognitioni-bus quafidirectis. Sediam,quòd àſolo intellectu fiant entia rationis, poterit quis dubitare, per quam operationem eius fiant : An per pri-mam,quæ eft apprehenfio fimplicium,autperſecundam, quæ eſtcompofitio,&diuifio , per diſcurſum:quiefttertia. Re-ſpondent quidam,nonpoſſe fieri perprimam , &probanthac ratione: Entia rationis fiuntper comparationem naturæ cum inferioribus,aut prædicati cumfubiecto:fed omnis compara-tio eft compofitio,autdiuifio,& actualis predicatio:ergo non poffuntfieri per fimplicem apprehenfionem. Communistamen fententiaànobis ſequenda tenet,(vtvi-dimusin quæſt. s.vniuerfali ) quædam entia rationis fieri per primam operationem intellectus,alia per ſecundum , & qux-damaliaper tertiam.Quodhoc argumento probatur. Adargumentum verò alterius opinionis, negandum eft, quòdomnis comparatiofit compofitio , autdiuifio, cùm pro-batum fit in quæſt. 5.vniuerfali,dari comparationem, quæ fit fimplicium apprehenfio,per quamcognofcimus vnum in or dineadaliud, veladmulta. An

its inferiors. The minor, however, is manifest, because this reflection cannot belong to the will, which knows nothing but tends to the object known by the intellect; nor can it be attributed to the senses, whose cognition is most imperfect; and therefore they cannot operate about a thing as already known by themselves; although it may happen that they know again the same thing already known, yet not by a reflex cognition, but by several cognitions that are as it were direct.

But now, granted that beings of reason are made by the intellect alone, someone could doubt by which of its operations they are made: whether by the first, which is the apprehension of simples, or by the second, which is composition and division, or by discursive reasoning, which is the third. Some reply that they cannot be made by the first, and they prove it by this reason: beings of reason are made through the comparison of the nature with its inferiors, or of the predicate with the subject; but every comparison is a composition or division, and an actual predication; therefore they cannot be made through simple apprehension.

The common view, however, to be followed by us, holds (as we saw in q. 5 on universals) that some beings of reason are made through the first operation of the intellect, others through the second, and some others through the third. Which is proved by this argument. Some beings of reason belong to simples before a composition is made out of them; others belong to the same simples as they already are in a composition, or to the composition itself; others, finally, to compositions as they are in a syllogism; therefore different beings of reason are made through each of these operations. The antecedent is proved, because through the simple comparison of the nature with its inferiors there is made the being of reason which is the universal; there are made also genus and species, all of which belong to the predicables before they are actually predicated, therefore before a proposition is made out of them. Wherefore it is necessary that they be made through simple apprehension, through which we know one thing in order to another; for this simple cognition is prior to composition. Of the beings of reason which belong to composition and to discursive reasoning, it is manifest that they are made through the second and third operation of the intellect; and such are the denominations of predicate and subject, and also of proposition; and moreover the denominations of argumentation and syllogism.

To the argument of the other opinion, however, it must be denied that every comparison is a composition or division, since it was proved in q. 5 on universals that there is given a comparison which is an apprehension of simples, through which we know one thing in order to another, or to many.

Whether beings of reason are made by the divine or the angelic intellect.

The first opinion affirms that the divine and the angelic intellect produce beings of reason; it is held by certain moderns. And it is proved, first, by the testimony of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 15, a. 2, ad 3, where these words are found: Respects of this kind, by which the ideas are multiplied, are not caused by things but by the divine intellect, comparing its essence to things, etc. From which this argument is gathered: The distinction of the ideas in God is not real, since the ideas agree with the divine essence, in which there can be no real distinction; therefore it is only a distinction of reason. But a distinction of reason is a relation of reason; therefore a being of reason is made by the divine intellect, according to the mind of St. Thomas. The consequence is proved, because he says that the distinction of the ideas is caused by the divine intellect.

It is proved also by a twofold argument. First, the divine intellect knows beings of reason most perfectly; but beings of reason have no other being than to be known; therefore they have being from the divine intellect, which is to be made by it.

Second, the divine intellect distinguishes things which are not distinct on the part of the thing; but this cannot be done except by producing a being of reason; therefore the divine intellect produces beings of reason. The major is manifest, because it distinguishes its justice and mercy, and also the ideas existing in itself, which are not distinguished on the part of the thing. The minor is proved, because distinguishing things which are not distinct is done through a relation of reason, which is a being of reason.

The second opinion asserts that the divine intellect does not produce beings of reason; and this is the more probable and is to be held. I explain it by two conclusions. The first: the divine intellect most perfectly knows the beings of reason which are made by our intellect. All grant this, and it is proved by an evident argument. Beings of reason are made by our intellect; therefore they are known by it. But whatever is known by the intellect is contained under its object; therefore beings of reason are contained under the object of our intellect. But the object of the divine intellect is not less universal than ours, since it comprehends things diminished and most imperfect; therefore it no less contains beings of reason, nor knows them less.

The second conclusion: the divine intellect makes no being of reason, nor can it make one. In order to prove this, it must be supposed that two imperfections are necessarily required for producing a being of reason, in the mode of understanding. The first, that things which are not distinct on the part of the thing, but one, be distinguished

by the intellect and conceived through several concepts. The second, that the object be represented to the intellect and understood by it, not as it is in itself or on the part of the thing, but in another mode. Both conditions are made manifest by this example. In order that the intellect may make the universal nature genus or species, it is necessary that it distinguish it from the inferiors from which it is not distinct, and abstract it from them, since it is not abstracted of itself but is joined to them on the part of the thing; and this is to understand it in another mode than it is on the part of the thing, that is, to understand by several and distinct concepts what on the part of the thing is one. But the intellect does both without falsehood, because without affirmation and negation. And what we say of these beings of reason is evident in the rest.

From these things an argument is gathered to prove our view effectively. Beings of reason cannot be made by the intellect except by distinguishing things which on the part of the thing, or according to themselves, are not distinct, and by conceiving through several concepts things which in themselves are one, and also by understanding them in another mode than they are on the part of the thing. But such a mode of understanding is most imperfect, and one that cannot belong to the divine intellect; therefore neither will it be able to produce beings of reason. The minor is proved: for the divine intellect understands all things by a single cognition and a single and most simple concept, and according to the same mode which they have on the part of the thing: so that if they are one, it knows them in the mode of one; but if they are distinct, as distinct. Therefore such an imperfect mode of understanding, through which a being of reason must necessarily be made, cannot belong to it; and therefore neither will it be able to produce one.

To the arguments of the other opinion I reply, and to the first, the testimony of St. Thomas, that his sense is gathered from another place, namely from De potentia, q. 17, a. 6, where he teaches that the distinction of reason which is found among the divine attributes, as between justice and mercy, or among the ideas, is found in a different way in the divine intellect and in ours: because in the former it is found as in its root and as it were virtually, but in ours formally. Which is to be explained in this way. An idea is nothing other than the divine essence as it can be participated by creatures. And since there are several creatures distinct according to essence, we distinguish in it several ideas, so that by the ratio by which it can be participated by man, it is the idea of man and not of lion; and as it can be participated by the lion, it is the idea of lion and not of elephant; and so of the rest. But although the divine intellect understands the divine essence as imitable by all creatures by a single and most simple concept,

and therefore does not distinguish several ideas in it, yet through that single concept it understands that, by our intellect conceiving it in an imperfect mode, that is, through several and distinct concepts, it is distinguished into several ideas, of man, of lion, and of other things. For by one concept we understand the divine essence as it can be participated by man, and by another, distinct concept as it can be participated by the lion; and this is to distinguish several ideas in the divine essence by a distinction of reason, and therefore to produce beings of reason by understanding the divine ideas.

From which is understood the difference between the divine intellect and ours: that the former does not distinguish the ideas in the divine essence by an actual or formal distinction, but by a fundamental or virtual one, inasmuch as it knows that they can be distinguished by ours; whereas our intellect makes an actual distinction of reason among the ideas. And because all our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine, St. Thomas taught that the divine intellect causes the distinction of the ideas, not by producing it actually, but only virtually, inasmuch as it understands the divine essence as it can be understood by our intellect through several concepts, and that therefore several ideas can be distinguished by us; which distinction, made by us, the divine intellect itself causes through its understanding. And this is the sense of that testimony.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted, that the divine intellect knows beings of reason by a most perfect cognition; but the consequence is to be denied, that it makes them. And the reason is that it does not know things with those two imperfections necessarily required for producing beings of reason. And to declare the solution in one word, it must be said that the divine intellect does not know beings of reason by a cognition productive of them, but by a cognition through which it understands them as made by us.

To the second, the major is to be distinguished: because “to distinguish things which are not distinct” can be understood in two ways. First, by producing an actual distinction among them; and in this sense it is to be denied. In another way, by producing the distinction only as it were virtually or fundamentally; and in this way it can be granted. For since the divine intellect understands things which are not distinct as able to be distinguished by us, who know imperfectly through several concepts, it is said virtually to produce the distinction which our intellect makes actually, inasmuch as our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine. And what we say of the divine intellect must also be understood, in its own way, of the angelic: which, since it understands perfectly, is not said to make beings of reason, but to know them as made by us.

To which science it pertains to treat of being of reason.

This doubt must be answered with two distinctions presupposed. The first is the one we adduced above, of being of reason having a foundation in things and not having such a foundation. And concerning the second it is certain that it pertains per se to no science. Which is proved by two arguments. First, because the things of which a science treats per se must be determinate; but beings of reason which have no foundation can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect; therefore no science can treat of them per se. Second, that of which a science treats must have determinate principles, through which determinate attributes are proved of it; but these beings of reason do not have determinate principles; therefore no science can treat of them per se. I prove the minor, because they are composed of disparate things, or things diverse in species; therefore no determinate principle can be taken from them, nor can such an impossible composite have determinate attributes.

The other distinction is of being of reason having a foundation in the thing. If it is a relation of reason, it can be considered in two ways. First, according to itself, or according to its proper entity; and in this way it pertains to Metaphysics, not per se, because the per se object of this science is real being, but as it were per accidens, inasmuch as it has a certain likeness to real relation, of which this science treats per se. Second, it can be considered as it is a denomination of the nature to which it is attributed, as the denomination of genus, species, predicate and subject. And according to this consideration it is called logical being of reason, of which Logic treats per se as of its proper object. But if it is a privation or a negation, it must be reduced to that science which treats per se of the form or essence which it denies or of which it deprives: as the privation of a natural form pertains to Philosophy, as one of the three principles of natural generation, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1; and a negation which is of the essence of this or that nature is reduced to the science which treats per se of such a nature, as not to be a horse to the science of man; and so of the rest.

In what way being of reason is reduced to the categorial order.

Concerning being of reason not having a foundation in things, it is certain that it cannot be reduced to the categorial order, because it is composed of things diverse according to essence,

and therefore it does not have some one determinate nature according to which it could be ordered in a category. But concerning being of reason having a foundation, as regards privation and negation, it is also certain that it has a certain likeness to qualities. Which I prove thus. Privation and negation are beings of reason as they are considered by the intellect as positive forms and are attributed to some subject in a proposition, as when we say that a man is blind; but so considered they have a likeness to qualities; therefore they are reduced to their category. The minor is proved: because blindness is predicated of a man just as whiteness or color is; therefore it has a likeness to these and to other qualities.

There remains only relation of reason, which could be ordered in a special category. This, however, will not be proper, because a category can properly be made only of real beings; but it will have the greatest likeness to the true category of relation, ordered out of real relations. The category of relation of reason, therefore, is to be ordered thus: that the supreme genus be relation of reason (for being of reason, the most universal, must be excluded from this category on account of its transcendence, just as real being is excluded from all the real categories), which can be divided into three genera, or subalternate species, according to its diverse foundations, which are the diverse operations of the intellect, namely simple apprehension, composition and division, and discursive reasoning. Just as Aristotle divided the supreme genus of the category of relation, which is the relative, or real relation, through its diverse foundations, so that the first genus is of relations which are founded on unity, as the relations of identity, likeness and equality; the second, of relations which are founded on action and passion, as paternity and filiation; the third, of those which are founded on measure, as are the relations of science to the knowable and of a power to its object: so relation of reason is to be divided into that which is founded on the cognition of simples and is attributed to the simples themselves, and this is the first genus, having under it diverse species, as the relation of universal, genus, species and the other predicables; next, into that which is founded on composition and division, to which genus the various species of propositions pertain; and finally into that which is founded on the third operation, which is discursive reasoning, under which genus are contained the diverse species of argumentations and syllogisms. And so these three genera have others under them, down to the lowest species, from all of which, so ordered, the proper category of being of reason results.

## OF FIRST AND SECOND INTENTIONS

t the end of the preceding treatise we said that Dialectic treats of

A          being of reason as it is a certain relation, or a denomination at‐

tributed to natures by the intellect; in which acceptation it is called logical being of reason. Therefore in this second treatise we must treat of the mode and order which it has with respect to the predications of concretes and abstracts, in which are exercised the denominations which natures receive from it. And since predications can be made in first intentions, which are real natures, and also in second intentions, which are beings of reason, we shall divide the present treatise into two parts: so that in the first we treat of the predications of concretes and abstracts of first intention, and in the second of the same abstracts and concretes of second intentions.

And in first intentions they can be exercised in four ways. First, so that a concrete is predicated of a concrete, as man is animal. Second, an abstract of an abstract, as humanity is animality. Third, an abstract of a concrete, as man is humanity. Fourth, a concrete of an abstract, as humanity is man. And so that we may suppose what is certain as regards the truth and falsity of propositions, we must speak only of those propositions in which the predicate and subject are in some way ordered, so that they are related as superior and inferior, or as equals, one of which pertains to the other because it is included in it, or is its proper attribute, or a common accident.

These things explained, it is certain, first, that a proposition is true in which a concrete is predicated of a concrete inferior or superior, or also equal, whether it be of its essence, or a proper attribute, or a common accident: such are these, man is animal, man is rational, man is risible, man is white. True also are the others into which these are converted, but indirectly and improperly.

Second, it is certain that propositions in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, or a concrete of an abstract, are false, whether they be related as superior and inferior, or be equals;

[p. 87]

as man is humanity, man is rationality, or risibility, or whiteness. And the reason for this is manifest. First, on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the terms: because the abstract is signified by way of a part, but the concrete by way of a whole; but a part is not predicated of the whole, as foot or hands of a man.

Second, because the subject in these propositions includes something which the predicate in no way includes, as white includes body, which whiteness does not include; or, conversely, the predicate includes something which the subject does not include, as in the indirect propositions made from the same terms. Which suffices for it not to be true that the one is the other, as is signified by the proposition.

From which it follows, first, that the opinion of Soto, q. 3 on Universals, is false, who asserts that a proposition in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, as man is humanity, is false only on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the terms; for they are false also on account of the inclusion of something in the one and not in the other: because, as we shall see in its place, no proposition can be true unless the whole that is included in the subject in some way includes the predicate.

It follows, second, that the opinion of Durandus, in 1, d. 24, last q., is even more false, where he laid down a universal rule, saying that in creatures all propositions are true in which a substantial abstract is predicated of a substantial concrete, as man is humanity; although they are false in accidental concretes and abstracts, as man is whiteness, and others like it.

It is certain, third, that propositions in which the abstract of a genus is predicated of the abstract of a difference, or conversely the abstract of a difference of the abstract of a genus, as rationality is animality, or animality is rationality, are false. And the reason for this is that the generic and the differential grade are formally diverse, and, signified in the abstract, they do not include each other, because neither does animality include rationality nor rationality animality; therefore neither is predicated formally of the other. The consequence is proved, for in order that a proposition be true, the predicate must be included in the subject.

Whether a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract.

that are accidental or essential. And if they are made in accidental terms, it is certain that all are false, as humanity is risibility, or humanity is whiteness. And the reason for this is that the predicate and the subject of these propositions are often distinguished really, and the one is never included in the other: for although man includes whiteness as its subject, yet humanity, since it is signified as a form, is not the subject of accidents, nor does it include them, as signified in the abstract. The question can therefore only be about the propositions of abstracts which are made in substantial terms, such as these, humanity is animality, humanity is rationality: whether they are true or false.

And the first opinion asserts that they are true; it is followed by Soto, q. 3 on Universals, Canterus, chapter on difference, and many of the moderns. And it is proved by two arguments. First, that proposition in which a superior concrete is predicated of an inferior, as man is animal, is true, because the predicate is included in the subject, as animal in man; but the superior abstract is also included in the inferior abstract, as animality in humanity; therefore this will be true, humanity is animality. The minor is proved, because humanity is composed of animality and rationality, just as man of animal and rational; therefore it includes both.

It is proved, second, in substantial and accidental forms. And first in substantial ones, such as are the rational and the sensitive soul, of which the latter is superior and the former inferior; and both are signified by an abstract name; and yet this is true, the rational soul is sensitive; therefore this too will be true, humanity is animality. The consequence is proved, because a superior form is predicated of an inferior precisely because it is included in it; but animality is a superior form with respect to humanity; therefore it is included in it, and consequently it will be truly predicated. In accidental forms too, such as whiteness and color, it is manifest: for this is true among all, whiteness is color; and in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract, just as in the other, humanity is animality; therefore this too is true and to be granted.

The second opinion holds that such propositions are false. It is followed by Scotus, in 1, d. 5, q. 1, a. 1; Nifo, Metaph. 3, q. 2, concl. 5, ad 3; Canariensis, 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, disp. 2; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 18, 2, 3, § Considerandum, and bk. 4, ch. 81; Cajetan, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 3 and 4. But Scotus maintains that they are false because he thinks that the predicate and the subject are distinguished from the nature of the thing, or formally, before the operation of the intellect; but the others, who posit only a distinction of reason between them,

do so on account of the mode of signifying of abstracts, by which animality is signified as a principle or part of animal, and humanity as a principle of man; and the principle of one is not predicated of the principle of another. And this opinion is gathered evidently from St. Thomas in the two places cited, and it seems to us more probable and to be followed.

15 But in order that we may prove it more effectively, two things are to be noted. The first is that the concrete and the abstract signify the same thing, but by a different ratio: for the concrete signifies it by way of the haver, but the abstract by way of the principle or form of that same haver. For example, man and humanity signify the same human nature; but man signifies it by way of an actual and complete whole, and therefore by way of the haver; humanity, on the other hand, only by way of the principle and form of that same complete whole, or haver. Which is manifest from the common way of speaking and understanding: for we say that a man is the same as one having humanity, and that humanity is as it were the principle and form of man.

From which it is gathered, first, that the concrete signifies the nature not as altogether prescinded from the singular conditions, but as containing them, at least confusedly and in potency. For although it is abstracted from singulars by an abstraction through which it becomes in some way universal, and therefore does not signify or contain the same singulars in act, yet it contains them in potency: because from its proper mode of signifying it can be determined through singular conditions to this and that individual, or to Peter or John. But the abstract signifies the same nature as altogether prescinded from singulars, and not as determinable through their singular conditions: because, since it does not signify it by way of the haver but of the principle or form, and a principle or form does not have the mode of what is determinable through another, but rather of what determines another, namely that whose principle or form it is, the nature signified in the abstract cannot be understood by way of the haver; and therefore, so signified, it can contain neither in act nor in potency the singular conditions through which it would be contracted to this or that singular. And what we say of the specific nature with respect to the singulars is to be understood in the same way of the generic nature signified in the concrete or in the abstract, as of animal or animality: so that animal signifies the sensitive nature as contractible or perfectible through the differences rational and irrational, which it contains in potency; but animality in no way, or rather as the form or principle of that same animal and of its species.

[p. 90]

It is gathered, second, that abstracts signify the nature by way of a part, just as concretes do by way of a whole. Which is proved by a twofold evident argument. First, because abstracts signify the nature by way of the principle and form of that same thing as it is signified by the concrete name: as animality signifies the sensitive nature as it is the principle and as it were the form of animal; but that which is the principle and form of another is related as a part of it; therefore the abstract signifies the nature by way of a part. Second, animality does not signify the sensitive nature by way of a whole; therefore by way of a part. The antecedent is proved: because if it signified it by way of a whole, it would be either of an actual or of a potential whole; but it signifies it in neither way; therefore not by way of a whole. I prove the minor: because a potential or actual whole signifies the thing by way of the haver, but the abstract only by way of the form of that which has it; therefore not by way of a whole but of a part. And hence it comes about that neither is animality predicated of animal, nor humanity of man: because a part cannot be predicated of the whole.

It follows, third, that abstracts are not genera or species, but principles of genera and species; which Avicenna asserted, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, as Cajetan testifies in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4; and St. Thomas proved it in the same place by this argument. A genus by its proper nature has the mode of a potential whole, and a species the mode of an actual whole; but abstracts do not signify the nature by way of a potential or of an actual whole, but by way of a part; therefore they are not genera or species, and for that reason they are not denominated by the second intentions of genus or species, or of the other predicables. All this doctrine that has been noted is found in St. Thomas, opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4.

From it two arguments are gathered for proving our view, that this predication, humanity is animality, and similar ones, are false. The first is: for any predication to be true, it is necessarily required that whatever the subject contains, the predicate contain in act or in potency; but animality does not contain, in act or in potency, whatever humanity contains; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of it. The major is most certain, because it cannot be true that this is that, as is affirmed through the proposition, unless the whole that this contains that also contains; and this is the reason why a part is not predicated of the whole, nor could a genus be predicated of a species unless it contained in potency the difference which the species contains in act, as St. Thomas says well in the place above. But the minor is proved: because humanity contains animality and rationality, of which it is composed; but it is evident

that animality does not contain rationality in act or in potency, since it does not have the mode of an actual or a potential whole, but of a part or form; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of humanity.

The second. An actual part is not predicated of the whole, as all grant; but animality is an actual part of humanity; therefore it is not truly predicated of it. The minor is proved: because just as man is composed of animal and rational, so humanity is composed of animality and rationality. And if you say that this argument also proves that this proposition is not true, man is animal, because animal is an actual part of man: I reply that animal is indeed a part, yet it is not signified by way of a part, but by way of a potential whole, and therefore it is truly predicated of man; animality, on the other hand, is not only a part but is signified by way of a part, which cannot be predicated of the whole. And this is the reason why this is true, Man is animal, and this false, Humanity is animality.

To the first argument it is replied that it is not enough for the truth of a proposition that the predicate be included in the subject: because if that sufficed, it would follow that a proposition in which a part is predicated of the whole is true, since it is certain that the part is included in the whole. It is required, therefore, not only that it be included in it, but that the whole that the subject contains the predicate contain in act or in potency, as has been explained. And since animality does not contain the whole that humanity contains, because it does not contain rationality in act or in potency, it follows that it is not truly predicated of it.

The second argument has two parts. The first proceeds about substantial forms, the second about accidental ones. To the first, therefore, I reply by denying the antecedent: that that predication, the rational soul is sensitive, is of an abstract of an abstract. And concerning the predicate, namely sensitive, it is evident that it is not an abstract name but a concrete one. Which is also true of soul: for although it is a form, yet it is signified by way of what has the grade of sensing; not indeed as man has it, who is composed of it, but as the form, which gives that grade to the composite, yet signified as it were by way of a whole, and therefore by way of a concrete. Which is made manifest from this: because unless soul were signified by way of a concrete, sensitive, which is a concrete name, could not be truly predicated of it; and by the very fact that it is truly predicated, signifying the same as what has the grade of sensing, it cannot be denied that soul too is signified by way of a concrete. Hence it is not well inferred that this too is true, Humanity is animality, in which it is certain that an abstract

is predicated of an abstract; and therefore it has a different ratio.

For the solution of the second part, a threefold difference is to be noted between the abstracts of substances and those of accidents. The first: that the former are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera, species or differences, as animality from animal and humanity from man; but the abstracts of accidents are abstracted by physical abstraction from the subject in which the accidental form signified really inheres. Hence, by the very fact that it is signified as abstracted from it, it is not signified as inhering in it or dependent on it, but after the manner of a complete nature subsisting per se. The second: because the abstracts of substances always have the mode of the form or principle of that from which they are abstracted, whereas the abstracts of accidents rather have the complete mode of a total nature, subsisting per se; which comes from the proper mode of physical abstraction. The last difference is that the abstracts of substances, because they are abstracted metaphysically, are ultimate abstracts, because metaphysical abstraction is ultimate; hence no other abstraction can be made from them: for nothing further can be abstracted from humanity or animality. But the abstracts of accidents are not ultimate, because neither is physical abstraction ultimate, but metaphysical abstraction can still follow upon it: so that from whiteness, which is abstracted by physical abstraction, another, metaphysical abstract can be taken, which will be the ratio of whiteness, or albedineitas [whitenessness] (a barbarous word, but one that signifies by explaining the nature of the thing). From which it is understood that the abstracts of accidents are called abstracts only in the physical order, but in the metaphysical order are rather concretes.

From these differences we can reply to the form of the argument, granting the major, that this is true, whiteness is color, but denying the minor, that in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract; rather it is a predication of concretes in the metaphysical order, like this, man is animal. Hence neither is the predicate signified by way of a part, but by way of a complete whole, subsisting per se and containing whatever the subject contains, which is related as genus to species, as in this, man is animal. But that one, humanity is animality, is a predication of abstracts in the same metaphysical order, and therefore it is false. And in the same way a predication of abstracts in accidents will be false if they are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction: as if from whiteness and color we metaphysically abstract albedineitas and coloreitas, or the ratio of whiteness and the ratio of color, this will be false, albedineitas is coloreitas: because metaphysical abstracts are signified by way of principle and form, and therefore cannot make a true predication.

S E C O N D PA RT O F T H I S

T R E AT I S E , O N T H E P R E D I C A-tions of Second Intentions.

econd intentions are certain relations of reason which the intellect

S        attributes to first intentions, that is, to real natures, which are denomi‐

nated by them: as the second intention of species is a relation of reason of the specific nature, which the intellect attributes to it when it compares it to the individuals; and all the predicables are certain relations of reason, diverse because they are attributed to diverse natures, and in order to diverse inferiors, or to inferiors of which they are predicated in diverse ways. Thus the predicable of genus is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species, of which it is predicated in quid as a potential whole. The predicable of difference is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species or individuals, of which it is predicated in quale quid. The predicable of property is a second intention, or a relation of reason of a proper attribute to species or individuals: as of sensible to man and horse, or of risible to man, and to Peter and John. And the predicable of accident is a second intention, or a relation of reason of an accident to several subjects distinct in species or in number: as the relation of reason of white to man and horse, or to Peter and John. And finally the universal, which is common to all the predicables, is a second intention, or a relation of reason to all and each of the predicables, of which it is predicated in quid as a genus.

These things supposed, second intentions can be compared in two ways. First, among themselves, inasmuch as one is predicated of another; and if they are compared in this way, whether in the concrete or in the abstract, they behave in the same way as first intentions: so that if one pertains in some way to another, concretes are predicated of concretes essentially or accidentally, as a proper or a common accident. Therefore all of these are true: Genus is universal, Species is universal; and also this: Universal is genus; but the former are essential, the latter accidental. This one, however, The universal is predicable, is a predication of a property, or of the fourth predicable. But concretes of abstracts, or abstracts of concretes, always make false propositions: as Genus is genericity, or Specificity is species, or Genus is universality. Only

in the predications of abstracts is there a difference: because in second intentions the predication of a superior abstract of an inferior abstract is true, as genericity is universality; which, however, in first intentions we said is false, as humanity is animality. And the reason for this difference is that second intentions are relations of reason, and therefore accidents of reason. Wherefore, just as real accidents signified in the abstract do not have the mode of parts but of a whole subsisting per se, because they are not abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera or species, but by physical abstraction from their subjects, in the same way second intentions have a likeness to accidental forms, and therefore are not signified through abstract names as forms or principles of genera or species, but by way of a whole subsisting per se. And this is the reason why they constitute a true predication, although in first intentions it is false.

Second, with first intentions. If second intentions are compared to first ones, they are always compared accidentally, since they are relations and accidents attributed to them; and they also behave in the same way in all things as we said first intentions behave among themselves when they are compared accidentally. In this alone they differ: that real accidents which are truly predicated of inferiors are truly predicated also of superiors; and if they are truly predicated of superiors, they are truly predicated also of some inferior: as if white is predicated of Peter, it must be truly predicated of man; and if it is predicated of man, it must be truly predicated of some singular man. Which is not found in second intentions, but the contrary: because neither can the second intentions which are predicated of inferiors be truly predicated of superiors, nor are those which are predicated of superiors truly predicated of inferiors, as is made manifest by these examples. Species is predicated of man, and not of animal, nor of Peter; and genus is predicated of animal, and not of man; and the second intention of individual is truly predicated of Peter when we say Peter is an individual, and yet it is not predicated of man, but this is false, man is an individual. And the reason for this difference is that real accidents belong to their subjects absolutely and as they are on the part of the thing; but second intentions, which are relations and accidents of reason, do not belong to natures absolutely, nor on the part of the thing, but as they are conceived in such a mode by the intellect, namely in common, in order to species or individuals, or also in the singular; and therefore those which belong to the inferior, namely to the individual, cannot belong to the species, nor can that which belongs to the species belong to the genus: because the second intention

## CHAPTER II

On Genus.

But it seems that neither genus nor species is said simply, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of genus, which is the first predicable. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he lays down two real acceptations of genus and compares them with each other; from their likeness, in the second part, he gathers its third, logical acceptation. And in the third he hands down the definition of genus and at the same time expounds it.

The first real acceptation of genus is that in which it is taken for some collection of men having an order among themselves and to one first, from whom all are derived: in which signification we are accustomed to call the Roman people the genus of the Romans, because they are ordered among themselves by such laws, and descend from Romulus as from their first principle.

Second, genus is taken for the very principle of generation from which others are derived, whether it be the father or the fatherland: in which signification the poet speaks when he says: Mantua begot me, etc., calling his fatherland his genus, or principle of generation. But properly speaking, it is not so much the father or the fatherland as the origin through which men are derived from them that is called genus: for we do not so much call him their genus as say that the Romans draw their genus from him. And of these two acceptations Porphyry teaches that the second is more proper than the first. First, because we use it more frequently. Second, because a collection of men is called a genus precisely because the men of it draw their origin from one first; therefore the origin through which they are derived from him is more properly called genus than the collection itself.

In the second part, from both real acceptations, Porphyry gathers the logical one, which he intends per se, saying: The logical genus is taken for that under which the species are placed, that is, under which they are set, as animal is a genus, because under it are placed man,

[p. 96]

and lion: which species have an order and a certain likeness among themselves by reason of the same nature, which they participate from the genus itself, from which they are also said in their own way to draw their origin.

In the third part of the chapter he defines the logical genus, taken according to the last acceptation; and the definition is this: Genus is what is predicated of many differing in species, in quid. Which he explains thus: Things that are predicated are predicated either of one, as the individual, or of many, as universals. By the particle of many, therefore, genus is separated from the individual, which is predicated of one alone. By the particle differing in species, it is separated from species, which is the second predicable and is predicated only of things differing in number. By the last particle, in quid, it is separated from the three other predicables, difference, property and accident: for difference is predicated in quale quid, property and accident in quale, genus only in quid; because to a question put through what we do not answer well through those, but through genus: as if you ask what man is, I answer well that he is an animal. Thus far Porphyry.

## QUESTION I

What the defined of the definition of genus is.

That the definition of genus assigned by Porphyry has no defined, I prove by two arguments. First: if it had any, it would above all be genus; but genus is not definable; therefore it has none. The minor is proved: A good definition must consist of genus and difference, or of something in place of the genus and something else in place of the difference; but there is no genus of genus: for if there were, there would be another genus of that genus, and so we should proceed to infinity. It follows, therefore, that genus is not definable, and therefore that the aforesaid definition has no defined.

Second: a definition must be given through genus and difference; therefore nothing can be defined except species, because this alone is composed of genus and difference; indeed, nothing can be defined except inasmuch as it is a species, because to have genus and difference belongs to the species inasmuch as it is a species; therefore genus cannot be defined. The consequence is proved, because it is not a species but another predicable distinct from species; and therefore the present definition will have no defined.

It must be held, however, that the definition of genus is good and has a definite defined, whose nature it explains. And that the definition is good is proved, first, from Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, where Aristotle laid it down; and it was from him that

Porphyry took it. Second, by argument: because a good definition is one that so explains the nature of the defined that it distinguishes it from any other things with which it could agree; but through this definition it is explained what genus is, namely a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, and it is distinguished from the individual and from the remaining predicables, as we saw in the explanation of the text. It is therefore good.

And the second point, that it has a definite and determinate defined, I prove thus.

3 To be predicated of many differing in species, in quid, is a common ratio, belonging in the same way and equally to all genera; therefore it is one and can be explained through one definition; wherefore this will be the determinate defined of that definition.

But in order that this truth may be better understood and the arguments solved, it should be noted that the second intention of genus, which is the first predicable, is a certain relation of reason, and a most universal ratio of denominating all generic natures, even if they are the supreme genera of the categories, as substance, quantity and quality; and at the same time it is a certain species of universal. Hence, since every species is composed of genus and difference, this second intention too is composed of universal, which is the common genus of the predicables, and of a difference, which is to be relative to several species of which it can be predicated in quid. And so genus agrees with the other predicables in the common ratio of universal, which is to be one in many; and it is distinguished from them because it is in many species, of which it can be predicated in quid. And therefore, although it is a most universal ratio of denominating, because the natures which it denominates as genera are also for the most part most universal, since they are the supreme genera of the categories, nevertheless according to its essence it is a particular and determinate species of a certain genus, which is universal. From which it is understood that it can be defined through a determinate definition, and that its definition handed down by Porphyry has a determinate defined.

To the form of the first argument it must be replied by denying the minor of the first syllogism; and when it is said in the minor of the second syllogism that there is no genus of genus, by distinguishing: because the second intention of genus can be taken in two ways, in the ratio of denominating or in the ratio of being. And in the first way it has no other genus by which it is denominated, because it is not a genus denominatively or accidentally, but essentially; but in the ratio of being it is a determinate species, and has a superior genus, which

is universal, of which, together with the difference, it is composed.

And if it is said that universal too is denominated genus by this second intention of genus, which is the first predicable, like the remaining genera, and therefore is inferior with respect to it: it is replied that the antecedent is true, but the consequent must be distinguished. For in the ratio of denominating it is superior to universal, but in the ratio of being inferior; and because denomination is accidental with respect to that which is denominated, as the denomination of white with respect to body, while the ratio of being is essential, therefore the second intention of genus explained by this definition is accidentally superior to universal, but essentially inferior, as its true species.

To the form of the second argument I reply: nothing is defined by a proper definition except a species; but genus, which is the first predicable, is a species of another genus, namely of universal, which it denominates accidentally; and therefore it can properly be defined. But to what is added in the argument, that everything which is defined is defined inasmuch as it is a species, it must be replied with this distinction. “Something is defined inasmuch as it is a species”

can have a twofold sense. The first, that the ratio of species is explained through the definition; and this is false: because although man is a species, when he is defined as rational animal, yet it is not explained through such a definition that he is a species. The second sense is “to be defined inasmuch as it is a species” in such a way that to be a species is a necessary condition for a proper definition; and this is true. But nothing is explained through the definition except the proper and essential ratio of the defined, which nevertheless is accidentally denominated species by the second predicable.

## QUESTION II

Whether the proper defined of the same definition is the real nature which is denominated genus, or the second intention of genus by which it is denominated.

6

Genus considered in common can be taken in four ways. First, for the nature which is denominated genus, considered according to its essence: as if we take animal for the sensitive nature. Second, it is taken for the aggregate of the nature denominated and the second intention denominating, just as white can be taken for the aggregate of body and whiteness. Third, it is taken for the generic nature, not according to its essence, but inasmuch as it is denominated genus by the second intention of genus. Fourth, for that same second intention denominating the same nature genus. And of these four,

it is certain that the aggregate is not the defined, because it is a being per accidens, composed of two beings in act, namely of the nature and of the second intention. But a being per accidens does not have one essence but a twofold one, and therefore it cannot be explained through one definition, as Aristotle expressly teaches, Metaph. 7, text 21.

The question therefore proceeds about the three others. And there are three opinions concerning it. The first asserts that the defined of this definition is the generic nature according to its essentials, so that animal is a genus and a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, as it is a sensible living thing; and so of the other genera. This is attributed to Scotus, who, since he affirms that the nature is universal according to itself and before the operation of the intellect, seems consequently to assert that it is a genus or a species essentially. And it is proved by argument: because that is the defined to which the definition belongs; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the nature according to its essence, and not as it is denominated by the second intention; therefore that is the defined. The minor is proved, because animal, according as it is a sensible living thing, is predicated of man and lion, and not as it is denominated by the second intention: for if it were predicated in this way, when we say man is animal, then the sense would be, man is a genus. The consequence is proved: because animal, as it is denominated by the second intention, is a genus.

This opinion is neither Scotus’s, nor true, but false. The first is proved: because although Scotus asserts that there is a formal unity on the part of the thing which is the foundation of genus and species, yet he teaches that genera and species are denominations attributed to natures by the intellect; wherefore he does not hold that the real nature according to its essence is the defined. But that this opinion is false is proved by this argument. If the generic nature according to its proper essence is the defined, then according to its proper essence it is a genus, or at least to be a genus will be its proper attribute; but whatever things are essential to the generic nature, or are its proper attributes, necessarily belong to its species, as whatever things are essential to animal, or belong to it as proper attributes, are essential to horse and lion, or are their proper attributes; therefore to be a genus, or to be predicated of many differing in species, will belong to the species; which is plainly false.

The second opinion is that of Cajetan in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4, where he holds that neither the generic nature according to its essentials, nor as it is denominated by the second intention, is the defined, but the second intention. Which, however, he says can be considered in two ways. First, as That by which, that is, as the ratio of denominating the generic nature, just as whiteness is the ratio of denominating

a white body; and this is to consider it in the abstract. Second, it can be considered inasmuch as it is referred to the species: for since it is a relation of reason, it essentially regards its term; but the term of the relation of genus is the species; and therefore it can be considered in order to them; and in this way it is taken as That which, and in the concrete, and it is the proper defined of this definition, but not when taken in the first way.

Cajetan proves it by this argument. A definition must belong to the defined essentially, if it is quidditative, or as a proper attribute, if it is descriptive; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the generic nature, as to animal or to color, accidentally, even considered in common; and to the second intention in the concrete essentially, because the second intention of genus essentially regards the species, since it is a relation to them; therefore this, and not that, will be the defined.

8 This opinion too is false, which I prove. First, to be predicated of many belongs to genus in the concrete, because what is predicated of many is a concrete, just as to disperse sight belongs to white in the concrete; but this opinion does not hold that genus in the concrete is defined; therefore it is false. The minor is proved: because an accidental concrete, such as genus is, signifies the form, namely the second intention, and connotes the subject, namely the generic nature, to which it belongs to be predicated of many. If, therefore, the generic nature is not the defined, but the second intention, then genus is not defined in the concrete but in the abstract, which contradicts the words of the definition.

Second, even if the second intention of genus is considered inasmuch as it is a relation to the species, it is not a concrete but an abstract; therefore Cajetan falsely calls it a concrete. The antecedent is proved, because the concrete of relation is the relative, just as the concrete of whiteness is white; but the second intention of genus, even in order to the species, is not the relative, because it is not that which is referred but the ratio of referring; therefore it is not a concrete but an abstract.

there results one adequate and per se defined, because it is not considered as an aggregate of them, but as including the one in order to the other; and things that are ordered per se do not make something one per accidens. We have an example in this definition, Dispersive of sight. Its material defined, and as That which, is body as denominated from whiteness, because to disperse sight belongs to it; its formal defined, and as That by which, is whiteness, which is rather the ratio of dispersing sight; but from both, as ordered to each other, there results one adequate and per se defined. This opinion is followed by Javelli in his Logic, tit. 4, ch. 2, Paul of Venice in the chapter on genus, Soto in the same place, the single question, Toledo q. 1. And it seems to us more probable, and to be followed.

And it is proved by this argument. That is the defined of a definition to which the definition belongs per se; but to be predicated in quid of many differing in species belongs per se to the generic nature as denominated by the second intention of genus, and is convertible with it per se, and it cannot belong to anything else; therefore this alone can be the defined. The minor is proved: because just as it belongs per se to body, as denominated or informed by whiteness, to be dispersive of sight, so the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention, is per se predicable of many differing in species; and whatever is predicable in quid of many differing in species is the generic nature as denominated by the second intention. That it belongs per se to it alone is proved because it does not belong essentially to the same nature, as was proved against the first opinion, but can only belong to it accidentally; and it can belong to the second intention only as That by which, since this is not predicated of many differing in species, but is only the ratio of predicating. Therefore it can belong per se only to the same nature as denominated by the second intention.

For the solution of the argument of the first opinion it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predication of any predicable on the part of the predicate.

First, the formal ratio which it predicates of the subject. Second, the condition under which it is predicated of it: as when species is predicated of the individual in this predication, Peter is a man, the formal ratio which it predicates of him is the essence of man, but the condition under which it is predicated is being a species, which is to be denominated by the second intention of species, which is the relation of the species to the individuals.

From this distinction I reply to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor in this way: if in the predication of genus of species, when we say Man is an animal, the formal ratio is considered which
