animal predicates of man, it is true that it is predicated according to essence, inasmuch as it is sensible living thing; but if the condition under which it is predicated is considered, it is the second intention of genus, by which it is denominated; and therefore by reason of such a condition it belongs to it to be predicated in quid of many differing in species, and not according to essence or essential predicates, although it predicates these of the same species. And from this the sense of this proposition, Man is an animal, is understood, and of the others in which genus is predicated of species: which is not that man is a genus, but that he is a sensible living thing; for this is the formal ratio which it predicates of him, from which the sense of the proposition is to be taken, and not from the condition under which it is predicated, which is the second intention.

For the solution of Cajetan’s argument something else should be noted, namely that the material significate of genus, in the concrete signified, is twofold, as of other accidental concretes: one proximate, adequate, and per se; the other remote, inadequate, and per accidens. As the material significate of white, adequate and per se, is body; inadequate and per accidens, a wall or any other particular body: so the material significate of genus, per se, adequate, and proximate, is the generic nature in common, which is denominated genus from the second predicable; the remote, or inadequate and per accidens, is animal or color. And from this one replies to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor: for although the definition of genus belongs accidentally to animal or to color, because they are remote and per accidens material significates, yet to the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention of genus, it belongs per se and not accidentally. Just as to be dispersive of sight belongs per se to body as having whiteness; but to the second intention, even in order to several species, the definition does not belong except as That by which, as was proved by us against Cajetan.

## QUESTION III

Whether the definition of genus is quidditative or descriptive.

Two things are to be explained in order that the present question may be solved. First, of what kind the definition of genus is, quidditative or descriptive. Second, what is placed in it for its genus: universal, or predicable, or something else; and so the question is to be divided into two parts. Concerning the first there are two opinions, as it were extreme, and another in the middle.

The first extreme opinion asserts that the definition of genus is not only not quidditative or essential, but that genus can in no way

be defined by a quidditative definition. It is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 1 of the Predicables, ch. 5; Villalpando on the present chapter, who also cites Ammonius for the same view; Toledo, q. 1 on this chapter. And it is proved by this argument. Genus is an accidental concrete, including as its material the generic nature, which can be a substance or a real accident, and as its formal the second intention, which is a being of reason; but these have diverse essences; therefore they cannot be explained by one definition; wherefore genus cannot be defined by a quidditative definition.

The second extreme opinion asserts not only that genus can be defined by a quidditative definition, but that this definition of it assigned by Porphyry is quidditative. So Scotus, q. 14 and 15 on Universals, whom Cajetan follows, q. 1 on this chapter, in the solution to the first. Scotus proves it by this reasoning. Genus is considered by Porphyry in this work under the ratio of predicable, as are the other predicables too; but it is defined by being predicated of many differing in species; therefore the definition is quidditative. The consequence is proved: because predicable means the potency of predicating, and to predicate is the proper act of such a potency; but a potency is defined quidditatively through its proper act, from which it takes its essence or species; therefore genus, as predicable, is defined quidditatively.

The third opinion is the common one, which affirms two things. First, that genus can be defined quidditatively. Second, that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative but descriptive. And as regards this second point it is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 84, tract. 1, ch. 2 and 3; Albert the Great, tract. 3 of the Predicables, ch. 34; Ammonius and Villalpando in the places above; Scotus, the single question on this chapter, the last §; Toledo, q. 2; Mercado, chapter on species, fol. 16, col. 2. And this is more probable and to be followed.

The first thing it affirms, that genus can be defined quidditatively, is proved by this argument. Universal is a genus to the five predicables, as we proved in q. 8 on Universals; therefore the first predicable, which is genus, is a species of universal; but every species is composed of genus and difference as of essential parts; therefore it can be defined through them; and a definition delivered through genus and difference is quidditative; therefore genus can be defined by a quidditative definition.

It is proved second that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative: first, from his words in the present chapter, which run thus: Which those describing it also assigned, saying that genus is that which is predicated of many, and differing in species, in what it is. Next, by reason, because the predicables have two things, as we proved above. First, that they are universals, that is, one in

many; next, that they can be predicated of the same; and the first stands as their essence, the second as a proper attribute. But genus is defined by being predicated of many; therefore it is defined through a proper attribute; and a definition that is given through a proper attribute is descriptive, as if man were defined through risibility; therefore the definition of genus is descriptive.

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that the things which genus includes are diverse, but ordered among themselves: for it includes the nature as ordered to the second intention, as to a denominating form, and the second intention as ordered to the nature, as to a denominated subject; and by this they make one order, so that it can be explained by one definition.

To Scotus’s argument I reply by distinguishing the antecedent: for if it is understood that genus and the remaining predicables are considered by Porphyry as predicables in the sense that predicability is their essential ratio, it is false, for the essential ratio is rather universality. But if it is understood that they are considered as predicables in such a way that predicability is a common attribute which is proved of them, it is true; and therefore they are all defined through it as through a common attribute, which is to be defined by descriptive definitions; and all are to be reckoned such.

S E C O N D PA R T O F T H E Q U E S T I O N . 13

But supposing that the definition is descriptive, it is asked in the second part of the question: What is placed in it for its genus? And the first opinion asserts that the genus of this definition is universal, because although it is not placed there in an express word, it is nevertheless referred to by that relative, which is predicated of many: for it is the same to say, Genus is that which is predicated of many, as to say, Genus is universal. This opinion, however, cannot in the first place be defended in Porphyry, which I prove thus. Porphyry, expounding the same definition, says that by the particle predicated of many the individual is excluded; which cannot be true if universal is the genus, for it would already be excluded by that, since the individual is not universal. Next, it cannot be defended that the definition is descriptive: for if you take away the particles predicated of many and put universal in their place, the sense of the definition will be: Genus is universal in many differing in species in quid; and thus the proper attribute will be taken away; and once it is taken away, the definition will not be descriptive, against the common opinion, proved from

Porphyry and by reason.

The second opinion asserts that the genus in this definition is predi

cable, which is expressed by the words which is predicated of many: for a verb in a definition does not express act but aptitude; it is the same, therefore, to say Genus is that which is predicated of many, as if one said, that which is apt to be predicated of many; but to be apt to be predicated of many is the same as to be predicable of many; therefore predicable is placed for the genus in this definition.

14 The third opinion is the common one and to be held: that in place of the genus the generic nature is put, not indeed taken in the same way as when it is said to be the defined, but in another: for when it is the defined, it is taken together with the second intention by which it is denominated, and with which it makes one per se defined, by a unity of order; but for the genus it is put only as it is taken in common, not as ordered to the second intention. This we can explain by the example of white: when it is defined in this way, White is dispersive of sight, the defined is body as denominated from whiteness, so that from both, namely from body and whiteness, as ordered, one complete and per se defined is made; but in place of the genus body is put, taken absolutely, that is, not considered under the denomination of whiteness, nor together with it. This opinion, so explained, is followed by Ammonius, Albert the Great, and Canterus, in the places cited above. And it seems to us more probable.

15 For in the first place it is gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, On Interpretation 1, ch. 1, lect. 4, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 7, where he teaches the mode of defining accidents: in the concrete, through the subject in place of the genus; and in the abstract, through a true genus, and the subject in place of the difference: as risible, that it is man apt to laugh; but risibility, that it is the aptitude of man to laugh. And that the reason of both is this: because to be able to inhere in a subject is of the essence of an accident; but inherence in a subject is properly expressed through the same subject placed in the definition; therefore accidents are properly defined through the subject, in place of the genus if they are defined in the concrete, and in place of the difference if in the abstract.

16 Next, from this doctrine this argument is constructed to prove that opinion. Genus is defined by Porphyry in the concrete, as the words of the definition signify: That which is predicated of many differing in species in quid. For what is predicated is the concrete, not the abstract; but genus is an accidental concrete, like white; therefore it is defined through the subject in place of the genus; and the subject is the generic nature, just as the subject of whiteness is white; therefore it is defined through this nature placed in the definition in place of the genus, and the sense of the definition is: Genus is a nature which is predicated of many differing in species in quid.

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that accidents are better defined in the concrete through the subject than through the genus, because through it the aptitudinal inherence, which is of their essence, is better expressed. Hence the subject of genus, which is the nature, is more properly referred to by the relative which is predicated than universal is. And in the same way one replies to the argument of the second opinion.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether genus includes the differences and species in act, or only in potency.

17

This question is very useful for understanding the nature of genus; but for a briefer resolution of it, it should be noted that one thing can be understood to contain another in act in three ways. First, in distinct act, as a definition contains each of its parts, namely genus and difference. Second, in determinate act, but not expressed: as the species contains genus and difference, as man contains animal and rational. Third, confusedly and indeterminately: as being contains the intrinsic modes of substance and of accident, which are per se and in another; not only confusedly, but determining neither one rather than the other.

Of these three modes, first, it is certain that genus does not contain the differences in distinct act, as a definition contains genus and difference. This is proved evidently: because if animal contained rational in distinct act, we could define man through it alone, saying that man is an animal, because in animal rational too would be included in act and distinctly; and therefore such a definition would consist of genus and difference, and would therefore be sufficient, which is plainly false.

Second, it is certain that genus does not contain the differences in determinate act, even if it contains them confusedly, as animal does not contain rational as man does. This is proved because if animal contained rational and irrational in act, all the predications in which it is predicated of its species would be false, as Man is an animal, A lion is an animal: because the sense would be, man is rational and irrational, and likewise the lion, which is absurd.

The only doubt, then, can be whether genus contains the differences in indeterminate and confused act, so that it expresses no particular one rather than another, but is said to contain them all indeterminately, in a different way from that in which any species contains its difference: for man, although he does not contain rational expressly, yet contains it determinately, so that this difference

and not another is contained in it; but animal cannot contain rational and irrational in that way, because it expresses the one no more than the other, but both under the same confusion. Nevertheless it could be understood to contain them in confused and indeterminate act, according to the third mode. And it is of this mode of containing the differences in act that the question proceeds; its sense is: whether genus contains the differences in confused and indeterminate act, or only in potency, as matter contains forms only in potency.

18 And the first opinion asserts that genus contains the differences in act in this third mode. It is proved by two testimonies of Aristotle. The first is found in Phys. 1, text 4, where he speaks thus: But the universal is a certain whole, for it comprehends many things as parts. The second in Phys. 7, text 31, where he speaks of genus thus: Genus is not some one thing, but in it many things lie hidden. From which I argue thus. Genus contains many things as parts; therefore it contains them in act, because every whole contains its parts in act, since it is composed of them; but the things that genus contains in this way cannot be other than the differences and species, as is known; therefore it contains them in act, and not in potency, according to the mind of Aristotle.

Next it is proved by this reasoning. For a predication to be true, it is necessary that the whole which contains the subject contain the predicate, not only in potency but also in act; but genus is predicated of species; therefore it must contain in act whatever the species contains, namely the difference, of which together with the genus it is composed. The major is proved: because when animal is predicated of man, the sense of the predication is that man is an animal in act; which will not be true if animal expresses in act only sensitive nature: for since this is a part of man, the part will be predicated of the whole; in order, then, that it be true, animal must also contain rationality in act, and in potency is not enough, since it is predicated in act and not in potency.

The second opinion holds that genus contains the species and differences not in act but only in potency, as animal contains rational and irrational. Posterior Analytics, text 17, where he speaks thus: For let genus be supposed to be such that it is in more according to potency. But to be in more than the species is to be more universal and to contain more than the single species, that is, other species and their differences; if, then, it is in more according to potency, it will contain the species and differences only in potency. This is also the express opinion of Porphyry in the chapter on difference, where, speaking of genus, he says thus: In potency indeed it has all the differences that are under it, but in act none. And St. Thomas on the words of Aristotle cited, and opusc. 42, ch. 9, whom follow

Albert the Great, tract. 5 of the Predicables, ch. 4; Javelli, tract. 4 of the Predicables, ch. 4, before the middle; Cajetan, Soto, Banterus, Toledo, on the chapter on difference, in the exposition of the text; Mercado, the single question on this chapter. And it is true and to be held. But in order to prove it, two things should be noted. First, that genus signifies a superior grade of the nature, and difference an inferior grade, by which it is determined to constitute the species: as animal signifies the grade of sensitive nature, which is superior to the grade of rationality, which the difference rational signifies; by this it is contracted to constitute the species of man.

Second, it should be noted that genus is considered in two ways. First, as an actual part composing the species together with the difference. Second, as a potential whole, contractible by the differences: as animal is an actual part of the human species, which it composes together with the difference rational; and as a potential whole it is that which is determined by the same difference to constitute man, and by the difference of horse to constitute horse.

19 From these two notes two arguments are gathered to prove our opinion. The first is: genus signifies a grade of nature diverse from and superior to the grade which the difference signifies, and it is abstracted from the species and differences, as animal from man and horse, and consequently from rational and irrational; but that which is abstracted from its inferiors, as so abstracted, does not include them, since to be abstracted from them is to be known without them; therefore genus cannot include in act the species and differences from which it is abstracted, but only in potency.

The second argument. Genus can be considered only as an actual part of the species, or as a potential whole contractible by the differences; but in neither way does it include them in act; therefore only in potency. The minor is proved: because it does not include them in act as it is a part of the species, for one actual part does not include another, since by the very fact that it included it in act it could not compose the whole with it, as the components must be distinct and therefore not including each other; but neither as it is a potential whole can it include them except only in potency, because they are only its potestative parts, of which it is composed as such a potestative whole.

And it can be confirmed: because if genus contained the differences in act, since these are altogether diverse, as rational and irrational, it would contain in act many diverse things, and would therefore be equivocal with respect to the species of which it is predicated, or at least analogous, like being with respect to substance and accident, which it contains in confused and indeterminate act, as genus contains the differences,

according to the opposite opinion; but the consequent is false, since genus is univocal; therefore it will also be false that genus contains the differences in act.

To the testimonies of Aristotle adduced for the other opinion I reply: genus contains many things in potency, that is, species and differences, not as actual parts but as potestative ones; for just as among wholes one is actual and another potential, so among parts some are actual and others potential. The actual are those which compose an actual essence; the potential or potestative, those through which, or to constitute which, the whole is contracted or determined: for it is the same to be the parts to constitute which in act the whole is determined, and to be the parts of its potency.

20 To the argument, the major is to be denied: because it is not required for the truth of a proposition that the predicate contain in act whatever the species contains, but it is enough that it contain something in act and something in potency; for thus it will predicate a part of the species, included in the species, yet not by way of a part but of a whole; and therefore it will make true the proposition in which it is said that man is an animal, whose sense is that man includes animal, which is determined by rational to constitute him. For this is to include rational and the other differences in potency. Which is to be explained thus. Contractible or determinable means potency, and the contracting means act; but genus is contractible by the difference as by an act; therefore it is a potency with respect to the difference and to the species which it can constitute with it; wherefore it cannot contain the species and differences in act, but only in potency.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether genus is predicated of species as a whole, or also as a part of it.

Genus can be considered in three ways. First, as it expresses the generic nature abstracted from the species, as animal inasmuch as it expresses sensitive nature abstracted from man and horse; and taken in this way it is not a part but a whole, because it is signified by way of something having the nature; yet it is not an actual whole but a potential one, because it is signified as having a nature perfectible by the differences; and what is perfectible is signified as in potency to further perfection, which is to be signified as potential. In another way genus is taken as the other part of the species, composing it together with the difference; and then it is not taken as abstracted from the species,

Vt prædicatio fit vera, prædicatum debet conti- nere totum , quod continet ſubiectum , fed genus vt pars actualis , non continet aliampartem ſpeciei,quæ eſt differen- tia, actu, necpotentia, ſedbenevepotentialis : quia vtpoteſt componere ſpeciem non confideratur , vt actu coniunctum cum aliquadifferentia, fedvt poteft coniungi: quare omnes continebit in potentia : quod fatis eft, vt dicatur contine- re totum , quod continet ſpecies , nempe vnam partem astu, & alteram in potentia: prædicabitur ergo vt parspo

but only as it expresses in act their partial nature. But further, signified by way of a part, it can be taken either as an actual part, inasmuch as it is joined in act with the difference in composing the species, or as a potential part, if we consider it not as composing in act but as able to compose.

And according to these three acceptations there are three opinions. The first holds that it is predicated of the species even as an actual part. It is followed by Cajetan on the present chapter, Paul of Venice on the following chapter toward the end, and others. And they prove it first from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 4, where he teaches that the whole definition and each of its parts are predicated per se of the defined; but the parts of the definition are actual, of which one is the genus; therefore it is predicated of the species as an actual part.

21 They prove it next by reason. First, because this is the difference between the predication of genus and of species, granted by all: that the predication of species is complete, but the predication of genus incomplete; genus is therefore predicated of the species as something incomplete; but the incomplete is a part; therefore it is predicated as a part.

Second, physical parts, such as matter and form, are more distinguished among themselves and from the whole than metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, since the former are distinct things, but the latter only distinct concepts of the same thing; but physical parts, signified in the concrete, are truly predicated of the whole, when we say Man is corporeal, or is animate; therefore the metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, signified in the concrete, will all the better be predicated of the species which they compose; and so this will be true, Man is an animal, even if the genus is taken as a part; just as this too is true, Man is rational, although rational is not a potential whole but an actual part.

The second opinion affirms that genus is predicated of the species not as an actual part but as a potential part, that is, not as composing in act but as able to compose together with the difference. Canterus holds this, on the present chapter, doubt 3, and proves it by this argument. For a predication to be true, the predicate must contain the whole that the subject contains; but genus as an actual part does not contain the other part of the species, which is the difference, either in act or in potency, but it does so well as potential: because as able to compose the species it is not considered as joined in act with some difference, but as able to be joined; wherefore it will contain all of them in potency; which is enough for it to be said to contain the whole that the species contains, namely one part in act and the other in potency; it will therefore be predicated as a potential part

, not as an actual part.

22 The third opinion is that of St. Thomas, in 1, d. 15, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 3, who asserts that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a whole. His words are: If animal were not the whole that man is, it would not be predicated of him, since no part is predicated of its whole. It is followed by Boethius, in the book On Division, near the beginning; Cajetan too, although he is cited for the opposite opinion, expressly asserts in the same ch. 3 of the opusc. On Being and Essence that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a potential whole. Likewise Soto, the single question on this chapter, and Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 15, sect. 11, no. 16. And it seems to us more probable.

23 But in order to explain its foundation, it should be noted first that both genus and difference are taken from the whole specific nature, or from its whole entity, considered under diverse grades, and not from a part alone, as will be explained in the chapter on difference; yet by a diverse ratio: for genus is taken from the whole nature of the thing under a more universal and imperfect ratio, which is nevertheless perfectible through the same nature considered under the specific grade; but difference, also from the whole nature, as determined and perfect. For example: animal, as it is the genus of man, is taken from his whole nature according to the superior and imperfect grade, that is, as sensitive, determinable by the same nature of man as rational; and rational, which is the difference, is also taken from the whole nature of man, as perfect and determinate. Whence it follows that both genus and difference signify the whole nature of the species: the former under the ratio of the contractible, the latter under the ratio of the contracting.

Second, it should be noted that genus taken as a potential whole is very diverse from itself taken as an actual or potential part: for as a potential whole it expresses not only a part of the species but its whole nature, considered under a superior and more imperfect grade, and contractible through the inferior and specific grades of the differences; but as it is a part of the species, it in no way expresses the entire nature of the species, but only a part. And the reason for this difference is that genus as a potential whole is abstracted from the species by universal abstraction, because the common is abstracted from the particulars, as animal is abstracted from man and lion, as a universal from particulars; and therefore it expresses their whole nature, but under the superior sensitive grade, signifying the same as that which has a sensitive nature determinable by rational. But if the same genus is taken as a part of the species, it is not abstracted by the abstraction of the universal from particulars, but rather by the abstraction

of precision, by which a part is prescinded from the whole, as the arm from man.

24 From this doctrine a twofold argument is gathered to prove that genus is predicated of the species as a potential whole and not as a part. First: genus is predicated of the species as a universal and superior predicate abstracted from them; but the universal which is abstracted from particulars contains their whole nature, considered under a superior ratio, the inferior rationes from which it is abstracted not being considered, as is plain in the species abstracted from the individuals; therefore it is predicated of them as a potential whole, contractible by the differences, and not as a part. The consequence is proved: because a part cannot be abstracted from the whole by the abstraction of the universal from the particular, but only prescinded from it, as the arm from man; which plainly is not predicated of the whole.

Second, for any predication to be true, it is not enough that the predicate be included in the subject, for if this were enough any part would be predicated of the whole; therefore it is required that it contain whatever the subject contains. The consequence is proved from the sense of the proposition itself, by which it is signified that this is that; which cannot be true unless the predicate contains the whole that the subject contains: for if it does not contain something of the subject, it will not be true on the part of that something that this is that. And this is the reason why no part can be predicated of the whole: because by reason of the other part, which the whole expresses, it cannot be true that the whole is the part, as that man is a head. And this argument proves in the same way of physical parts, such as matter and form: because although these are not really distinguished from the whole, it is enough that they are distinguished by formal ratio, on account of the diverse mode of being and of signifying of the whole and of the part as conceived by the intellect, for them to make a false proposition.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion I reply that the parts of the definition are predicated per se of the defined, the due mode of predicating being observed, namely taken by way of a potential or an actual whole: for under the form of a part it is impossible. But for Aristotle’s intent in that passage it is enough that they are predicated in this or that way.

To the first argument of the same opinion one replies by distinguishing the antecedent. For a predicate can be incomplete on two counts: on the part of what it predicates of the subject, and from the mode in which it predicates it; and in the first sense genus is predicated incompletely of the species, because it predicates only sensitive nature, which is a part of the species; but on the part of the mode it is rather predicated completely, because it predicates the same sensitive nature

not by way of a part but by way of a whole, because by way of something having it; not indeed of an actual whole, but of a potential one, because by way of something perfectible and determinable by the differential grades.

25 To the second one replies by granting the antecedent, that a physical part signified in the concrete is predicated of the whole: because it is not signified as a part but under the ratio of a whole, since it is signified by an adjectival name; which, since it signifies by way of something adjacent, also signifies the thing by way of something having: as when we say that man is material, it is the same as if we said that he is having matter; and to be material, signified by an adjectival name, is signified by way of something adjacent, as if it were an accident of man, although it is truly a substantial part. But genus, even signified in the concrete, can be taken as a part, because it is signified by a substantive name; and taken thus it cannot be predicated of the whole according to the true sense of the proposition, by which it is said that this is that. Which cannot be true on the side on which the whole imports something else, diverse from any part per se.

To the argument of the second opinion one replies that the difference between genus as an actual part and as a potential part does not consist in this, that as an actual part it is joined to one difference only, while as potential it can be joined to all: for in both ways it regards only one determinate difference; but only in this, that as an actual part it is distinguished from itself as a potential part, because as joined in act it is considered with such a determinate difference, but as a potential part it is considered as able to be joined, not to all, but only to the same determinate difference. Hence it is false that as a potential part it contains some difference in potency, and consequently it is false that as a potential part it can be predicated of the species.

## QUESTION VI

Whether genus is separated from difference by the mode of predicating in quid.

25

The negative part, that it is not distinguished by the mode of predicating in Quid and in Quale quid, is proved from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, text 12, where he teaches that both parts of the definition, namely genus and difference, are predicated of the species in quid; and more expressly in Topics 7, ch. 2, place 31, in these words: Of those things which are in the assigned expression, this one is genus, that one difference; and genus and difference are predicated in what it is.

It is proved also by reason: because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being; but difference has a more perfect mode of being in the composition of the species than genus, since it stands as form, and genus as matter; therefore it will have a more perfect mode of predicating. But the more perfect mode of predicating is to be predicated in Quid; therefore it will be predicated in this mode rather than in Quale. I prove the minor: because the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, and the mode of predicating in quale is the mode of an accident; which it seems cannot be denied, since it is an essential predicate. Nevertheless the common opinion of Porphyry and of all his interpreters, that genus is distinguished from difference in that the former is predicated in quid, the latter in quale quid, is true and to be held. It is proved by an express testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 6, place 81, where he speaks thus: Since difference always signifies a quality of the genus, but genus does not of the difference: for he who says gressible says a certain animal; but he who says animal does not say a certain gressible thing; difference, therefore, is to be separated from genus in this way. And this mode of distinguishing these two predicables, genus and difference, by the mode of predicating in quid and in quale quid, is followed by St. Thomas, opusc. 58, tract. 1, ch. 4. It is proved next by reason: because genus is predicated of the species by way of a substance, that is, of something standing per se, of which an evident sign is that it is signified by a substantive name; but the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, which is the quiddity of the thing; therefore it is predicated in quid. But difference is predicated by way of a form, which is not the mode of a thing standing per se, but of one inhering in matter and determining and modifying it, after the likeness of a quality; therefore it is not predicated in quid but in quale; not, however, as a true quality, because it pertains to the essence of the thing; and therefore it is not predicated in quale simply, but in a certain respect and with an addition, that is, in quale quid; and in this it is distinguished from genus. For the explanation of the testimony of Aristotle adduced to prove the negative part, it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predicate of any predication. First, the thing itself that is predicated. Second, the mode in which it is conceived and signified, according to which it is attributed to the subject; and the first is as it were the material element in the predication, from which the mode of predicating that distinguishes the predicables is not taken, but from the second, in which the formal ratio of predication consists. Aristotle, then, considered both in different places: in the one whose words we adduced for the negative part he considered the first; but the mode of conceiving the predicate and of attributing it to the subject he considered in the second place, which we adduced for our opinion [p. 115] ; and therefore he distinguished genus from difference by the modes of predi‐

cating in quid and in quale; but in the other he taught that they are predicated in the same mode, which is true on the part of the thing that is predicated, considered in itself: for both difference and genus are a part of the quiddity of the species.

To the argument I reply by distinguishing the major: for the mode of being can be taken in two ways, according to itself, or as it is conceived by us; and the mode of predicating is taken from it taken in this latter way, because things are not predicated as they are on the part of the thing, but as they are known in such a way; and although according to the first consideration difference is more perfect than genus, yet in the latter way the latter has a more perfect mode of predicating than the former, by which it constitutes a distinct predicable.

## CHAPTER III

On Species.

1

Porphyry’s intent in this chapter is to explain the nature of the second predicable, which is Species. It is divided into four parts. In the first he proposes two acceptations of species: the first physical and real, from whose likeness he gathers the second, the logical. In the second he defines species by a twofold definition. In the third he sets out the categorial ordering of the category of substance, so that through it the twofold relation of species may be understood: one which it has to the genus under which it is placed, the other to the individuals of which it is predicated. In the last he defines the individual by two definitions. The first, real acceptation of species is that in which it is taken for the form and beauty of a thing. In this acceptation it is customarily said: Praestantissimam speciem dignam esse imperio [the most excellent species is worthy of rule]; that is, that the most beautiful man is worthy of rule, because beauty of body is a sign of virtue existing in the soul. And similar to this real acceptation is the logical acceptation, for species is taken for that which is placed under the assigned genus, says Porphyry, that is, under the genus already defined and explained in the preceding chapter. And the likeness of the two acceptations consists in this: that just as the form of a thing, in which beauty usually consists, includes and shows in an accidental way the essential perfection of the thing, so the species, which is placed under the genus and constituted by it together with the difference, includes in a substantial way the whole essential perfection of the thing: as the human species the whole essential perfection of man. And this is in the first part of the chapter.

In the second part Porphyry defines species, according to this logical acceptation, by a twofold definition. The first definition is this: Species is that which is subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species.

The second definition of species is: Species is that which is predicated of many differing in species in what it is. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the individuals, and as it is the second predicable; and this Porphyry does in the 2nd part. In the third he proposes the categorial order in the category of substance, which consists of these five predicates: Substance, Body, Living thing, Animal, Man. But in order that it may be understood, he says three things are to be considered in it. The first is that three things are found in it, namely: the supreme genus, which is a genus in such a way that it is not a species, as substance; the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus, as man or lion; and the intermediate genera, which are at once genera with respect to the inferior species and species with respect to the superior genus. The individuals, however, are not placed in the category as its parts, but as the foundation of all the essential predicates, of which, as of parts, the category is composed. For example: Substance is the supreme genus; Man, the lowest species. And these are as it were the extremes of the category. Animal, Living thing, and Body are called intermediate, because they are genera in such a way that they are at once species: for animal is the genus of man, the species of living thing; and therefore these are called subalternate genera, because they are genera in such a way that they are placed under another genus, with respect to which they are called species; and this is to be at once genera and species with respect to different things.

Second, it is to be considered that the supreme genera are ten, namely Substance, Quantity, Relation, Quality, Action, Passion, Where, Position, When, Having; and since these are as it were the heads of the categories, there are also ten categories; but the lowest species are finite, and in the same way the intermediate genera; but the individuals proceed to infinity, because, whatever ones are given, others and others multiply to infinity; and so they fall outside the science of the categories.

3 Third, it is to be considered that the difference between categorial ascent and descent is this: that descent takes place by the division of one into many, namely of the genus into several species through the differences; but ascent by the gathering of many into one: as when we descend from the supreme genus of substance down to the lowest species of man, we predicate by dividing it into corporeal and incorporeal substance, and this into

living and non-living, down to man. But when we ascend, we gather several species into one genus, as man, lion, and the other species of animal into one genus of animal; and so on up to the supreme genus of substance. And this

Porphyry does in the 3rd part. In the last, since he defined species as predicable through the individuals, as through the term of its relation, he explains the nature of the individual by two definitions, of which the first is: The individual is that which is predicated of one alone: as Peter of himself, in this identical predication, Peter is Peter.

The second definition: The individual is that whose collection of properties, which is in one, cannot be found in another. Which is explained thus. The specific properties, such as risibility and wonder, are common to all the individuals of the human species; and even many individual properties of any individual can belong to others; but the collection of all that are found in one cannot be found in another. For example: any individual property of Peter can belong to John, but all of them taken together cannot belong to him. Porphyry, in the whole chapter.

## QUESTION I

Whether species was defined by Porphyry with two definitions or three. 4

Concerning the number of definitions by which species was defined by

Porphyry, it is certain among all his interpreters that it was defined by at least two definitions, according to the two relations or respects which it has: one to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species, the other to the individuals, from which it is called predicable species. But whether it was defined by two only, or by three, there are different opinions.

The first is that of Soto, who asserts that it was defined by two only, so that the first, which asserts that species is that which is placed under the assigned genus, is not a definition but only the logical acceptation of species, or a bare explanation of the word. But the other, in which it is said that species is that which is subjected to the genus and of which the genus is predicated in quid, is a definition; not, however, a twofold one, but one only, because it explains the same respect: for it is the same to be subjected to the genus and for the genus to be predicated of it. And since besides this there is only another, by which species is explained as predicable, there will be only two. He proves it by this argument. Species has only two respects, one to the genus, as it is subjicible, the other to the individuals, as it is predicable; therefore it has only two formal rationes explicable by definition; and therefore it can be explained by two definitions only.

But all the others assert that it was defined by three definitions, yet they do not enumerate them in the same way. For Toledo says that only the first is an explanation of the word, but he divides the second into two, so that one is: Species is that which is subjected to the genus; and the other: Species is that of which the genus is predicated in quid; and that therefore, with the other, by which species is explained as predicable, there are three. He proves it because each explains the same respect to the genus in a different way: for it is one thing for the species to regard the genus, another for the genus to regard the species when it is predicated of it.

But Cajetan and Canterus assert that there are three definitions in such a way that the first is not only an acceptation or explanation of the word but at the same time a definition, while the second is only one, because all those words explain only one relation to the genus. And this seems to me the more probable opinion, and more in accordance with the mind of Porphyry.

5 And the first point is proved, that the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus are not only an acceptation but also a definition: because Porphyry, when he proposed the other definition, asserted thus: They assign species thus too: Species is that which is placed under the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By which words he teaches that he is assigning another definition after the first one already delivered. Moreover, before proposing the second definition, he gives the reason why, since he defined genus through species in the preceding chapter, he has now explained species through genus: because, since they are relatives, one had to be defined through the other; therefore he admits that he had already defined species before proposing the second definition; which would not be true if the first were only an acceptation and not a definition.

The second point is proved, that the first and second, by which species is defined as subjicible, are distinct definitions, by this argument. Species, as it is subjected to the genus, has two diverse formal rationes; therefore it had to be explained not by one but by two definitions. The consequence is evident, because one definition can explain only one formal ratio. The antecedent is proved: because in genus there are diverse formal rationes, to be universal, that is, one in many species, and to be predicable of them; and the ratio of universal is prior and essential to it, while the ratio of predicable is posterior, and its proper attribute; and under each ratio it regards the species; therefore in the species too diverse formal rationes must correspond, namely to be the subject in which the genus is, and to be the subject of which it is predicated; so that the former is prior and as it were essential to the species as subjicible, the latter posterior and as it were a proper

attribute of it; but those diverse formal rationes in genus are explained by diverse definitions, namely one in many species, and predicable of them; therefore the diverse rationes on the part of the species too must be explained by diverse definitions. And so it was done by Porphyry, who by the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus explained the subjicible species as it is the subject in which the genus is, but by the second as it is the subject of which it is predicated.

But that the second definition is not twofold but one is proved because the words Species is that which is subjected to the genus explain altogether the same ratio of species that had been explained by the first definition, namely to be the subject in which the genus is; wherefore they seem to be only a repetition of the first definition. But the other words, namely Of which the genus is predicated in quid, explain another formal ratio of the same subjicible species, namely to be the subject of which the genus is predicated. Porphyry therefore delivers two definitions of subjicible species, according to its two formal rationes, and a third of the same species as predicable.

6 To the argument of Soto and Toledo one replies with the same solution: for when it is said that species has only respects to the genus and to the individuals, this is to be granted; it must be said, however, that the respect to the genus has a twofold diverse formal ratio, by which it regards the genus in a diverse way, namely as the subject In which and as the subject Of which; just as the genus regards the same species by a diverse ratio, namely as the subject in which it is and of which it is predicated; therefore it had to be explained by diverse definitions.

But two very brief doubts remain. The first: for what reason Porphyry treats of subjicible species: for since this is a work on the predicables, species does not pertain to it except as predicable; but it is not predicable as it regards the genus, but the individuals; therefore it should not have been defined except with respect to them, and therefore by a single definition, and not by several. The reply is that Porphyry treats of subjicible species, first, because it is the subject of the genus, and the subject pertains to the same consideration as the predicate, because it is the term of its relation, without which it cannot be known. Second, because the subject is opposed to the predicate, and of opposites the science is the same; and therefore species had to be defined by two definitions as subjicible, because it is the subject of the genus in two formally diverse ways.

7 But concerning each of its definitions there is the second doubt: because it seems to belong to individuals, since they are placed under the assigned genus, as this or that animal under animal, and also

Peter and John, and they are subjected to the same genus, which is predicated of them in quid, as of the species. I reply that to be placed under the genus, or to be its subject, can be understood in two ways: per se, by reason of itself and immediately; and through another, by reason of something else and remotely. And in the first way it belongs to the species alone, but to the individuals only in the second way. And the reason for this is that genus descends per se and immediately to the species through the differences, but to the individuals only by reason of the species; therefore the species alone is what is placed per se and first under the genus, but the individuals only through the species. The definitions of subjicible species, then, are understood by Porphyry according to the first way, so that the sense of the first is: Species is that which is placed per se, first, and immediately under the assigned genus. And the sense of the second: Species is that which is per se, first, and immediately subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is per se, first, and immediately predicated in quid; and so the individuals are excluded, which are not so placed under the genus, nor subjected to it.

## QUESTION II

Whether subjicible species, as subjicible, is universal, or in what way these relations of species are related among themselves: universality, predicability, and subjicibility.

To understand the question, two things are to be presupposed as certain among all. First, that these two respects of species, namely predicability and subjicibility, are as it were opposed, since they belong to it with respect to diverse and as it were opposed terms: for the respect of subjicibility belongs to species in order to the superior genus, the respect of predicability in order to the inferior individuals.

Second, it is certain that the respect of predicability belongs to species as universal. This is proved because, as was proved above, universality stands as the essence of the universal, and predicability as its proper attribute; therefore it is true that species, as universal, is predicable, just as it is true that man is risible as he is rational. The question, then, is whether the respect of subjicibility also belongs to species inasmuch as it is universal.

On this there are two opinions. The first is Cajetan’s, on the present chapter, where he says that these two rationes of species, namely universality and predicability, are so connected with the third, which is subjicibility, that this stands as the essence from which those two proceed as

proper attributes. Whence it follows that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is true that man is risible inasmuch as he is man: because risibility proceeds from rationality, as a proper attribute always does from the essence.

The second opinion is that of Cardinal Toledo, q. 1 of this chapter, where he asserts: Universality is the essence of species, and from it proceed two attributes: one is predicability of many, with respect to the individuals; the other, subjicibility, with respect to the genus. From which it follows that species, as it regards the genus, is a subjicible universal, and as it regards the individuals, a predicable universal; and, to explain this opinion in a word, he says that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is universal inasmuch as it is predicable.

This is proved by a twofold argument. First: The universal (he says) is a genus to the five predicables, as animal to man and lion; therefore each predicable regards it as its proper genus, whose ratio it participates. But the species are subjicible with respect to the genus; therefore the predicables, as subjicible species, participate the generic ratio of the universal, as man and lion that of animal; wherefore, as subjicible, they are universal.

9 Second: Subjicible species, as subjicible, is not singular; therefore it is universal. The consequence is necessary, because between universal and singular there is no middle. And the antecedent is proved: because subjicible species is not a nature contracted by singular conditions, as is the nature of Peter, but abstracted from them; but an abstracted nature is common to many; therefore it is universal; and therefore inasmuch as it is subjicible it will be universal.

And this is confirmed: because subjicible species, inasmuch as it is subjicible, is common to this and that subjicible species, of which it is predicated in these predications: This subjicible species is a subjicible species, and That subjicible species is a subjicible species; therefore it is universal. The consequence is proved: because the predicable follows from the universal, as a proper attribute from the essence.

Each of these opinions is false. This is proved by this argument. Universality and predicability are respects of the nature to its inferiors, whereas subjicibility is a respect of the same to its superiors; therefore this respect is opposed to those. But one of two opposites cannot proceed from the other, as a proper attribute from the essence; therefore universality and predicability do not proceed from subjicibility, as from an essence, as Cajetan affirms, nor does subjicibility proceed from universality, as from an essence, as Toledo affirms.

The true opinion, then, affirms three things. First, that universality and predicability are not opposed respects, but are related as essence and proper attribute. This is proved because each respect has the inferiors for its term, although considered in a different way, as was explained in the preceding question.

Second, that these respects are as it were opposed to subjicibility, and therefore neither can they proceed from it, as a proper attribute from the essence, nor subjicibility from them. Both have been proved against Cajetan and Toledo.

Third, that subjicible species, as it is subjicible, is not universal but the common and proximate subject of the genus. This follows evidently from the first two, and is proved by this argument: Opposed respects cannot belong to the same thing under the same formal ratio; but universality and subjicibility are opposed respects, as has been proved; therefore they cannot belong to species under the same ratio; and therefore neither is it subjicible as universal, nor universal as subjicible.

To the first argument of the second opinion, the antecedent must be granted, that the universal is a genus to the five predicables, and also the first consequence, that they participate its nature; but it must be denied that they participate it as they are subjicible species. Rather, they participate it according to their proper essence; and from the participation there results in them accidentally the respect of subjicibility, according to which they are not universal but subjects of the genus. This is made clear by this example. Animal is the genus of man and of lion according to their proper sensitive natures, and in this way they participate its nature and are formally animals. But from this there results in them the denomination of subjicible species: an accidental one, indeed, since it is attributed to them by the intellect; and therefore, as they are subjicible species, they are not animals but subjects. By the same reasoning the predicables, according to their proper natures, participate the essence of the universal, which is their genus. But the proper nature of the predicables is to be second intentions denominating universal natures: that of the first predicable, to denominate a universal nature in many species; that of the second predicable, in many things differing in number, in quid; and so of the rest. Whence in this way they participate the nature of the universal, and are essentially universals; but the denomination of subjicible species follows on them accidentally; and therefore according to it they cannot be universal, just as neither are man and lion animals as they are subjicible species.

To the second, the antecedent must be granted, namely that

[p. 123]

species, as subjicible, is not singular; but the consequence must be denied, that it is universal: for between universal and singular there is a middle, which is the common subject, that is, the abstracted nature, common negatively, because it is appropriated to no singular, nor does it regard them, but only the genus to which it is compared and under which it is placed; whereas for it to be formally universal it is necessary that it be compared and referred to the individuals.

To the confirmation I reply that subjicible species, compared to this and that subjicible species, is not subjicible in reality but in name only, because it is not compared to the genus nor does it regard it; but it is truly predicable and universal, since it is one in many and of many. Wherefore it is not proved that, as subjicible, it is in reality universal.

From what has been said in this question three things are understood. First, that of the twofold respect of predicability and subjicibility, the second belongs to species first. The reason for this is that the first thing species has is to be composed of genus and difference; and after it has been composed of them, it is participated by the individuals; therefore it follows on its nature with respect to the genus before it does with respect to the individuals.

The second thing understood is that the respect of predicability is nobler in it than the respect of subjicibility, and therefore a nobler denomination of species follows from it. I prove this thus. The predicate is nobler than the subject, since it is its form; therefore the respect of the predicable is nobler than the respect of the subjicible. Finally, it is understood third that species, with respect to the subjicible and the predicable, is an equivocal name. This is proved: because the respects of subjicibility and predicability are opposed and altogether diverse, so that under the name of species they agree in nothing; therefore they have only a common name, which is proper to equivocals.

## QUESTION III

Whether a species can be preserved in a single individual, and a genus in a single species.

12

That the question may be more easily understood and solved, it should be noted that genus and species can be considered in three ways. First, according to their physical and real entity. Second, logically, inasmuch as genus is predicable in quid of many things differing in species, and species of several things differing in number. Third, metaphysically, inasmuch as genus is a potential whole,

contractible by opposed differences, or a part of the species, composing it with the difference. And according to the physical consideration it is certain among all that the genus can be preserved in one species, indeed in one single individual, and the species as well; and the reason for this is manifest: because the whole entity of the genus and of the species, as of animal and of man, is found in any individual whatever, as in Peter or John.

According to the logical consideration, too, it is certain that the genus is not preserved in one species, nor the species in one individual. This is proved from the definitions of each: for genus is predicable of many species, and species of many individuals; therefore each requires several for its preservation, in which they are equal. But whether the genus requires several actually existing species, and the species several individuals, or whether one in act suffices them for their preservation, provided there are several in potency: concerning species no one doubts that it can be preserved in one individual if several are possible. This is proved by evident experience: because the Sun and the Moon are logical species, and they have only one actually existing individual, yet several possible ones; therefore this will suffice for the preservation of a logical species.

13 But concerning the logical genus, Toledo asserts, in the single question of this chapter, that it cannot be preserved in one actually existing species, although several are possible, but requires several actually existing ones for its preservation. He proves it first by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 3, where he speaks thus: But since several species are to be placed under every genus, see whether it is not possible for there to be another species of the said genus: for if it is not manifest, then it will not be a genus at all. Then by reason: because the genus is contracted to the species by the difference; but the difference does not constitute the species except by distinguishing it from others; therefore the genus requires several actually existing species. The consequence is proved: because the difference does not distinguish the species from others that do not exist, but only from those that actually are.

This opinion, however, is false. This is proved by this argument. The logical genus is predicable of several things differing in species, even if it is not actually predicated, as its definition shows; but even if it is in only one actually existing species, it suffices that others be possible for it to be predicable of several; therefore it will be preserved in one if several are possible, and it does not require several actually existing. But as regards the logical consideration, the reasoning is equal concerning genus and species, so that each requires several for its preservation, not actually existing, but one in act and several in potency. Concerning the third, metaphysical, consideration, it is first certain among all concerning the genus, as it is a whole

potential, that it cannot be preserved in a single species unless others are possible. And the reason is manifest: because as it is a potential whole it is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species; therefore it requires several, at least possible ones, for its preservation.

Second, it is certain concerning the same genus, as it is an actual part of the species, that it can be preserved in one species even if several are not possible. This is proved: because as it is an actual part of the species it requires only one difference, to which it is actually conjoined; therefore for its preservation it requires only one species, which it composes with it.

But concerning the metaphysical species it is not so certain whether it can be preserved in one individual, or requires several, at least possible ones. On this there are two contrary opinions. The first is held by Oña, q. 2 of this chapter, a. 2, who affirms that genus and metaphysical species are equal: so that, just as the genus requires several species, one in act and another at least in potency, so the species cannot be preserved in one individual if several are not possible.

14 He proves this by an argument. The genus cannot be preserved in one species for this reason, that it is contractible by opposed specific differences, that is, such as cannot be in the same species, as animal by rational and irrational; but the species too is contractible by opposed individual differences, that is, ones not able to belong to the same individual, as man by the differences of Peter and of John; therefore, just as the genus cannot be preserved in one species, so the species will not be able to be preserved in one individual. But this opinion too is proved false by this argument. The metaphysical species, according to its essence, signifies only something composed of genus and difference, and is defined by genus and difference alone; but in one single individual, even if others are not possible, the composition of genus and difference can be saved; therefore the metaphysical species too will be saved, or preserved. The minor is proved: because the individual differences are outside the genus and the difference; therefore the composition of the species from genus and difference does not depend essentially on them; and therefore it will be preserved no less in one individual than in many, and consequently the species too. And this is confirmed: because it is probable that the species of the angels neither have nor can have more than a single individual; and yet no one denies that they are true species, composed of genus and difference.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First, that genus and species according to the logical consideration are equal, so that neither can the genus be preserved in one species unless others at least

[p. 126]

> fitpoſſibilis,necſpecies invno indiuiduo,nifi alterum faltem fitpoffibile:neutrum tamenpoftulareplura actu exiftentia ad fui conferuationem . are possible, nor the species in one individual unless at least another is possible; yet that neither requires several actually existing ones for its preservation.

The second thing it asserts is that genus and species according to the metaphysical consideration are not equal; but that the genus, as it is a potential whole, cannot be preserved in one species unless at least another is possible, although as it is a part of the species it can be preserved in one; whereas the species can be preserved in one individual even if no other is possible. Both of these have already been proved from the refutation of the other opinions.

15 But that the truth of the second may become more manifest, and the opposing argument be more easily solved, it should be noted that there is this difference between genus and species considered metaphysically: that the genus is a potential whole, and essentially imperfect, yet perfectible by the specific differences as by other grades of perfection, essentially distinct. As animal signifies a sensitive nature, essentially imperfect, but perfectible by rational and irrational as by diverse grades of essential perfection. Whence it follows, first, that the genus is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species. But the species is an actual and perfect whole, so that it cannot receive a further essential perfection (we are speaking of the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus); wherefore it is not contractible by essential differences which are grades of essential perfection, but is only multiplied in individuals by individual differences, which are not essential but altogether outside its essence: for they are accidental, or at most certain substantial modes. It follows, second, that the species is not essentially contractible by individual differences, but without such contraction is essentially perfect and complete; and therefore, whether it is determined by several to several individuals or by one only to one, and whether others are possible or not, it will be a species essentially perfect and complete in one no less than in many; and therefore it will be preserved in that one alone, because determination by such differences is not essential to it, but either accidental or modal, and altogether outside the essence.

16 To the testimony of Aristotle which Toledo adduced, I reply that the sense of Aristotle is that the logical genus cannot be preserved unless it is cognized by the intellect in order to several species, because it is made by the intellect only through comparison to several, nor has it any other being than to be cognized by it; yet it does not require

several existing on the part of the thing, but it is preserved in one, if others are possible.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the difference constitutes the species and distinguishes it from others, whether existing or possible:

for since specific distinction through differences is essential, it does not necessarily depend on the actual existence of the species. This is proved evidently: because the diverse species of flowers are no less distinguished in species in winter, when they do not actually exist, than while they actually are. The difference, then, can well constitute the species and distinguish it from others, even ones not actually existing but only possible.

To the argument of the second opinion, which proceeded concerning the metaphysical species, the reply has been given from the doctrine noted above. It is to be applied to its form thus: when it is said that the genus cannot be preserved in one species because it is contractible by opposed differences, the antecedent must be granted; but the minor must be distinguished: for the species is not essentially contractible by individual differences, as the genus is by specific ones; rather, the determination to individuals is outside its essence; and therefore it can be essentially preserved no less in one than in many.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the last definition of species belongs to those species which can have only one individual.

17

No specific nature is found of which it is certain that it cannot have several individuals; but concerning the angels and the heavenly bodies many are of the opinion that they are so constituted that each species neither has nor can in any way have several, but that all the angels are distinct in species and cannot be distinguished in number alone, as Peter and John. This question, then, is conditional and not absolute, and its sense is: Whether, supposing that there are some species to which it is repugnant to have several individuals, the last definition of

Porphyry belongs to them, namely that they are predicable in quid of several things differing in number.

But before we propose the probable opinions concerning it, we must refute what certain people assert without any foundation in reason: namely, that

Porphyry’s definition belongs to these species by non-repugnance. They explain this thus: although it does not belong to them to be predicable of several inasmuch as they are such species, not multipliable through several individuals, yet if they are considered under the common ratio of species, it is not repugnant to them to be predicated of many: because species, as species,

is predicable of many. That this is false is openly proved. First, because definitions ought to belong to things positively, since they explain their positive nature; but non-repugnance is only a certain negation; therefore it does not suffice for the definition to belong to them. Second, because if such non-repugnance sufficed for it to be said to belong to these species, it follows that it also belongs to any individual whatever, as to Peter or John. The consequence is proved: because although it is repugnant to him to be predicated of many inasmuch as he is a singular thing, yet if he is considered under the common ratio of man, it will not be repugnant, since man is predicable of many; therefore any individual whatever will be a predicable species, which is absurd.

18 This, then, being refuted: the first opinion is Cajetan’s, 1 p., q. 13, a. 9, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 5, and on the present chapter, doubt 3, concerning the last definition of species, who asserts that it truly belongs to these species. To explain this, he distinguishes a twofold potency in a nature toward several individuals, physical and logical. He calls physical potency the real one, which it has on the part of the thing, inasmuch as from its own principles it can be multiplied in several individuals, as human nature; but logical the one which it has only as it is understood by us. And because we understand the spiritual natures of the angels through the likeness of material species having several individuals, and we abstract them from that one individual which they have, as we abstract material natures from many, as man from Peter and John, hence it is that we attribute to them the denomination of predicable of several individuals no less than to those which have several individuals.

This opinion, so explained, is proved by the authority of Aristotle, who in the chapter on substance asserts two things. First, that second substances are genera and species, as man and animal, but first substances individuals, as Peter and John. Second, that these same second substances are predicable of the first. But the natures of the angels are genera and species: as spirit is a genus, Michael and Gabriel are species; therefore they are second substances, and consequently they will be predicable of several.

It is proved also by reason: because if the species of Michael cannot have more than that single individual of Michael, it follows that its specific and its individual difference are the same in reality, yet distinct in reason: as specific, it is distinct from itself as individual; because as specific it composes the species together with the genus, but as individual it determines the species already composed to such an individual. This supposed, the intellect will be able to consider the nature of Michael as composed of genus and difference

[p. 129]

> &differentia,vt ſpecificam, non confiderata eademdifferen tia,vtindiuiduali: & hoc erit abſtrahere naturam ab illo yno Indiuiduo. Sicautem abſtracta,prædicari poterit de illo, non prędicatione identica:qua ratione formali diſtinguiturab in-diuiduo:necprædicatione æquali , quia indiuiduum inferius eſtreſpectu ſpecici: ergo prædicatione ſuperioris de inferioris ſedprædicatio fuperioris eft prædicatio vniuerfalis:ergo præ-dicabitur prædicatione vniuerfalide fingulari : eritque verò prædicabilis de multis, cui conueniat definitio ſpeciei.Proba-turconfequentia:quia vniuerfale, & prædicabile conuettun-tur.
