Quia licèt intelligamus naturasſpirituales per ſpecies corporú,non tameniis attribuimus proprietates cof-porú eis repugnantes,fedpotiùs easremouentes abillis,intel. ligimus incorporeas effe.ergo fuppofito,quòd intelligamus nopoffehaberepluraindiuidua, ficuthabet corporegnaturæ, perquarú ſpecieseasintelligimus:împoſſibile eft,quòd eis tri-buatintellectusdenominationesvniuerfalin,autpredicabilić, I

as specific, without considering the same difference as individual; and this will be to abstract the nature from that one individual. And so abstracted it will be able to be predicated of it, not by an identical predication, by which it is distinguished from the individual by a formal ratio, nor by an equal predication, because the individual is inferior with respect to the species; therefore by the predication of a superior of an inferior. But the predication of a superior is a universal predication; therefore it will be predicated by a universal predication of the singular, and it will be truly predicable of many, so that the definition of species belongs to it. The consequence is proved: because the universal and the predicable are convertible. This opinion is followed by Canterus, on part 2 of this chapter, doubt 2, and Mercado, single question, arg. 2.

19 The second opinion is that of many moderns: that Porphyry’s definition in no way belongs to these species. And it seems to me more probable and to be held.

But in order to prove it efficaciously, one thing should be noted: namely, that we understand God and the angels through the species or likenesses of material things in such a way that from them we do not form concepts repugnant to them, but proper ones, that is, ones that belong to them alone and are convertible with them. For example, through the likeness of a bodily thing we understand God by removing imperfection from him, and therefore conceiving of him that he lacks a body and is pure spirit; and through a nature composed of genus and difference, removing from him the imperfection of composition, we understand that he is most simple. And in the same way we understand the angelic nature through the species of bodily things, forming a proper concept of it: namely, that it is incorporeal and spiritual; and through the species of material natures, which are multiplied in several individuals, we understand that the angels cannot be multiplied, according to the probable opinion of many. And this doctrine is true: because if we did not form proper and true concepts of spiritual things, although imperfect and through the alien species of bodily things, we would not truly understand them; indeed we would attribute to them many things false and repugnant to their nature.

20 From this same doctrine, then, our view is proved first against Cajetan. Because although we understand spiritual natures through the species of bodies, yet we do not attribute to them the properties of bodies that are repugnant to them; rather, removing these from them, we understand that they are incorporeal. Therefore, supposing that we understand that they cannot have several individuals, as the bodily natures through whose species we understand them have, it is impossible that the intellect should attribute to them the denominations of universals or predicables,

I

[p. 130]

> Etinhocdecipitur primò Caiet. quia putat ex eo,quòdper ſpecies rerum materialium ànobis intelliguntur , denominari ab intellectu vniuerfales,& prædicabilesde pluribus:quodnó eft verum,ficut nec verum eft,quòd intelligamus effe corpo- reas. Secundò,decipitur in fua illadiuifionepotentiæ Phyficæ & Logica: nam potentia Logica,fundamentum faltemremo- tum habere debet in natura , etiam vtà nobis intelligitur, vt vera fit,&non ficta:fed nullum habet fundamentum innatu- raangelica,etiam vtà nobis intelligitur, multiplicatioindiui- dorum,cum potius intelligamus eirepugnare:ergo nec habet potentiam Phyficam, nec Logicam, fecundum quam poffit denominatiprædicabilis de multis. Ad teftimonium Arift, pro fententia Caietani adductum, refpondentaliqui,negando, quòd naturæ Angelorum fintfe- cundæ fubftantiæ; fedhoc cotrarium eſt verbis eiufdem Arift. quoditaprobo : Quia Ariftoteles afferitexpreſſe, General fpecies,eſſeſecundasſubſtantias ſed naturæ Angelorű funtſpecies copofitæ ex genere,&differentia:ergo funtfecundæ ſubſtan-

And in this Cajetan is deceived, first, because he thinks that from the fact that they are understood by us through the species of material things, they are denominated by the intellect universal and predicable of several; which is not true, just as it is not true that we understand them to be bodily. Second, he is deceived in that division of his into physical and logical potency: for logical potency, in order to be true and not fictitious, must have at least a remote foundation in the nature, even as it is understood by us; but the multiplication of individuals has no foundation in the angelic nature, even as it is understood by us, since rather we understand it to be repugnant to it; therefore it has neither a physical nor a logical potency according to which it could be denominated predicable of many.

It is proved second: because we understand God through the species of material things, just as we do the angels; therefore, if the angelic nature is universal as so abstracted and understood by us, God too will be universal and predicable of many, which is plainly false. And if you reply that the reasoning is still different concerning God and the angels, because the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, and therefore the intention of universality can be attributed to it, whereas it cannot be attributed to God, because he lacks such composition: this solution is worth nothing, because the denomination of universal or predicable is not attributed to the species from the fact that it is composed of genus and difference, but because it is compared to several individuals. This is proved in the subalternate species, which, although they are composed of genus and difference, are not predicable species but only subjicible; therefore, although the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, it is not on that account capable of the denomination of universal or predicable; rather, that is repugnant to it, as is the multiplicity of individuals.

21 From which it follows that not every subjicible species is predicable (even if it is lowest), but that it can be subjicible and not predicable. This is evident in the subalternate species, which are not predicable but only subjicible; and in the lowest too it will be true, if plurality of individuals is repugnant to them. And the reason for it is that for a subjicible species it is enough that it be composed of genus and difference, but for one predicable of many there is necessarily required a multitude of individuals, actually existing or possible.

To the testimony of Aristotle adduced for Cajetan’s opinion, some reply by denying that the natures of the angels are second substances; but this is contrary to the words of the same Aristotle, which I prove thus: because Aristotle asserts expressly that genera and species are second substances; but the natures of the angels are species composed of genus and difference; therefore they are second substances

[p. 131]

> tia.Continent etiam prædicata fuperiora , & fpiritualia acci dentia ſuſtentant: &ideò dicuntureis fubſtare , non minùs quam ſpecies materiales: nec folùm prout fingulares funt , aut primæ fubftantiæ , fed etiam,vt funtſpecies: ergo negari non poteſt in doctrina Arift.quòd fint fecundæ fubftantiæ. Concedendum eſt ergo ,quod tales ſpecies fint fecunda ſubſtantie:negandum verò,quòd eis non conueniat vniuerfa-lis proprietas,aflignata ab Ariftotele , neimpe , quòd de primis prædicentur:namhæcproprietas fingulis ſpeciebus applican-da eft,iuxta earumnaturam, itavt fiplures habuerintprimas ſubſtantias , de omnibus prædicentur, fi vnani tantum, folùm de illa: quod fatis eſt adveritatemvniuerfalis locutionis,vide-licet, proprium eſt ſecundis ſubſtantiis prædicari de primis. 22 Alarg.concedendum eft, quamlibetharumfpecierum abftrahi poffe, à ſuo indiuiduo , negandum tamen , quòd fic abstractæ, poffit ei attribui relatio rationis,per quam fitprædi cabilis demultis , nam idemmet intellectus eam abftrahens, præfupponit ei repugnare plura indiuidua. Nec ſequitur, Quòd intellectus eam abſtrahatper ſpecies rerum materia-lium, quibus abſtrahitalias naturas, pluraindiuidua haben-tes,ergo ficuthas denominat vniuerfalis, fic illas.Nam ex eo, quòdper tales ſpeciesrerum materialium eas intelligit, non formateundem conceptum earum, ac materialium rerum,fed diuerfum,iuxta naturam cuiufcunque ita vthas intelligateffe multiplicabiles inpluribus indiuiduis , illas verò ad vnicum effedeterminatas. De quo conceditius , prædicari poffe, non prædicatione identica, nec prædicatione fuperioris,ſed æqua-lis, admodum,quo differentia vltima prædicaturdeſuaſpecie Etratio huius eft:quiafuppofito, quòd natura Michaelis non poteſthabere plura indiuidua, folùm dicit ordinem ad ynam differentiam indiuidualem, etiam fiabilla abſtrahatur ideo non magis coarctatur per illam :fedquomodocunque accipia tur, cum ea conuertitur. Talis autem prædicatio, eiufdem fpe. ciei de ſuo indiuiduo,licèt fumilis fit prædicationi vltimæ , dif-ferentiæ, de ſita ſpecie, ratione æqualitatis, ſed prædicatur in Quis, tanquam totum actuale, & completum, ad fecundum prædicabile potius reducenda eft. Speciesigitur , quibus repu-gnatpluralitas indiuiduorum fubiicibiles tantum funt:quibus conueniunt duæ definitiones aſſignatæ à Porphyrio : nam ſpecies Michaelis,fubiiciturſuo generi proximo, quod eſt ſpi-ritus,& etiam remoto , quod eſt ſubſtantia corporeaautſpiri-tualis: fednon fant ſpecies prædicabiles : ideò non conuenis eis vltima definitio. Ii

They also contain the superior predicates and sustain spiritual accidents, and therefore they are said to stand under them, no less than the material species; and not only as they are singular, or first substances, but also as they are species; therefore it cannot be denied in Aristotle’s doctrine that they are second substances.

It must be granted, then, that such species are second substances; but it must be denied that the universal property assigned by Aristotle does not belong to them, namely that they are predicated of the first: for this property is to be applied to the single species according to their nature, so that if they have several first substances they are predicated of all of them, and if only one, then of that one alone; which is enough for the truth of the universal statement, namely: It is proper to second substances to be predicated of the first.

22 To the argument, it must be granted that any one of these species can be abstracted from its individual; but it must be denied that, so abstracted, a relation of reason can be attributed to it through which it would be predicable of many: for the very intellect that abstracts it presupposes that several individuals are repugnant to it. Nor does it follow: The intellect abstracts it through the species of material things by which it abstracts other natures having several individuals; therefore, just as it denominates those universal, so too these. For from the fact that it understands them through such species of material things, it does not form the same concept of them as of material things, but a different one, according to the nature of each: so that it understands the former to be multipliable in several individuals, but the latter to be determined to a single one. Of which we grant that it can be predicated, not by an identical predication, nor by the predication of a superior, but by an equal one, in the way in which the last difference is predicated of its species. And the reason for this is that, supposing that the nature of Michael cannot have several individuals, it signifies an order only to one individual difference, even if it is abstracted from it; and therefore it is not further narrowed by it, but in whatever way it is taken it is convertible with it. Such a predication, however, of the same species of its individual, although it is similar to the predication of the last difference of its species by reason of equality, yet, because it is predicated in quid as an actual and complete whole, is rather to be reduced to the second predicable. The species, then, to which plurality of individuals is repugnant are only subjicible; and to them belong the two definitions assigned by Porphyry: for the species of Michael is subjected to its proximate genus, which is spirit, and also to its remote one, which is substance, corporeal or spiritual; but they are not predicable species; therefore the last definition does not belong to them.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether species is distinguished from genus by those particles of its definition, “to be predicated of several things differing in number.” 23

This question took its occasion from Porphyry, who in the chapter on genus taught that species is distinguished from genus, because genus is predicated of several things differing in species, but species of several things differing in number. But in the present chapter, and also in the last of this book, he grants that genus too is predicated of several things differing in number:

because, since it is a superior predicate with respect to the species, as animal with respect to man, it must be predicated of whatever things the species is predicated of. Wherefore it does not seem that it can be excluded from the last definition of species by those particles, to be predicated of several things differing in number; nor is there any other by which it is excluded. And therefore it will not be a good definition, because it does not distinguish the second predicable from the first.

The first opinion, then, is that of Albert the Great, in the treatise on the

Predicables, ch. 1, who asserts that species is distinguished from genus by those particles (to be predicated of several things differing in number), because they are understood by Porphyry in this sense: that species is predicated of the individuals through itself and immediately, but genus not through itself or immediately, but by means of the species. And the reason for this opinion is that species is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore through itself participates the nature of the genus; but the individuals are not per se composed of genus and difference, but only participate the nature of the genus because they participate the nature of the species in which they are contained: for Peter is an animal for this reason, that he is an individual of the human species, composed of sensitive and rational nature.

This exposition is proved false by two arguments. First: Genus is predicated of the individuals through itself, or immediately; therefore species is not distinguished from it by this. The antecedent is proved: in these predications, This animal is an animal, This living thing is a living thing, which are truly immediate, and not in name only: for the predicate signifies the sensitive nature in common, and the subject the same nature singularized; but between the nature taken in common and in the singular there can be no middle; therefore the genus is predicated immediately of the individuals.

24 Second, because individuals can be considered in two ways. First, as they are on the part of the thing; and thus there is none that is not contained under some species and by means of it participates the generic nature; and therefore they are called individuals of a species, as Peter

[p. 133]

> trus,& Ioannes, fub his nominibus. Alio modo,inquantum concipiunturab intellectu, ſub gradu naturæ fuperioris , non confideratogradu ſpecifico: quem reueraparticipant,vt fi Pe- erus confideretur ſub gradu naturæ fenfitiuæ,non confiderato gradu rationali,quem participat ab ſpecie humana,in qua ac- ceptione fignificatur nominehuius animalis.Etindiuiduahoc modo confiderata,vocanturgenerica : quia formaliter,&im- mediatè fignificant,& participant naturam genericam. Vnde ſequitur , quòd licètdeindiuiduis ſpecificis prædicetur genus media ſpecie , degenericis tamenper feipfum& immediate prædicatur: quaredum prædicatur de indiuiduis , hoc modo confideratis,non diftingueturab ſpecie. Propterea tertiaopinio tenet,Non diftingui per illas mate rialiter confideratas,ſed formaliter;hoc eſt,ſub tali modo pre-dicandi ſpeciei proprio:quia ſpecies prædicatur de indiuiduis, complete,hoc eft,vt totum actuale,& completum, prædicans deillis totam effentiam : genus verò prædicatur incomplete, quialicèt per modum totius potentialis prædicetur, tamen folùm prædicat partem : vt animal non prædicattotamna-turam Petri , fed folum ſenſitiuam, quæ pars illius eſt. Er hocmodo intelligidebet Porphyrius,dumdiftinguit ſpeciem

and John, under these names. In another way, inasmuch as they are conceived by the intellect under the grade of the superior nature, without considering the specific grade which they really participate: as if Peter is considered under the grade of sensitive nature, without considering the rational grade which he participates from the human species; in which acceptation he is signified by the name this animal. And individuals considered in this way are called generic, because they formally and immediately signify and participate the generic nature. Whence it follows that, although the genus is predicated of the specific individuals by means of the species, yet of the generic ones it is predicated through itself and immediately; wherefore, when it is predicated of individuals considered in this way, it will not be distinguished from the species.

Therefore the second opinion, that of Avicenna, granting that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals, asserts that those words of the definition (which is predicated of several things differing in number) are to be understood with a twofold limitation, so that by them species may be distinguished from genus: namely, of those which are distinct in number alone, and of those only, and not of others which are distinguished by more than number. Whence, since genus is predicated not of individuals only but also of species, it is excluded from the definition of species by those words so expounded.

But this opinion too is insufficient. This is proved first: because, just as a definition must belong to the thing defined positively, and not only through negation, so too it must distinguish it from others by a positive difference, and not by negation alone; because negation alone cannot be a difference distinguishing species; but to be predicated of individuals, and not of others more diverse, is a pure negation; therefore it cannot distinguish the second predicable from the first.

25 Second: if it is once granted that genus is predicated immediately of individuals, as species is, even if it is predicated of species, it does not follow that it is not a species, but that it is not only a species but also a genus, since the definition of each belongs to it; therefore it is not distinguished from species by those particles.

For this reason a third opinion holds that it is not distinguished by them considered materially, but formally, that is, under such a mode of predicating as is proper to species: because species is predicated of the individuals completely, that is, as an actual and complete whole, predicating of them the whole essence; but genus is predicated incompletely, because, although it is predicated by way of a potential whole, yet it predicates only a part: as animal does not predicate the whole nature of Peter, but only the sensitive nature, which is a part of it. And in this way Porphyry is to be understood when he distinguishes species

Prímò : Cùm genus prædicatur immediate de indiuiduisge-neris , concipitur natura generica, vt immediatè participata ab eifdem indiuiduis: ergo vtimmediatè contracta per dif-ferentias indiuiduales fibi proprias : fed immediate contra-hi perdifferentias indiuiduales , conuenit fpeciei, & non ge-neri, vtgenus eft : ergo in his prædicationibus , non habet modum generis , ſed ſpeciei. Probaturminor ; quia genus vtgenus,noncontrahitur immediatèperdifferentias indiui- 4

from genus by to be predicated of several things differing in number.

This opinion too is proved false by an argument ad hominem, taken from what it grants: namely, that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals of the genus, as animal of this and that animal. This supposed, I argue thus: Animal is predicated per se and immediately of this and that animal; therefore the sensitive nature is taken in these predications as immediately participated by them, and not by means of some species. But genus is not taken as a potential and incomplete whole, contractible by differences, except inasmuch as it descends through them to the species; therefore neither is it predicated incompletely except of the species, or of individuals with the species as means. Therefore it is impossible for it to be predicated immediately of the individuals and to be predicated incompletely. Wherefore neither can it be distinguished from species by an incomplete mode of predicating of the individuals.

27 These opinions being refuted, ours is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself and immediately as genus, but by way of species; and therefore such predications pertain not to the first predicable but to the second. This conclusion is first to be explained, then proved. It is explained in this way: Genus is not predicated through itself or immediately except of generic individuals, as animal of this and that animal; and in these predications the generic nature is signified as immediately participated by the individuals, and not by means of some species; wherefore it is not considered as contractible by essential differences, and therefore not as imperfect and incomplete, but as complete from genus and difference, immediately determined to the individuals by individual differences proper to it and not to another inferior nature, which are proper to the lowest species. Whence in these same immediate predications it is formally taken by way of a lowest species, and not as a genus; nor is it predicated with the predication of a genus, but as a species and with the predication of a species.

28 The conclusion so explained is proved by a twofold argument. First: When genus is predicated immediately of the individuals of the genus, the generic nature is conceived as immediately participated by those same individuals; therefore as immediately contracted by individual differences proper to it. But to be immediately contracted by individual differences belongs to species, and not to genus as it is genus; therefore in these predications it does not have the mode of a genus, but of a species. The minor is proved: because genus, as genus, is not contracted immediately by individual

[p. 135]

> duales,ſed ſpecificas : ergo dum formaliter concipitur in eif-dem prædicationibus, tanquam contractum immediatè per differentias indiuiduales propriæ naturæ,non concipitur tan-quamgenus:fed permodum ſpeciei.. Secundò: Id quod concipiturtanquamimmediatè contra- Etum, per differentias indiuiduales concipitur, vt quid iam cópletum in fua natura: fed animal in hacprædicatione,Hoc animal eft animal, confideratur,vt immediate contractum,per differentias indiuiduales eiufdem naturæ fenfitiuç:ergo figni-ficaturvtquid completumin fua natura, compofita ex genere, &differentias; nempe ex viuenti , & fenfibili : & ideo non vt incompletum,neque vt genus, fed per modum ſpeciei. Talia autem indiuidua ita confideratata, non exiftunt à parterei,ſed formaliter accipiuntur ab intelle- Etu,tub gradu naturæ fuperioris, &generica . QUÆSTIO VI . Andeturuna ratio communis, atque realis indiuiduorum, qua definiatur per fecundam definitionem indiuidui . E Indiuiduo agit Porphyrius cap. prætenti , quia eft Dterminus relationis ſpeciei,per quem definira eſt ſpecia

differences, but by specific ones; therefore, when in these same predications it is formally conceived as contracted immediately by individual differences of its proper nature, it is not conceived as a genus, but by way of a species.

Second: That which is conceived as immediately contracted by individual differences is conceived as something already complete in its nature; but animal in this predication, This animal is an animal, is considered as immediately contracted by individual differences of the same sensitive nature; therefore it is signified as something complete in its nature, composed of genus and differences, namely of living and sensible; and therefore not as incomplete, nor as a genus, but by way of a species.

The second conclusion: Genus as genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself, but through the species. This is manifest enough, supposing the preceding one: for if genus is not predicated immediately of the individuals as genus, but by way of species, it follows that when it is predicated of them as genus it is not predicated through itself and immediately, but through the species, and also in a different mode from the species: because by way of a potential and contractible whole they predicate only a part of the essence, whereas species is predicated as a complete and perfect whole. And from these things it is understood that genus was well excluded by Porphyry from the definition of species by those particles, which is predicated of several things differing in number, understood by him in such a way that species is predicated of the individuals per se and not through another, and also completely, whereas neither can belong to genus as it is genus.

29 To the form of the argument of the first opinion I reply that species alone is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore species alone per se participates the nature of the genus as it is genus, but the individuals by means of the species; but the same generic nature, as it is considered immediately contracted to its proper individuals, is also immediately participated by them, yet not under the ratio of genus but of species, to which it belongs to be immediately contracted by individual differences. Such individuals, however, so considered, do not exist on the part of the thing, but are formally taken by the intellect under the grade of the superior and generic nature.

QUESTION VI. Whether there is one common and real ratio of individuals which is defined by the second definition of the individual.

Of the individual Porphyry treats in the present chapter because it is the term of the relation of species, through which species

I iiij

[p. 136]

> es vltimadefinitione: & ideo ex eius notitia dependet notitia ſpeciei. Sed duplicidefinitionedefiniuit indiuiduum. Prima, Inquantum eft pradicabiledeuno, per terminos fecunde intentio- nis:&propterea fecundo intentionaliter intelligitur talis de- finitio ab expoſitoribus, Secundam verò tradidit, per proprie- tates reales, dicens,Indiuiduum eſſe, cuius collectio proprietatem queinunofunt,inalio reperirinonpoffunt: quare hæc velutifun- damentumprimæ,& ideoprius eſt ànobis examinanda,quàm illa.Etquiadefinitio quæcunque explicaredebet aliquamra- tionem communem omnibus,quæ fub definito continentur. vt definitio hominis , rationem hominis communem omni- bushominibus,quærittitulus quæſtionis,An per hanc defini- tionem Indiuidui, definiatur aliqua ratio realis communis omnibus' indiuiduis . 30 Eteſt primaopinio Soti , quæftione vnicahujus capitis, infolutionead ſecundum afferentis, Nihil dari reale , quod omnibus indiuiduis fit commune, &perhanc definitionem explicetur:ſeddefinitum Formale, & vt Quo , effe fecundam intentionem indiuidui,Materiale verò, & vtQuod reale In- diuiduum non ſecundùm eſſe commune omnibus , fed vtde. nominatur à ſecundaintentione, ficut indefinitione generis diximus, definiri naturam genericam,proutdenominatur à fecunda intentione. Habet autemhæc opinioduo argumenta,quibus probatur nihildari reale communeomnibus indiuiduis , quod definiri poffit, Primum,Quia indiuidua duo habent : Vnum eſtparti- :     cipatio naturæ ſpecificæ, fub qua vniuocè conueniunt, vtPe- trus,& Ioannes,in eo quòd vterque eſt homo. fed communis hæc ratio, ſpecifica eft, &non indiuidualis : quare non poteft eſſedefinitumhuius definitionis,fed per definitionem potius ſpeciei explicatur.Alterum quodhabent, eſtdifferentia indi- uidualis,propria atque diſtincta,per quam contrahiturnatura ſpecifica& fit fingularis; & per hanc differentiam conftituun- turin ratione fingularium,aut indiuiduorum , & diftinguun- turinterſe.Gratia exempli,Petrus habet naturam humanam, perquam eſthomo,&conuenit cum Ioanne,&differentiam indiuidualem , perquameſttalis homo fingularis , &diſtin- guituràIoanne,&fub prima ratione, certum eſtnon definiri, quiafub eaconfideratus,non eſt ſingularis, fed fub fecunda. Sedfub ratione fingularium , non poffunt conuenire indiui- dua:ergo nihilrealedatur eis commune,quod definiatur Mi- norem ficprobo:differentiæ indiuidualesfunt primò diuerfæ, &perquasvltimòdiftinguunturindiuidua: ergo rationeilla

is defined in the last definition; and therefore knowledge of species depends on knowledge of it. And he defined the individual by a twofold definition. The first, inasmuch as it is predicable of one, through terms of second intention; and for this reason such a definition is understood by the expositors in the manner of second intention. The second he delivered through real properties, saying that the individual is that whose collection of properties, which are in one, cannot be found in another. Wherefore this is as it were the foundation of the first, and therefore it is to be examined by us before that one. And because any definition whatever ought to explain some ratio common to all things contained under the thing defined, as the definition of man explains the ratio of man common to all men, the title of the question asks whether by this definition of the individual some real ratio common to all individuals is defined.

30 And the first opinion is Soto’s, in the single question of this chapter, in the solution to the second, who asserts that nothing real is given which is common to all individuals and is explained by this definition; but that the formal thing defined, and as that by which, is the second intention of the individual, while the material, and as that which, is the real individual, not according as it is common to all, but as it is denominated by the second intention; just as we said in the definition of genus that the generic nature is defined as it is denominated by the second intention.

This opinion has two arguments by which it is proved that nothing real is given common to all individuals that can be defined. First: because individuals have two things. One is the participation of the specific nature, under which they agree univocally, as Peter and John in that each is a man; but this common ratio is specific and not individual; wherefore it cannot be the thing defined by this definition, but is rather explained by the definition of species. The other thing they have is the individual difference, proper and distinct, by which the specific nature is contracted and becomes singular; and through this difference they are constituted in the ratio of singulars, or individuals, and are distinguished among themselves. For example, Peter has the human nature, through which he is a man and agrees with John, and the individual difference, through which he is such a singular man and is distinguished from John; and under the first ratio it is certain that he is not defined, because considered under it he is not singular, but under the second. But under the ratio of singulars individuals cannot agree; therefore nothing real is given common to them which is defined. I prove the minor thus: the individual differences are primarily diverse, and are those by which individuals are ultimately distinguished; therefore by reason of them

[p. 137]

> rumnonpoffunt conuenire : quare nihil reale commune ha-berepoffunt, quoddefiniatur, ficut inquantum diuerfa funt, non poffuntconuenire. 31 Secundum,Singularia vt diſtincta funt, propriis,ac diuer-fis nominibus ſignificantur, vt Petrus ,& Ioannes : ergo fub propria,&vltimaratione fingularitatis non conueniunt. Pro-baturconſequentia:quia fifub ea conuenirent per alias diffe-rentias indiuidualesdeberentdiftingui,quarumratione con-uenire etiam poffent , fi ratione earum, quas modò habent, conueniunt:& tunc per alias differentias diftinguerentur, das retúrqueproceſſfus in infinitum. Etam à Petro,& foanne,ac cæteris:fequiturſpecies etiamrea-les atomas , vtdistintas, habere conuenientiam realem vni-uocam :ita vt ab homine & equo non folùm vt conueniunt in animali, fed etiam,vtfunt ſpecies diſtinctæ per rationale , & irrationale, poffitabſtrahi vnus conceptus realis eis commu-nis & vniuocus; quodpatet eſſefalfum. 32 Secunda opinio affirmat, Dari aliquid reale commune, & vniuocumindiuiduis,quod per hancdefinitionem Porphytij definiatur.Hæc eft D.Th.1.par.qu.30.art.4 Caie.ca.præf.& 1.part.q.29.art.1.&Canteri in expoſitionehuius definitionis &ca,de ſubſtantia,in expofitione definitionisprimæ ſubſtan-tiæ,quam ſequuntur plures moderni. Et mihi videtur proba-bilior. Sed duo funt probanda, aduerfus primam opinionem , vt maiorprobabilitas ſecundæ conftet. Primum eft ,quòd non definiaturfecundaintentio, velnatura indiuidui, vtab eade-nominatur.Secundum.quoddefiniatur aliquid rea'e, Probaturprimum,Quia omnia verba in definitione pofita, ſignificant proprietates reales indiuidui , per quarum colle tionem diftinguitur vnum ab altero:nam licèt in multis conuenire poffint, tamen quodlibet habet aliquam fibi pro-priam, diuerfam à propriis aliorum : vnde collectio , quæ ex communibus, &propria conftat, diſtincta eſt in fingulis, & per illamdiftinguuntur:ergo collectio,per quam definiturin-diuiduum,conftat ex proprietatibus realibus,vt reales funt,& nou vedenominantur à lecunda intentione. Probatur confe-quentia: quia indiuiduum conftituitur per, proprietates rea-les,ante operationem intellectus:ergo fine vllo ordine ad fe-cundamintentionem, Probatur fecundum,dupliciratione,Primo: Definitiohee,

they cannot agree; wherefore they can have nothing real in common which is defined, just as, inasmuch as they are diverse, they cannot agree.

31 Second: Singulars, as they are distinct, are signified by proper and diverse names, as Peter and John; therefore under the proper and ultimate ratio of singularity they do not agree. The consequence is proved: because if they agreed under it, they would have to be distinguished by other individual differences, by reason of which they could also agree, if they agree by reason of those which they now have; and then they would be distinguished by other differences, and there would be a process to infinity.

And the argument can be confirmed in this way: if individuals, as individuals, are real and have a univocal agreement, as abstracted from Peter and John and the rest, it follows that the real atomic species too, as distinct, have a real univocal agreement: so that from man and horse, not only as they agree in animal but also as they are species distinct by rational and irrational, one real concept common to them and univocal could be abstracted; which is plainly false.

32 The second opinion affirms that something real is given, common and univocal to individuals, which is defined by this definition of Porphyry. This is the opinion of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 30, a. 4; of Cajetan, on the present chapter and on 1 p., q. 29, a. 1; and of Canterus, in the exposition of this definition and in the chapter on substance, in the exposition of the definition of first substance; and many moderns follow it. And it seems to me more probable.

But two things are to be proved against the first opinion, so that the greater probability of the second may be established. The first is that what is defined is not the second intention, or the nature of the individual as it is denominated by it. The second, that something real is defined.

The first is proved: because all the words placed in the definition signify real properties of the individual, through whose collection one is distinguished from another: for although they can agree in many, yet each has some property proper to itself, diverse from the proper ones of the others; whence the collection, which consists of common properties and a proper one, is distinct in each, and by it they are distinguished. Therefore the collection by which the individual is defined consists of real properties, as they are real, and not as they are denominated by second intention. The consequence is proved: because the individual is constituted by real properties before the operation of the intellect; therefore without any order to second intention.

The second is proved by a twofold argument. First: This definition,

[p. 138]

> cominunis eft omnibus indiuiduis fubftantiæ , quæ per cam definiuntur: ergo aliquid commune definitur peream, non fola vox : quia æquiuocum eflet, quòd definiretur , vt canis, quod conftatnon poffe definiri; ergo definitur aliquid com-mune,per vocem fignificatum, vt reale: vt probatum eft,nem-pe,ratio indiuiduationis realis in concreto . 33 Secundò:A quacunque conuenientia reali vniuoca, ab-ftrahi poteft conceptus realis vniuocustled indiuidua conue-niuntvniuocè in modo particulari eflendi: ergo talis modus abſtrahi poteft ab eis,vtin eo æqualiter conueniunt,poterunt definiri. Probatur minor: quia æquè conuenit Petro,& Ioan -ni,modus particularis effendi, per quemdeterminatur natura humana, vt fit fingularis in vtroque. Hoc autem commune definitur, & confirmari poteſt hocmodo : Syllogifmus ifte conftituitur inDarij: Omne indiuiduum eft incomudicabile : Petrus eftindiuiduum:ergo eft incommunicabilis:fedfi nihil commune datur indiuiduis , ſequitureſſe vitiofum : ergo di-cendum eſt, aliquid reale commune eis dari. Probatur minor: quia medium erit æquiuocum,nempe indiuiduum,nihil com. mune indiuiduis fignificans prætervocem . 34 Pro folutione argumentorum notandum eft,Tribus mo-dis confiderari poffe indiuidua. Primo,in quantum conueniût innatura ſpecifica:vt Petrus,&Ioannes,in natura humana: ra-tione cuius conuenientiæ, quilibet vocaturhomo,& concep-tus ifte non eft indiuiduorum, vt indiuidua funt : fed concep-tusſpeciei.Secundo modo confi lerantur, vt funtparticulares : acdeterminati homines,per proprias differétias indiuiduales : & ifte conceptus,non eft naturæ, fed indiuiduationis. Quem adhuc dupliciter cófideramus, primò , vt talisindiuidui eſt,no-mineparticulari,&proprio fignificati,Petri, aut Ioannis. Se-cundo,vteſt rei fingularis, &indiuiduæ, non determinando hancdifferentiam indiuidualem, Petri aut Ioannis : fed diffe-rentiam indiuidualem,vt fic,abftrahendo à determinatis , Pe-tri & Ioannis : & fecundum primam confiderationem , nihil comune habere poffunt: in ſecunda verò, comunis eſt eis con ceptus indiuidui,vt fic,per quem fignificatur differentia indi-uidualis,& nă aliqua determinata,& in concreto indiuiduum fub ratione indiuidui,non determinando hoc,vel illud . 35 Vnde fequitur, Conceptum communem,quem indiuidua habere dicimus,non effe conceptum rei,autnaturæ fed con-ceptum modi determinantis naturam : & fub tali conceptu definiti indiuiduum in hac definitione. Ad primum arg. Conceffa maiori,negatur minor, quod

is common to all the individuals of substance, which are defined by it; therefore something common is defined by it, not the word alone: because what was defined would be equivocal, as canis [dog], which, it is agreed, cannot be defined; therefore something common is defined, signified by the word, as real: as has been proved, namely the ratio of real individuation in the concrete.

33 Second: From any real univocal agreement whatever a real univocal concept can be abstracted; but individuals agree univocally in a particular mode of being; therefore such a mode can be abstracted from them, and, as they agree equally in it, they can be defined. The minor is proved: because the particular mode of being, by which human nature is determined so as to be singular in each, belongs equally to Peter and to John. And this common thing is defined. And it can be confirmed in this way: this syllogism is constituted in Darii: Every individual is incommunicable; Peter is an individual; therefore he is incommunicable. But if nothing common is given to individuals, it follows that it is faulty; therefore it must be said that something real common to them is given. The minor is proved: because the middle, namely individual, will be equivocal, signifying nothing common to the individuals besides the word.

34 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that individuals can be considered in three ways. First, inasmuch as they agree in the specific nature, as Peter and John in human nature; by reason of which agreement each is called a man; and this concept is not of the individuals as they are individuals, but the concept of the species. In the second way they are considered as they are particular and determinate men through their proper individual differences; and this concept is not of the nature but of individuation. This we consider further in two ways. First, as it is of such an individual, signified by a particular and proper name, of Peter or of John. Second, as it is of a singular and individual thing, not determining this individual difference of Peter or of John, but the individual difference as such, abstracting from the determinate ones of Peter and of John. And according to the first consideration they can have nothing in common; but in the second the concept of the individual as such is common to them, by which is signified the individual difference, and not some determinate one, and in the concrete the individual under the ratio of individual, not determining this or that one.

35 Whence it follows that the common concept which we say individuals have is not a concept of the thing or of the nature, but a concept of the mode determining the nature; and under such a concept the individual is defined in this definition.

To the first argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, that

[p. 139]

> indiuidua vt indiuiduafunt,nihil commune haberepoflint, nam licètdifferentiæ indiuiduales fintprimò diuerſæ, & vt ta-lesnihil propriis rationibus communehaberepoffint : tamen inofficioconueniunt, nempe, indeterminando naturam ſpe-cificam, ad particularem modum eſſendi : quod eft confti-tuere eam in indiuiduo; licèt quælibet fecundum propriam rationem , conftituat indiuiduum determinatum ac diuer-fum. Adfecundum refpondetur: Diftinguendo confequens:nem-pe,fingulariafub vltima ratione fingularitatis,non conuenire. Nampropriæ fingularitates Petri ,& Ioannis , duobus modis confideraripoffunt.Primo,vt fingularitates funt. Secundo , vt tales fingularitates. Et fiprimo modo confiderentur, conue-niunt : quia commune eſt eis officium fingularizandi natu-ram:fi verò fecundo modo , conuenire non poffunt. Necda-tur proceſſus in infinitum : quia fub illa ratione communi, confiderata indiuidua , non diftinguunturperalias differen-tias indiuiduales fedper eafdem , confideratas fub vltima ra-tione particulari , ac determinata : quibus hoc modo fumptis, nihil communedatur: & ideo neceft neceffarium , per alias differentias diftingui. 36.Et quod de indiuidualibus differentiisdicimus,deſpeci-ficis intelligendum eft: quælicèt fecundum proprias rationes, non conueniantin aliquo,ſed fintprimo diuerfa :vtrationale, &hinnibile:tamen in officio diuidendi genus,& conftituendi ſpeciem conueniunt. Quam conuenientiam definiunt Por-phyrius cap.dedifferentia,dicens: Differentia eft,qua diuiditge-nus, & constitui fpeciem.Et conuenientiahec ſpecierum, vtper differentias ſpecificas conftituuntur, etiam eft modalis : quia non eft ratione naturæ differențiarum,fed folum ratione offi-cij conftituendiſpeciem; & ideo non eſtmedia inter proximu genus,& fpecies,fed natura generis proximè deſcenditadfpe-cies , per differentias licèt differentiæ ipfæ, & fpecies , per eas modaliter conueniant,vt expofitum eft.Si autem inquiras,Ad quod præ licabile pertineat indiuiduum reale,fub hac ratione communi,fub qua definitur: Refpondet Caiet,ſpeciale prædi cabile, diftinctum àcæteris,pro eo effe ponendum:quia habet modum prędicandi diſtinctum:non enim predicaturin Quid, neq; in Quale quid,ſedin cuiufmodi: neceftprædicatumAc-cidentale,fed Subſtantiale, Dicendumtamen eft : Non pofle ſpeciale prædicabile conftituere: quia non eftprædicatum na turæ,autalicuius gradus eſſentialis eius, fed mod: ſubſlatialis, eiufdem nature ſpecificæ: & ideo ad prædicabileſpecicireduci

individuals, as they are individuals, can have nothing in common. For although the individual differences are primarily diverse, and as such can have nothing in common by their proper rationes, yet they agree in function, namely in determining the specific nature to a particular mode of being, which is to constitute it in an individual; although each, according to its proper ratio, constitutes a determinate and diverse individual.

To the second the reply is by distinguishing the consequent, namely that singulars do not agree under the ultimate ratio of singularity. For the proper singularities of Peter and of John can be considered in two ways. First, as they are singularities. Second, as they are such singularities. And if they are considered in the first way, they agree, because the function of singularizing the nature is common to them; but if in the second way, they cannot agree. Nor is there a process to infinity: because individuals considered under that common ratio are not distinguished by other individual differences, but by the same ones considered under the ultimate particular and determinate ratio; and to these, taken in this way, nothing common is given; and therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished by other differences.

36 And what we say of the individual differences is to be understood of the specific ones: which, although according to their proper rationes they do not agree in anything but are primarily diverse, as rational and able to neigh, yet agree in the function of dividing the genus and constituting the species. This agreement Porphyry defines in the chapter on difference, saying: Difference is that which divides the genus and constitutes the species. And this agreement of the species, as they are constituted by specific differences, is also modal: because it is not by reason of the nature of the differences, but only by reason of the function of constituting the species; and therefore it is not a middle between the proximate genus and the species, but the nature of the genus descends proximately to the species through the differences, although the differences themselves, and the species through them, agree modally, as has been expounded. But if you ask to which predicable the real individual belongs under this common ratio under which it is defined, Cajetan replies that a special predicable, distinct from the others, must be posited for it, because it has a distinct mode of predicating: for it is predicated neither in quid nor in quale quid, but in cuiusmodi; nor is it an accidental predicate, but a substantial one. It must be said, however, that it cannot constitute a special predicable, because it is not a predicate of the nature, or of any essential grade of it, but of a substantial mode of the same specific nature; and therefore it ought to be reduced to the predicable of species

[p. 140]

Definitum quod, eſſe naturam genericam,vt denominata àſecunda intentione generis, & definitum ,quo:

on account of its very great similarity with it: because it is predicated of several things differing in number, substantially.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the second intention of the Individual, defined by the first definition of the

Individual, is one. 37

This question presupposes one thing and asks another. What it presupposes is that the second intention of the Individual considered in common, that is, abstracted from this and that second intention of the Individual denominating Peter and John, predicable of one, is the thing defined by the first definition of the Individual: namely, The Individual is that which is predicated of one. What it asks is whether it is one, that is, whether it has one common and univocal ratio with respect to the second intentions denominating the particular Individuals.

But what it presupposes seems false, as these arguments prove. First: The second intention of the Individual, considered in common, is predicated of this and that second intention of the Individual denominating Peter and John; therefore it is predicable of many. But the definition asserts that the Individual is predicable of one; therefore it cannot belong to it; rather, the definition of species will belong to it, since it is predicated in quid of several things differing in number.

Second, it is proved that it is not one, from which it is also gathered that it is not the thing defined: because the thing defined must be one, that is, univocal with respect to all to which the definition belongs; but not every individual is predicated of one, but some of several; therefore the second intention of the

Individual, which is their ratio of predicating, will not have one common univocal ratio with respect to all. The consequence is evident: because from that which is predicated of one, and from another which is predicated of several, a common ratio of predicating of one, to which this definition belongs, cannot be abstracted. The antecedent is likewise proved: because the vague Individual, as some man, is predicated univocally of several, as of Peter and John; and the

Individual by demonstration, as this white thing, is predicated of the same; therefore one second intention of the Individual will be the ratio of predicating of one, but another the ratio of predicating of many.

38 For the solutions of this question it should be noted that, just as we said in the definition of genus that the defined is twofold, That by which and That which: the defined That which is the generic nature as denominated by the second intention of genus, and the defined That by which,

the same second intention, as denominating the nature; and that from both, so ordered, there comes to be one total and complete defined. Moreover, that both the defined That which and the defined That by which are twofold: Adequate and Proximate, and Inadequate and Remote; so that the generic nature taken in common is the adequate and proximate defined, while the remote and inadequate defined is any particular generic nature whatever, as animal or color; and that the adequate and proximate defined That by which is the second intention of genus taken in common, while the inadequate and remote is the particular intention denominating animal or color. So now it must be said that the proximate and adequate defined That which is the nature of the Individual taken in common, as it is denominated by the second intention, predicable of one; and the inadequate and remote, any Individual in particular. And that the adequate and proximate defined That by which is the second intention of the Individual taken in common, as it is the ratio denominating the Individual in common, predicable of one; while the remote and inadequate is any intention of the individual whatever denominating Peter and John, predicable of one. And from both defineds, That by which and That which, as ordered to each other, there comes to be one complete and adequate defined, which is explained by the definition: which belongs to the defined as That which, to the nature of the individual as denominated by the second intention, predicable of one; and to the second intention, as denominating that same nature.

39 From which a single conclusion is gathered, by which we answer the question, and it is this: The second intention of the Individual taken in common, as it is the ratio denominating the nature of the individual, also taken in common, is one and univocal; and it is also the formal defined of this definition, just as the denominated nature of the individual is one and is the material defined. Both are proved by this argument: The second intention of the Individual equally denominates every Individual predicable of one; and the nature of the Individual in common is equally denominated by it; therefore each is univocal and, in its own way, the defined of this definition.

For the solution of the first argument it should be noted that the second intention of the Individual in common can be considered in two ways: as That by which, and as That which. The first consideration is formal, because it is considered as the form denominating the nature of the individual, predicable of one. The second is material, because it is considered as that which is predicated of many, namely of the second intentions of the Individuals. Hence according to the first consideration only does it pertain to the present definition, as its formal defined; but according to the other, to the predicable species

[p. 142]

> ciei pertinet:quia prædicaturde pluribus differentibus nume- ro , in Quid : pertinet quidem, non propriè,fedreductiuè, & impropriè: quia ficutindiuiduum quodcunque, non prædica- turprædicatione propria , pertinente ad artem, & fcientiam, fedimpropriiflima, & quæ vocatur identica, & naturalis : ita fecunda intentio indiuidui, tanquam incompletum quid , & impropriè , prædicaturde hac & illa fecunda intentioneIndi- uidui: & ideò folùm per quandam fimilitudinem denomina- tar,àfecunda intentione ſpeciei,ficut naturæ completæ,deno- minanturpropriè. because it is predicated of many differing in number in quid. It does pertain to it, but not properly; rather reductively and improperly: because, just as any individual whatever is not predicated with a proper predication pertaining to the art and science, but with a most improper one, which is called identical and natural, so the second intention of the individual, as an incomplete quid, is also predicated improperly of this and that second intention of the Individual; and therefore they are denominated by the second intention of species only through a certain likeness, whereas complete natures are denominated by it properly. The argument, however, proceeds of the second intention of the Individual considered materially, and therefore proves nothing against our conclusion.

40 To the second I reply that by this definition not every Individual whatever is defined, but the proper and determinate one, which is predicated of one, that is, of itself, with an identical predication; and therefore the formal defined is nothing but the proper second intention of the Individual, which is the ratio of predicating of one. Of the vague individual, however, some assert that it is not defined by this definition because it is complex, as some man. Others say that it is not defined because it signifies nothing determinate, but a vague something that extends itself to all the singulars of the same nature, determining none. But both are false. The first, because Some or A certain are certain signs that do not signify a thing distinct from the noun to which they are joined, but a particular mode of being, which is the individual difference by which it is denominated; but the thing determined by the mode is one and the same; therefore the vague Individual, or the demonstrative one, is a simple thing, and the noun by which it is signified is incomplex, although in word it seems complex: as some man signifies human nature singularized, without signifying the ultimate rationes of the singulars by which it is distinguished into diverse individuals. But that this thing is determinate, or a determinate concept, is manifest, although it does not determine some individual of which it is verified in the proposition, but it suffices that it be verified in one or another. From which it is plain that the second is false. Wherefore it must be said that the vague Individual is not properly an Individual, since it is predicated of many, and therefore does not pertain to the present definition.

to follow that the Individual is in no way predicated, and consequently not of one either, as is said in the definition: the reply is that predication is twofold. One proper and doctrinal, whose predicate is in some way diverse from the subject.

The other improper and not apt for doctrine or science, but as it were natural, in which predicate and subject are the same. When, therefore, Aristotle asserted that of first substance, or of the individual, there is no predication, he is speaking of doctrinal predication, and does not exclude the natural or identical, of which this definition of Porphyry is understood: The Individual is that which is predicated of one alone.

C H A P T E R I V.

On Difference.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

But difference is said commonly, and properly, and most properly, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T. 1

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of the third predicable, which is Difference. And the chapter is divided into two parts, in the first of which he divides Difference by five divisions; in the second he defines it by five other definitions.

The first division is: one Difference is Common, another Proper, and another

Most proper. Common difference is that by which some things differ by a common accident, as the whiteness of Peter is a common difference, by which Peter, white, differs from John, black. Proper difference is that by which some things differ by an inseparable accident, as the whiteness of the swan, through which it differs from the raven. Most proper difference, finally, is called that by which some things are distinguished in species, as rational, through which man differs from the lion.

The second division of difference is according to its proper office, which is to make diverse, and it runs thus: some Difference makes diverse per se, as the essential; another makes diverse per accidens, as the accidental. This division is no less universal than the preceding, although it has only two members, because under its second member are contained two members of the first, namely common and proper difference.

By the third division Difference is likewise divided, according to its whole latitude, into Separable and Inseparable, so that under the second member are comprehended common and proper difference. For separable difference is that by which some things differ by a separable accident, as the whiteness of a wall; inseparable, however,

[p. 144]

that by which they differ inseparably, as by rationality or risibility.

The fourth division is of inseparable Difference into Inseparable per se, as rational, and Inseparable per accidens, as the whiteness of the swan; and it is less universal than the preceding ones, because it is a subdivision of one member of the third division, namely of inseparable difference; and it contains only two members of the first, namely proper difference and most proper.

The last division is: one Difference is that which divides the genus, another that which constitutes the species. He gives the example in animal, whose constitutive difference is sensitive, while its divisive one is rational. And this division comprehends less than the preceding, since it is a certain subdivision of one of its members, namely of inseparable difference per se. And both of its members can belong to the same difference, yet not by the same ratio, nor with respect to the same thing, but to diverse things: for rational can exercise both offices, since it is a difference divisive of animal and constitutive of man.

2 In the second part of the chapter he defines difference by five definitions, of which the first is this: Difference is that by which the species exceeds the genus, as man exceeds animal: because, besides its sensitive nature, it contains the rational, which is not contained in act in the same animal. And he asserts that this difference has its being not from itself nor from nothing, but from the genus itself, in whose potency it is contained, and is educed by the intellect from its potency and attributed to the species, so that the species may be composed of it together with the genus.

The second definition is this: Difference is that which is predicated of many differing in species in quale quid. Porphyry proves that difference is predicated in quale quid: because to a question put concerning the species through What we properly answer by the Genus, but to a question put through Of what sort, no less properly by the Difference. As, if it is asked, What is man? we properly answer that he is an animal; but if What sort of animal?, we no less properly say that he is rational. Therefore Genus is predicated in quid, but Difference in quale; not, however, absolutely, because it is not an accidental quality but an essential part of the species; and therefore it is predicated in quale with quid added, so as to denote that it is predicated in essential quale.

The third definition is: Difference separates those things that agree under the same genus, as rational separates man from the lion, with which he agrees in animal.

The fourth definition: Difference is that by which singular things differ from one another, as by rational man differs from the lion. For Difference constitutes the Species and separates it from the others.

The last definition seems more proper than the preceding ones, because it explains its chief act. For he says: Difference contributes to the substance of the thing, and is a part of its essence and definition. Rational has both: for it contributes, that is, it helps per se, to the substance of man; and since it composes him together with animal, it is a true part of his essence, and indeed the last, so that by this it is distinguished from the Genus. By these five definitions Porphyry defines only most proper Difference, because this alone is essential, and this alone pertains to the third predicable.

## QUESTION I

Whether the first division of Difference into Common, Proper, and Most proper is sufficient.

In two ways a Division can be understood to be insufficient: either because some member is lacking to it, or because it contains another that is superfluous. And this division of Difference is proved insufficient in both ways. And first, that it contains some members which are not contained under the divided, by this argument: The divided of this division is the third predicable; but common and proper Difference do not pertain to the third predicable but to the fifth; therefore they are not contained under the divided. The minor is proved: because common and proper Difference are separable and inseparable accident; but these pertain to the fifth predicable, as is known; therefore they cannot pertain to this division.

But that other members are lacking to it is proved by two other arguments. First, because the individual Difference, by which one Individual differs from another, is neither common nor proper, since it is not an accident; nor is it most proper; therefore it is not contained under any member of the division, but another must be added for it. That it is not most proper is proved: because most proper Difference is specific, as Porphyry expressly teaches in the same division; but the individual is not specific, as is known; therefore neither is it most proper Difference.

Second: the proper attributes of species, such as risibility, make those same species differ by an inseparable accident; and yet they are not proper differences; therefore they do not pertain to this division. The consequence is evident, because they cannot pertain to the two other members, since they are neither separable accidents nor specific Differences. The minor is likewise proved: because proper Differences, as Porphyry asserts in the explanation of the fourth division, admit of more and less, which is plainly established to belong to the proper attributes of species.

It must nevertheless be held that this Division is sufficient. This is proved not only by the authority of Porphyry and of all the expositors, but by this argument: A sufficient division is that to which no member is lacking, and which has nothing that is not contained under the divided; but this one is such; therefore it is sufficient. The minor will be proved from the solution of the arguments. And to the first, by which it was proved that common and proper difference do not pertain to this division, the minor must be distinguished: for common and proper Difference can be considered in two ways. First, as they are certain accidents; and in this way they pertain to the fourth or fifth predicable. Second, as they make one thing differ from another by a separable or inseparable accident; and in this way they pertain to this Division, whose divided is not the third predicable but something more universal, namely Difference according to its common ratio, as related to the essential and the accidental; but the third predicable is constituted by the most proper alone. The others, however, are explained so that from their rationes most proper Difference may become more manifest; hence they do not pertain to two predicables, but to one only, although in this third one they are brought in for the easier understanding of it.

Concerning the individual Difference, from which the first argument of the other side proceeds, certain moderns assert that it is essential, because the individual can neither be nor be understood without it; and if this is true, it will be most proper difference. But it is proved false by this argument: Those predicates alone are called essential which are taken from some grade of the essence itself, as rational from the grade of rationality, and sensitive from the grade of sensing; but the individual Difference is not taken from any grade of the essence; therefore it is not essential. The minor is proved: because the last grade of the essence or nature is the last Difference, by which the last species is constituted; but the individual Difference determines the last species already constituted by the last Difference; therefore it cannot be essential, but is outside the essence of the individual.

6 And so it must be held that it is rather a substantial mode, outside the essence or nature which it determines and constitutes as singular or individual; and therefore it is not most proper Difference, but on account of the likeness it has with specific difference it is reduced to most proper Difference. But that the individual can neither be nor be understood without it does not prove that it is essential, but only that it is an intrinsic mode determining the nature or essence: for in relatives it is known that one cannot be nor be understood without the other, as a father

without a son, and yet the one is not of the essence of the other.

Concerning, finally, the properties of species, the first opinion is that of Soto, Mercado, and Canterus, in their exposition of the text, who assert that they do not pertain to this division. Toledo too seems to hold this, in his explanation of this division. And their argument is: because Porphyry, speaking of proper difference, always gives examples in the properties of Individuals, by which individuals differ by an inseparable accident. And in the fourth division he calls proper Differences Inseparable per accidens, which does not belong to the proper attributes of species, which are rather inseparable per se.

Others, however, affirm that the proper attributes of species are to be reduced to most proper Difference, because Porphyry, in the 4th division, gave the example of Differences inseparable per se (which are plainly most proper) in proper attributes, as in the capacity for learning; therefore he holds them to be most proper differences.

The common opinion, however, which is also true, asserts two things. First, that the attributes of species properly pertain to this Division, against the first opinion. Second, that they are not most proper differences but proper ones, and are therefore placed in the second member of the division, against the second. The first is proved by this argument: the properties of individuals are proper differences for this reason, that they make individuals differ by an inseparable accident; but the properties of species make those same species differ by an inseparable accident; therefore they are proper differences.

7 The second, that they are not most proper, is proved by the testimony of Porphyry and by reason. For Porphyry in the second Division speaks thus: Universally, then, every difference added to something makes it altered; but those which are common and proper make it altered, while those which are most proper make it other. But the proper attribute of a species makes it altered, and not other; therefore, in the mind of Porphyry, it is not most proper Difference, but proper. The first is proved: because the altered is the accidentally diverse, since alteration is a motion concerning Quality; but the proper attribute of a species is a true accident and a true quality, as risibility; therefore it makes altered. The second is proved: because that is other than another which differs from it in essence or nature; but a proper attribute does not make one species differ from another in essence or nature, but by a certain proper accident; therefore it is not most proper difference. It is proved also by reason: because most proper Difference is the greatest of all, since it effects the greatest difference, namely the essential and specific; but a proper attribute does not make an essential Difference between species; therefore it is not the greatest Difference, nor will it be most proper Difference.

To the last argument, therefore, the minor must be denied, namely that the proper attributes of species are not proper Differences; and what

Porphyry asserts, that proper Differences admit of more and less, he does not understand of all of them, but of those which belong to individuals, in which he gave his examples, rather than in the proper attributes of species, because they are commonly better known to us.

## QUESTION II

Whether the Division of difference into Common, Proper, and Most proper is of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into analogates.

3

That the difficulty of the question may be understood, it must be supposed, as certain among all, that the members of this Division do not agree in the word alone, as the significates of an equivocal name agree, but also in some way in the thing signified, which is to be Differences by which one thing differs from another: for this concept of making to differ is common to them. Whence it is certain among all that the Division is not equivocal. But whether it is Univocal or Analogous, in this consists the difficulty of the question.

Its solution depends chiefly on another, namely, whether the Division is taken really, that is, for the real differences that make one thing differ from another before the operation of the intellect, or for second intentions, or for the real differences not as they are real but as they are denominated by second intentions; and therefore this must be determined first of all.

On this there are two opinions. The first holds that the Division is not taken for the real differences as they are real, but for the same as they are denominated by second intentions, or for those second intentions themselves as they denominate them, in the same way as Genus and Species in their definitions. This is Cajetan’s, on the present chapter, whom some of the more recent follow.

It is proved by this argument: Because if it were taken for the real differences, its members would coincide, so that the same Difference would be

Common, Proper, and Most proper, and therefore there would be no division. The antecedent is proved: because the difference of whiteness is common with respect to a wall, proper with respect to the swan, and most proper with respect to itself.

It is proved, second: Because the divided of this Division is Difference considered formally and in common, and the members are particular differences, also taken formally; but Difference taken formally is a being of reason, as are Genus and Species;

therefore the Division is to be taken for second intentions.

9 The second opinion is the common one: that the division is taken neither for second intentions nor for the differences as they are denominated by second intentions, but for the same differences according to their real acts of making to differ. So hold Avicenna, Albert the Great, Soto, and many moderns, on the present chapter. And to me it seems the more probable opinion.

It is proved by the testimony of Porphyry and by reason. The words of Porphyry are: Difference which, joined to something, makes it diverse from another: one is Common, another Proper, another Most proper. But to be joined to something and to make it diverse from another does not belong to second intentions, nor to the differences as they are denominated by them, but to the real acts of making one thing differ really from another; therefore they are taken really in the Division by Porphyry, and not for second intentions.

10 The argument from reason is this: these Differences can be taken as they are predicable, or as they make one thing differ from another. And in the first consideration they do not pertain to the third predicable, but to the fourth and fifth, since they are predicated in accidental quale, and not in quale quid; but in the second they cannot be taken as they are denominated by second intentions, because the act of making one thing differ from another is real, and belongs to them before the operation of the intellect, indeed without any dependence on the intellect: as is plain in whiteness, which without dependence on the intellect makes a white man differ from a black one; therefore this Division cannot be taken for second intentions.

To the first argument I reply that the members of a good Division can coincide in the same thing, provided they are distinguished by a formal ratio: which is plain in the Division of the Good into the Virtuous, the Useful, and the Pleasant, whose members coincide really in virtue; but it is enough that their formal rationes be distinguished, because the ratio of virtuousness is one, that of usefulness another, and that of pleasantness another, in the same virtue. So, then, common, proper, and most proper Difference coincide in the same thing, but always have distinct formal rationes: because the ratio of the same difference of whiteness as it is a Common difference is one, and as it is proper or most proper another.

11 To the second, the major must be distinguished: because the formal ratio of Difference is twofold. One is the ratio of the predicable, the other the ratio of making to differ. When, therefore, it is said that Difference in this Division is taken formally, if the sense is of the formal ratio of predicating, the antecedent is false; but if of the formal ratio of making to differ, it is true; but then the minor must be denied, namely that Difference

considered in this way is formally a being of reason: for it is rather real, through the real act of making one thing differ from another.

This being now supposed, we must treat of the other point, which is principally asked: whether the Division is univocal or Analogous. And the first opinion is that of those who hold that the Division is taken for second intentions, and that it is therefore a Univocal Division of a genus into species, so that Difference in common, as it is denominated by the second intention, is a Genus with respect to Common, Proper, and Most proper Difference, considered as they too are denominated by second intentions.

They prove it from Porphyry, who in the text calls the members of this Division three species of Difference; he holds, therefore, that it is divided as a genus into its species.

Next, by reason: because, although, if the Division is taken really, its members cannot agree univocally, since most proper Difference alone makes to differ simply, while the others do so only in a certain respect, because they make to differ only accidentally; nevertheless, as they are denominated by the second intention of Difference, the ratio of Difference belongs to them equally: just as the ratio of Genus, for the second intention, belongs equally to the genera of substance and of accident.

12 The second opinion is that of all the others, who have held that this Division is taken really by Porphyry, and consequently have asserted that it is of an analogous term into analogates: which Cajetan also holds, although he thinks it is taken for second intentions. And this is the more probable opinion.

We assert, then, two things. The first is that the Division, taken really, is of an analogous term into analogates, which the authors of both opinions grant. And it is evidently proved: because things that differ substantially differ simply, while things that differ accidentally differ in a certain respect; but most proper Difference alone makes to differ substantially, while the two others do so only accidentally; therefore in the ratio of making to differ really they cannot agree univocally, but only analogically.

Second, we assert that, even if the Division is taken for second intentions, or for the differences as they are denominated by them, it is not of a Genus into Species but of an analogous term into analogates, as Cajetan asserted. This is proved by this argument: The members of this division are considered either under the ratio of the predicable or under the ratio of making to differ; and in the first consideration Common and Proper do not pertain to the third Predicable, because they are not predicated in quale quid, but to the fourth and fifth, since
