they are predicated in accidental quale, proper or common. And certainly, if in the ratio of the predicable Difference in common were a Genus and the members were Species, they would be distinguished in species in the ratio of the predicable; and therefore two or three predicables of Difference would have to be multiplied. In the second consideration, however, they are not denominated by second intentions, because to make to differ by a proper or common accident does not depend on the intellect, but is a real act belonging to them before the operation of the intellect; in which they cannot agree univocally with most proper Difference, because these do not make to differ except in a certain respect, and by attribution to most proper Difference, which alone makes to differ substantially and simply; therefore it is repugnant that the members of this Division should have a univocal agreement. But even if, in the ratio of making to differ, they were denominated by second intentions, they could not agree univocally. It is proved: Because to make to differ, taken in common, is Analogous, since it belongs first and per se to most proper Difference, which makes to differ substantially, and only in a certain respect to the others, which make to differ accidentally; therefore neither can the second intentions denominating these members agree univocally. The consequence is proved: Because one is the ratio of making to differ simply, another that of making to differ in a certain respect; therefore, just as to make to differ in common is Analogous, so too the ratio of making to differ in common will be Analogous.

13 To the testimony of Porphyry for the other opinion I easily reply that he called the members of this division three species of Difference, that is, three modes of difference, not speaking properly of Species but by likeness.

To the argument: the antecedent must be denied in the part where it says that the members of this Division, as they are denominated by second intentions, agree Univocally: because they are not even denominated by them, since in the ratio of making to differ they do not depend on the intellect; and even if they were denominated, they could not be denominated Univocally: because the concept of making to differ, however much it is abstracted, cannot be participated equally by those which make to differ only accidentally and by that which makes to differ substantially; just as the concept of being cannot be abstracted without being participated in a diverse mode by being simply, which is substance, and by being in a certain respect, which is accident.

and color the ratio of Genus belongs univocally, because they are equally denominated by the second intention, although, taken really, they can have nothing univocal in common. I reply that the ratio is diverse for Genera and for differences taken under the ratio of making to differ: because the Genera of Substance and of

Accident are in many species in the same mode, and are predicated of them in quid; and therefore the denomination of Universal and of Genus by the second intention is univocal to them. But for substantial and accidental differences the ratio of making to differ cannot be univocal, but is always unequal: because it is participated simply by the Most proper, as by the substantial, and in a certain respect by the others, as by the accidental ones; just as the ratio of Being is participated by

Substance and Accident. Whence, however much it is abstracted, or considered in order to second intentions, it always brings inequality and Analogy with it.

## QUESTION III

Whether it is true that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form, and how it is to be understood.

15

These expressions, Genus is taken from matter and difference is taken from form, are used by Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 9, where he says: The definitive ratio signifies something of something, and it must be that this one is as matter, and that one as form. And the whole school took them from him, especially St. Thomas in the opusc. On

Being and Essence, ch. 7 and 9, and 1 p., q. 85, a. 5, ad 3.

But they are proved false by this argument: There are many things in which true Genera and true differences are found which cannot be taken from matter nor from form; therefore these expressions are not universally true. The antecedent is proved: In Angels there is, or can be, a specific distinction; therefore a true Genus and a true Difference; but they do not have matter or form from which these might be taken, since they are spiritual and simple substances, that is, not composed of matter and form; therefore it is not true that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form.

The whole difficulty of this question consists in explaining these expressions:

for from their explanation it will be established in what sense they are true. Now there are three things in which Genus and Difference are found, namely Corporeal

Substances, Spiritual Substances, and Accidents; therefore it must be explained of each, in the same order, how and from what Genus and Difference are taken in them.

16 And first, of Corporeal Substances, in which, in order that the truth of these expressions may be understood, three things are to be noted. The first is

that the composition of the species from Genus and Difference is not Physical but Metaphysical; and therefore it is not from things but from concepts: not, indeed, from formal ones, because formal concepts are Qualities and accidents inhering in the intellect, but from objective ones, which are represented through the formal ones. As the composition of man is not from the formal concepts of Animal and Rational existing in the intellect, but from the grades of the Sensitive and Rational nature, which are represented through them. Whence Genus and Difference are not diverse things, even partial ones, as matter and form are; nor is some third thing, distinct from each, composed of them, as from matter and form there is composed a certain third Physical thing, distinct really from each, though not from both taken together and united; but Genus and Difference are diverse objective concepts of the same thing, and the species composed of them is not a thing distinct from both, nor from either of them, but a certain total and complete objective concept, composed of the concepts of Genus and Difference.

17 Second, it should be noted that the concept of Genus and that of Difference are so related that the former is potential and imperfect, yet determinable and perfectible by the concept of the Difference; and the concept of the Difference has the mode of an act, determining and contracting it. Whence it follows that Genus is taken from a more imperfect grade of the nature, and Difference from a more perfect one. And because the root of all potentiality in material things is matter, which in its essence has no act, but is pure potency determinable by form as by its proper act; and the root of all actuality is form, by which matter is determined to such a Species: therefore it was said by Aristotle, Genus is taken from matter and difference from form; which he understood only in material things, in which the Metaphysical composition from Genus and Difference presupposes, as its foundation, the Physical composition from matter and form.

Third, the difference must be noted which St. Thomas lays down in the place cited above between Matter and Form on the one side, and Genus and Difference on the other: namely, that the former have only the mode and office of parts, and therefore are never predicated of the whole (for it is never true that man is soul or body); but Genus and Difference have both with respect to the species, namely the ratio of whole and of part. And the reason of this is that they exercise two offices with respect to it, those of Predicates or Universals, and of Parts: for each, taken by itself, is predicated of the Species, and of the same, as of parts concurring together, it is composed. Whence, since to compose is the office of a part, and on the other

[p. 154]

side nothing is predicated of another formally by way of a part, but by way of a whole, it follows that Genus and Difference, as they compose the species, have the mode of a part; and as they are predicated of it, the mode of a whole: Genus, indeed, the mode of a potential whole, but Difference the mode of an actual whole; so that Genus includes its own grade of the imperfect nature in act, but the Difference only in potency; and the Difference includes both grades in act, but the generic one as it were presupposed and as the material, and its own as the formal: as Animal includes the grade of the sensitive nature in act and that of the rational in potency; but rational includes the grade of the sensitive nature as the material and as it were presupposed, but the grade of the rational nature formally.

18 Lastly, it should be noted that the composition of the Species can be considered in two ways: in Becoming and in Having-been-made; or more clearly, while it is being made, or when it has already been made. And if it is considered in Becoming, it is true that the Species is composed of Genus as it is formally genus, that is, as a potential whole, and of Difference as an actual whole; but in Having-been-made it is not composed of Genus as it is genus, nor of Difference as it is difference, but of the generic and differential Nature, as of parts. And the reason of this is that, although Genus at the beginning of the composition is also a potential whole, yet when it is already conjoined in act with the Difference, it is restricted and determined, so that as such it does not extend itself to other species. In this it differs from Matter, which even while it is conjoined to one form has potency to others; but Genus, as already conjoined in act to one difference, does not have potency to others. And the reason of this difference is that the potency of Matter to all forms is natural, and therefore is not lost by conjunction with one form or another; but the potency of Genus comes to it from this, that it is conceived by the intellect in such a way, namely by way of something having, but imperfect and perfectible by another, which is to be conceived as a potential whole; but when it is conjoined in act by the intellect with the Difference, it is conceived in another way: not by way of something having, but by way of something actually composing this determinate Species and pertaining to its nature, with which it is the same, because animal in man is Man. Whence, as so conceived in a limited way, it does not have potency to be conjoined with the Difference of Lion. Thus the potency of genus came to it only from this, that it was conceived by way of a contractible whole; but when it is now considered as conjoined in act with the Difference, the same mode of conceiving does not remain, but it is conceived in another, diverse way; therefore the same potency does not remain. Which, however, remains in matter, because matter has it from nature, and nature does not vary.

19 From this whole doctrine two conclusions follow, by which we answer the first part of the question. The first conclusion is: In material things the first root of all potentiality is Matter, and the first root of all actuality is form. The second conclusion: And therefore it is true that in them Genus is taken formally from the whole nature itself as it is conceived under an imperfect grade, perfectible through the Difference, but radically from Matter; and that difference is likewise taken formally from the whole nature as conceived under a perfect grade, but radically from form. The first part is known per se in Physical things; wherefore it needs no proof. The second is proved: because the proper and formal ratio of the Metaphysical Genus is to be a potential whole, contractible by opposed differences; and the proper ratio of the Difference is to be the act by which the same Genus is contracted to constitute the species; and each is a Universal Predicate of the Species, which must contain the whole that the Species contains, according to its proper mode: Genus, indeed, in act and in potency together, but the Difference in act, though by a diverse ratio; and the species contains it. Whence each must be taken from the whole nature of the Species formally; but radically Genus from Matter, and difference from Form; because it is true that the first root of Genus in things is Matter, and the first root of Difference is Form. In which sense it was said by Aristotle, and is understood by all the others, that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form: namely in material things, in which alone it can be true. And from this the argument proposed at the beginning is solved.

Second, it must be explained briefly from what the ratio of Genus and of Difference is taken in spiritual substances. In these it is certain that they are not taken from matter nor from form, since they do not have them; we say, therefore, that in these too Genus is taken from something having a likeness to matter, and Difference from something having a likeness to form. Which is to be understood in this way.

20 The actuality and perfection of a created essence, by which it is and comes to be outside its causes, is the being of actual existence, distinct from that same essence really or by reason alone. Whence, the closer the grades of the essence, or the essential predicates, are to this act, the more perfect they are understood to be, and therefore to have more of act and less of potency; and the farther they are from it, the less actual and the more potential. For example, among the essential grades of man, Rational comes closest to the act of being, because existence belongs to it proximately or immediately: for it is the last grade of essential perfection, beyond which there is no other, but only the substantial mode of actual existence. of Animal less proximately, and most remotely the grade of Substance; wherefore this grade will be more potential, since it is more distant from act. Since, then, Genus is something potential and contractible by Differences, and Difference is the act by which the Genus is contracted, the first Genus of any substantial Species whatever is taken from the whole essence itself according to the grade of substance, as from the first potency in the Metaphysical Genus, similar to matter; and so of the other intermediate genera, according to their greater or lesser approximation to the last Species, which is closest to actual existence. As the genus of Body is taken also from the whole nature of man itself, taken under the grade of corporeity; and the Genus of Living, from the whole nature conceived under the grade of life; and finally the Genus of Animal, from the whole nature under the grade of sensing; and this is the last genus, since beyond it there is no other potential grade of the nature, but only the lowest Species. But the last grade, according to which the same nature of man is proximately capable of actual existence, is Rational; whence, since the Difference is the act contracting the genus, it is taken from the whole nature of man considered under the grade of Rational, as from an act similar to form; and so of the other Differences of species.

From these things it is understood in what way Genus and Difference are taken in Angels. For they agree with bodies in the grade of substance, which is most remote from actual existence; and therefore their first genus is taken from the whole spiritual nature itself under the grade of Substance, which is most potential and similar to matter. The second, from the same whole nature under the grade of the spiritual or incorporeal, still common to all, but less remote from actual existence. And if there are any other Intermediate genera, unknown to us, they are taken in the same way from the whole nature conceived under some grade more or less remote from existence. But the Difference is taken likewise from the whole nature, under the grade closest to that actual existence. I am speaking, however, of the last Difference: for the subalternate ones, which contract the Intermediate genera, are taken, as more imperfect, from other, more imperfect grades of the nature, in the same way as the Differences of corporeal Substance, which can easily be understood.

Of Accidents, finally, we say that they are of two different kinds. For some are Relative, of which it will be said in the category of Relation in what way, or from what, they take their Genus and Difference. Others are absolute, of which this is certain: that there is in them an essential attribution to substance, since they are something of it; and they are not so much called Beings as Beings of a Being, that is, of the substance in which they are naturally apt to inhere from their own nature. genus of these, therefore, is taken from the grade of Being which they participate from the most universal Being, with attribution to substance, as most remote from actual existence, and therefore more potential, after the likeness of matter. As the first Genus of Quantity is taken from the grade or mode of extending substance; and the other intermediate Genera from other grades, according to the proportion already explained.

The Difference, however, is taken by order to the proper principle or cause by which it is caused: which is manifest in proper attributes; for the Difference of Risibility is to be taken by order to Rationality, from which it proceeds naturally as from its proper principle; and so of the others. And in almost the same way in common Accidents: because, although they have several subjects, yet they always have some proper cause in them to which they are ordered, and by order to it their difference is taken. And this is the cause on account of which

Accidents are always and necessarily defined through the subject, whether they are defined in the Concrete or in the Abstract: because in their Genus as well as in their Difference there is essentially included the order to the Subject, which they are accustomed to call aptitudinal Inherence.

## QUESTION IIII

Whether the composition of the species from Genus and difference is real, or only of reason. 22

The question proceeds of Species of a real nature: whether their

Metaphysical composition is real or of reason, as the composition of man from animal and rational. For of the Species that are found in beings of reason it is certain that they are not real, because the nature of a being of reason is not real, but made by the intellect; therefore no composition can take place in it which is real.

Now for a real composition two conditions are necessary, and they suffice for it to be called such. The first is that the parts, or components, be real. This is proved: Because from a real composition something real too must result; but if the components are not real, nothing real will result from their composition, as is known; therefore they must be real.

23 The second condition is that they be distinct really, or from the nature of the thing: for if only through the intellect, they will not effect a real composition, but only one of reason. And the reason of this is that composition is as it were a union of many; but if these many are not distinguished really, they will not be many really; therefore they will not effect a real composition.

[p. 158]

Vtraque conſequentia poteft probari,hoc exemplo. Quia gradus rationalitatis, per-ficitgradum naturæ fenfitiuæ , & perficit perfectione reali: quianatura fenfitiua , magisperfecta eſt realiter in homine, quàm in animali : ideorealiterdicitur contraheregenus: quia contrahere,nihilaliudeft,quàmdeterminare,atqueperficere.

And of the first condition it is certain among all that it concurs in the Metaphysical composition of the Species from Genus and Difference: for the objective concepts of which it is made are grades of the generic and of the differential nature, which are truly real: as the grade of the sensitive nature, which animal expresses, and the grade of the rational nature, which rational expresses, are real; therefore the components are real.

24 To the second condition, then, the whole difficulty of the question is reduced: whether these grades, or objective concepts, are really distinct. For if they are really distinct, the composition will be real; but if they are distinguished by reason alone, the composition will not be real, but of reason. Since, indeed, Distinction is threefold: one real, another from the nature of the thing, and the third is the distinction of reason. That is called Real which is between two things, as between Peter and John. The distinction from the nature of the thing is posited between a thing and its mode, as between the point and the line; or it is also posited by others between formal rationes of the same thing, but distinct before the operation of the intellect, as between action and passion, which are really the same motion. Scotus posits the distinction from the nature of the thing because he asserts that the formal ratio of action and of passion are distinguished before the operation of the intellect. But the distinction of reason is called by all that which is not between things distinct on the part of the thing, but is made by the intellect.

These things supposed, there are two opinions. The first is that of Scotus, in 2, d. 3, q. 1, and Metaph. 7, q. 16, where he affirms that the grade of Genus and that of Difference are distinguished from the nature of the thing, inasmuch as they are distinct formal rationes before the operation of the intellect; and since the composition of the Species is made from them, he must consequently grant that such a composition is real, if not from diverse things, at least from formal rationes of the same thing distinct before the operation of the intellect. Scotus is followed by Antonius Andreas, in 2, in the place cited; Ferrara, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 24 and 42; Fonseca, Metaph. 2, ch. 2, text 11, and bk. 4, ch. 2, q. 4, sect. 3.

25 It is proved, first: Because the differential grade perfects the generic grade really, and not only through the intellect; therefore the Difference contracts the genus from the nature of the thing; but to contract the Genus is to compose the Species together with it; therefore it composes the species really; wherefore the composition will be real. Both consequences can be proved by this example: Because the grade of rationality perfects the grade of the sensitive nature, and perfects it with a real perfection, because the sensitive nature is really more perfect in man than in animal, therefore it is said to contract the genus really: because to contract is nothing other than to determine and perfect.

[p. 159]

Primò, vefuntin diuerfis Speciebus, & in-diuiduis : vtAnimalin Leone, aut hoc Leone , & Ratrona-le in Homine & in hoc , aut illo Homine. Et hoc modo , certum eft, non folum ex natura rei,fed reas

It is proved, second: Because if rational were not really distinct from animal, it would not be really distinct from horse; the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also. The consequence is proved: for whatever things are the same as one third are the same as each other; if, therefore, rational is the same as animal, then neighing too, which is the Difference of horse, will be the same as that same animal; and so rational and neighing will be really the same, and consequently rational and horse: which is plainly false. And it can be confirmed: because those things are distinguished really of which one can be separated from the other; but any Difference whatever can be separated from the Genus, and will be separated if the species it constitutes perishes; therefore it is distinguished really from it.

The second opinion holds that the Grade of Genus and that of Difference, or the objective concepts of each, are distinguished neither really nor from the nature of the thing, but only through the intellect, and therefore only by a Distinction of reason; and consequently that the composition of the species is not real, but made by the intellect. This is St. Thomas’s, in the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 4; Metaph. 7, lect. 4; and 1 p., q. 50, a. 4, ad 1, and q. 76, a. 3, ad 4; whom Alexander of Hales follows, Metaph. 7, tit. 11, and bk. 5, tit. 10; Durandus, in 2, d. 3, q. 2, no. 14; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 1, q. 9; Gregory, in 1, d. 38, and Gabriel in the same place, with the other nominalists; Capreolus, in 1, d. 8, q. 2, a. 3; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, § ad 2. dubium; Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 36; Javelli in the same place, q. 18; Nifo, in the Elucidarium, bk. 7, disp. 15, ch. 3 and 4; Soto, q. 1 on Universals, concl. 3, and q. 2, a. 2; Toledo, q. 3 on Universals. And it is now common in the school, and true.

26 But it must first be explained, then proved. And for its explanation it should be noted, first, that the composition of the Species from Genus and Difference is Metaphysical and not Physical; and therefore it is not made from them as from diverse things, as the Physical composition is made from matter and form, which are diverse things, but as from diverse essential grades of the same thing, as the composition of man from the grade of the sensitive nature and of the rational. Wherefore of the Physical composition there is no doubt that it is real; but of the Metaphysical Composition there can be the greatest reason for doubting, because it is not certain whether these grades, or concepts, are distinct from the nature of the thing, or are distinguished only through the intellect.

27 Second, it should be noted that Genus and Difference can be taken in three ways. First, as they are in diverse Species and individuals: as Animal in Lion, or in this Lion, and Rational in Man, and in this or that Man. And in this way it is certain that they are distinguished not only from the nature of the thing, but really

[p. 160]

Primò:Quia fi Genus diftinguitur ex natura rei,a Differétins, aut diftinguitur vtabſtractum ab eis,hoc eft tanquam gradus Vniuerfalis,àparticularibus,vt animalin communi,ab Equo, & Leone, vel vtcontractum in Speciebus , & indiuiduis , vt in Petrohoc Animal, &hoc Rationale,ſed neutro modo di-ſtingui poteft : ergo nondiftinguunturiſti gradus ex natura rei.

: for the Animal that is in Man is essentially other than the Animal that is in Horse, because through conjunction with the difference of Horse it becomes horse; although, as abstracted from the Differences, it is one and the same by a Generic unity only, which does not take away the specific distinction that it has in diverse Species through diverse Differences: as the Animal that is in this Man and the Animal that is in this Lion have a distinct real entity. In the second way they are taken as they are in the same Species or in the same individual: as in Man, Animal and Rational, and in Peter, this animal and this Rational. Third, as Genus is considered abstracted from the Species and Differences, and as contractible by them; and in this way it is said to be outside the ratio of the differences, because it does not include them in act, but the proper grade of its nature: as animal abstracted includes in act only the grade of the sensitive nature, not of the rational or the irrational, except only in potency. And of the grade of Genus and of Difference, taken in these last two ways, Scotus affirms that they are distinguished before the operation of the intellect and from the nature of the thing; but St. Thomas and those who follow him deny it, and assert that they are distinguished only through the intellect, and therefore only by reason.

Third, it should be noted that, although Scotus and others hold that all the generic and differential grades of the same Species proceed from diverse substantial forms, St. Thomas, whose opinion is now common in the school, holds that they emanate from the same substantial form: so that all the essential grades of man, namely the grade of Substance, the grade of Body, the grade of Living, the grade of the Sensitive and of the Rational nature, proceed from the same rational soul, and there is no other substantial form in man. Whereas Scotus, for the grade of Substance and the grade of Body, posits one substantial form, which he calls the form of Corporeity, and for the remaining lower grades another, really distinct, namely the rational soul. And this diversity of Forms seems to argue some Distinction from the nature of the thing between the essential grades proceeding from them, just as the Identity of the substantial form, according to St. Thomas, argues their identity.

28 These things noted beforehand, the common opinion is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because if Genus is distinguished from the Differences from the nature of the thing, either it is distinguished as abstracted from them, that is, as a Universal grade from the particulars, as animal in common from Horse and Lion; or as contracted in the Species and individuals, as in Peter this Animal and this Rational; but it cannot be distinguished in either way; therefore these grades are not distinguished from the nature of the thing.

The major is necessary, because only in these two ways can they be considered in the metaphysical order, as we noted. The minor is proved: for if they are distinguished as the universal from the particulars, then the universal is given before the operation of the intellect, which we proved above to be false. That they cannot be distinguished as diverse grades singularized in Peter, I prove. Because in one individual there is really given only one individual difference, through which all the generic and differential grades become singular, although to each grade there corresponds its own individual difference, distinct by reason alone: as to the grade of body, this body, and to the grade of animal, this animal, etc.; but all the grades, and each of them, are the same from the nature of the thing with the individual difference of Peter which contracts them; therefore they are the same among themselves. The minor is proved: for if they were distinguished from the nature of the thing, it would follow in the same way that a universal is given from the nature of the thing, and before the operation of the intellect, distinct from the singular.

Second: all these generic and differential grades are bestowed by the same substantial form; all are taken from the same real nature; indeed all are found in the same physical form, which is the same simple entity; therefore they cannot be distinguished except by the intellect alone. The consequence is evident, because in the same simple entity, in the same essence and nature, nothing can be distinct from the nature of the thing. Accordingly the antecedent is proved: because from the same real human nature are taken all the generic and differential grades, from substance down to sensitive and rational nature; all of them are also found in the same real nature of Peter, with which they are the same thing; finally, all of them exist in the same most simple entity of the rational soul, in which they are founded: for the corporeal, vital, sensitive, and rational substantial form is the same; therefore, just as these grades, speaking physically, cannot be distinguished except by the intellect, so much less will they be able to be distinguished taking them metaphysically.

29 But if they are not distinguished except by reason alone, it must be explained by which distinction of reason: because a twofold one is customarily given. One having a foundation in the thing itself that is conceived, which is called the distinction of reason reasoned about; the other in the intellect alone, conceiving imperfectly, that is, through several concepts, things that can be conceived through one, which they call the distinction of reason of the reasoning intellect: such as that by which Peter is distinguished from himself in this identical predication, Peter is Peter. I reply that genus is distinguished from difference by a distinction of reason reasoned about. And the reason is manifest: because in the same specific essence is found each

grade, and according to them it has really distinct operations: as man, according to the generic grade of animal, has sensitive operations, such as seeing and hearing; and according to the grade of difference, he has the operations of the rational intellect and will; therefore it has a foundation on its own part for the intellect to distinguish in it the generic grade from the differential. It is indeed true that our intellect would not distinguish these grades unless it cognized in an imperfect manner; but neither would the imperfect mode of cognizing suffice unless a foundation were given in the thing itself; and since there is not given in Peter a foundation for distinguishing him from himself, the intellect cannot distinguish him by such a distinction, but only by another, lesser one, which is called the distinction of reason of the reasoning intellect.

30 From all these is gathered this conclusion, by which the question is answered: Although the composition of the species from genus and difference is real on the part of the real components, nevertheless on the part of their distinction it is not real but of reason; and since both conditions are necessary for a real composition, namely that the components be real and really, or from the nature of the thing, distinct, then, speaking simply, it is not to be called a real composition but one of reason, made by the intellect in the same way as it would be made from the nature of the thing if the generic and the differential grade were distinct from the nature of the thing.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be denied, that the differential grade perfects the generic from the nature of the thing: for since they are not distinct from the nature of the thing, but the same, neither can they be conjoined from the nature of the thing; and therefore neither can one perfect the other: for if they are not distinct, they will not be one and another. It perfects it, then, only on the supposition of a distinction made by the intellect between them; and therefore one perfects the other only through the intellect, just as it is conjoined to it only through the intellect distinguishing them. Thus the perfection which the generic grade has in the species through the differential grade is real, and not a being of reason; but just as they are not distinct from the nature of the thing, so from the nature of the thing the perfection in it is always the same; but because the intellect, distinguishing those things which are not distinct from the nature of the thing, considers the one without considering the other, and therefore under a certain imperfect being, perfectible by the other, the one is said to perfect the other: which is not true from the nature of the thing, since they are not distinct, but only through the intellect distinguishing them. Real, therefore, is the perfection itself which the one receives from the other, on the supposition of the distinction which the intellect makes; and therefore, for lack of a distinction, it is false that one perfects the other from the nature of the thing: for both are required for it to be true, namely that they be distinct from the nature of the thing, and also that from the nature of the thing one

[p. 163]

contract or determine the other: wherefore, if one of the two is lacking, the truth of the antecedent also fails.

31 To the second, the consequence is to be denied; and when it is proved thus: if rational is the same as animal, therefore also as horse, again the consequence is to be denied: for animal is not some third thing with respect to rational and neighing except through the intellect alone, because on the part of the thing animal is distinct in man and in horse; and therefore it does not follow that, if rational is the same as animal, and neighing also, they are the same among themselves: because they are not the same as it as with some third thing from the nature of the thing, but as with some third thing according to reason. But it can well be understood that two things are the same as some third thing distinct from them by reason alone, and yet are not the same among themselves: as Peter and John are the same as man abstracted from them, and are really distinguished among themselves. Thus, in order that that principle be true, Whatever things are the same as one third thing are the same among themselves, it is required that the third thing be distinct from the nature of the thing from each of them. From the lack of distinction, then, it comes about that, since genus is not a third thing with respect to the differences and species before the operation of the intellect, they cannot be compared with it from the nature of the thing, but only through the intellect abstracting and distinguishing it; and therefore that a real identity of the opposed differences among themselves cannot be inferred from the fact that they are the same as the genus abstracted from them by the intellect.

To the confirmation the reply is made in almost the same way: that since genus is not distinct from the differences except through the intellect abstracting it from them, they are not said to come to it, or to be separated from it, really, but only through the intellect and according to reason; and only in this way can any of them be separated from it with its essence preserved: from which it does not follow that they are distinguished really, or from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone.

32 One argument, not an easy one, remains against our view: because if the composition from genus and difference is not real but of reason, then it posits nothing real in the nature in which it is found; and if nothing real, then nothing of perfection or imperfection either. Each consequence is proved: because from the fact that the intellect understands something in one way or another, there accrues to it only the extrinsic denomination of being understood in that way; but an extrinsic denomination can posit nothing of imperfection in it. If this is so, it follows that composition from genus and difference can be found in God: which does not seem in any way to be granted, since every composition is repugnant to his supreme simplicity. The reply is: Such a composition

is not to be admitted in God, according to the common opinion of the school.

Of this there is a twofold reason, setting aside others. The first: because the concept of genus implies three things intrinsic to itself, namely to be limited, and to be imperfect outside the ratio of the differences, and to be essentially perfectible through another; and this indeed with a foundation in the thing itself; all of which signify imperfection intrinsically; and therefore they are alien to God, who is supremely perfect, in whom we conceive nothing limited or finite, nor anything which is essentially outside others, or essentially imperfect and perfectible through another; but the divine immensity and his infinite perfection, and his being most pure act, exclude these things, even as he is understood by us in an imperfect manner.

33 The second reason: because the generic concept has two other things intrinsic to it. The first, that it can be common and univocal to many species; but it is repugnant that such a concept be found in God; therefore it is repugnant that genus and difference be given in him. The minor is proved: because a concept formed by us of God cannot be common to many gods differing in species, whom we evidently know to be impossible; therefore it can only be common to

God and creatures, which differ more than in species; but less can something common and univocal be given to God and creatures than to substance and accident; therefore, just as being cannot be a genus to these, so neither can there be given in God a univocal concept, formed by us, which is univocal, and consequently neither one which is a genus.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether a superior difference is included in an inferior one, and is predicated of it.

34

A     twofold distinction of difference is necessary for explaining the title of

the question. The first is of superior and inferior difference: and that difference is called superior which constitutes a more universal species; inferior, that which constitutes an inferior species: as corporeal is a superior difference with respect to the difference living, and this with respect to sensible, and sensible with respect to rational. The title of the question therefore asks whether corporeal is included in living, and sensible in rational; and whether the predication Rational is sensible is true.

The second distinction is of any difference whatever, which can be taken in two ways, materially and formally. It is taken materially inasmuch as it implies the whole that the species itself implies, namely the grade of the genus, as for the material, and its proper grade, as for the formal: as rational implies for the material the nature

sensitive, but for the formal the grade of rationality; but formally it is taken for the grade of rationality alone: just as white, taken materially, implies a body affected with whiteness, but when it is taken formally, only the whiteness denominating the body. And difference, signified in the concrete, has both acceptations, just as white has both. For rational is taken both for the whole nature of man and also for its last grade alone, though signified in the concrete. Hence some falsely think that difference is taken formally when it is signified in the abstract, as by the name rationality or sensibility: for signified in this way it is not difference but the principle of difference, just as the nature of the genus signified by an abstract name is signified only as the principle of the genus, and not as genus. It is signified, then, in the concrete even when it is taken formally, but only for the last and proper grade.

35 And indeed, if we take the inferior difference materially, it is certain that it includes the superior and that the latter is predicated of it; hence this is true, Rational is sensible, although it is not formal. For rational, at least for the material, implies the nature of animal, in which its difference, namely sensible, is included; therefore it also includes sensible, which is the superior difference.

The difficulty of the question, then, concerns the inferior difference taken formally: whether it includes the superior, and the latter is predicated of it; as, whether rational, taken as it implies formally the last grade of rational nature, through which man is constituted, includes sensible and the other superior differences.

And the first opinion affirms that it is included and predicated formally: which Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 37, asserts he defends for the sake of exercise, although the opposite pleases him more. Soto too inclines to it, ch. on genus, q. 1, ad 3; but Cant. expressly holds it in his exposition of this chapter.

It is proved first from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 45, where he teaches three things about differences. First, that it makes no difference whether the last difference alone is placed in the definition, or also all the superior ones, because the last includes all. Hence we define man in the same way if we only say that he is a rational animal as if we placed all the superior differences, saying: Man is a corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational substance. Second, he asserts that the last difference is the whole substance of the species, and therefore, if it is placed in the definition, it is not permitted to add another superior one, because the fault of nugation would be committed, by repeating the same thing twice: as if we should say, Man is a rational

sensible animal, we assign a nugatory definition. He asserts third that, in order to find the last difference of some species, the superior must be divided by two opposed inferior ones: as biped, which is a difference of animal (an accidental one, indeed, but one which Aristotle uses in place of an essential one), by having cloven and not cloven feet, that is, split or not split. For to have cloven feet (he says) is an inferior difference with respect to biped, since the cleaving of the foot is a certain footedness: that is, since the cleaving of the foot includes footedness, which signifies the same as to have feet.

But from each of these three it seems evidently to follow that the inferior difference includes the superior. From the first, indeed, because difference is taken formally when it is placed in the definition; but the last difference, which is the inferior, placed in the definition, is worth as much as if all the superior ones were placed; therefore it includes them: for if it did not include them, it would not be worth as much. From the second: because it could not be the whole substance of the thing unless it included the superior ones, which it is certain pertain to the substance of the lowest species. But from the last it follows more efficaciously: because if, in order to find the last difference, the superior is to be divided by two opposed inferior ones, then it is included formally in each and is predicated formally of each. The consequence is proved evidently: because in a good division the divided, taken formally, is included in each of the dividing members and is predicated of them, also formally: as animal of rational and irrational animal. And finally Aristotle himself predicates the superior difference of the inferior, taken formally, when he says, It is true that the cleaving of the foot is footedness: for this is the superior difference, and that is called the inferior.

37 It is proved next by reason. First, because rational, taken formally, is a substance: therefore corporeal or incorporeal; and since it is corporeal, it will include formally the superior difference, as this syllogism in Datisi also proves: Every man is formally sensible; man is formally rational; therefore the rational is formally sensible.

Second: if the inferior difference did not include the superior, this would happen chiefly because it is a simple concept, and therefore cannot be composed of or resolved into several other concepts, since then there would be a process to infinity; but the generic concept is also simple, and nevertheless it includes the superior genera, as animal includes living, body, and substance; therefore even if difference is a simple concept, it will be able to include the superior differences.

The second opinion denies that the inferior difference, taken formally, includes the superior, and consequently denies that the latter is predicated of it formally. It is followed by Scotus, 4, d. 11, q. 3, § ad rationes; Capreolus, 1, d. 8, q. 2, in the solution to the 5th argument; Soto; Cardinal Toledo, ch. on substance, doubt 2; Mercado, 1 post ch. 4, q. 3, ad 3; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 28, q. 18, sect. 1. And it seems to me not only more probable but true, and evidently gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle and St. Thomas.

38 But in order that we may prove these things to be so, two things are to be presupposed as certain and necessary foundations. The first is that any difference whatever, whether inferior or superior, is included formally in its species, which it constitutes: as rational is formally in man, and sensible is formally in animal. This is proved evidently: because difference formally constitutes the species; therefore it is a formal part of it; but a part is included formally in the whole; therefore difference is included formally in the species.

The second foundation is that all subalternate species are genera with respect to their inferiors: as animal with respect to horse and lion, and living with respect to animal and plant. From which it follows that in whatever a subalternate difference is formally included, the subalternate genus, which is the subalternate species constituted through the same difference, is also formally included. For example: animal is a subalternate species, constituted formally through the difference sensible, which it necessarily includes formally; therefore in whatever sensible is formally included, animal is also formally included, just as in whatever rational is formally included, man is formally included. The question, then, is the same: whether the inferior difference, taken formally, includes the superior, and whether it includes the genus which is the subalternate species constituted through it; just as it is the same question whether rational, taken formally, includes sensible, and whether it includes animal. Hence, if it has been proved that it does not include the superior genus, it will have been proved that it does not include the superior difference, and concluded that our view is true.

Now it is proved by express testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and then by reason. For Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 2, place 18, speaks thus: It is manifest, therefore, that difference does not participate in genus: wherefore neither will odd be a species, but a difference, since it does not participate in genus. And in place 22: Genus (he says) must be said of more things than difference, and must not participate in difference. And

St. Thomas, Metaph. 3, lect. 8, says: Genus taken per se cannot be predicated of difference, because difference does not participate in genus, as is said in Topics 4, etc.

It is proved also by reason. First: because genus and difference, taken formally, have two things. The first, that they formally import diverse grades of essential perfection: as animal the grade of sensitive nature, and rational the grade of rational nature. Second, that the one is related as contracting and the other as contractible, and therefore as act and potency; but from each it follows that they do not include each other formally; therefore neither will the inferior difference include the superior. I prove the minor thus: grades of diverse essential perfection have diverse rationes; act and potency also differ formally; therefore neither the former nor the latter can include each other formally, and consequently neither can genus and the difference by which it is contracted. But the consequence, that neither does the inferior difference include the superior, is proved by this syllogism: That which is not formally animal is not formally sensible; but rational, taken formally, is not animal; therefore neither will it be formally sensible: wherefore it will not formally include the superior difference.

39 Second: if the inferior differences included the superior formally, then rational and irrational would include sensible formally, and consequently would agree in it formally, as man and horse do; but whatever things agree essentially in some grade of essential perfection must be separated from such agreement through differences, as man and horse are separated from the essential agreement in the same sensible through the differences rational and neighing; therefore the differences themselves would have to be separated through other differences from such essential agreement in the grade of sensible, and so there would be a process to infinity: because those differences also through which they were separated would have a similar agreement in the superior difference which they would include, from which they would have to be separated through other differences; nor could they be separated through themselves, because through themselves they agree formally; but they would have to be separated through other grades of perfection, and consequently through other differences.

be contrary to the other; but that the reason of the first is that the intermediate differences constitute the subalternate species, which are the intermediate genera; therefore, when the same differences are placed in the definition, their formal rationes are sufficiently explained. Which is plain if we define man thus: Man is a corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational substance. And the reason of the second, that the proximate genus formally contains the rationes of all the superior ones; therefore, when the last difference alone is added to it, the whole ratio of the defined is sufficiently explained; and therefore, if after it some one of the superior ones is added, the fault of nugation or of useless repetition is committed, because such a difference is sufficiently explained once the proximate genus is placed, in which it is formally included. For example, animal formally contains living, body, and substance, and all their differences; wherefore, when rational alone is added to it, it sufficiently explains the whole essential ratio of man; and if after rational you add sensible or corporeal, you commit a useless repetition, because such differences are sufficiently explained once animal is placed, in which they are formally included.

41 And from this explanation the reply is made to the first: that the way of defining through the supreme genus and all the intermediate differences down to the last, and through the last alone with the proximate genus, is the same: not because the last includes the superior ones, but because they are formally included in the proximate genus, and therefore, once it alone is placed, they are sufficiently explained.

But when Aristotle asserts that the last difference is the whole substance of the species, they teach that this is to be understood not totally but completively, so that, presupposing the proximate genus, which it contracts and upon which it falls in the definition, it completes the whole substance of the thing. And the third thing which Aristotle asserts, on the division of the superior difference into opposed inferior ones, they expound thus: that the difference is divided not by reason of itself but by reason of the genus which it constitutes as a subalternate species, and which it formally includes; and not, indeed, into differences, but into species through differences: hence neither is the superior genus included in the inferior differences, but in the species, and much less the superior differences in the inferior. And those words of Aristotle, The cleaving of the foot is footedness, are not to be understood as if he meant to predicate the one of the other formally; but his sense is that cleaving is a per se difference dividing footedness, and not a per accidens one.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished, namely, Rational is a substance: for if it is taken for complete substance, which is the supreme genus of the category, it is false;

since rational, and any difference whatever, is formally a part of the species, and therefore an incomplete substance; but if substance is taken more universally, as it abstracts from complete and incomplete, it is true that rational is a substance, not the categorial one, but one analogous to complete and incomplete substances. Hence, to the form of the argument, it is to be denied that it is a substance which is divided into corporeal and incorporeal, and consequently that it includes the superior difference.

42 The syllogism which is adduced we grant to be in mood and figure, and therefore to conclude evidently that the inferior difference includes the superior; not, however, in the formal sense: nor is this necessary to the syllogistic form, by virtue of which it is indeed inferred that the conclusion stands in truth with the premises, but not always in the same sense: as can be proved by this altogether similar example: Every man is an animal; every man is risible; therefore the risible is an animal; whose premises are true in the formal sense, but the conclusion cannot be true formally, but only in the material sense.

To the second, the major being granted, the minor is to be distinguished:

because genus is not as simple as difference; for since it is a subalternate species, it is composed of genus and difference; but difference cannot have such a composition, because, since by its proper ratio it is the last act of the species, it cannot be composite in any way; nor yet is it pure act, because, since it is a part, it includes potency for composing the whole, and an intrinsic imperfection coming to it from the ratio of a part.

## QUESTION VI

Whether difference is always and necessarily more perfect than the genus which it contracts.

For example, animal is contracted by rational and irrational: and rational elevates it to the higher grade of rational nature, whereas irrational does not elevate it, but leaves it within its proper grade of sensitive nature. question is whether they are nobler than the genus, or less noble, or equal in nobility.

And the first opinion holds that not all differences are nobler than the genus which they contract, but only those through which it is elevated to the grade of a more perfect nature; but that the others are less noble than it, or at most of the same nobility: as all the differences of animals, except rational, and all the differences of angels, through which their genus, which is spiritual or incorporeal substance, is not elevated to a higher grade of essential perfection. Certain moderns follow this.

And they prove it by a twofold argument. The first is: because a more perfect grade of nature is the root of perfection of operation; therefore that difference which does not elevate the nature of the genus to a more perfect operation, or at least to a more perfect mode of operating, cannot be more perfect than it; but there are many differences which elevate the genus in neither way; therefore none of them will be nobler than the genus. The minor is proved in the differences of animal, of which none constitutes a species having another operation more perfect than the sensitive, which is proper to the grade of the genus; and also in the species of angels, which have no other more perfect operation besides intellection, nor another more perfect mode of operating besides understanding without discursive reasoning.

44 The second: among the species of animal several are found so imperfect that they lack several senses, as is manifest of moles, oysters, and leeches, and of others always fixed to rocks, which seem to have no other sense besides touch; therefore in these a less perfect grade of sensing is found than in the genus animal, which signifies sensitive nature abstracted from these defects.

The second opinion is the opposite, affirming that any difference whatever is more perfect than the genus which it contracts. This is the express view of St. Thomas, and not only more probable but true. It is proved first by two testimonies of the same: for in 2, d. 13, q. 1, a. 6, ad 1, he speaks thus: Difference is not nobler than genus as one nature is nobler than another, or as one form is nobler than another: because difference implies no form which is not implicitly contained in the nature of the genus; but it is said to be nobler than genus as the determinate than the indeterminate; and in this way to have intellect thus is nobler than to have intellect simply, and to have sense thus than to have sense simply, etc. And 1 p., q. 75, a. 7, ad 2, he says: The last specific difference is most noble inasmuch as it is most determinate, in the way in which act is nobler than potency: but in this way the intellectual is not nobler

than the sensitive, because it is indeterminate and common to many grades of intellectuality, as sensible is to many grades in sensible being, etc.

45 From these two arguments are gathered for proving the same opinion. The first is: every difference elevates the genus to a higher grade of being, or to a higher mode of being within the same grade of its nature; therefore every difference is nobler than its genus. The consequence is evident: because a thing is more perfect not only because it implies a more perfect grade of being, but because it participates the same grade in a more perfect mode. But the antecedent is proved: because difference has two things in which it exceeds the genus: namely, to be the act determining and perfecting it, whereas the genus is related as a determinable potency; and also to be a determinate and distinct grade of nature, and to imply it in a determinate and distinct mode, whereas the genus, although it includes a determinate grade, includes it indeterminately and as it were confusedly; but to include a determinate grade of nature, and determinately, is more perfect than to include it only confusedly; therefore difference, by its proper mode of being, is always more perfect.

Second: genus is related as matter in the composition of the species, and difference as form; but form always elevates matter to a more perfect being; therefore difference always elevates genus to a more perfect being. And form is always nobler than matter; therefore difference will always be nobler than genus. The minor of the first syllogism is proved: because form elevates matter in the physical order to the determinate and actual specific being which it bestows on it; and in the same way difference elevates the genus in the metaphysical order; but specific, determinate, and actual being is more perfect than the confused and potential being which the genus has; therefore difference is always nobler than genus.

46 To the first argument of the other opinion the reply is made by denying the consequence of the first enthymeme: because, besides elevation to a more perfect operation or a more perfect mode of operating, there is found a more perfect mode of being, actual and determinate, to which every difference elevates the genus; and therefore it is always more perfect than it.

To the second, the antecedent being granted, the consequence is to be denied: for although the grade of sensing is found imperfectly in those species, it is still found more perfectly than in the genus, because it is determinate and specific; but in the genus it is neither determinate nor more perfect, but confused, abstracting from the perfect and the imperfect. But what is determinate and distinct is more perfect than the indeterminate and confused. And therefore still

## QUESTION VII

Whether the second definition of difference can belong to the last differences.

he title of the question presupposes two things as certain. First,

T           that difference is twofold, subalternate and last. The subalternate

is that which constitutes a subalternate species, as corporeal and sensible; the last, that which constitutes a last species, as rational. It presupposes second that the second definition belongs to subalternate differences, since it is known that they are predicated of many things differing in species: as sensible of man and lion. But it calls into doubt whether it can also belong to the last ones. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because they are not predicated of many species, but of one only and its individuals: as rational of man alone and of singular men; therefore the definition does not belong to them which asserts that difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species in quale quid.

47 And there is a first opinion, which holds that it belongs also to the last differences; and in order to explain the way in which it belongs to them, it teaches that the definition is to be expounded thus: that when it is said, Difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, the sense is: of many things which are distinguished in species either among themselves or from others. In which sense it is manifest that it belongs to the subalternate differences and also to the last: for the former are predicated of many things differing in species among themselves, as sensible of horse and lion; but the last difference, as rational, is predicated of many things differing in species, not among themselves but from others: as of man, who differs in species from the horse, and of Peter and John, who are distinguished in species from the individuals of other species through the same rational. Some held this opinion, whom Avicenna brought forward in the present chapter.

But it is proved false by a twofold argument. First: this definition of difference is assigned by Porphyry in the same way and in the same sense in which the definitions of the other predicables were assigned; but the other definitions, as those of species and genus, are understood thus: that the former is to be predicated of many things differing in number among themselves, the latter of many things differing in species among themselves, as the examples adduced in them by Porphyry prove; therefore this definition of difference is to be understood in the same way; but, so understood, it is plain that it does not belong to the last differences; therefore they were not defined by Porphyry.

[p. 174]

Second: if that sense were to be admitted, so that it belonged to the last differences, it follows evidently that the definition of genus also belongs to species. The consequence is proved: because it is predicated of many things differing in species, not indeed among themselves, but certainly distinct from the individuals of other species.

48 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, in his exposition of this definition, in the single doubt, where he presupposes two things for explaining the sense of the definition in which it belongs to the last differences. The first is that by this definition difference is defined under the common ratio of difference, abstracting from subalternate and last, because under the common ratio it is denominated by the second intention of the third predicable. Second, that the words of any definition can be applied in two ways to those things which are contained under the defined: positively, that is, affirmatively, or else negatively, that is, by non-repugnance; and this definition is applied in each way to diverse differences: positively, indeed, to the subalternate ones, which are truly predicated of many things differing in species; but to the last ones by non-repugnance, because it is true that it is not repugnant to them, inasmuch as they are differences, to be predicated of many things differing in species. Thus the last differences are considered in two ways, namely under the common ratio of difference, and under the particular ratio of last ones; and in this latter way the definition is altogether repugnant to them, but not in the first. For if it were repugnant to them as they are differences, it could not belong to any differences, not even the subalternate ones; and since they are not defined as last, but as differences, it is to be said absolutely that the definition belongs to them negatively, or by non-repugnance.

This opinion of Cajetan is followed by Soto in the present chapter, in the single question, ad 6; for it are also cited Avicenna, in the last chapter of the Predicables, and Iamblichus, in the chapter on difference. And Toledo, in the single question of this chapter, teaches that it is probable, although not according to the mind of Porphyry. Cajetan proves it by this argument: the definition of quantity is that it is divisible into parts, and it does not belong positively to a celestial body, because, since it is incorruptible, it cannot be divided; otherwise it would be corrupted by division; but it belongs to it negatively, that is, by non-repugnance, as it is quantity, not as it is an incorruptible body: because as it is quantity it is not repugnant to it to be divided, although division is repugnant to it as such an incorruptible quantity. And yet it suffices for it to belong to it in this way for the definition to be said to belong to it absolutely; therefore it will suffice that it belong to the last differences by non-repugnance, as they are differences, although it is repugnant to them as last.

49 But to me it seems to have almost no probability. Hence hardly anyone now defends it. It is proved first: the definition of a thing, if it is essential, contains the essence of all the things that are defined; and if it is descriptive, some proper attribute of them; but essence and proper attribute cannot belong to things negatively, or by non-repugnance, but it is necessary that they belong to them positively; therefore it is repugnant to a definition to belong to anything by non-repugnance.

Second: because, if the definition belongs to the last differences only from the fact that it is not repugnant to them, considered under the common ratio of difference, to be predicated of many things differing in species, although it is repugnant to them as they are last differences, it follows that the definition of man belongs to the lion; indeed, that the definition of any species whatever belongs to the other species of the same genus. The consequent is absurd; therefore the antecedent will also be false. The consequence is proved: because, although the definition of man is repugnant to the lion under the specific ratio of lion, it is nevertheless not repugnant to it considered under the common ratio of animal.

The third opinion, common and true, holds that by this definition Porphyry defined only the subalternate differences, and not the last. So the Commentator, Avicenna, and Alfarabi, whom Albert the Great cites and follows, tract. 5 on difference, ch. 6; Javelli, the Louvain commentators, Soto, Canterus, Mercado, Villalpando, Toledo, and Fonseca, in the present chapter, in the explanation of the same definition. And it is proved from the refutation of the other opinions: because in no way can it belong to the last differences.

But why did Porphyry not define these? Some reply: because he did not know them. But this is false, because it is certain that he knew the last species, of which he made mention in the chapter on species, in the categorial ordering; therefore he also knew the last differences, at least in the common ratio of last ones, although he was ignorant of the particular ones; and in this chapter, and in the last of this book, he said that the last difference of man is rational mortal: whence it follows that he also knew some in particular.

Therefore others assert that he did not define them because he thought they were not simple but composite or complex, as rational mortal is the difference of man; but complex ones do not pertain to the predicables, which must be simple, or incomplex, as we said in the last question on universals. This reason, however, is against the mind of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where, comparing difference with species, he speaks thus: Difference indeed is often considered in many species; but species only in those things which are under the species

of the individual, etc. If, then, difference is often in many species, not always according to the mind of Porphyry, there will be given with him a predicable last difference, which is compared with the species.

It is to be said, therefore, that Porphyry defined only the subalternate ones because, since they are better known to us, we use them more frequently in definitions. Which can be proved from a like case: for since property is twofold, subalternate and lowest, he defined only the latter in the following chapter, because we use it more frequently in demonstrations. And it suffices to have defined the subalternate differences: because, since all are predicated in the same way, namely in quale quid, from the knowledge of these it is easy to know the lowest differences, inasmuch as they pertain to the third predicable; it is also easy to assign a definition common to the subalternate and the lowest, which will be this:

Difference is that which is predicated of many in quale quid.

To the argument of Cajetan the reply is that it is false that the definition of quantity designated by Aristotle does not belong positively to a celestial body:

because, since it has true quantity, it is truly, per se, and positively divisible into parts, although actual division is impeded per accidens on account of the substantial incorruptibility of the same body.

C H A P T E R V.

On Property.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

But property is divided in four ways, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T. 1

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of property, which is the fourth predicable. And it is divided into two parts. In the first, Porphyry hands down four acceptations, or modes, of property. In the second, he teaches that only its fourth acceptation is proper, but that the others are common to other accidents.

Property in the first mode is taken for that which belongs to some one species alone, yet not to all its individuals: as to be a physician or a philosopher is said to be a property of man, because it belongs to man alone, although it does not belong to every man. In the second mode it is taken, in the opposite way, for that which belongs to every individual of some species, yet not to it alone, but also to the individuals of others: as to be a biped, or to have two feet, belongs to all men from their own nature, yet not

to them alone, but also to certain other animals of other species. In the third mode it is taken for that which belongs to some species, and to all its individuals, yet not at every time, but at a certain determinate one: as to grow gray belongs to all men and to men alone, but not always, only at the time of old age. In the fourth mode property is taken for that which belongs to some species, and to all its individuals, not for a determinate time but always: as risible belongs to man, and to every man, and also always: because, although a man does not always laugh, he nevertheless always has the aptitude for laughing, and therefore he is always risible.

Of these four acceptations, only the fourth is proper (says Porphyry): because property properly taken is only that which is convertible with that of which it is the property; but only property taken in the fourth mode is convertible; therefore only in the fourth acceptation is it taken properly.

## QUESTION I

Whether property taken only in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable, or also according to the other three modes. 2

The title of the question presupposes as certain that property according to the fourth mode pertains to the fourth predicable; but it doubts whether this alone constitutes the fourth predicable, and the other three modes rather pertain to the fifth, or whether the fourth is made up of all four modes.

And the first opinion holds that property not only according to the fourth mode but also according to the others constitutes the fourth predicable: that is, either according to all, or at least according to the third mode. So Albert the Great seems to think, tract. 6 on property, ch. 1, and tract. 7 on accident, also ch. 1; the Louvain commentators, in the present chapter; and in the same place Canter., whom some of the moderns follow, at least as regards property in the third mode.

It is proved first: because, although the properties of the other modes, taken for the act, are common accidents, yet if they are taken for the aptitude or potency, they are proper attributes emanating from the essence; therefore they do not pertain to the fifth predicable, but to the fourth. The antecedent is proved in property of the first mode: for to be a physician or a philosopher, that is, to have some science among these, is a common accident; but the aptitude for having them, as for having the others, is a proper attribute of man, which they are accustomed to call the capacity for learning.

Second: because property in the third mode belongs to every and to only; therefore it is a proper attribute. The consequence is proved: because to be a proper attribute consists only in this, that it emanate from the essence; but emanation is not removed by the fact that it does not always belong, but at a time fixed by nature: because at that time, and not at another, a disposition for such emanation is found in the subject; therefore neither is the ratio of proper attribute, which consists in emanation, removed.

3 The second opinion is common and true. It denies that any acceptation of property besides the fourth constitutes the fourth predicable, but affirms that the three prior ones pertain to the fifth predicable, and that only property in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable. It is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 7; Javelli, tract. 4 on the predicables, ch. 5; Cajetan, Soto, and Toledo, in the present chapter; and it is expressed in the doctrine of Aristotle, in which the definition of property is contained as belonging only to property in the fourth mode. And moreover property according to the other acceptations is said to pertain to the predicable of accident. Both are found in Topics 1, ch. 4: the definition of property in these words: Property is that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. Of the other acceptations of property, too, he speaks thus: For no one will call property that which can belong to another, nor perhaps that which belongs to it alone for some time, etc. And at the end of the chapter he says: But it is manifest from these things that nothing prevents an accident from becoming a property both when and relative to something; but simply it will not be a property, etc. Property relative to something he calls property taken in the first and second mode, because it is called such in order to other things, that is: because it belongs to only and not to every, or to every and not to only. But property when is the same as property in the third mode: for when signifies time; and since property in the third mode belongs only for a determinate time, it is called by Aristotle property when.

4 No less express is the opinion of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where he teaches that the fourth and the fifth predicable are distinguished in three things. In the first, indeed, because property belongs only to one species, whose essence it follows, and to its individuals; but an accident belongs to many others. In the second they differ because property is predicated convertibly of the subject, but not so a common accident. In the last, because property does not admit of more and less, but common accidents do admit of them. But this threefold difference with respect to accident belongs only to property in the fourth mode.

It is also proved by a reason drawn from the testimonies of Aristotle: Not in the common mode of conceiving and speaking, says Aristotle, is that
