alone called property which so belongs to all that it is not common to others; and moreover, which always belongs to those of which it is the property; but only property in the fourth mode has these two conditions; therefore this alone will be property, but the others common accidents; and therefore this alone will constitute the fourth predicable, while the others will rather pertain to the fifth. The minor is proved: for property in the first and second mode either does not belong to all, or is common to others as well; but property in the third mode never belongs to many individuals, and to all the others it does not belong at least for a long time; therefore it is to be understood that none of them ought to be called truly property, nor pertain to the fourth predicable.

5 And if you say: Why, then, are the properties of the other modes adduced by Porphyry in this chapter? I reply: they are adduced only because they have some likeness and analogy with true property in the fourth mode, from which likeness the nature and essence of true property is better known, and also from their unlikeness and impropriety. Wherefore, if property is taken in common, it is said of all not univocally but analogically: and of property in the fourth mode simply, but of the others only in a certain respect and by attribution to it.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished: for aptitude for the sciences is twofold, universal and particular. The universal is called the capacity which man has through the intellect; the particular, that with respect to particular sciences. For one man has a particular inclination and aptitude for one science or art which others do not have, although they do not lack the universal aptitude of the intellect. To the form of the argument, then, the reply is that it is true that property in the first and second mode, taken for the universal aptitude, is a proper attribute; but in this way it is not property in the first or second mode but in the fourth, because it is a property flowing from the specific essence of man; but if it is taken for the particular aptitude, it is only a property of individuals, not belonging to all, although it belongs to them alone; and therefore it is not property simply, but a common accident pertaining to the fifth predicable.

6 For the solution of the second argument, a twofold property is to be distinguished, specific and individual. The former flows from the essential principles of the species, which are genus and difference, as risibility from the proper principles of man. The individual, on the other hand, from the individual complexion, to which the humors and other qualities and dispositions of matter concur. Hence it follows that the former always

belongs, because the specific essence is always disposed in the same way; but the individual property need not always belong, because the humors are not in the same disposition: hence it is not called a proper attribute simply, but a common accident. Such is grayness of hair, even if it is taken for the aptitude: which, although it belongs properly to man alone, and to other animals only by likeness to man, as is gathered from its causes which Aristotle hands down in On the Generation of Animals 4, ch. 5, nevertheless does not flow from his specific essence, but from the particular complexion of men, and also from other extrinsic causes concurring in the same men, and in men alone, at the time of old age; therefore it pertains not to the fourth predicable but to the fifth.

7 To the form of the argument, then, the consequence is to be denied, that property in the third mode is a proper attribute simply; it only has a likeness with a proper attribute. And when it is said that it is not necessary for it always to belong in order to be a proper attribute, this too is to be denied: because a proper attribute simply follows from the bare essence; hence it does not vary, but is disposed in the same way as the essence itself; but the properties of individuals depend on other accidental and extrinsic causes, which are disposed in a different way at a different time; therefore such properties are not proper attributes simply, nor are they comprehended under the name of property constituting the fourth predicable.

QUESTION II. Whether property is a universal, or the fourth predicable, with respect to the species or to the

individuals.

For an easier understanding of the question it should be noted, first, that property is twofold. One, which follows the nature of a genus or of a subalternate species, and therefore is called subalternate property, and is predicated convertibly of the genus itself, but is not convertible with any species whatever; and therefore with respect to the genus it is adequate property, and with respect to any species inadequate: as sensible is a subalternate property, which follows the nature of animal, with which it is convertible, but with none of its species; therefore it is an adequate property with respect to animal, but inadequate with respect to the species; yet it is predicated of all of them in the same way as of the genus, although not proximately but remotely: that is, in quale as a property, according to the antepredicamental rule handed down by Aristotle in ch. 3 of the Antepredicaments: That when something is predicated of something,

whatever things are predicated of such a predicate are predicated of its subject and of all things contained under it, and in the same kind of predication, according to all interpreters: as animal is predicated of man and of lion, and sensible of animal, with the predication of a property; and therefore it is necessary that the same sensible be predicated of man and of lion, contained under the same animal, also with the predication of a property. The other property is the one that follows the lowest species, and is predicated of it proximately, adequately, and convertibly; but of the individuals of that species inadequately, because it is convertible with none of them, and remotely, because by means of the species: yet with the predication of a property, because in quale proper.

8 It should be noted second that each property was defined by Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, with this definition: A property is that which does not indicate what the being of a thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. For a subaltern property is no less convertible with the subaltern species which it follows (as sensible with animal) than a lowest property with the lowest species (as risible with man); although the former is not convertible with the inferior species, nor the latter with the individuals, because with respect to inferiors neither is an adequate property. And when it is said that it does not indicate what the being of a thing is, this signifies only that it does not pertain to the essence but is an accident of it; although a posteriori we know the essence through it, and in this sense it might seem to indicate what the being of a thing is; but the sense of the definition is the former. Each is also defined by Porphyry, when he says that a property in the fourth mode (which alone is a property simply) is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always.

Concerning each property too, the subaltern as well as the lowest, it is asked whether it is a universal and the fourth predicable with respect to the subaltern or lowest species which it follows, or only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because nothing is universal except with respect to many; but the species which each property follows is only one, for it is convertible with it; therefore with respect to it the property will not be universal or predicable, but only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals, which are many.

9 The first opinion asserts that property is not a universal, nor the fourth predicable, with respect to the genus or species which it proximately follows, but with respect to the inferiors. So the Louvain commentators, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 28, q. 19, sect. 2; and several moderns. They prove it, first, because the universal extends to more things than the subject of which it is predicated; therefore if it is convertible with it, it will not be universal with respect to it. the antecedent: for the universal, by the force of the name, signifies that which is not particular but extends to many particulars; therefore it is repugnant for it to be universal with respect to one particular subject; whence, since the species is one particular subject, the property will not be universal with respect to it.

Second, because the ratio of universal and the ratio of property are opposed; therefore they cannot belong to the same thing with respect to the same thing; but something is called a property with respect to the species which it follows; therefore it is repugnant for it to be called universal with respect to the same. The antecedent is proved: for the universal is so called with respect to many, as its definition proves, that which is one in many; but a property with respect to one only, as is also plain from its definition, in which it is said: but belongs to it alone; therefore they are opposed rationes.

The second opinion affirms that property is a universal and predicable with respect to the species which it follows, and not only with respect to the individuals. This is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 5, on property, ch. 1; Cajetan; and Soto, q. 1 on this chapter; Toledo, at the end of the same; and also several moderns.

10 It is proved from Aristotle and Porphyry. From Aristotle indeed, because the definition which he gives of property does not belong to it with respect to the inferiors, but only with respect to the species; for he says: but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, that is, to the species alone, of which alone it is predicated convertibly, and not of the inferior species or individuals; therefore Aristotle holds that property, with respect to the species alone, is a property, and therefore a universal and the fourth predicable. Porphyry too says that property in the fourth mode is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always: which conditions it does not seem to have except with respect to the species; and in the last chapter of this book, enumerating the things that belong to the fourth predicable, he says that it is predicable of the species which it follows.

Again, it is proved by reason. First, because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being which a thing has from its own nature, or from the mode in which it is conceived by the intellect; but property, from its natural mode of being, and also as it is conceived by the intellect, regards the species as the proximate principle from which it flows, but the inferior species or the individuals only remotely and through participation in the species; therefore property has the ratio of universal and of predicable in quale primarily with respect to the species, and as it were secondarily with respect to the individuals.

Second, the predicables are ordered to demonstration, as the categories are; therefore the necessary and per se propositions of which demonstration is composed pertain to the predicables; but such are those in which a property is predicated of the species, as

“man is risible”: they will therefore pertain to the fourth predicable, since there is no other to which they could pertain; and therefore property will be universal and predicable with respect to the species.

11 Our view is explained in two conclusions. The first: Property is not universal with respect to the species alone, but with respect to the inferior species or individuals. This is proved from the definition of the universal, namely one in many and of many; but the species is not many simply, but one, although it is many according to a virtual ratio, by which it is participated by many; therefore with respect to it the property cannot be universal. The consequence is proved: because only those things are, and are called, many simply which are in act many and distinct; but in the species neither are the individuals many or distinct, but one, nor is the species itself many in them, but likewise one; therefore property with respect to the species alone is not universal.

Second conclusion. Property does not have its being such a universal, that is, a property or the fourth predicable, in relation to the species alone, nor in relation to the individuals alone, but in relation to the individuals as they participate the ratio of the species. In order that this conclusion and the preceding one may be better understood, it should be noted that in property, as in any other predicable, two things are to be considered: both the common ratio of universal, which all participate and in which they agree, and the special ratio, taken from such a mode of predicating, by which they are distinguished. The ratio of universal as such, then, requires several things for its term; and therefore property does not have it with respect to the species, as was proved in the first conclusion, because the species is not many simply, but one. But the special ratio of such a universal and predicable it does not have with respect to the individuals alone: because it does not flow from them, nor is it primarily and per se their property, but the species’, from which it flows primarily and per se, and of which it is predicated per se and primarily in quale proper; whence in relation to it, it has per se and primarily the special mode of predicating by which it is distinguished from the other predicables. But because for the ratio of such a universal such many are required, just as for the ratio of the universal in common many simply, property is still not such a universal with respect to the species alone except with an order to the individuals, by which its essential ratio, and consequently the property itself flowing from it, is participated.

12 From this doctrine not only is each conclusion explained, but this argument is gathered by which the second is proved. Property, as it is the fourth predicable, is to be defined thus: A property is that which is predicated of many in quale proper; but it does not have the first with respect to the species alone, namely to be predicable of many, nor

the second, namely in quale proper, with respect to the individuals, except with an order to the species, by reason of which it is predicated of them in quale proper; therefore it has the complete definition of the fourth predicable neither from the species alone, except with an order to the individuals, nor from the individuals alone, except with an order to the species.

The arguments of the first opinion prove only that property does not have the ratio of universal as such with respect to the species, but with respect to the individuals; not, however, that it does not have from the species, with an order to the individuals, the special ratio of such a universal, taken from the mode of predicating.

The argument of the second opinion proves only that it has the same special ratio of such a universal, or of the fourth predicable, from the species, yet not without an order to the individuals; and since our view contains both, it is not necessary to solve the arguments of the other opinions in particular, but from the doctrine noted they will easily be solved by anyone.

It remains only to explain in one word what some are accustomed to doubt:

whether property, as it is the fourth predicable, is referred by one and the same relation, according to species, to the species and the individuals, or to the genus and the inferior species, or by different ones, so that one is to the species and another to the individuals. To which I reply that it is referred by one and the same. Which

I prove thus: A relation takes its specific unity from the formal term; but the species and the individuals have the same ratio of terminating the relation of property; therefore it will be one with respect to all. The minor is proved:

Property is referred to the species and the individuals as to the principle from which it flows and as to the subject with which it is convertible; but the species and the individuals have the same ratio of principle and of subject, since the individuals have both by reason of the species; therefore they have the same formal ratio of terminating, and are to be taken for a single formal term, from which the relation of property has its specific unity.

three things in the whole chapter. First, he defines accident by three definitions.

Second, he divides it by a certain division. Third, he replies to a certain tacit objection.

The first definition of accident is: An accident is that which comes and goes without the corruption of the subject. As whiteness inheres in a wall and can be separated from it without its corruption. The second definition is almost the same: An accident is that which can both belong and not belong to the same thing. The last definition: An accident is that which is neither genus, nor difference, nor species, nor property, but inheres in a subject. This definition is given by Porphyry through the negation of the other predicables, so that the proper mode of predicating of accident may be explained.

2 The division of accident is: One accident is separable, as to sleep; another inseparable, as whiteness in a swan. But someone could object against Porphyry that the first definition of accident is not good, or that this division is bad: because according to the first definition every accident can be separated from the subject; therefore none will be inseparable; but the division asserts that one accident is separable and another inseparable; therefore they contradict each other. Therefore

Porphyry replies in the 3rd part with this distinction: It happens in two ways that something is separated from the subject: according to the thing, or according to the consideration of the intellect; and in the first way not every accident can be separated from the subject, but it can in the second way; and the definition is understood in the first or in the second way, but the division only in the second way; therefore they are not contrary.

## QUESTION I

Whether accident is a universal, and with respect to which things it has this.

3

It is proved that accident is not a universal by two arguments. First, because the universal does not have on the part of the thing an aptitude for being in many or for being predicated of them, nor does it regard its inferiors by a real relation, but it has such an aptitude only through the intellect abstracting it or comparing it to the inferiors, to which alone it bears a relation of reason; but accident on the part of the thing has an aptitude for being in a subject; therefore it will also have an aptitude for being predicated of it; and since it is really distinguished from it, it will regard it by a real relation, as whiteness regards man; therefore accident is not a universal with respect to the subject; indeed, it cannot even be predicated of it, because what is really distinguished from another cannot be predicated of it, since a real distinction makes the predication false.

Second: the universal is said to be in many and to be able to be predicated of many, even if those many do not exist in act in the nature of things but only in potency, as is plain of the Sun and the Moon; but accident cannot be predicated of subjects except of those actually existing; therefore it is not universal or predicable. The minor is proved: because if no man existed in the nature of things, it would be false to say: Man is white, or Peter is white.

For the solution of this question it should be noted first that accident is considered in two ways. First, in relation to its quidditative inferiors, as color with respect to whiteness and blackness, or whiteness with respect to this and that whiteness; and in this way it does not constitute the fifth predicable, but the first, second, or third, for it is either a genus, or a species, or a difference. Second, it is considered in relation to the subjects in which it inheres, as white in relation to man or a wall. And in this way it constitutes the fifth predicable, because it is predicated in quale accidental.

It should be noted second that accident is considered in two ways: in the abstract and in the concrete. Considered in the first way, it does not express the subject but the form alone, as whiteness and color; and since this is really distinguished from the subject, it is not predicated of it, for it is false to say: Man is whiteness. But considered in the concrete, it expresses the subject, as white; and abstracted by the intellect from diverse subjects, as from man and a wall, it is universal and predicable with respect to those from which it is distinguished only by reason; nor does it have an aptitude for being predicated of them on the part of the thing, but only through the intellect; nor, finally, is it referred to them by a real relation, but by one of reason, just as the other predicables are to their inferiors. But because accident regards the subject according to the mode of actual inherence in it, and in this way is predicated of it, it requires the actual existence of the subjects of which it is predicated; otherwise the predications would not be true. And in this it is distinguished from the other predicables, which, since they are essential, as genus, species, and difference, or proper attributes following upon the essence, as the fourth predicable, abstract from existence and are predicated of their inferiors according to the natural connection of the extremes; and therefore they do not require their actual existence.

5 These things supposed, the conclusion answering the question is: Accident taken in the concrete is the fifth predicable, not with respect to its quidditative inferiors but with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted and of which it is predicated in quale accidental; and taken in this way it is defined by Porphyry by a twofold

[p. 187]

> definitione, inferius explicanda. definition, to be explained below. This conclusion is proved: because accident taken in this way is one in many accidentally, and therefore predicable of many in quale accidental, and distinct from the other four predicables.

To the first argument, the minor is to be denied, namely that accident has a real aptitude for inhering or being in many on the part of the thing: for if it is taken in the abstract, this is true; but so taken it is not universal or predicable, but expresses an accidental form really distinct from the subjects and really inhering in them, which cannot really be predicated of them, on account of the real distinction; but if it is taken in the concrete, with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted, it is universal and predicable, as has been explained.

To the second, the minor is to be distinguished: for in order that accident be universal and predicable, it is enough that it regard several subjects existing according to potency; but for the exercise of predications it requires the actual existence of the subjects; and in the first it agrees with the other predicables, from which it is distinguished in this second, on account of the distinct, accidental mode of predicating which it has; for accident regards the subject according to actual inherence in it, and actual inherence requires the actual existence of the subject, because nothing can inhere except in what actually exists; but of the other predicables the ratio is different as regards the exercise of predicating, as has already been explained.

## CHAPTER II

Whether the division of accident into separable and inseparable accident is good.

t seems to be proved by two arguments that it is not good. First, be‐

I       cause accident according to Porphyry can be separated from the subject

in two ways, according to the thing and through the intellect; therefore no accident is inseparable. The consequence is proved: because an accident inseparable according to the thing is separable through the intellect; whence accident is not well divided into two members.

Second: because if every accident is separable through the intellect, then this division comprehends the proper attribute, which although it cannot be separated according to the thing, can nevertheless be through the intellect, as risible can be separated from man: because, since it is not of his essence, man can be understood without it. And from this it follows that the fourth predicable and the fifth are not distinguished. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute, which constitutes

the fourth predicable, pertains to the fifth, since it is an inseparable accident.

For the solution of the question, the distinction is to be noted which St. Thomas gives in the single question On Spiritual Creatures, last article, ad 7, where he says that the operation of the intellect by which it separates one thing from another is twofold. One is simple abstraction, by which it knows that one thing without the other, without affirmation or negation: as when we understand the whiteness existing in a wall without understanding the wall, yet without denying that it is in it. The other is composite abstraction, by which we understand one thing without the other while denying it of it: as if, when we understand whiteness without the wall, we deny it of the wall, saying: The wall is not white.

8 It should be noted second that this is the difference between the inseparable accident and the proper attribute as regards the second mode of abstraction from the subject: that the subject of an inseparable accident can be understood not only without it but also with its opposite, its essence remaining intact; as a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but with blackness, which is not repugnant to its essence. But the subject of a proper attribute, although it can be understood without it, yet cannot be understood with the opposite one; the reason for which is that, since the proper attribute flows from the essence, and it is impossible that the opposite should flow from it, it is also impossible that it be understood with the opposite; but the inseparable accident does not flow from the essence of the subject, and therefore it is not repugnant that the same subject be understood with the opposite accident. For example, man can be understood without risibility, yet not with the capacity to neigh, because it is repugnant that the capacity to neigh should flow from his essence; but a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but also with blackness, because, since whiteness does not flow from its essence, it is not repugnant that it be understood with the opposite blackness.

Our conclusion is that the division is good. It is proved: because each member is truly found in things, is truly an accident, and together they contain as much as the thing divided; therefore it is an adequate and good division. But it is to be understood really, and not through the intellect, so that the sense is: one accident is really separable from the subject, and another really inseparable from the same; and by this the first argument is solved.

9 To the second, the consequence is to be denied: because a common accident can be separated through the intellect by both abstractions, simple and composite, so that not only can it be denied of the subject, but its opposite can also be attributed to it; which the attribute does not have, because, since it flows from the essence, it is repugnant that the opposite attribute should belong to the subject. And so every common accident

can be separated from the subject through the intellect in all ways, but a property not in all ways; and this suffices for it not to pertain to the fifth predicable.

10 But in order that the nature of this predicable may be better understood, a further threefold difference is to be noted which it has with respect to property. The first is that a property flows from the essential principles of the subject; a common accident does not flow from them, but comes from other causes. The second: that an attribute belongs primarily to the species and secondarily to the individuals; a common accident, on the contrary, belongs primarily to the individuals, and by reason of them to the species. And the reason for this difference is that a property flows chiefly from the specific nature, but a common accident follows from particular individual causes. The third difference is that a property is predicated per se of the subject, but an accident, which is the fifth predicable, per accidens.

## QUESTION III

Whether the definitions of accident are understood by Porphyry of the real inherence of the accident in the subject, or in terms of second intention, of affirmation and negation.

11

It seems that they are understood in this second way and not in the first, which is proved from the same Porphyry, who assigned the last definition through the negation of the other predicables; therefore he defines accident as a predicable, and consequently not through real inherence but through predication. And moreover, because, in order to explain that the division is not contrary to the first definition, he taught that accident can be separated from the subject not only according to the thing but through the intellect; therefore when he asserts in the first definition that it can come to and go from the subject, he speaks not of real inherence but of predication.

And it is then proved by reason. First, because accident according to real inherence does not pertain to the Dialectician but to the Philosopher; therefore in Dialectic it ought not to be defined through it, but through predication, which is proper to Dialectic.

Second, accidents of reason, such as second intentions are when they are predicated of first ones, pertain to this predicable, and do not have real inherence in the subject, but are only objectively in the intellect; and yet the definitions of accident belong to them; therefore they are not understood of real inherence, but of predication. This opinion is held by Cajetan on the present chapter, doubt 1; Javelli, tract. 4, on the five predicables, ch. 6; Soto in the exposition of the text; and Toledo, doubt 3, says that it is probable.

[p. 190]

12 The second opinion affirms that the same definitions are understood by

Porphyry of the real inherence of the accident; and this is more probable. It is proved effectively from Porphyry, who, in order to explain that the first definition is not contrary to the division, gives different modes of separation of the accident from the subject, namely real and through the intellect; which would not be necessary if the definition were understood of predication and not of real inherence: for predication, if it is negative, expresses separation through the intellect.

It is proved second: because accident is taken in the definitions in the same way as in the division; but the division cannot be understood of predication, but of real separation, for in the first sense no accident would be inseparable; therefore the definitions are understood of real inherence.

To the first testimony it is replied that Porphyry defined accident not through the negation of the other predicables alone, but through real inherence, which he placed in the last word of the definition. The second testimony rather proves our view.

To the first argument it is replied that real inherence is the foundation of the second intention, which it was necessary to explain through the definitions, so that the nature of this predicable might be better understood.

To the second we say that beings of reason do not have real inherence in a subject, but are understood by us through likeness to real accidents, which have it; and therefore we also speak of them as if they really inhered; wherefore the definitions of accident are applied to them through likeness.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the first definition of accident is good.

13

The reason for doubting is that there are many accidents which corrupt the subject, as a lethal disease, burning, and death; therefore the definition does not belong to them, because they cannot come and go without the corruption of the subject.

The difficulty of this question consists in this: whether the things enumerated in the argument are accidents or not. And the first opinion denies that they are accidents, but says rather that they are destructions of substance, or substantial predicates taken privatively. It proves this: because corruption or death is the dissolution of the principles of life; but the principles of life are substantial; therefore corruption and death will be something substantial rather than accidental.

[p. 191]

Quod verò ad veritatem pro- pofitionumattinet,nempe: Homoeſtmortuus , vel Domus

For the solution of the question it should be noted that death can be taken in two ways: first, for the corruption of a thing in its becoming, that is, while it is coming to be; or for the corruption in its having been made, or already made. And it is certain that, taken in either way, it has at least the mode of an accident, and consequently a subject; and since it is as it were a privative change, it has not only a subject but also a term, as it were the thing made through it. And its subject is the matter, which is changed from the form that is corrupted to the form newly supervening: as from the form of man, which ceases to be in the matter, to the form of the corpse, which newly supervenes. But the term of corruption is the not-being of the thing, as the not-being of the man. And corruption denominates the matter as its subject, inasmuch as it is its change, and also the term, namely the thing corrupted, at whose not-being it terminates; and so the matter is denominated privatively, changed through corruption, as the subject of this privative accident; and that which ceases to be through it is said not to be, or to be dead or corrupted. And just as it is an accident of the matter as of the subject in which it is understood to inhere, so with respect to it the definition of accident belongs to it, because it comes to and goes from the matter without the matter’s corruption; but it does not denominate the term as a subject, but as the term which it destroys, and therefore it is not an accident with respect to it, nor does the definition of accident belong to it.

14 Our view, then, is that all the things enumerated in the argument are accidents, or at least have the mode of accidents, to which the definition belongs in its own way. This is proved evidently of disease, even lethal disease, by this argument: Disease comes and goes without the corruption of the subject; therefore the definition of accident belongs to it. The antecedent is proved: because as long as the disease lasts the subject remains, and when it is absent it also remains; therefore it can come and go without its corruption.

Second, it is proved of burning and death: for these have the mode of a privative change; but the subject is one in many, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1 and 5; therefore it is an accident: wherefore they must have the mode of accidents, to which the definition may belong.

From these things the reply would be given to the argument: disease is an accident and can come to and go from the subject without its corruption, because as long as it lasts the subject is not corrupted but remains. But of burning and death we say that they are privative accidents of the matter, to which they come and from which they go without its corruption; yet they are not accidents of the man or of the house, but they denominate the one and the other as terms. As for the truth of the propositions, namely The man is dead, or The house

is burned, we say that they are true, as the common mode of conceiving and speaking holds, because the sense is: The man has ceased to be, or the house; and it is true indeed, because they are denominated not as subjects but as terms of the corruption, as if it were said that the man and the house have perished through death or burning; for death is called the corruption of the man, because it is the privation of life; but burning is not the corruption of the house, but such a burning.

15 Finally, concerning the ratio of accident, two things are to be noted. The first: accident is taken in two ways, namely for the accident of the categories and for the predicable accident; and this acceptation is more universal, because it comprehends not only true accidents but also those which, although they are substances, yet relate to others in a certain accidental mode, and therefore, on the part of the mode of relating, seem to regard them as subjects: as difference, with respect to the genus, is called a predicable accident, although it is often a substance, because it can come to and go from the genus, its essence remaining intact. But categorial accident comprehends only true accidents; yet on the other side the same accident, as predicable, is less universal: because categorial accident comprehends all true accidents absolutely, but predicable accident does not comprehend them except under a limited consideration, that is, insofar as they can come to and go from the subject, or be predicated and not be predicated of it. For whiteness or blackness, and so of the other accidents, are considered in two ways. First, according to their own essences, as there are in them genera, species, and individuals; and so they pertain to the special categories, and not to the fifth predicable, but to the first, second, or third. In another way, in relation to the subject to which they can come and from which they can go; and so they pertain to the fifth predicable.

From these things a certain quite necessary distinction of accidental predication is understood: for one is accidental from a categorial accident, when what is predicated is a true accident inhering in the subject of which it is predicated. The other is accidental from a predicable and not categorial accident, whose predicate is not a true accident of the subject, but relates to it in an accidental mode, inasmuch as it can come to and go from it without its corruption: as this predication, Man is white, is accidental from a categorial accident and also from a predicable one; but this one, Animal is rational, not from a categorial accident, but only from a predicable accident.

16 It should be noted second that accident, as it is the fifth predicable, is not to be defined through several species or several individuals

as through its subjects: because, although both the former and the latter are true subjects of the accident, yet each is inadequate; and so it is to be defined through that more universal thing which is as it were its adequate subject and, taken in the plural, the adequate term of the relation of the same accident as predicable.

Whence its adequate definition will be this: An accident is that which is predicated of many in quale accidental. By this definition, by reason of the last particle, it is plain that it is distinguished from the other predicables. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the predicables.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident.

17

Inherence is twofold, actual and aptitudinal. Actual inherence is a certain mode through which the accident is united to the subject, so as to be sustained by it; and it is proportioned to the per se mode of substance, through which it subsists in itself and per se independently of another. Whence, just as the mode of subsistence is the ultimate term of a substantial nature existing per se, by which it is completed and constituted in a supposit, so actual inherence is the ultimate term of an accidental nature actually existing, completing it and constituting it in act in the subject. And finally, just as subsistence, presupposing actual existence (not really distinct from the substantial nature, but through which it is outside its causes), is distinguished from the nature of the thing from the same substantial nature existing per se, by the same reason the actual inherence of an accident, presupposing, in our mode of understanding, the accidental nature actually existing, is distinguished from it from the nature of the thing.

The other is aptitudinal inherence, which is nothing other than the aptitude of the same accidental nature for actually inhering in the subject: as, if God should separate an accident from the subject, the mode of its actual inherence, through which it actually inhered in the subject, will perish; but it will still be apt to inhere in it; and this aptitude for inhering is called aptitudinal inherence.

And concerning actual inherence it is certain among all that it is not of the essence of accident, because without it there can be an accident, if not naturally, at least by divine power; and indeed the quantity of the Eucharist remains without the actual inherence which it had in the substance of the bread. From which an evident argument is deduced proving that it does not pertain to its essence; and since the same reason holds of the other accidents, it follows that actual inherence is essential to no accident; in which it is also likened to substantial subsistence, of which it is evident that it does not pertain to the essence

of the substantial nature, since it is certain in faith that the human nature of Christ does not have its own subsistence, but is terminated by the subsistence of the divine Word. Therefore the title of the question asks only about aptitudinal inherence, whether it is of the essence of accident.

18 And the first opinion is that of Scotus, In 4, d. 12, single q., and of Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 7, q. 1, with the other disciples of Scotus, who assert that it does not pertain to its essence, but is outside it. They prove this, first, because inherence is a relation of the accident to the subject, or at least includes a relation; therefore it cannot be of the essence of any absolute accident; indeed, it must presuppose some accidental ratio in that to which it belongs, through which such a relation is founded, and consequently the essence of the accident founding it; wherefore it will be altogether outside it.

Second: if aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident, it must belong to all equally, because the things that are essential must belong equally to all of that order; but it neither belongs to all nor can belong equally; therefore it is not essential. The minor is proved: because the mode which the quantity of the Eucharist has, separated from the substance, is an accident, since it terminates an accidental nature; and the aptitude for inhering is repugnant to it, since it is a mode of being per se and independently of the subject; therefore it does not belong to all accidents; nor yet equally, because then it would belong to them univocally, which we shall see is false.

The second opinion is the common and true one: that aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident. So St. Thomas, In 4, d. 18, q. and a. 1, q. also 1; Capreolus, In 4, d. 2, q. 1, ad 1 against the 5th and 6th conclusions; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 4, q. 9; Javelli, Metaph. 7, q. 1; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15. And it is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 2, where he asserts that accidents are not beings, but beings of a being, that is, of substance, to which in their entity they bear an attribution; but to be beings of substance is to be able to affect it according to their own intrinsic modes; therefore the aptitude for inhering in it is essential to them, according to the mind of Aristotle.

19 It is proved also by reason: because to be per se and to be in another are the intrinsic modes of substance and accident, dividing being per se; but to be per se according to aptitude, that is, to be apt to subsist per se, is of the essence of substance; therefore to be apt to inhere in the same substance will be of the essence of accident. The minor is proved: because for substance to be such an entity that subsistence per se is due to it is essential to it; and this is for it to be essential to it to be the root from which subsistence arises; therefore it is also essential to accidents to be such a nature that there is due to it

actual inherence in a subject: that is, to be the root of actual inherence; and this root is aptitudinal inherence, which will therefore also be essential to it.

To the first argument, the major is to be denied, namely that actual inherence is a relation; rather it is an absolute mode including a certain transcendental respect, of which the minor is to be denied, namely that it cannot be of the essence of an absolute thing, just as the other transcendental predicates, as we shall see in the category of Relation; where we shall prove that, although categorial relation, which is called relation secundum esse, cannot pertain to the essence of an absolute thing, yet transcendental respects, or respects secundum dici, necessarily pertain to the essence of many absolute things.

To the second, the first consequence is to be denied, namely that aptitudinal inherence belongs equally to all accidents, or univocally: for since it belongs to them through attribution to substance, or is itself the attribution to substance, it cannot belong to them univocally, because attribution is repugnant to univocation. And moreover, it belongs to each according to its own mode of attribution to substance, which suffices to constitute analogy, as we shall show in the Antepredicaments, ch. 2. But as for the per se mode of the quantity of the Eucharist, it is not certain that it has it, but it is probable that it is sustained immediately by God; and even if it be said to have it, it is not an accidental nature to which actual inherence is due, but a mode to which it is not due per se; just as to actual inherence another inherence is not due, otherwise there would be a process to infinity; but since it is the ratio or mode of inhering, it is not properly said to inhere. Nor is inherence due to that mode of per se being of quantity, because it is not an accidental nature, but a certain modal entity supernaturally granted to the accident, so that it may be per se, that is, without actual dependence on substance; which entity is accidental, because it gives the accident a mode of being. And so aptitudinal inherence belongs per se only to the accidental nature, just as actual inherence is due to it alone; but it does not belong to the modes per se, but by reason of the nature whose modes they are; just as neither do they inhere per se, but by reason of the nature; and since that mode is neither an accidental nature nor a mode belonging per se to the accident from its own nature, actual inherence is in no way due to it, nor will aptitudinal inherence be essential to it.

## COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK

B R I E F P RO E M .

On the title of this book.

lthough the Greek word Categoria, from its first imposition, is 1

A          so called from predication or from the predicate, yet by the com‐

mon consent of Dialecticians and Philosophers it is now taken for the entire ordering of essential predicates; and the same is the signification of predicament, which we can describe thus: A predicament is the arrangement of essential predicates, superior and inferior, under some one supreme genus, than which nothing is higher, down to the individual, than which nothing is lower.

Whence this work is entitled the book of the Categories or Predicaments:

that is, the book of the orderings by which predicates are arranged according to the different grades of being, from the supreme genus, which is as it were the head of the whole ordering, down to the lowest species and individuals.

On the inventor of the categorial art.

The common consent of the school now holds that the first inventor of this art was Aristotle. For he was the first who taught how to arrange all the grades of being in such a way that all the things of the world might be reduced to certain definite classes, and that we might easily find the nature and essence of anything by recurring to its proper category or predicament.

On the end of this work.

Since the categories are made from simple or incomplex things, it is plain that they pertain to the first operation of the intellect, which is the apprehension of simples, and that they are ordered, for specifying the second, which is concerned with composition and division,

[p. 197]

proximately; but as to their ultimate end, to Demonstration, to which it is established that all the things treated in Dialectic are ordered.

Whether the categories treat of words or of things.

By all is refuted the opinion of the Nominalists, who said that this work, like the whole science of Dialectic, treats principally of words. Which is proved false from this: because words are only instruments which we use in place of things, since we are unable to bring the things that are disputed about into the schools, as Aristotle teaches in Sophistical Refutations 1. It is things, therefore, from which the categorial ordering is constituted, signified by means of words; and therefore the categorial art treats principally of things, and less principally of words, as of necessary conditions.

On the object of this work.

The object of this part of Dialectic is the category or predicament considered in common, as it comprehends under itself all the categorial orderings.

Which is proved from this: because under it are proximately contained all the things treated in this art, and they proximately participate its ratio; which two are the proper conditions of an object.

On the mode of proceeding, and on the ordering of this work with the other parts of

Dialectic.

2

The mode of proceeding which Aristotle observes in this work is simple, because he proceeds by definition and division, through which he teaches in what way simples are to be ordered in the categories.

As for the order of this work among the other parts of Dialectic, it must be explained thus: that it holds the first place among them all, because the ordering of simples, and the ordered cognition of them, is as it were the door through which we enter the remaining parts of Dialectic and the whole science itself.

To which science it pertains to treat of the categories.

Although some assert that the categorial art pertains to no determinate science, but that the intellect

through the natural light, without any intermediate science, can have cognition of this art, and that it therefore pertains neither to Dialectic nor to Metaphysics; nevertheless, since the orderings of predicates cannot be made without an art or science, it must necessarily be said that it pertains to a science, and first of all to

Metaphysics. The reason for this is sufficiently manifest and known per se: because Metaphysics treats of the most universal real being; therefore it pertains to it to consider all the modes of real being according to its proper ratio of abstracting from matter; but the categories are nothing other than orderings of things, from which we know the proper modes of being; therefore this art of ordering things according to the different modes of being will pertain properly to

Metaphysics; and also to Dialectic, but under a different ratio: for to the former according to their proper entities, but to Dialectic in relation to predications, enunciations, and syllogisms.

## CHAPTER I

On Equivocals, Univocals, and Denominatives.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Those things are called equivocal whose name alone is common, but the ratio of substance according to the name is different.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

3

The intent of Aristotle in this first chapter is to explain the nature of

Equivocal, Univocal, and Denominative names: for since the categories are made from things as they are signified by words, the distinction of the things that are to be placed in a category depends chiefly on the mode of signifying of words; and so, from the application of these three words, three other things will be established. First, which things are to be excluded from the categories. Second, from which things the categories are to be constituted. Third, in what way the things of one category can be predicated of the things of another.

And the chapter is divided into three parts, in the first of which Aristotle proposes the definition of Equivocals; in the second, the definition of Univocals; and in the third, the definition of Denominatives.

The definition of Equivocals is this: Those things are called equivocal whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is different. Which contains two parts. In the first it is said that equivocals must have a common name, so that it may be signified

that they are distinct from that same name and are the things signified by it: as the barking dog, the heavenly constellation, and the sea fish, which are the things signified by this name canis [dog]; these are indeed distinct from it, but they are not called equivocals except as they are signified by the name, because things do not pertain to Dialectic except as they are signified by words.

And from this is taken that common distinction by which equivocals are distinguished into equivocated equivocals and equivocating equivocals: so that equivocated equivocals are the things which, as they are signified by such a name, are said to become equivocal in it; but equivocating equivocals are the words themselves, which, from such a mode of signifying, make the things equivocal.

4 The second part of the definition is the one in which it is said that the ratio of substance accommodated to the equivocal name is different. By ratio is understood the definition, or the quidditative concept in those things which do not have a definition. The definition, therefore, or the concept of equivocals, as they are signified by the equivocal name, must be altogether different, so that they in no way agree in it, but have only the name in common.

The definition of Univocals is this: Those things are called univocal whose name is common, and the ratio of substance according to the name is the same. In which by the ratio of substance is understood the definition or concept of univocals, which must be the same and not different, as we said it is different in equivocals.

The definition of Denominatives runs thus: Those things are called denominative which, differing only in case, have their appellation according to the name from something:

as from fortitudo [courage], fortis [courageous]. In which three things are contained, because in denomination there are three: the denominating form, the thing denominated, and the denominative name; to be understood in such an order that the thing denominated is called such from the denominative name, and this is called denominative from the form; and so the form is as it were the origin of the whole denomination. For example: courageous is a denominative name, in which the thing denominated is Peter himself; but the form from which he is denominated is courage. From which the denominative name itself must differ in case, so that the derivation of that denomination which the thing denominated receives from the form may be signified.

from another, they are called denominatives; but in relation to the things denominated, of which they are predicated, they are truly univocal: as white, with respect to whiteness, from which it is denominated, is called denominative; but with respect to this and that body, namely a wall and a man, of which it is predicated, it is univocal; wherefore the definition of univocals belongs to all denominatives. So Soto, in the single question on this chapter, ad 2. Which opinion Cajetan says is probable, in the exposition of the definition of denominatives. And it seems to be proved from the definition of univocals: because the denominative name is common to all the subjects of which it is said, as white to man and to a wall; and the ratio signified, which is the accidental form, is also the same in them, as whiteness in the same; therefore the whole definition belongs to them.

And it can be proved second: because every universal must be univocal, as we said in the last question on universals; but among the universals, the fourth and fifth predicables are denominatives, as risible and white prove; therefore denominatives are univocal, and the definition of univocals truly and properly belongs to them.

The second opinion is that of Toledo, who, although he seems altogether to deny that denominatives are univocal, nevertheless asserts one thing from which the contrary seems to be gathered: namely, that that particle of the definition of univocals (ratio of substance) is understood of the quidditative or of the descriptive definition, so that it suffices for the ratio of a univocal that the descriptive definition be the same in all the univocates. From which it is gathered that the names of proper attributes, as sensible or risible, are univocal with respect to the subjects of which they are predicated, as sensible with respect to man and horse.

6 Our view, however, is that the definition of univocals in no way belongs to denominatives. So holds Cajetan on the present chapter, and it is the express opinion of Aristotle in the chapter on substance, where he asserts that denominatives are not predicated of their subjects in name and in ratio: because the form signified by the name is not in them quidditatively, but accidentally.

And it is proved by reason: because in the definition of univocals it is said (whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same); but by the ratio of substance all understand either the quidditative definition or the quidditative concept, which properly pertain to the substance of the thing; but this is not found in denominatives: because the thing signified by them is neither the quidditative definition with respect to the inferiors nor their quidditative concept, but an accidental form; therefore they are not univocal.

To the first argument, the minor is to be distinguished: for the ratio signified

by the name can be common in two ways: either as the same in the inferiors essentially, or accidentally. And in the first way it must be common for the name to be univocal; for this is what Aristotle means by those words (the ratio of substance accommodated to the name) in the definition of univocals, because the ratio of substance is the same as the essential ratio. But the significate of denominatives is common and one in the inferiors only accidentally; and therefore the definition of univocals cannot belong to them.

7 The second argument is solved by another distinction. Univocal is taken in two ways: properly, for that of which not only the name is common to the univocates, but also the definition or quidditative concept; and only this did

Aristotle define in the present chapter. The other is improper univocal, whose significate is common to the inferiors only accidentally; and in this way, improperly, denominatives can be called univocal. And although this does not suffice for the definition of univocals to belong to them, it does suffice for them to be universals and predicables: for to the ratio of universal it suffices that something be univocal only as it is distinguished against the equivocal and the analogous, which denominatives have through an improper univocation.

T R E AT I S E O N T H E A N A L O G Y

## OF NAMES

he treatment of the nature and ratio of analogy pertains for the 8

T           most part to Metaphysics, since it is found chiefly in being taken

most universally, which is its proper object, and also in its attributes, and in accident, a name common to the categories. But it pertains properly to Logic in order that from it we may know that analogous terms are to be excluded from the categories, and also from syllogisms and other argumentations, which can conveniently be made only in univocal terms. Aristotle, however, did not define analogous terms in the present chapter, but only equivocal and univocal ones: because, since analogous terms are as it were midway between these extremes, once univocals and equivocals are known it is easy to know analogous ones. Concerning these only five things are to be disputed. First, what analogy is. Second, how manifold it is. Third, whether the analogous term can be abstracted or prescinded from the analogates. 4. Whether being is analogous with respect to God and creatures, and to created beings, substantial and accidental; and by what analogy it signifies all these. 5. Whether accident, with respect to the nine categories of accidents, is analogous or univocal.

It is explained what analogy is.

9

If we wish to define analogy from the very signification of the name, we shall have to say that it is nothing other than a proportion, or agreement, or comparison among many things signified by the same name. For it is a Greek name, which Quintilian, rendering it in Latin, calls proportion; while Cicero in one place calls it agreement, and in another comparison, or proportion. And all these significations can belong to different analogous terms, or to the same ones under different consideration, as will be able to appear when we enumerate the different species of analogy.

But if we consider rather the thing signified by the name of analogy than the etymology of the same name, we can easily gather the definition of analogous terms from the definitions of equivocals and univocals assigned by

Aristotle in the present chapter. For analogous terms, according to the common opinion of the school, are something midway between equivocals and univocals. Now Aristotle defines equivocals thus: Those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether different: as dog, with respect to the barking animal, the fish, and the heavenly star. Univocals: those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether the same. Analogous terms, therefore, will be those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether different nor altogether the same. According to this, analogous terms participate in both extremes: for they agree with equivocals and univocals in the name, which must be common in all of them; but in the thing or concept signified by the name they partly agree and partly differ. They agree with equivocals in this, that it must be different simply; and in this they differ from univocals, in which it must be the same simply. But they differ from the same equivocals in this, that it is not altogether different, but in some way one or the same; and in this they resemble univocals. From which it follows that they have greater similarity with equivocals. And this is the reason why they are customarily enumerated with equivocals, and are even called equivocal: because they are distinguished from them only a little.

10 Thus the concept of the analogous term, as regards the things signified, is not one but several, because the analogates are different; yet by reason of proportion, or attribution, or proportionality, they have a certain similarity, and by reason of it some unity; and this is for the ratio of substance accommodated to the name to be neither altogether different nor altogether the same, but proportional or similar.

How manifold analogy is.

11

Cajetan, in the opuscule On the Analogy of Names, ch. 1, 2 and 3, distinguishes a threefold analogy. The first, of Inequality, which is found in genera with respect to their species, by which, by reason of the differences, they are participated according to an inequality of perfection: as in animal with respect to man and lion; for it is participated more perfectly by man, by reason of the more perfect difference, and therefore unequally by the two.

But he says that this analogy is not such simply, nor does it make a name analogous, because it is found in truly univocal genera; and it can only be called physical analogy, because it proceeds from different physical forms of greater and lesser perfection.

The second species of analogy is that of Proportion of one to another, or of several to one; and this is also called analogy of Attribution, because the proportion that one has to another, or many to one, is a certain relation to it, which is also called attribution. Thus healthy is called an analogous term of proportion and attribution, because it is said of urine and medicine according to the proportion they have with the health of the animal, inasmuch as urine is a sign of health and medicine a cause; and this is to be said by attribution to it. Wherefore healthy, with respect to animal, urine, and medicine, is called an analogous term of proportion or attribution.

12 The third species of analogy is that of Proportionality. Proportionality is nothing other than the similarity or proportion of two proportions. For example: between three and six there is found a double proportion, and the same is found between four and eight; then between these two double proportions there is found another proportion or similarity, consisting in this, that as three is to six, so four is to eight. This proportion and similarity of two proportions, therefore, is called proportionality. And therefore the name that signifies several things among which it is found is called an analogous term of proportionality. Thus laughter signifies the true laughter of man and the as it were metaphorical laughter of a meadow, which, when it flowers, shows a certain cheerfulness similar to that which a man shows when he laughs. Now the name laughter is said of both, namely of the laughing man and of the flowering meadow, according to proportionality: because as the laughter of a man is to the man, so the floweriness of the meadow is to the meadow. Wherefore it is called an analogous term of proportionality.

Of these three species of analogy, the first is reputed by no one to be true, nor sufficient to constitute an analogous name; but all say that it is not analogy simply, but only

in a certain respect. And the reason of all is that it is found in genera and in many other univocals without prejudice to univocation.

13 But the analogy of proportion, or of attribution, all receive as true and sufficient to constitute an analogous name. And the reason is manifest: because attribution alone, of one to another or of many to one, brings it about that not all are signified in the same way or equally, but that the one is called such simply, while the others are not, except in a certain respect; therefore attribution alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is proved from the definition of analogous terms: Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but by the very fact that the significates are so related that all are said by attribution to one, the ratio under which they are signified belongs to that one first, per se, and principally, and to the others by attribution to it; therefore it is not altogether the same in all: because if it were the same, it would belong to each one equally first and without dependence on the others, as is plain in univocals. Wherefore it is necessary to say that attribution alone produces analogy.

Second, attribution alone takes away univocation; therefore it alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is evident: because where there is attribution of the significates there is no equivocation of the name, since something is common to them besides the name, namely that similarity and correspondence which attribution produces. If, therefore, attribution takes away univocation, it must make the name analogous, because no middle is given between univocal and equivocal besides the analogous. Moreover, the first antecedent is proved from the definition of univocals: Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether the same; but attribution brings it about that the ratio is not altogether the same, nor equally participated by all, but first by one, and by the rest with dependence on it; therefore it takes away univocation.

14 But concerning the analogy of proportionality it is not certain that it is such simply, so that it alone suffices to make a name analogous. The first opinion holds that it is sufficient, no less than the analogy of attribution. So Cajetan in the place cited above; so also St. Thomas seems to think, On Truth, q. 2, a. 11; so, finally, many moderns.

The second opinion is that of other moderns, who use this distinction. Proportionality can be found among the significates of a name in two ways. First, such that it is not itself signified by that name, but another ratio common to them; and taken in this way it does not suffice to make a name analogous

That it is not signified by the name seems manifest: because animal signifies only the sensitive nature common to the species, not the proportionality found among them.

15 Second, such that the analogy itself is signified by the name; and this will be sufficient to constitute that name analogous. And because no name has been imposed by which it is signified, no such analogy is given; it would be given, however, if a name were imposed to signify it. Of which they do not bring a reason or an example. But we can bring both: an example, indeed, in this name principle, which is said analogically of the foundation of a house, of the point, which is the principle of a line, and of the premises of a demonstration known per se; and among these there is no attribution, but all are signified equally and per se; only proportionality is found: because as the foundation of a house is to the house that begins from it, so the point is to the line, and the principles of a demonstration to the demonstration. And because it is signified by the name (since they seem to signify those three by reason of proportionality, and not by reason of another concept common to them), it suffices to constitute analogy.

It can also be proved by reason: because proportionality necessarily presupposes that the things among which it is found are different, but that they receive from it some similarity and unity; therefore it brings it about that the ratio signified by the name is not altogether different, but not altogether the same either, because there is some similarity and unity in it. Wherefore it alone will make a name analogous.

16 The third opinion holds that proportionality, found in whatever way among the significates of the same name, does not suffice to constitute an analogous name; but it is necessary that it be found in such a way that one of them is absolutely such through its form or through its being, while the other is not absolutely such through its being, but as it underlies such a proportion or comparison to another. An example can be in laughter, which signifies the laughter of man and the floweriness of the meadow in such a way that the former is absolutely such through its own being, but the latter not, except inasmuch as it has such a proportion or proportionality with it. For it is manifest that the floweriness of the meadow neither is nor is called laughter except through its order to the laughter of man. So thinks Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaph., disp. 28, sect. 3, no. 11.

Our view is explained in three conclusions. The first is: Proportionality is not true analogy, nor does it suffice to make a name analogous, unless it is signified by it. This seems to me evident, as this argument proves. Things do not have analogy, or

[p. 206]

> vniuocationem,nifi in quantumper vocesſignificantur: ergò nec funtanalogaproportionis vel attributionis, nifi inquan tum,vt eamhabentes,ſignificantur.Cuius euidens fignum eſt quòd quia diuerfo modo fignificantur,perdiuerías voces,fieri poteſt,vt æquiuocèpervnam, vniuocè verò per aliam fignifi-centur: vt Canis , nomine beſtiæ latrabilis , Pifcis, &Sydus, æquiuocè ſignificantur,&vniuocè eademdeſignanturperno-men ſubſtantia : ex eo, quòd ſubſtantia fignificat conuenien-tiam eſſentialem corum: canisverò nullam. Vtigiturnomen fit vniuocum:neceſſe eſt,ſignificet conuenientiammultorum: & codem modo , vtfit analogum, neceſſe eſt , vtſignificetdi-uerfitatem fimul,& conuenientiam multorum, fed analogata, habent conuenientiam,autfimilitudinem, rationeproportio-nalitatis:aut attributionis : cùm diaerſa ſimpliciter: ergo non poffunt,vtanalogata fignificari: niſi proportionalitas ipfa, vel attributio fignificetur. 17 Secundò probatur:Quia licètſignificata alicuius nomi-nis , vniuocamhabeant conuenientiam, fitamennon fignifi-centur,vteamhabent, non eruntvniuocata, necnomenquo fignificantur,vniuocum, fed conuenientiafehabebitmateria-litertantum,aut concomitanter ,& erit, quaſinon effet,ad ef- -fectum efficiendi nomen analogum:ergo licèt aliqua habeant interfe conuenientiam analogicam ,fihæcnon fignificetur, materialiter, & quafi concomitanterfe habebit, & erit quafi non effet,ad effectum conſtituendi nomenanalogum. Quare neceſſe eſt pernomen ſignificari. Secunda concluſio: Proportionalitas, aliquando ſignifica-tarpernomen analogum : & ideo ſi ſignificata ſufficit confti-tuere ſpeciem diſtinctam , ab analogia attributionis , efficiet camdiſtinctam:&ita fatendumerit,eſſeactu, in rerum natu-ra, diuerfas ſpecies analogiæ. Hæc eft contra ſecundam opi-nionem quæ negat, diuertas eſſe ſpecies analogiæ,& analogo-rum,nempeproportionalitatis , & attributionis : quamuisfa-teatur, effepoffibiles, fi nomen imponatur,ad fignificandam proportionalitatem multorum. univocation except inasmuch as they are signified by words; therefore neither are they analogous terms of proportion or attribution except inasmuch as they are signified as having it. Of which there is an evident sign: that, because they are signified in different ways by different words, it can happen that they are signified equivocally by one and univocally by another. Thus dog, the barking beast, the fish, and the star are signified equivocally by the name dog, and the same are designated univocally by the name substance, because substance signifies their essential agreement, but dog none. Therefore, for a name to be univocal it is necessary that it signify the agreement of many; and in the same way, for it to be analogous it is necessary that it signify at once the diversity and the agreement of many. But analogates have agreement or similarity by reason of proportionality or attribution, since they are different simply; therefore they cannot be signified as analogates unless the proportionality itself, or the attribution, is signified.

17 Second, it is proved: because, although the significates of some name have a univocal agreement, yet if they are not signified as having it, they will not be univocates, nor will the name by which they are signified be univocal; but the agreement will stand only materially or concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of making the name univocal. Therefore, although some things have an analogical agreement among themselves, if this is not signified it will stand materially and as it were concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of constituting an analogous name. Wherefore it is necessary that it be signified by the name.

Second conclusion: Proportionality is sometimes signified by an analogous name; and therefore, if when signified it suffices to constitute a species distinct from the analogy of attribution, it will make it distinct; and so it will have to be admitted that there are in act, in the nature of things, different species of analogy. This is against the second opinion, which denies that there are different species of analogy and of analogous terms, namely of proportionality and of attribution, although it admits that they are possible, if a name is imposed to signify the proportionality of many.

It is proved effectively by the example of laughter, by which the floweriness of the meadow is signified together with the true laughter of man, solely because the meadow, when it flowers, displaying a certain cheerfulness, is related as a man is related when he laughs; but this is proportionality; therefore the floweriness of the meadow is signified inasmuch as it has proportionality with the laughter of man. Wherefore it will be false that proportionality is never signified by an analogous name; and consequently it will be necessary, according to the same opinion,

[p. 207]

Conclufiohęc, eft contra ſecundam &tertiam opinionem: &priùs declaranda eſt,deinde probanda.
