should be concerned with a being of reason: for there are many real sciences which are concerned with beings of reason, such as the science of the commonwealth (which they call politics), Music, and Dialectic.

But this solution too is insufficient, and supposes something false. For although sciences are divided into real and rational, and the rational are those which are concerned with directing the works of reason, to which it is not repugnant to be concerned with a being of reason, as is evident of Dialectic, yet no one has called the mathematical disciplines rational sciences, namely Geometry, which deals with line, or Arithmetic, which deals with number; rather they are truly real, by the common consent of all: because they are not concerned with directing operations, as Dialectic is, but with determinate things. But neither can politics be numbered among the rational sciences: because it is concerned not with directing the works of reason, but with ordering the actions of the citizens and of the commonwealth; otherwise Ethics and all the moral sciences would be called rational, which is quite false. Thus, therefore, of politics, as of these, it is true, in the judgment of all, that they are not rational sciences, but real ones, and ones which must be concerned with real beings, not with a being of reason. From which it follows that if number is formally a being of reason, as this solution asserts, it could not be the object of Arithmetic.

56 Our view is proved, second, because number is sensible per se, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, ch. 6; therefore it is a real being, and one per se. The consequence is proved: because the operations of the senses do not depend on the intellect, but are prior to its acts; therefore neither can the objects of the senses depend on the intellect, but they are given in the nature of things before its operation; and therefore they are true real beings. That they have per se unity I prove, because the sensitive power receives its unity from its per se object, under which number is comprehended; therefore it must be one per se, not as it is conceived by the intellect, but on the part of the thing: because the senses are not concerned with sensibles as they are apprehended through the intellect, but as they are in things.

But in order that the probability of the common opinion which we are defending may be more evident, and that the arguments, which are truly difficult, may be solved, it must be explained in what way number is a real being, and from what it has its being one per se: for in this consists the whole difficulty of this opinion. And as for number with respect to its unities, no one can doubt that it is a real being, because three quantities of men or of stones are real; but what that real ratio is by which they are constituted in the ratio of one real number, so that it is separated from a heap of stones, is explained with difficulty, and not in the same way by all who follow this opinion.

[p. 343]

Thus the first opinion is that of Toledo, q. 2 of this chapter, concl. 2, who asserts that number is a real being on the part of its unities, but receives its essential complement from the intellect; and this complement, he says, is the order of prior and posterior which the intellect attributes to the unities, numbering one after another, the third after two, and the fourth after three, and thus constituting the number three and the number four. According to this opinion, therefore, number is composed of a real being, namely of the unities, and of a being of reason, which is the order of prior and posterior; and through such an order the unities are united and make something one per se.

57 This way of speaking, however, cannot be sustained: because according to it number can be neither a real being nor a species of quantity. I prove the first: because either three unities make the number three before the operation of the intellect, or the operation of the intellect must be awaited for them to make the number. If the first is said, it will be false that it depends on the intellect, or receives its essential complement from it; but if the second is said, it follows that it is not formally a real being, but a being of reason; nor is it one per se, because from a real being and a being of reason there cannot come to be something one per se which is a real species of a category. Therefore, if number on its material side is real, and on its formal side a being of reason, it cannot be a categorial being, nor a categorial species. Number, therefore, must have both before the operation of the intellect: both that it is a real being and that it is something one per se. And in order that we may show how it has them, it should be noted that the unities of which number is made have two things. The first, that each is a continuous quantity, distinct from the other. The other, that they are numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; and this too is real and intrinsic in them, just as the aptitude of any thing whatever to be understood by the intellect is real; and just as this aptitude is called intelligibility, so the aptitude of the unities to be ordered according to the order of prior and posterior is called numerability. But just as a thing’s being actually understood by the intellect is not something real intrinsic in it, nor is it a being of reason, but a real extrinsic denomination from the real act of the intellect by which it is understood, so the actual numbering of the unities is not something real intrinsic in them, nor is it a being of reason, but a real extrinsic denomination from the real act of the intellect by which they are numbered. Therefore, although the unities of a number are several beings in act, considered according to continuous quantity, yet the real aptitude to be really numbered according to prior and posterior gives them unity: because from it they have their constituting one real number per se. For example, three men or three stones are real unities according to the real quantities which they have,

and according to the real aptitude which each has to be really numbered by the intellect after another or before another, they make the number three, one per se: composed in its own way of potency per se and act per se. For each unity is in potency to be numbered before another or after another; and the one that is numbered before another stands as potency, determinable by another that is numerable after it. And since the unities have both before the operation of the intellect, namely, being real quantities and being really numerable according to prior and posterior through a real act of the intellect, they make something one per se, real and categorial, receiving no complement from the intellect.

58 From this doctrine two things are gathered. The first, that just as Aristotle often asserts that the same certitude is not to be sought in every matter, or object of which there can be science, nor in every science, but that some sciences are more certain than others, because the matter with which they are concerned is more certain according to a greater or lesser abstraction from matter, so neither is the same unity, or the same mode of being one per se, to be sought in all categorial things whatsoever; but some have a greater unity and are more one per se, while others have a far lesser one, according to the lesser perfection of their nature. But provided they have some unity, it will suffice for them to be placed per se in a category, as its genera or species. For example, in substance a greater unity and a more perfect mode of being one per se is found than in accidents; and among accidents, a greater one in one than in another; but some degree suffices for them to be per se categorial species, at least imperfectly. And of this condition is number, and all discrete quantity, which, since by its own nature it must have parts separated in act, can have a lesser unity, yet one sufficient to constitute certain imperfect categorial species.

59 It is gathered, second, that things which are beings per accidens in one genus are beings per se in another: as a house, in the genus of nature, is a being per accidens, since it contains several natural beings in act, such as timbers and stones; but in the artificial genus it is one per se. So, then, it must be said of number that its unities, in the genus of continuous quantity, are many in act, which in that same genus do not make something one per se, even if they are gathered into a heap; but in the genus of discrete quantity they make per se one number, on account of the real numerability through which they are united per se in their own way, as has been explained.

From this doctrine the reply is made to the arguments. And first, to the testimony of Aristotle, we say that he is speaking of number with respect to its material significate,

Eteodemmodo refpondetur ad confirmationem , Negan-dominorem,quòd numerus nihilaliud dicat,præter vnitates; dicit enim aptitudinem numerabilitatis, fecundum prius , & pofteriuscarundem vnitatum,in ordinead intellectum , à quo

namely, for the unities; and in this way they are called certain quantities and certain ones; but by reason of the formal numerability they become one per se, which numerability Aristotle does not exclude there, but rather seeks it: hence those testimonies contain nothing against our view.

60 To the first argument. The minor must be distinguished: for the unities of a number are considered in two ways. First, according to their material ratio, by which they are several quantities, separated in act; and in this way they do not make something one per se. Second, they are considered as they are numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; and from this they have a unity through which they constitute one number. And when it is said that the order of prior and posterior among the unities is not real, this too must be distinguished: for prior and posterior can be taken as connoted through the aptitude of numerability, and thus it is something real in those same unities, because each, by its own nature, can be numbered according to prior and posterior; but if it is considered in the actual numbering, it is only an extrinsic denomination in those same unities: just as intelligibility in any thing whatever is something real, but being actually understood is only an extrinsic denomination. And to the other point, which is said at the end, that it is not enough that number be one by order, but it is required that it be one by entity: the reply is that numerability does not signify only a respect, but also something absolute in which all the unities agree, namely the aptitude of numerability; and therefore, although number is one by order, yet in some respect it is also one by entity; and this suffices for it to be a categorial species.

61 To the second. The antecedent must be denied, namely that the unities do not concur to compose number through some union: for although they are separated inasmuch as they are continuous quantities distinct from one another, yet through the aptitude of numerability which they have in order to the intellect they are united with one another to make one discrete quantity, of whose ratio it is that its parts are not joined by a common material term, that is, by an indivisible point or any other, but not that they are not united formally to constitute one discrete thing. Hence, although the unities are separated with the separation of the continuous, they are nevertheless united with the union of the discrete; and therefore, although they do not make one continuous thing, they nevertheless make one discrete thing, as has been set forth.

And in the same way the reply is made to the confirmation, by denying the minor, that number signifies nothing other than the unities: for it signifies the aptitude of numerability of those same unities according to prior and posterior, in order to the intellect, by which

[p. 346]

they have a unity sufficient to make one discrete thing per se, which the same unities do not have as they are in a heap, in which they do not signify such an order of numerability; and therefore a heap is one per accidens, but number one per se.

62 To the third. Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished, namely that the unities of a number do not stand as potency per se and act per se: for potency is twofold. One receptive of act by way of information, such as is physical matter, from which a natural being comes to be. The other not receptive, but determinable by the act; and it is like the potency of a genus, which does not receive in itself the act of the difference, but is determined by it to the constitution of the species. And such is the potency in each unity, to be determined by another to constitute number; and thus the determining one stands as act per se, and the determined one as potency per se; and this suffices for something one per se to come to be from them, by a certain imperfect unity, through which they constitute one species of discrete quantity. This doctrine is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 8, ch.

8, text 15.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the form of number is to be taken from the last unity, or from all.

his question proceeds on the supposition of the common opinion, 63

T           which we followed in the preceding question, that number is a true

species of discrete quantity: for if it were a being per accidens and did not pertain to the category, it would have no form or difference; and therefore it would not need to be inquired whether it is to be taken from the last unity or from all.

The first opinion, then, is that of Capreolus, on 1, d. 24, q. 1, concl. 5, who distinguishes a twofold form of number, Partial and Total, as must be distinguished in any species of substance whatever. As in man, the partial form is that which with matter composes the nature of man; and the nature itself, composed of matter and form, is called the total form: as humanity is called the total form of man, because together with its substantial mode, which is subsistence, it composes man, signifying the complete nature in the supposit. The partial form of number, then, he says is the last unity, which determines the preceding ones; and thus it stands by way of act and form, and the preceding ones by way of matter: as the form of the number two is the second unity, determining the first to the constitution of such a species; the form of the number three is the third, presupposing two as matter and determining them by way of form. But the total form (he says) is not

the last unity, nor all of them, but the very nature of number resulting from the composition; from which nature, together with the mode of actual inherence, the complete number in the concrete comes to be. He proves this last point by this argument: because in any things whatever the total form, which is the nature, results from the union of the parts; but neither the last unity nor all of them together result from the union of the parts, but rather they are the parts from which the very nature of number results; therefore they cannot be its total form. The first point, however, he does not prove, because it is manifest of itself. This opinion was followed earlier by Albert the Great, in the Categories, the treatise on quantity, and in his Commentary on ch. 5 of St. Dionysius, On the Divine Names; indeed also by St. Thomas, Metaph. 8, lect. 3; and afterward by Javelli, Metaph. 8, q. 10.

64 The second opinion is held by Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 9, where he distinguishes number in another way: into that which is abstracted from particular unities, and signifies only two, three, or four; and into that which is contracted to particular unities and is considered in them, as when we say three bodies, three stones, or three men. The form of abstract number, then, he says is the last unity, but not that of contracted number; rather contracted number is constituted in its species by itself, that is, by its unities taken together, without an order of first or last: as the number three of men, or the number four of stones. And this opinion seems opposed to the preceding one, because this question proceeds concerning real number, taken for the quantities themselves, whose form the first opinion says is to be taken from the last unity, which this second one denies.

65 Soncinas, further, proves the first part of his opinion, that the form of abstract number is the last unity, by this argument: because abstract number is found only objectively in the intellect, which constitutes the order of prior and posterior among one, two, and three, so that just as it does not arrive at two except through one, so it does not arrive at three except through two, and so always to the others; therefore the last unity, in the apprehension of the intellect, presupposes the others, and therefore stands to them by way of a determining form.

But the second part, that the form of contracted number is not the last unity, he proves by a twofold argument. First, because where there is a first and a last really, there is some real order between them; but among the unities of number there is no real order; therefore neither is there really a first unity, nor a last, which could be the form of number. The minor is proved: because, if a real order were given among the unities, that order would be either of nature, or of dignity, of place, of where, or of position; but none such is given; therefore they will not have a real order. I prove the minor again: because two or three bodies, from which the number three is made, can come to be at the same time; and thus

one is not the cause of another, nor is it more worthy than it; nor is it necessary that they have an order of place or of position, since they can be constituted in a vacuum: wherefore they will have no real order.

Second: Either the last unity is the form of real number inasmuch as it is a unity, or inasmuch as it is last. Not as a unity, because this ratio is common to all; but neither as last, for two reasons. First, because it has its being last from the intellect that numbers; therefore it cannot be a real form. Second, because the form of a thing must be fixed and invariable; but being last often varies according to the will of the one numbering, so that a unity which is now numbered after the others can in turn be numbered first; hence being last varies through all of them; wherefore it cannot be the form of number.

66 For the solution of this question it should be noted, from St. Thomas, 1- 2, q. 54, a. 4, in the body, that in accidents there is no essential physical composition of matter and form, but that they are certain natures so imperfect that they are rather forms of the subject, through actual inherence in it. And the reason for this is manifest: because matter and form are essential parts of a natural being, which is substance; but accidents are not natural beings, but something of a natural being; therefore they cannot have composition of matter and form. Hence, of the three compositions which are found in substance, namely the physical essential one, of matter and form; the quasi-entitative or substantial one, of integral parts; and the metaphysical essential one, of genus and difference, only the last two are found in accidents; in which it must be explained whether the last unity has the ratio of difference, or whether the essential difference is taken from it.

And let us begin with the composition of genus and difference, as with the essential one. In it form and difference are the same: because, since it is made of genus and difference, the genus stands as matter and the difference as form. It must be seen, then, from what the difference in the species of numbers is taken: whether from the last unity, or from all. And concerning the genus it is certain that it must be defined from all taken together: because the proximate genus of number is discrete quantity, and discreteness is not found in one single unity, but in all; wherefore the genus is taken from all. But the difference too must be taken from all: because the difference contains a grade of perfection determining the genus; hence, since the genus contains the common ratio of extension, or of discrete divisibility, the difference must contain a grade of perfection of such extension or divisibility, which likewise is not found in one single unity, but in many,

and therefore it must be taken not from the last alone, but from all, under a special ratio. And thus the genus of the number three will be discrete quantity, and the difference the extension or divisibility into three unities; and so the number three is defined: It is a discrete quantity extended according to three unities, so ordered according to prior and posterior.

67 But in the composition of the whole from integral parts neither matter nor form is found: because all the integral parts are in act in such a way that none receives another nor is received by another: as among arm, head, and feet there is no matter or form, properly speaking. Nevertheless, among the integral parts of number one part stands to the others as form, inasmuch as it determines them; and thus the last unity stands in number, determining another or others to make a certain number: as the second unity determines the first to make two, and the third determines two to make three, and so of the rest.

Our view, therefore, asserts two things. The first is: The essential form which number can have is not taken from the last unity alone, but from all, inasmuch as they have a special ratio of discrete extension.

This is proved by this argument, drawn from the doctrine delivered: Essential form is only twofold, physical and metaphysical; but number does not have a physical essential form; and the metaphysical one which it has is taken from all the unities so ordered according to prior and posterior; therefore not from the last alone. The minor is proved: because the difference in any things whatever is taken from the whole nature, conceived under a special grade, as in man from his whole nature under the grade of rationality; therefore the difference of number is taken from its whole nature, considered under such a grade of discrete extension. But such a grade of discrete extension is not found in the last unity alone, but in all so ordered, just as discreteness itself is not found in one alone, but among many; therefore neither can the difference of number be taken from the last unity alone, but from all so ordered: as the form of the number three from the unities so ordered that two are presupposed and are determined by the last.

68 The second thing our view asserts is: In number considered as an integral whole, although no proper physical or metaphysical form is found, yet a certain likeness of form is found, and it is taken from the last unity alone; indeed that alone stands as form. This is proved by this argument: That which is determinable by another has the mode of matter, and that which determines another has the mode of form; but among the integral parts

of number, the last unity stands as determining the preceding ones, and these as determinable by it; therefore these stand as matter and that one as form. And this is what the first opinion meant when it asserted that the last unity is as it were the partial form of number, and especially St. Thomas, who understood this same point not of a true form but of some likeness of it. And therefore it is not necessary to reply to the arguments of that opinion.

This only should be noted: the integral parts of number have this special feature, that, since one stands by way of form and the others by way of matter, when the one that stands as form is varied, the essential difference of number is consequently varied: because the mode of extension from which it is taken is varied; as, when the third unity is varied, the same number has an extension in order to two or to four, which is different.

The second opinion, however, did not do well in adducing that distinction of abstract and contracted number: because we are now speaking of categorial number, which is a species of discrete quantity and is found in things; but abstract number is transcendental, since it is found in substances and in the other accidents; and therefore it pertains no more to this category than to the others; indeed, to none; and therefore we need not concern ourselves with it.

To the first argument, then, of that opinion: the minor must be denied, namely that there is no real order among the unities of number. For although there is no order of time, nor of nature, of place, or of position, yet there is an order of numerability, which each unity signifies to the others, inasmuch as it is numerable by the intellect as prior or posterior, that is, as presupposing them or as presupposed to them.

To the second. The major must be distinguished: because the unities of number can be considered in two ways, either as they are actually numbered or as they are numerable; and therefore each has a twofold consideration of being last, namely in the actual numbering or in the aptitude. When, then, it is said that the last is the form either as it is a unity or as it is last, a distinction must be made: for as last in the ratio of numerability it has the mode of a real form; not as last in the actual numbering, because this is an extrinsic and variable ratio, that one intrinsic and invariable, belonging in the same way to all, since any one can be numbered after the others; and therefore being last according to aptitude belongs invariably to each one. And they do not have this from the intellect, but from their own nature; although not without respect to the intellect, yet they have it before its operation. The ratio of last, therefore, is real in each unity, as is the ratio of first or of middle, as has been explained.

## QUESTION VIII

Whether categorial number is found not only in bodies, but also in spiritual things.

70

The sense of the question is: whether, just as three men, three stones, or any three other bodies make a number which is a species of discrete quantity, so three angels or three souls do; and the question proceeds on the supposition that number is per se in the category.

The first opinion affirms that the number of spiritual things is no less a species of discrete quantity than the number of bodies. So Richard, on 1, d. 10, q. 1, ad 4, and d. 24, a. 1, q. 1, and a. 2, q. 1; Marsilius, on 3, q. 27, a. 1 and 2; Gregory, d. 24, q.

2, a. 3; Auriol, as reported by Capreolus in the same distinction and question, where also Major, Ockham, and Gabriel, whom a great part of the moderns follow.

It is proved by the testimonies of St. Augustine, On Free Choice, bk. 2, ch.

16, where he asserts that number is something intelligible, and is found in all things; and of Damascene, On the Faith, bk. 3, ch. 8, who teaches that numbers in any things whatever, different among themselves, are so found that the two natures, divine and human, in Christ pertain to discrete quantity.

It is also proved by reason: because the entire ratio of number consists of many real unities, separated from one another and numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; but all this belongs to three angels; therefore they have the true ratio of categorial number. The minor is proved: because three angels are really distinct, and also really separated, and each is numerable by the intellect before the others and after the others.

71 The second opinion denies that categorial number is found in spiritual things, and thinks that it is to be posited only in bodies. So St. Thomas, q. 9

On Power, a. 7; on 1, d. 24, q. 1, a. 3; and 1 p., q. 3, a. 3; Capreolus, on 1, d. 24, q.

1; Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 13; Javelli, bk. 8, q. 11. And it is gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle, Phys. 4, 6 and 7, where he teaches that number comes to be from the division of the continuous; and On the Soul 2, 6, he asserts that number is sensible per se. But the number of spiritual things neither comes to be from the division of the continuous nor is sensible, because the senses can perceive only bodily things; therefore it is not categorial number in the mind of

Aristotle.

72 It is likewise proved by reason. First, because every species must participate the nature of its proximate and remote genus, placed in the same categorial line; but the proximate genus of number

is discrete quantity, and the remote one common quantity, continuous and discrete; therefore it is repugnant that any number be categorial unless it participates in these two genera. Further: the number of spiritual things participates in neither genus; therefore it is not a species of this category. The antecedent is proved: such a number is not quantity; therefore it is not discrete quantity. The consequence is evident, from the superior to the inferior negatively; and the antecedent is known per se.

Second: because transcendentals do not pertain to any special category, as is manifest of being and accident; but number, in the way in which it is found in spiritual things, is found in any things whatever of any category; therefore it is transcendental and not categorial. I prove the minor: for just as we say three angels or three souls, so we say three whitenesses, three relations, three actions and passions, and so of the other categories.

73 For the solution of the arguments of the opposite opinion it should be noted that, just as unity is taken in two ways: first, as one is an attribute of being, and unity is convertible with entity, and so taken it is transcendental, because it is found in all things; second, as it is a special unity, which is founded on the quantity of a thing, and this is proper to this category: so number is twofold, transcendental, which consists of transcendental unities, and special, which is made of quantities; and the latter is a species of discrete quantity, while the former ranges through all the categories, and therefore pertains neither to this one nor to any other.

This distinction explains the sense of the holy Fathers, who, as is evident from what precedes and what follows, are speaking of transcendental number, not categorial. And even if some word of theirs seems to signify categorial number, it must be understood only by way of likeness.

To the argument. The antecedent must be distinguished: because if it is understood of categorial number, it is not true that it signifies only any discrete unities whatever, numerable according to prior and posterior; rather it must signify special and quantitative unities; and since the number of spiritual things does not have these, but transcendental ones, it is not categorial number, but transcendental.

## QUESTION IX

Whether speech is a true species of quantity.

More difficult is the question concerning speech: whether it is a true species of discrete quantity. And we understand the question as concerning

spoken speech alone: for mental and written speech do not pertain to this category, since each is a quality, the former natural, the latter as it were made by art; but spoken speech, which is either uttered by the human voice or made by other instruments, seems to have a certain extension of syllables; and therefore we ask concerning it whether it is a species of discrete quantity.

And the first opinion is that of the Louvain commentators, in their exposition of this chapter, who deny that speech is a species of discrete quantity, thinking that it is a certain quantified thing per accidens, like white or motion; and Cajetan seems to follow it, in the present chapter, and all the moderns who exclude number from this category follow it.

74 And it is proved by all those arguments by which it was proved of number that it is a being per accidens, and therefore does not pertain to this category, q. 6; which are not to be repeated in this place.

But it must be proved by two other special ones. First, because only these things are in speech: namely the sounds of the syllables; the motion of the instruments or of the utterance, through which come to be the times consumed in that utterance; the order of the syllables; and the signification of the whole speech; but from none of these can speech be quantified per se; therefore it is not to be admitted to this category. The minor is proved: because sounds are qualities; motion is quantified per accidens; times are indeed quantified per se, but continuous ones, which cannot make another species of discrete quantity; the order of the syllables, according to length and shortness, can be changed at will, and therefore cannot make speech quantified per se; and far less the signification of the syllables, which it is certain they do not have from their own nature, but from the free imposition of men.

Second: because successive things cannot have unity except through continuation, as is plain in motion, whose parts, if they are once interrupted by a delay of time, become so diverse that they in no way make one thing; but syllables are certain interrupted motions of the utterance of the instruments; therefore they are altogether diverse, having no union or unity; wherefore they cannot make one quantity. And if you reply that they are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, like the unities of number, and through such orderability have unity, against this is the following: because if motions of utterance once interrupted are orderable according to prior and posterior, then even if they are interrupted for a long time they will be orderable; hence if one syllable is uttered today and another after a year, they will make a speech no less than if it were uttered after half an hour,

indeed even if by different men: which seem not only false but absurd.

75 The second opinion is that of Javelli, in his Epitome of the Metaph., bk. 5, ch. 8, who distinguishes a twofold consideration of speech. For if it is considered, he says, in the ratio of quantitative extension, speech is not distinct from motion, nor is it quantified per se, but per accidens, like motion, since syllables are nothing other than certain motions of utterance. But if it is considered in the ratio of measure, it is quantified per se, and a true species of discrete quantity, distinct from number, since it is a discrete and successive measure. And therefore, he says, Aristotle, considering in the

Dialectic the ratio of measure in quantities, taught that speech is a species of quantity; and he also proved it from the same ratio of measure, because, he says, it is measured by the long and the short syllable. But in the Metaph., where he principally considered the ratio of extension of that same quantity, when he had enumerated the other species he made no mention of speech; by which it is proved, from his mind, that it is not a species of quantity in the ratio of extension, but only in the ratio of measure.

The third opinion holds that speech is the second species of discrete quantity:

which Aristotle not only asserted, in the present chapter, but proved. So St.

Thomas, opusc. 42, and on 4, d. 3, the single question, a. 2, ad 5; Albert the

Great, the treatise on quantity, ch. 2; Scotus, the present chapter, q. 8;

Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 4; Soto, q. 2 of this chapter, and in the same place

Cant. and Toledo, and many moderns. And this opinion, although difficult, seems to us more probable and to be held.

76 And it is proved by this argument: Speech consists of syllables truly extended according to prior and posterior, as number consists of unities; therefore, just as number is a species of discrete quantity, so is speech. The antecedent is proved: because one syllable is longer, and has a greater extension of sound, than another, not only by reason of the time consumed, which is plainly greater, but by reason of itself, namely as it is an extended sound; just as three stones have a substance extended through quantity, and by reason of it they make a species of number. That syllables are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, by reason of length or shortness, is proved: because the speech, or the foot of verse, which consists of two long syllables is distinct from that which consists of two short ones, or of one short and the other long, from the fact that the syllables are ordered in a distinct way; therefore of themselves they are orderable

In what the quantity of speech is to be placed. 77

which it is said to consist; concerning which those who follow our view do not think in the same way.

But the first opinion is that of many moderns, who teach that the quantity of speech consists neither in the syllables nor in anything else of those which can be considered in speech, but in the motions of utterance, discontinuous and orderable by the intellect: as in the three motions of utterance by which this speech, Dominus [Lord], is uttered, they say its discrete and successive quantity consists.

This opinion, however, is false, which I prove by this argument: Motion is quantified per accidens; therefore a number of several motions is not categorial. The consequence is proved, from the superior to the inferior negatively: the number of three motions is not quantity per se; therefore neither is it discrete quantity. Second, because the number of motions is like the number of white things or of angels: it is transcendental, and not categorial.

Therefore the second opinion, that of many, places the quantity of speech not in the syllables, nor in the motions of their utterance, but only in the times by which the motions of the utterance themselves, and also the syllables, are measured, inasmuch as two or three times consumed in them are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior.

This they gather from Aristotle, in the present chapter, who proved that speech is a quantity because it is measured by the long and the short syllable; but the length or shortness of syllables is taken from the greater or lesser time by which they are measured; therefore the quantity of speech consists in these times, in the mind of Aristotle.

But neither does this opinion seem true to me, which I prove thus: Just as number is a multitude of unities orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, so speech is a multitude of syllables orderable according to length and shortness, from whose diversity all distinguish the diverse speeches; but times are not syllables; indeed, they are very different from them; therefore a multitude of times cannot be speech.

Second: Either distinct times constitute speech according to themselves, or inasmuch as they are the measure of syllables; each way is impossible; therefore they cannot constitute speech. The minor is proved: because the species of quantity are constituted through diverse rationes of extension; but times, from the fact that they are the measure of syllables, do not have a special ratio of extension distinct from the one they have according as they are many times; for no new ratio of extension accrues to times from their being the measure of syllables, just as none does from their being the measure of motions; for the utterance of syllables is a certain local motion of the instruments: therefore, if this

taken in this way they do not make a species of discrete quantity, neither will they make one as they are the measure of syllables. That distinct times as such do not make speech is proved: because if they did so make speech, then wherever they were found, even without syllables, they would make it. The consequence is evident, because what belongs to something as such will belong to it wherever it is found. And moreover, because three times receive nothing from the syllables by reason of which they could make a discrete quantity. But the consequent is false: because no one has ever said, nor can it be understood, that three durations of three heatings are speech.

In order, then, that we may understand in what the quantity of speech consists, it should be noted that two things are to be considered in a vocal sound. The first, that it is a sound made through the local motion of the tongue, teeth, and palate, and of the other instruments. The second is the extension or corpulence of that same sound or vocal sound, which is nothing other than its dilation or prolongation. For it is known that a syllable uttered slowly has a greater dilation or prolongation than one which is uttered quickly; indeed, the very nature of syllables composed of several letters, and of certain others, is such that they are uttered more slowly, e.g. (stirps), (traps), than these two, (e), (a). Such a dilation or prolongation of the vocal sound, then, is as it were its corpulence or magnitude, and so it is called its extension: just as the length or breadth of a substance is its extension. Hence, just as substance is extended per accidens, and its length or breadth is quantity or extension per se, so sound or vocal sound is extended per accidens, but its dilation, prolongation, and corpulence is quantity per se. And thus from many extensions of syllables succeeding one another speech comes to be, as from many extensions of substance number comes to be. Nor is it surprising that sound so made has its own extension, since it is a bodily quality: as whiteness and the other qualities have their own extension, belonging to them accidentally. But this extension of speech, which we call the prolongation or dilation of the sound, is not another one really distinct from the extension or quantity of the struck air; just as the vocal sound is not anything other than a sound caused by the striking of the air through such instruments and extended in the same air; but it is the same extension of the air by which the sound itself (which is a certain bodily quality) is extended. And this extension of the syllables is distinct from the motion of utterance, as is evident, and also from the time consumed in the utterance; but it is comprehended under the syllable and signified by the name of syllable. And therefore a multitude of syllables succeeding one another, as orderable

by the intellect according to prior and posterior by reason of length and shortness, is called speech.

79 And from this doctrine the testimony of Aristotle adduced for the second way of speaking, concerning times, is easily explained: for his argument by which he proved that speech is a quantity, because it is measured by the long and the short syllable, is as it were from an exterior sign: for times are an extrinsic measure of the syllables, but through such extrinsic measuring we know the proper extension of speech, consisting in the magnitude of the syllables, or in their dilation or corpulence, through which they are formally called long or short, formally and as it were intrinsically.

The arguments of the first opinion are also easily solved. For to the first the reply is that in the antecedent the things that are in speech are not sufficiently enumerated, but the principal one is left out, namely the extension or dilation and corpulence of the sound, in which the proper quantity of syllables consists; just as the extension of substance, or of other qualities, consists in breadth or depth.

To the second. The minor must be denied, namely that syllables are motions of utterance; rather they are certain articulated sounds, made through the motions of utterance; of which it must be denied that they do not have a unity sufficient to constitute speech: for they have the same unity as number, namely that they are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, by reason of length and shortness. It must also be denied that a syllable uttered today can be ordered in the manner of speech with one that is uttered after a year: because, since syllables are orderable by the intellect of the one uttering them, and in order to human concord and harmony, they must have an interruption in order to such an end, that is, so much and no greater as would be repugnant to that same end; and it would be repugnant if the second were uttered after a year, indeed if after a month or a day, and perhaps if after an hour. Wherefore they will not be orderable with so great an interruption, nor make speech.

## QUESTION X

Whether, if a line, surface, or body, or another quantity infinite in act were given, it would be placed in this category.

80

This question is not absolute but conditional: because we are not now disputing whether it is possible or impossible that some quantity infinite in act be given; but the title of the question asks under a condition: whether, if it were given, whether possibly or impossibly,

some quantity infinite in act, it would be placed in this category.

And the negative part, that it would not be placed in the category, is proved by the testimony of Aristotle and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, Metaph. 5, text 10, speaks thus: A multitude, then, is a quantity if it is numerable; and a magnitude, if it is measurable. But if a multitude infinite in act were given, it would not be numerable, nor would a body infinite in act be measurable; therefore they would not be quantified things in the mind of Aristotle, nor consequently would they be placed in this category.

And St. Thomas, in his Commentary on the same place, lect. 15, teaches that if a length were infinite in act, it would not be a line: because a line is a measurable length, and therefore it is placed in the definition of line that it is a length closed by two extreme points.

81 And it is proved by reason. First, because quantity stands in its categorial order as substance does in its own; but a substance infinite in act, such as God is, is not placed in the category, as we said in q. 2 of the preceding chapter; therefore neither would an infinite quantity be placed in the category.

Second: The ratio of continuous and discrete quantity is the same, as far as pertains to the present question; but if an infinite multitude of bodies were given, it would not be placed in the category under the genus of discrete quantity; therefore, if a continuous quantity infinite in act were given, it would not be placed in the category under the genus of continuous quantity. The minor is proved: because the species of number are varied by the addition of a unity: as, if you add one to two, it passes at once into another species, of three; if, therefore, a multitude infinite in act were given, it would not have a determinate species; and what does not have a determinate species cannot be under a determinate genus; therefore neither under a determinate category. Wherefore an infinite multitude could not be placed in this category.

The common opinion of the school, however, holds that if a line or body infinite in act were given, it would be placed in this category no less than a finite body. So Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 15; Javelli, in the same place, q. 17; Durandus, on 4, d. 5, q. 3; Nifo, Topics 8, topic 73; Soto, q. 1 of this category.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 8, topic 73, where he teaches that a finite and an infinite line are of the same species: from which it follows that they have the same genus and difference, and therefore are placed in the same category. And St. Thomas holds this same, 1 p., q. 58, a. 8, ad 2.

The same is proved by reason: Because whatever is composed of genus

and difference is placed in a category; but a line infinite in act would be composed of genus and difference; therefore it would be placed in this category. The minor is proved: because the genus of line is continuous quantity, and its difference extension according to the formal dimension of length; but an infinite line would have both: for it would be a continuous quantity, because it would be joined by points; and it would be extended according to the formal dimension of length; therefore it would be in this category. And if you reply that it is finite quantity, not infinite, from which the category is made, and that therefore it is excluded from the category, against this is the following: that being infinite in act is only having integral parts infinite in act; but integral parts do not pertain to the essence of a thing, as is manifest of itself; therefore, even if they are infinite in act, they will not vary the essence of line, but the infinite line will be of the same species as the finite line, as we adduced from Aristotle. And therefore it will be placed under the same genus, and will be in the same category.

83 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that it is one thing for something to be infinite according to substance, another according to some accidental ratio: because substance signifies the essence of a thing; therefore it is the same for something to be infinite according to substance and to be infinite according to essence; and what is infinite according to essence is infinite simply; but what is infinite according to an accidental ratio can be finite according to essence, because accidents are outside the essence of a thing. Hence it follows that, since all things are placed in a category according to their essences, if they are infinite according to essence they cannot be placed in a category. The reason for this is: because the categories are grades of being, of finite and limited perfection; and the things placed in them under the supreme genus must be composed of a determinate genus and a determinate difference containing a limited grade of perfection under such a genus; therefore what is infinite according to essence can neither be placed under a determinate genus, nor be constituted by a determinate difference, and consequently cannot be placed in a determinate category. But things which are infinite only according to an accidental ratio can well be comprehended under a determinate genus, and also be composed of a determinate difference, and therefore be placed in a category: because, since the accidental ratio is outside the essence, it does not vary it, but leaves it under its proper limitation. And for a line or body to be infinite in act is an accidental ratio: because it is nothing other than having more integral parts, from which the essence is not varied, nor does it grow in perfection.

84 As, if a body has more or greater integral parts, it is not on their account more perfect than another which has fewer or smaller ones, except only accidentally; therefore having infinite parts is also an accidental perfection, by which the essence is not varied; and therefore it will be no less finite and limited to a certain genus and to a category.

To the testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas the reply is that each is speaking of existing quantities, which are finite in act. But what they think of infinite ones, if they were given, as regards their placement in the category, they explain in other places cited by us for the common opinion; and they assert that they are placed in the category no less than other quantities finite in act. That definition of line, however, is the mathematicians’, who deal only with finite lines and therefore describe only these.

To the first argument. The antecedent must be distinguished: because substance and quantity can be considered in two ways. Either according to the ratio of finite and infinite; and in this way quantity does not stand to the category as substance does: because the latter, if it is infinite in act, cannot be under a determinate genus, nor be composed of genus and difference, and therefore cannot be placed in a category either; but infinite quantity can well have all these, and we have already given the reason for this difference. But if they are considered according to the categorial order, they are ordered in the same way, through the division of genera into their species.

Whether infinite number would be in the category. 85

But whether the ratio is the same for continuous and discrete quantity, so that, just as continuous quantity infinite in act would be placed in the category, so also would discrete quantity, such as an infinite number, is not certain. For Soncinas, in the place cited above, asserts that the ratio is the same for both. And he proves it: because, just as for a line to be infinite in act is only to have more integral parts, which does not pertain to its essence, so for a number to be infinite in act is only to have more unities, which are its integral parts; therefore, just as a line infinite in act would be in the category, so would a number infinite in act.

But I hold the contrary: that if a multitude of bodies infinite in act were given, it would not be per se to be placed in this category. This I gather from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 15, where he speaks thus of number: Just as with number, when something of those of which the number consists is taken away or added, it is no longer the same number, but a different one, even if the least is taken away or added, so neither the definition

nor the what-it-was-to-be itself will any longer remain, once something has been taken away or added, etc. From these words there follows a manifest difference between continuous and discrete quantity, in that continuous quantity is not varied by the addition of some part, or of several, but the same line or body remains; whereas number is varied by the addition of a unit. From which it is understood that the units are not related in number altogether as integral parts, but are the foundation of the genus and difference in such a way that through the addition or subtraction of a unit the difference and the species of number is varied. The reason for this is quite probable: because when a unit is added, the disposition of the whole number is varied, and so too its discreteness, or discrete extension, which consisted in such a disposition of the units: as the specific extension of the ternary consists in this, that two are disposed under a third, in which its essential difference consists; and therefore, when a unit is added, the species of number is dissolved, and another comes to be. And that this is the mind of Aristotle is not doubtful: because if it did not cease to be a species of number, or did not pass into another, the likeness of numbers with species would not hold, as is manifest of itself.

86 Hence from this it is gathered that number, in Aristotle’s view, is a subalternate species, which is divided as a genus into the binary, the ternary, and the rest: all of which are lowest species, having under them only individuals: as the ternary has this and that ternary.

It is gathered, finally, that number infinite in act is not placed in the category. I prove it thus: When a unit is added, the species of number is changed, and another comes to be; therefore, when units are added to infinity, the essential perfection of number will also grow to infinity; and therefore number infinite in act will have an essential perfection infinite in act in the ratio of discrete quantity: wherefore it will not be able to have a species, because a species is constituted through a difference of determinate perfection; nor will it be under a genus or a category.

Second: The difference of number is taken from units orderable according to prior and posterior, so that the rest are ordered under some one, as presupposed to it; but units infinite in act are not orderable by the intellect; therefore they cannot constitute a determinate species of number; and what is not determinate according to species cannot be under a genus; therefore neither will it be in the category. The minor is proved: because among things infinite in act no determinate unit can be given under which the rest may be ordered; therefore neither will they be orderable by the intellect.

But the argument for the opposite view concerning continuous quantity has been solved from the doctrine we have handed down.

## LAST QUESTION

Whether quantity is a thing distinct from corporeal substance and from the other absolute accidents.

87

We inquire not only about the real distinction of quantity from corporeal substance, but also from the other absolute accidents to which it gives extension of parts, as from qualities: because the ratio is the same for them as for substance.

And the first opinion denies that it is distinct. It was held by Ockham, in his Dialectic, the chapter on quantity; on 4, q. 4; Quodlibet 4, q. 30 also; and in the treatise on the venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, through several chapters: in which places he affirms that quantity is substance itself, inasmuch as it has parts disjoined in position and locatable, and corresponding to the different parts of place. Gabriel on 4, d. 10, single q., and d. 12, q. 1, a.

1, and lect. 45 on the Canon of the Mass; Adam on 4, q. 5; Aureolus in

Capreolus on 2, d. 10, single quest., a. 1. And it seems to have been the opinion of the ancient Philosophers, such as Plato, who, as Aristotle affirms in

Metaph. 1, text 5, speaking of the material principle of things, posited one matter for natural things, whose differences he said were the great and the small, meaning that matter and quantity are the same thing.

88 And it is proved by reason. First: Because God can separate corporeal substance from every absolute accident, since it does not depend on it essentially; therefore, if quantity is an absolute accident really distinct from substance, it will be able to be separated from that substance. And then, if it remains without quantity, it is asked whether it would have parts distinct in place, as before, or not. If you say that it would have them, it follows that it does not have extension from quantity, but is extended and occupies place of itself: which is to be quantity itself, and not to be distinct from it. But if you say that it would not have them, it follows that its parts are conjoined in place: which is impossible, because, since they were separated before, they could not have been conjoined except through local motion, of which they are not capable without quantity; therefore they are not really distinguished from it.

Second: If quantity is a thing distinct from substance, it will inhere in it; and then either the whole quantity is received in the whole substance and part in part, or the whole in the whole substance and the whole also in each of its parts, in the way in which the rational soul is received whole in the whole body through information and whole also in each part. But this last is repugnant to a corporeal and divisible accident having integral parts; therefore the first is necessary,

From which it follows that substance has integral parts of itself, and not from quantity, since its parts are presupposed to the parts of quantity as subjects in which they are received; but nothing has integral parts of itself except quantity alone, from which the other things receive them; therefore substance, having them of itself, will be quantity itself, and will not be distinguished from it really.

89 The second opinion holds: Quantity is distinguished really from substance and from the other absolute accidents. So St. Augustine, On the Trinity 5, ch. 10; St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15, at the end; Scotus on 2, d. 2, quest. 9, and on 4, d. 14, q. 2; Richard on 4, d. 12, a. 1, q. 1; Durandus and Thomas of Strasbourg in the same place, q. 5; Giles of Rome on 1, d. 2, q. 4; Albert the Great, Phys. 5, tract. 2, a. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 19; and the other interpreters of Aristotle in the present chapter. And this is true and to be held.

It is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Phys. 1, text 15, where he argues thus against Melissus, an ancient Philosopher, who posited only one principle of natural things, and that infinite: If there is only one principle, and infinite, since the finite or the infinite is a proper attribute of quantity, it follows that besides substance there is also quantity, and that therefore there is not one thing or one principle, but a manifold one, etc. Which argument plainly would prove nothing unless quantity were distinguished really from substance; therefore, in the mind of Aristotle, it is really distinguished. And in On the Soul 2, text 65, he teaches that substance is sensible per accidens, but quantity per se: which cannot be true without a real distinction.

The same is proved by a twofold reason. First: Because it is naturally repugnant that several magnitudes or quantities be in the same place, since this could not be without their penetration, which is naturally impossible, from the fact that each occupies a distinct place and is naturally apt to expel another from the same; but both follow if quantity is not distinguished really from substance and the absolute accidents; therefore it is necessary that it be really distinguished. The minor is proved: Because if quantity is the same really with substance, and with the whiteness existing in it, then each will have its own magnitude and extension, distinct from the other; but it is established that they are in the same place; therefore they will penetrate one another.

Second: Because it is certain in the Catholic faith that in the Eucharist the substance of the bread does not remain, but is wholly converted into the body of Christ; yet the experience of sight and touch teaches that the same quantity of the bread remains; therefore quantity is separated really from substance. And things that are so related that one can be without the other are distinguished really; therefore quantity is distinguished really from substance. Here I note in passing that it is dangerous to deny that in the Eucharist there remains the same quantity

of the bread, and to assert that that quantified body of the sacramental species is not the dimensions or true quantity of this category, but the proper extension of the other accidents, such as of whiteness and the others.

To the first argument: We grant the first enthymeme. But to what is asked afterwards, whether substance remaining without quantity would have parts occupying place, or separated according to place, I reply that substance so remaining does not occupy place, nor do its parts; nor does it have local extension, but an indivisible mode, as far as occupying place is concerned. Nor, however, are the parts conjoined through local motion: because they would not be positively conjoined by a local conjunction, but only negatively, from the fact that, quantity being taken away, they have no distance or local order.

But we dispute these things expressly in the books of the Physics.

To the second: We grant that substance has its own integral entitative parts, but not extended nor occupying place, which nevertheless are extended by the quantity received in them. In these parts, then, the parts of quantity are received; and so the whole quantity is received in the whole substance, and the parts in the parts. We deny, however, the consequence, that substance is quantity itself: because it is one thing to have integral entitative parts per se, another to have parts of extension; and the first is granted to substance and to the absolute accidents, but the second to quantity alone, from which all things receive extension: which suffices for a real distinction.

## CHAPTER VII

Containing the category of relation.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Those things are called relatives which, the very things that they are, are said to be of others, etc.

Prima igiturconditio eſt , quòd vno exiſtente in rerum natu-ra,necefle fitexifterealiud :& vno fublato,neceſſe etiam fit

from the solution of which he proves that it is not good. And finally, in the third, he gives a proper definition, from which he gathers the true property of relatives.

The ancient definition of relatives was this: Those things are called relatives which, the very things that they are, are said to be of others, or are in any way whatever referred one to another: as the double is said with respect to the half, and the great with respect to the small, a habit, a science, and a power with respect to their objects.

The first property of relatives was, in the ancient view, that relatives have a contrary: an example of which can easily be pointed out: because if habits and virtues are relatives, among them are found virtue and vice, and other particular contrary habits; from which it is proved that relatives have a contrary.

The second property is that relatives admit of more and less: for one thing is said to be more like another than something else is, and the same thing is more like the same thing at one time than at another.

2 The third property is that relatives are said by reciprocation. Now to be said by reciprocation is not to be predicated conversely one of the other in recto, because one relative cannot be predicated of the other in this way: for it is false that the father is the son. But it is for one to be predicated of the other in obliquo, as the nature of relatives requires: so that if someone is a father, he is the father of a son, and if he is like, he must be like to something. But in order that this property may belong to all relatives, the due assignment of the term must be made; and the due assignment of the term will be made if the term per se, and not per accidens, is assigned.

3 Now the term per se is that which signifies the formal ratio of terminating. And the formal ratio of terminating is that which sufficiently terminates the relation, all other things whatever that can be in the term of the relation being excluded. For example: father is a relative, for which man, or white, or musical is not well assigned as the term, but son: because, although the son must necessarily be a man, and is sometimes white or musical, even if these were per impossibile removed from him and filiation alone remained, it would sufficiently terminate the relation of the father, and it is said by reciprocation with it, not with the others: for we do not say that a father is the father of a man, or of a white thing, or of a musical thing, because these are material or accidental terms, but that he is the father of a son, because the son is the term per se and formal.

4 The last property is that relatives are simultaneous by nature: for which two conditions are required, of which Aristotle touches the first in the present chapter, but the second in the Postpredicaments, ch. 3. The first condition, then, is that when one exists in the nature of things, it is necessary that the other exist; and when one is taken away, it is necessary also that

the other be taken away: as, when a father is posited, it is necessary that a son be posited; and when either one fails, it is necessary that the other fail, at least under the ratio of relative: as, when the son is dead, even if the man remains who was a father, he no longer remains in the ratio of father. But this condition is not sufficient, because man and risible are so related, and are not simultaneous by nature, but man is prior by nature. The other condition, then, is that one relative not be the cause of the other according to the formal ratio of relative, although it can be a cause according to the material ratio: as the father, inasmuch as he is a man, is the cause of the son, not inasmuch as he is a father. When these two conditions concur, then, this property remains explained: that relatives are simultaneous by nature.

5 But against this ancient definition Aristotle proposes a doubt: whether it belongs to substance, either according to itself or according to its parts. And he replies that it cannot belong to substance according to itself: for water is not said to be of something as of a term (although it can be of some possessor); therefore substance according to itself is not relative. But he says that it belongs to its parts, such as the arm or the head: because a head is the head of some man or animal, and so also is an arm. But from the fact that such a definition belongs to substance, at least according to its parts, Aristotle gathers that it is not good: because substance is altogether absolute, and constitutes a category primarily diverse from the category of relation; wherefore, as substance, it cannot be relative.

Therefore in the last part of the chapter Aristotle teaches that it is necessary to assign another definition, which belongs only to true relatives. And he assigns this one: Relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to another: as the whole being of the father is to be referred to the son, and the whole being of the son is to be referred to the father. Relatives, then, as relatives, must have nothing absolute, but the whole being they have is to be referred to another.

6 From this definition Aristotle gathers that the property of relatives is not only that they are simultaneous by nature, but also simultaneous in cognition and in definition: so that whoever knows one relative definitely also knows the other definitely: as if to say, whoever knows one relative must at the same time know the other; and whoever knows how to designate the proper definition of one must know how to designate the definition of the other: as, if someone knows a father, he must by that very fact know a son; whoever knows how to define father must also know how to define son. This is what Aristotle says in the letter.

[p. 367]

## QUESTION I

Whether relation, or the relative, constitutes a special category.

7

We can consider the categories of accidents in two ways: namely, according to the order of dignity, and according to the order in which they inhere in substance, prior or posterior, more or less immediately. And

Aristotle had the first consideration in the Metaphysics, where he treated of them according to their proper entities; but the second in Dialectic, where he had rather to attend to the mode in which they are predicated of substance and inhere in it. And therefore in Metaph. 5 he placed the category of quality before relation, because quality is nobler, since it is an absolute accident; but in Logic he placed relation first, because it inheres in substance before quality does. Which is proved thus: Quantity is what most proximately inheres in corporeal substance, extending its parts; but immediately after quantity relation follows, because before substance is understood to have qualities it is understood to be great or small, double and half, and equal to another; therefore it is understood to be relative before it is understood to be affected by qualities. Hence relation affects substance before quality does:

not indeed by a priority of time, but of reason; because, although in the first instant of time in which it is generated it has relations and qualities, we understand it to have the former before the latter.

But concerning relation, which we understand by the name relative, it must first be inquired whether it is a special genus of being: which is nothing other than to inquire whether it is a most universal ratio, transcending all the categories, or a special one, which contains a special mode or genus of being, as quantity and quality do.

And the first opinion was that of the ancient Philosophers who, following

Zeno, said that the relative is intermixed with, or included in, all the categories, and therefore is not one special genus of being. It is proved by this reason: because relation necessarily presupposes other accidents in the subject: as, if it is a relation of equality, it presupposes quantity; and if a relation of likeness, quality; and so of the other accidents: because relation is found among all; therefore it is included in all and intermixed with all; wherefore it cannot be a special genus of being.

8 The second opinion was that of Plato, from whom Aristotle took it: that the relative is a special genus of being. And this is also the common one in the school, and altogether true. It is proved by this reason: Being is divided into ten categories as into diverse modes of being; and accident is divided into nine, as into diverse

modes of affecting substance; but relation contains a diverse mode of being and of affecting substance; therefore it will be a special genus of being. The minor is proved: because the being of relation is to be toward another, and it affects substance in a mode distinct from the other accidents: for quantity affects it by extending it, quality by qualifying it, but relation by ordering it to another: which mode no other accident has; therefore, as its mode both of being and of affecting substance is special and distinct from the others, it will therefore be a special genus of being.

9 But in order that the truth of this view may be understood, and the argument of the other may be better solved, one thing should be noted: namely, that relation taken universally is divided into three members. The first relation is a universal respect, intrinsic to all accidents, by which they regard the subject, as being able to inhere in it. Another is a certain less universal respect, which is included essentially not in all but only in certain special absolute accidents: such as the respect which habits and sciences, and also powers, bear to their object, by which respect, together with the absolute ratio explained through it, they are distinguished in species. The last relation is a respect that does not pertain to the essence of any absolute accident, nor orders the thing in which it is to another as to a subject or object or something similar, but only as to a term. And the first genus of relation is called transcendental, because it is included essentially in all accidents, and therefore is not a special genus of being. But the second is called relation according to being said, and pertains reductively to those absolute categories in whose intrinsic ratio it is enclosed: as the respect of science to its object pertains to the species of habit, and the relation of power to its object, to the species of natural power: reductively indeed, because they are something as it were completing the essence of these species. The third genus of relation has a twofold condition. The first: it does not belong to all accidents, but only to some, such as quantity, action, and passion, in which it is founded; and not essentially but accidentally. And in this it is distinguished from the first and second genera of relations: because it does not transcend all the categories of accidents, as the first does, although it is predicated accidentally of many of them; for this does not suffice for it to be reduced to their categories, but essential inclusion is required; otherwise all accidents would pertain to the category of substance, since they are predicated of it accidentally. Nor does it pertain to some absolute category, as the second does, because it is not of the essence of anything absolute:

hence it follows that its ratio is special, distinct from all others; and this is its second condition. And the third: that its essence has the mode of a complete being and of a potential whole, contractible by differences, as will be explained in the following question.

11 To the argument of the opposite view, then: granting the antecedent, the consequent must be distinguished, namely that it is included in all: for if it is understood of essential inclusion, it is false; but if of accidental, it can be granted that it is included in every category in some mode, not however an essential one but an accidental one. Hence it does not follow that it is transcendent, or that it pertains to several categories: for to both essential inclusion is required, as is manifest of itself.

## QUESTION II

Whether relation is a special genus of real being.

Having established in the preceding question that relation is a special genus of being, it follows that we should dispute in the present one whether it is a special genus of real being: which is the same as if it were asked whether there is given a real relation which constitutes a special category.

And the first opinion altogether denies a real relation and a real category of relation, and holds that whatever is referred to another, such as a father and a like thing, is called such through a relation of reason alone. So hold many of the more ancient Philosophers, whom the Commentator cites in Metaph. 12, comment 19; whom have followed, among the Theologians, Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 9, quest. 3; Ockham on 1, d., q. 1; Aureolus in Capreolus on 1, d. 3, q. 1, in the arguments against the first conclusion. And certain moderns hold the same: because they think that there is no convincing reason why some real relation should be posited in things.

12 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. 5, text 10, where he affirms that motion does not terminate per se at relation; and he proves it because it is acquired without change of the subject: as, if while one white thing exists at Alcalá another comes to be at Rome, the first white thing begins to be like without a new change of itself, through the change alone of the other, in which whiteness is newly produced at Rome. From which such an argument is gathered: Something becomes relative without real change of itself; therefore without some new real entity received in itself; therefore relation is not a real entity. The last consequence is proved evidently: because if it were a real entity, since it is newly acquired, nothing would newly become relative without a new entity received in itself, nor without a real
