change of itself: because it is repugnant that something newly receive a real entity in itself without change of itself.

It is proved next by reason. First: Because real being is adequately divided into substance and accident; but relation is neither substance nor accident; therefore it is not real being. The minor is proved, that it is not an accident (for that relation is not substance is evident): it is of the intrinsic ratio of a real accident to inhere in a subject, if not in act, at least in aptitude; but relation does not inhere in a subject in any way; therefore it is not an accident. I prove the minor: because the proper concept of relation is to be the ratio of referring something to a term; therefore relation as relation does not regard the subject but the term, nor can it inhere; wherefore it will not be an accident.

13 Second: If relation were a special category, it would be of its own nature a real accident, since it is established that it is not a substance; wherefore it could not be either a substance or a being of reason; but it is sometimes a substance and sometimes a being of reason; therefore it will not be a special category.

The minor is proved: because in the divine persons there are real rationes of paternity, filiation, and spiration, or procession; and they are not accidents, because accident is repugnant to God, but they are substantial relations; therefore relation can be substance. Next, the relation of the genus to the species, and of the species to the individuals, is a true relation, since the whole being of the genus is toward the species, and the whole being of the species toward the individuals; and it is not a real accident but one of reason, as we saw in the Predicables; therefore a true relation can be a being of reason; and therefore it will not of itself be a special genus of real being.

Third: Because relation is nothing other than a comparison of two extremes, as likeness is a comparison of two white things of the same degree; but comparison is a work of reason, which the intellect makes after it has known the nature of both; therefore it will not be a real being, but one of reason.

The second opinion is that of the whole school, which with Aristotle posits a special category of real relation, under the name of the category of the relative. And this is true and to be held; which (unless I am mistaken) can be proved efficaciously by these reasons: not indeed reasons drawn from the doctrine of Aristotle, which in this matter our adversaries do not accept, but from the very nature of things and from the Catholic faith.

14 The first reason is founded on the nature of things, in this way: From the nature of the thing, and before the operation of the intellect, one man is more assimilated to another man than to a horse or a lion; and also one white thing to another of the same degree more than to one that does not have so intense a whiteness; but a like thing is not called such with respect to itself, but to another; therefore, if it is naturally like another, by nature

it is ordered to the other, and a natural ordering is real; therefore the one is ordered to the other from the nature of the thing and by a real ordering; and a real ordering is a real relation; therefore real relations are given in things. And it can be confirmed from creation: for the rational soul, from the fact that it is created by God, is called and is a creature; but a creature is not said with respect to itself, but to another; therefore it is referred really to the creator, and there will be given in it a real relation.

15 The second reason is deduced from the Catholic faith, according to which real relations of Paternity, Filiation, and Spiration are posited in the Divine persons; but one Divine person is referred really to another because it proceeds from it, or because it is the principle from which another proceeds: as the Son to the Father, because he proceeds from him by natural generation. And in creatures one man proceeds from another by natural generation, as the begotten from the begetter; therefore the latter will be son and the former father through true real relations.

16 But in order that the nature of relation may be better understood and the arguments more easily solved, note what St. Thomas asserts, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1: namely, that every category has a twofold concept: a Common one, in which all agree, at least analogically; and a particular one, through which they are distinguished. The common concept is to be in a subject, in act or in aptitude; in which relation agrees with the absolute accidents. But the Particular and proper concept is not taken in the same way in the absolute accidents and in relation, but in the former through special modes of inhering in the subject; and therefore they are called absolute, because they affect the subject as it is in itself. As the particular concept of quantity is to inhere in substance by extending its parts, and that of quality by qualifying it, and so of the others. But the particular and proper concept of relation is not taken through order to the subject, but to the term to which it refers the subject: as the proper concept of paternity is taken through order to the son, as to its term. Hence the absolute accidents are completed by these two concepts, namely of inhering in the subject and of inhering in such a mode; but relation by two others: first, of inhering in the subject, therefore common with the absolute accidents; and second, of ordering it to the term. Therefore it is customarily said to have a twofold concept: one which is called esse in [being in], the other which is called esse ad [being toward].

17 The testimony of Aristotle is to be explained by this distinction. Change is twofold. One is proper and per se such, and intended by nature, which proceeds from an intrinsic principle of the thing, through which a body is moved to receive in itself some absolute perfection: as matter, to receive a substantial form; or a body, to receive an accidental one. The other, Common,

improper and per accidens, which does not proceed from an intrinsic principle of the thing, nor is intended per se primarily by nature, but follows as it were per accidens. And relation cannot be acquired or come to be through the first genus of change: because nature does not intend relation per se, since it is not an absolute perfection of the thing; but it follows as it were per accidens, in both extremes, upon the acquisition of some absolute form, intended per se in them, or at least in one of them. As in the example adduced in the argument, of the white thing newly made at Rome: from whose intrinsic change another white thing, which was at Alcalá, is changed extrinsically. Aristotle rightly asserts, then, that a proper and per se change or motion does not terminate at relation, but that it is acquired without it: he does not, however, mean that it is acquired without an improper and common one at least, since it is true and necessary that the subject, in whatever way it newly acquires a real relation, should be otherwise now than before: which is the common definition of improper change. And it is enough that it be acquired through improper change for it to be a real being.

18 To the first argument: It must be denied that relation is not an accident. And when it is said that according to its proper concept it does not inhere, a distinction must be made: for if the sense is that the proper concept of relation is not of inhering but of referring to a term, it is true. And if again it is said that according to this proper concept, which is toward, it is not an accident, it must be granted: because it is not an accident except according to the common concept of inhering; but it is such an accident, just as any other category whatever is not an accident according to its proper concept, but according to the common concept of inhering, in which all agree. And if finally it is said that the common concept of inhering is transcendental, and therefore necessarily included in the particular concepts of the categories, because if they do not include it they will not be concepts of accidents, nor consequently real: I reply that they necessarily include it, on account of its transcendence, just as they necessarily include the concept of being; yet they do not express it, or do not signify it expressly, but as it were implicitly or confusedly: just as rational includes the concept of being, but does not express it, because expressly it signifies only the grade of rational nature; in which, however, since being is included, it is said to signify the concept of being implicitly or confusedly, not distinctly or expressly. And so the proper concept of relation, through which relation is distinguished from the absolute accidents, expresses only the mode of referring to the term; but because it is the concept of a real form, inhering in and referring the subject, which it constitutes toward the term, it also includes

implicitly the being in, just as it includes the concept of being.

19 And the reason why it does not express it is that the name of relation was not imposed to signify the concept of inhering, but the concept of referring; in which, however, the same concept of inhering is implicitly included.

To the second: The antecedent must be distinguished. For relation is taken in two ways. First, most commonly, inasmuch as it only implies the ratio of referring to a term, abstracting from a real ratio or one of reason, indeed from a substantial or accidental ratio; and in this way it does not make a real category, because it does not imply the determination of a real accident.

Second, it is taken in a more special way, for a real and accidental ratio of referring; in which acceptation it constitutes the third category: from which are excluded, first of all, relations of reason, because they are not real; and to which substantial or divine relations do not pertain, because the divine ones, on account of their excellence and immensity, are not limited to the categorial order.

20 To the third: Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: because things are compared in two ways. First, from the nature of the thing, because their natural rationes are not such absolutely, but toward another, as they are like or equal; and such a comparison is not a work of the intellect, but is found without dependence on it in the nature of certain things. The other is a comparison which things do not have from their own nature, because they are not distinct, or, though they are absolute, they are conceived in order to another; and such a comparison is a work of reason. Real relations, then, include the first comparison, but relations of reason the other; and therefore the first comparison, as real, pertains to this category, but the second, as not real, is excluded from it.

## QUESTION III

What is the supreme genus of the category of relation. 21

There is a special reason for inquiring about the supreme genus of this category: because by this argument it seems to be proved that it can have none, and that therefore no categorial ordering can be made of relatives either. Because the intrinsic ratio of relatives is to be ordered to a term; therefore, whether the relative in common, or relation, is posited as the supreme genus, it will be ordered to a term; and then either to an inferior term, or a superior one, or an equal one; not to a superior or an inferior, for two reasons. First, because a real relation must be between real extremes, really distinct, as will be proved below; but the superior and the inferior

are predicates distinct only by reason, as is manifest; therefore a real relation cannot be given between them. Second, because relatives are simultaneous by nature, but the superior is prior by nature to the inferior, as Aristotle teaches in the Postpredicaments; therefore there cannot be a real relation between them. Wherefore the relative in common will be ordered to a term equal to itself and really distinct from itself. Hence it follows that there are either two supreme genera of this category, or none. The consequence is proved: because neither is placed under the other; but that there be two is repugnant, as are two heads in the same body: otherwise there would be two categories of relation; therefore it will have no supreme genus.

22 On account of this argument the authors are divided. And the first opinion holds that the supreme genus of this category, properly speaking, is not the relative in the concrete, or ad aliquid, but relation in the abstract, which is the ratio of referring to another; and in this way they seem to escape the difficulty of the argument: because relation is not referred to another, but is the ratio of referring; therefore it is not gathered that there are two supreme genera. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 6, sect. 2 and 3; which he proves by a universal reason: because the abstracts of accidents, rather than the concretes, are placed in the category, since they are signified as beings per se, but the concretes as beings per accidens. This opinion, however, cannot satisfy the argument: because, although it were true that abstracts are more properly placed in the category, nevertheless that concretes too are placed there in some way must necessarily be granted, and this opinion grants it; and on that supposition it does not solve the argument.

The second opinion says that ad aliquid, or the relative, is the supreme genus, rather than relation. So Albert the Great, treatise on the category of relation, ch. 2 and 10; Scotus on 1, d. 21, single q. And then to the argument they reply: The supreme genus of the category is ad aliquid, or the relative in common, inasmuch as it implies an abstracted concept in which all relatives agree. And taken in this way it is not referred per se to another, but through the inferior relatives in which the act of referring is exercised: as through paternity and filiation, through like and unlike; but it itself implies only the common ratio of those things that are referred. And so there is a single supreme genus in the concrete, having under it the inferior genera and species, in which it has the exercise of referring.

23 But this opinion is proved false by a twofold argument. First: A common concept abstracted from the inferiors must contain the essential ratio of the inferiors, as the concept of man abstracted from Peter and John contains the essential ratio of man; but the essential ratio of any particular relatives whatever,

[p. 375]

is to be referred to a term; therefore the common concept of the relative, abstracted from the particulars, must contain this. Hence it follows that the relative in common is referred to a term in common, just as the relative in particular is referred to a term in particular; or else that it is not the concept of the relative abstracted from the particulars.

Second: Whoever wishes to define father in common cannot define him except also through a common term, namely through the begotten in common, or through son in common; therefore father in common is referred to son in common, just as this father to this son; and consequently the relative in common to a term in common.

24 But what is said, that relation has the exercise of referring only in singulars, is false, and seems to proceed from ignorance: because the exercise of relation does not consist in some efficiency, nor in some act of the relation itself which it would have in singulars and not when considered in the common concept; but it is only the natural ordering of one to another, always holding itself in the same way; therefore it is exercised not only in singulars but also in universals. This alone can be the difference: that in singulars it is exercised according to the actual existence in them, but considered in the universal it abstracts from existence. And only in this sense can the distinction of relation assigned by some be true, into relation as Conceived and as Exercised: as if to say that relation, as actually existing, is exercised among singulars, which it does not have in the universal, but only the concept of the same exercise. And if the same opinion, or the same distinction, means anything else, it is not to be admitted.

25 Therefore the third opinion holds that the supreme genus of this category in the abstract is Relation in common, and in the concrete the Relative or Ad aliquid, also in common. Toledo holds this, q. 2 on this Category. And it is more probable and to be followed. And it is proved from the common mode of conceiving and speaking about the other categories of accidents, which, as we proved in the Antepredicaments, can be taken in both ways, in the Concrete and in the Abstract; and they are taken in both ways in different places by Aristotle; nor can the concrete be altogether excluded from the category, nor the Abstract either.

But for the solution of the argument it should be noted, first, that the formal ratio of the relative and of the term is diverse: for the formal ratio of the relative is to be referred to the term, but the formal ratio of the term is not to be referred to another, but to terminate the relation of another; and to terminate is nothing other than to be that to which the relative is ordered; and this does not seem to posit anything in the thing which terminates, but is as it were an extrinsic denomination: as being seen in a wall, or something similar.

26 It should be noted, second, that although there are diverse opinions about the term of relation, whether it is absolute or relative, it is nevertheless certain that in relations of the third genus, which are those of the measurable and the measure, the term is not relative but absolute: for the measure is something absolute, not depending on the measurable. For example: science, under the ratio of the measurable through its object, is referred to it by a relation of the third genus; which relation the object terminates under the ratio of measure; but the object does not depend on the science, although the latter depends on the object. And therefore science is called measurable through a true relation; but the object is not called measure through a proper or intrinsic relation, but through the extrinsic denomination alone of the measurable existing in the science. And therefore Aristotle said that the object is not called a measure because it is referred to the measurable, but because the measurable is referred to it as to something absolute. Hence it follows that either every term of relation is absolute, or at least some one is: which suffices for us to say that the term of relation, considered in common, either is absolute or abstracts from the absolute and the relative: because in some relations it is absolute, and in others relative.

27 And from this it is not difficult to reply to the form of the argument: by granting the first consequence, that the relative in common, or ad aliquid in common, is the supreme genus of this category, and also that it is referred to a term in common, not inferior nor superior, but equal to itself; but by denying the second consequence, that there are two supreme genera: because the term in common, under the formal ratio of term, is not a relative, but abstracts from the absolute and the relative, and implies only a certain extrinsic denomination of terminating, not a categorial one, but one which can be reduced to the same category which the relative in common constitutes as the supreme genus, of which it is itself the term. And so the term in common cannot be the supreme genus of the category, because it is not formally relative; indeed it cannot even pertain per se to the category, but only be reduced to the same category of relation, inasmuch as it pertains in some way to the relative in common, which per se constitutes this category.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the definition of relatives handed down by Aristotle in his own view is good.

18

The definition is contained in the text in these words: Relatives are those for which to be is the same as to be related in some way to something.

[p. 377]

Its sense is: relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to a term. But that it is not good can be proved by these arguments. First, because relation regards two things: namely the subject in which it inheres, which it formally denominates such, and also the term to which it refers; therefore it will have a twofold formal ratio: one according to which it regards the subject and inheres in it, the other according to which it regards the term and refers to it. From which I infer that the whole being of relation is not to refer or order to the term, but to have something absolute, insofar as it regards the subject and inheres in it. And therefore what is said in the definition is false: that the relative is that whose whole being is to be referred to another. The consequence is proved: because the relative is called such from relation; but the whole being of relation is not to refer to the term; therefore neither will the whole being of the relative be to be referred to the term.

And it can be confirmed: because this definition belongs equally to relatives of reason and to real ones; indeed to divine and created relatives, of which we have already said that they are not placed in the category; therefore it is not good. The antecedent is proved: because it is common to all that their whole being is to be referred to a term; for it is no less true that the whole being of the species is to be ordered to the genus, and that the whole being of the eternal Father is to be ordered to the son, than that the whole being of a like thing is toward another like thing.

Second: The words in a definition do not imply act but aptitude; but this definition cannot imply the aptitude of referring alone, but also the act; therefore it is not good. The minor is proved: because the relative is not that which can be referred, but that which is referred in act; otherwise that which does not have a relation would be a relative from this alone, that it can have one: because just as it can have it, it can also be referred; which is plainly false.

In order that the definition may be understood, it should be noted that Aristotle, before proposing the several categories, handed down the universal division of real being into ten categories, and consequently the division of accident into nine. Hence it follows, in his mind, that real being is to be understood in the explanation of substance, so that we say: Substance is a real being per se; and in the explanations of the categories of accidents, real accident. And so the definition of relatives must be assigned thus: Relatives are real accidents whose whole being is to be referred to another. And by the first particle divine relations are excluded, which are not accidents; by the second, relations of reason, which are not real accidents; but by the rest, relations according to being said and transcendental relations are excluded, because they are not rationes of referring to a term, but to a subject or an object;

or something similar; whereas the relatives of this category are ordered to another as to a pure term, of which Aristotle understood that particle to another, according to the common exposition of all the interpreters.

Our conclusion, then, is that Aristotle’s definition, so explained, is good: which is proved from the common consent of the whole school, which accepts it, and also by reason. For a good definition is one which explains the nature of the defined and distinguishes it from the others; but the present definition of relatives does this, as is established from the exposition of it handed down; therefore it is good.

To the first argument some reply that relation has a twofold concept: a Common one, with the other accidents, which is that of inherence in a subject, in act or in aptitude, and is called esse in [being in]; and a Particular one, through which it is distinguished from them, which is to refer to a term, and is called esse ad [being toward]. And by reason of the first concept they grant that relation regards the subject, as the other accidents do, but by reason of the particular one, that it does not regard the subject but the term; and therefore that the whole being of relation as relation is to be toward the term, not of relation as accident. And this way of speaking could be proved from St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, where, against a certain Gilbert (who asserted that relation posits nothing in the subject or relative, and therefore is not inherent in it, but as it were assisting from outside), he teaches that relation, according to the common concept of inhering in a subject, posits something in the relative, and that by reason of this it is inherent; but that according to the proper concept of relation it posits nothing in it, but is only the ratio of referring to another.

31 This solution, however, is false, and contrary to the same holy doctor. I prove the first: because relation according to its proper concept, toward, is a relative form and constitutes the subject formally relative: as paternity, under the proper concept of paternity, is a relative form and constitutes the man in the formal and intrinsic ratio of father; therefore according to its proper concept it posits something real and intrinsic in the subject or relative. The consequence is evident; and the antecedent is proved: because the denomination of father, or of like, and any other relative denomination whatever, is not extrinsic but formal, just as the denomination of white or hot; therefore it posits a formal effect in the subject; but the formal effect of any real form whatever must be real; therefore it is necessary that it posit something real in the subject.

32 Second, because if relation according to being toward posits nothing in the subject or relative, then according to this concept it is not something real. The consequence is proved: because every real being either is

Refpondeo adprimum : Secundum verumque conceptum,

substance or accident; therefore it is either a being per se or in another. But relation according to being toward is not a being per se, since it is not substance; nor in another, since it posits nothing in the subject; therefore it will not be something real, nor will it make a real category.

32 For the true solution of the argument, then, it should be noted that real relation, according to both concepts, in and toward, posits something in the subject, yet in a different ratio. For according to being in it posits a certain common ratio, abstracting from the particular ratios of the categories (in the way in which we said above that the analogous is abstracted from the analogates); but according to being toward it posits a proper relative ratio, distinct from the particular ratios which the other categories posit. As the relation of paternity posits the real ratio of father in the man; but this ratio, although it is posited in the subject, is purely relative: because it is posited in the subject in such a way that through it the subject is not such toward itself, but only toward another, namely toward the term. The other categories, however, posit something in the subject according to their proper concepts in such a way that through that proper ratio the subject is such toward itself, and is not referred to another. For example: quantity, according to its proper concept, posits the extension of parts in the subject, through which it is called extended in itself and toward itself; but paternity posits the real ratio of father in the man in such a way that through it he is not such toward himself, but toward the son; and so of the other relations.

And in this way St. Thomas must be understood when in the place cited he asserts that relation according to being in posits something in the subject, but according to being toward posits nothing special through which it is such toward itself, as the other categories posit, but purely and altogether toward another. Which sense he set down most clearly in another place, through which we have explained this one, namely on bk. 1 of the Sentences, d. 8, q. 4, a. 3, ad 4, where he says thus: The weakness of the being of relation is considered according to its inherence in its subject, because it posits nothing absolute in the subject, but only by respect to another.

33 But if someone should say: Then relation will inhere in the subject not only according to the common concept of accident, but also according to the proper and ultimate concept of relation, which is called being toward; against what we adduced from St. Thomas in the preceding question, namely that the proper concept of relation is not taken in order to the subject, as the proper concepts of the absolute accidents are taken, but in order to the term. Moreover, relation will have two concepts which are called in: one common with the absolute accidents, and another proper to itself. The consequence is proved: because it posits something in the subject both according to the common ratio and according to the particular one; therefore according to both it inheres in it and is in it.

I reply to the first: According to both concepts,

[p. 380]

Th. dixit, pro- prium conceptum relationis , non fumi in ordinead fubie- Etum,vt in accidentibus abſolutis , veriffimum eſt : fic autem intelligendum, vt non fumatur in ordine ad fubiectum, vtIn fe,&Adſe eſt,ſed vtrefertur ad aliud, pereandem rationem relatiuam, in eopoſitam. In quo valde differt ratio, propria relationis,à rationibus particularibus accidentium abfoluto- rum, quæ fumunturin ordineab fubiectum, vt eſt in ſe, & ad ſe,non vteſt adaliud,pertales rationes. 34 Adaliud verò refpondeo, Relationem habere effe, In, commune, cum cæterisaccidentibus,&efle,In,particulare,per quodfubiectum refertad terminum,&perhoc efle, in, parti- culare,determinatur aliud,In, commune , & fit vna ratio præ . dicamentalis ex vtroque : quia ex determinante per te, & de- terminabili,per ſe,femper fit vnumperſe: ficutquodlibetac- cidens abſolutum,habet efle,In commune,&particulare,& ex vtroque efficitur vnum. Ad formamigitur primi argu. Concedendum eſt primum enthymema,quoprob atur relationem habere duplicemcon- ceptum : Vnum,quo refpicit ſubiectum, Alium,quo refpicit terminum. Negandum tamen eft, quod infertur,totum effe relationis, & relatiui , non effe ad terminum : quia illudeſſe, quod habet infubiecto,ſi conſideretur in communi, abſtrahit ab abfoluto , & relatiuo, & contrahiturper eſſe ad terminum: ↑ &pertalem contractionem,ordinatur ad illu,& fit relatiuum ; fi verò confideretur inparticulari,eſt eſſe proprium relatio- nis, & ideo eft effe relatiuum: vnde fequitur, relatiuum effe, quidquidhabet relatio,& quidquidhabetrelatiuum: & hoc cit totum efferelationis , &relatiui , effead aliud, vt dicitur in definitione Arift. Ad confirmationem, refponfum eſt,per ex-plicationem definitionis . 35Circa folutionemfecundi arg aliqui diftinguunt relatum, & relatiuum, dicentes: Relatiuum dicere potentiam ad refe-rendum, relatum verò,actuale exercitium referendi; &in defi-nitionepotiùs explicari ad aliquid, vt relatum , quàm vt rela-tiuum.Hæctamen distinctio,nonhabet fundamentum :: quia vt fuperiusprobauimus, exercitium referendi , velactus refe-rendi,non eft aliud quam naturalis ipſa ordinatio , vnius rela- tiui ad aliud: quæ ſemper eodem modofe habet, & femper eft

it inheres in the subject, yet in a different ratio: for according to the common concept it inheres by a common inherence, together with the others, abstracting from absolute and respective inherence; but according to its proper concept it inheres by a purely relative inherence, which is to inhere by referring to another. And what St. Thomas said, that the proper concept of relation is not taken in order to the subject, as in the absolute accidents, is most true; but it must be understood thus: that it is not taken in order to the subject as it is in itself and toward itself, but as it is referred to another through the same relative ratio placed in it. In which the proper ratio of relation differs greatly from the particular rationes of the absolute accidents, which are taken in order to the subject as it is in itself and toward itself, not as it is toward another, through such rationes.

34 To the other I reply that relation has a common being in, with the other accidents, and a particular being in, through which the subject is referred to the term; and by this particular being in the other, common being in is determined, and one categorial ratio is made from both: because from what determines per se and what is determinable per se there always comes to be something one per se: just as any absolute accident whatever has a common and a particular being in, and from both one thing is made.

To the form of the first argument, then: The first enthymeme must be granted, by which it is proved that relation has a twofold concept: One by which it regards the subject, Another by which it regards the term. But what is inferred must be denied, that the whole being of relation and of the relative is not to be toward the term: because that being which it has in the subject, if it is considered in common, abstracts from the absolute and the relative, and is contracted through being toward the term; and through such contraction it is ordered to it, and becomes relative; but if it is considered in particular, it is the proper being of relation, and therefore it is a relative being. Hence it follows that whatever relation has, and whatever the relative has, is relative; and this is the whole being of relation and of the relative to be toward another, as is said in Aristotle’s definition. To the confirmation the reply has been given through the explanation of the definition.

35 Concerning the solution of the second argument, some distinguish the related and the relative, saying that the relative implies a potency for referring, but the related the actual exercise of referring; and that in the definition the relative (ad aliquid) is explained as related rather than as relative. This distinction, however, has no foundation: because, as we proved above, the exercise of referring, or the act of referring, is nothing other than the natural ordering itself of one relative to another, which always holds itself in the same way, and is always

[p. 381]

> actualis , & femper exercetur inter relatiua: quòd neceffariò dicendum eft:nam eoipſo,quòd vnum relatiuum non refera-turactu,vel in exercitioad aliud,no habebit actu in ſe relatio-nem,nec erit relatiuum formaliter:& eo ipſo,quod habetinſe relationem,non poteſt nonreferri actu , & fecundùm exerci-tium.Idem ergoprorfusfunt,ſecundum rem , & fecundumra-tionem,relatum,&relatiuum: fed illud magis distincte expli-cat actum referendi , quia etiam minus diftinctè dicitaliud: ideo in definitioneArift. pro vtroque ſamitur nomen, adali-quid: & actum referendi dicit,non potentiam. Adargum, ergo reſpondetur,Diftinguendo illudaxioma, quòdverba indefinitionenon dicutactum, ſed aptitudinem: nam res quæ definiuntur,ſuntinduplici differentia. Quædam enimfunt,quarumratio,veleſſentia in aptitudine, vel poten-tia confiftit : & iftæ,licèt definiantur per verba ſignificantia actum, nonpro actu,fed pro potentia accipiuntur in defini-tione:&ratiohuius eft:quia actusin his,nonpoteſt elle eſſen-tialis: & ideo nonbenedefiniuntur per actum. Aliæ funt,qua-rum ratio,vel eſſentia,non confiftit in aptitudine, ſed in actu: &in definitioneharum,nonpoſſunt verbaaccipi pro aptitu-dine,quia fi ita accipiantur,non explicabunt naturam definiti: Sedpro actudebent accipi, vtrationem eius explicent. Vufi definiaturquantum, pro co,quòdhabetpartem extra partem, ſecundùmextenfionem molis:nonpoffunt verba huius defi-nitionis,dicere aptitudinem,ſed actum:quia ratio extenfionis, inactu confiftit,nonin aptitudine;ficquede cæteris. Et ita ſe habet relatiuum,cuius ratio,in actuali ordinatione, & relatio-neconfiftit : ideo verba definitionis eius pro actu,& non pro aptitudine accipiuntur. QUÆSTIO V Vtrùm omnesrelationespetineantadhoc predicamentum.                   1 36     Anquam certunt præfupponendum eſt, necDiuinas relationes , nec etiamrelationes rationis , collocari in hocprædicamento:quia vt in præcedenti quæſt probauimus, præditamentum ad aliquid,eſt membrum quoddam genera-lis diuifionis accidentis realis,in nouem prædicamenta:&ideo relatiuum,quod eſt ſupremum genus, eſtaccidens reale,atque finitum:quarenec relationes Diuinæ , cùm fintfubftantiales, &infinitæ,poffunt pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum ,necre-lationes rationis: quia non funtaccidentia realia,

actual, and is always exercised between relatives: which must necessarily be said; for by the very fact that one relative is not referred in act, or in exercise, to another, it will not have relation in act in itself, nor will it be a relative formally; and by the very fact that it has relation in itself, it cannot fail to be referred in act and according to exercise. Therefore related and relative were altogether the same, according to the thing and according to the ratio; but the former explains the act of referring more distinctly, because the latter also says the same thing less distinctly; and therefore in Aristotle’s definition the name toward something is taken for both, and it says the act of referring, not the potency.

To the argument, then, the reply is made by distinguishing that axiom, that the words in a definition do not say act but aptitude: for the things that are defined are of two different kinds. For some are those whose ratio or essence consists in aptitude or potency; and these, although they are defined through words signifying act, are taken in the definition not for act but for potency; and the reason for this is that act in these cannot be essential, and therefore they are not well defined through act. Others are those whose ratio or essence consists not in aptitude but in act; and in the definition of these the words cannot be taken for aptitude, because if they were so taken they would not explain the nature of the thing defined; but they must be taken for act, in order to explain its ratio. As, if the quantum is defined as that which has part outside part according to the extension of bulk, the words of this definition cannot say aptitude but act: because the ratio of extension consists in act, not in aptitude; and so of the others. And so it is with the relative, whose ratio consists in actual ordering and relation:

therefore the words of its definition are taken for act and not for aptitude.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether all relations belong to this category.

36

As something certain it must be presupposed that neither the Divine relations nor even relations of reason are placed in this category: because, as we proved in the preceding question, the category of relation is a certain member of the general division of real accident into nine categories; and therefore the relative, which is the supreme genus, is a real and finite accident. Wherefore neither can the Divine relations, since they are substantial and infinite, belong to this category, nor relations of reason: because they are not real accidents.

[p. 382]

> Solùm ergo procedit quæſt. de relationibus realibuscrea-turarum :An omnes ponantur inhocpredicamento? verum non diſtinguntur ab omnibus eodemmodo : nam quidam affe-runt,Effeeasres in triplici differentia : Quædam funt tranſcen-dentales , quæ in rebus diuerforum prædicamentorum repe-riuntur,eiſque eſſentialiter conueniunt,quafi complementum effentiæ:tales funtreſpectusincluſi,ineffentia cuiufliberacci-dentis,per quos ordinatur adſubiectű, cui inherere aptű eſt. 38 Aliæ funt relationes , quæ non omnibus accidentibus vniuerfaliter conueniunt,fed quibufdam tantum: inquorum eſſentiis, etiam includuntur : vtreſpectus, quem dicunt habi-tus,potentiæ,& fcientiæ adpropria obiecta , & iſtæ vocantur relationes ſecundum dici. Aliæ deniquefunt relationes, quæ nulli conueniunt effen-tialiter,ſedaccidentaliter conueniunt multis : & dicuntur re lationesſecundumeſſe: vtpaternitas,fimilitudo,& æqualitas. Alij verò folùmhas vltimas relationes admittunt : & nullam prorfus ex iis , quæ ad eſſentiam alicuius abſoluti pertineant. Sicvidetur ſentire Scot. in 4.d.12.q. vnica. Probantque non eſſeadmittendas.Primò,quia quidquid pertinetadeſſentiam ſubſtantiæ,eſt ſubſtantiæ : & quidquid pertinet ad effentiam quantitatis,eſtquantitas : ergo ſi relationes talesdantur, quæ pertineantad eflentiamomnium rerum abfolutarum, erunt resabſolutæ:vtin ſubſtantia, eruntſubſtantiæ , in quantitate, quantitas,&in qualitate,qualitas.Et fiadeſſentiam aliquarum rerum tantum pertineant,vt ad effentiam habitus autpoten-tiæ,erunt etiam potentiæ ,& habitus. Hæc autemfalſa ſunt: ideofalfum erit talesrelationesponere. Probatur ſecundò:quia fi intra effentiam abſolutorum ad-mittantur relationes iſtæ,aliud abſurdum erit concedendum: nempe,quòd tales effentiæ componantur, ex entitate abſolu-ta,&relatiua,diuerfisnonfolum ſpecie, ſedgenere. 39 Alij denique præter relationes accidentales, vel ſecúdum efle,admittuntintra eſſentiam abſolutorum traſcendentales: nontamenrelationes ſecundum dici , niſiſolo nomine : nam habitus inquiunt,potentia,& fcientia,purè abfoluta funt, nec dicuntreſpectumrealemadobiecta,ſedabſolutamproportio. nem cumeis:quamproportionem nonpoſſumus intelligere, nec explicare,nifiper quendam reſpectum, quem intellectus concipit in eis : & ideo de eis loquitur , quafi de reſpectiuis : cùmtamen non fint verè reſpectiua, ſed abfoluta:licètin com-munimodoloquendi,reſpectiua dicantur:&propterea appel-lentur relatiua fecundùmdici.

The question, therefore, proceeds only concerning the real relations of creatures: whether all are placed in this category? But they are not distinguished by all in the same way. For some assert that they are things of three different kinds. Some are transcendental, which are found in things of diverse categories and belong to them essentially, as it were a complement of the essence: such are the respects included in the essence of any accident whatever, through which it is ordered to the subject in which it is apt to inhere.

38 Others are relations which belong not to all accidents universally, but only to certain ones, in whose essences they are also included: as the respect which habit, power, and science bear to their proper objects; and these are called relations according to being said.

Others, finally, are relations which belong to none essentially, but belong accidentally to many; and they are called relations according to being: as paternity, similarity, and equality. But others admit only these last relations, and none at all of those that would pertain to the essence of something absolute. So Scotus seems to hold, in 4, d. 12, single q. And they prove that they are not to be admitted. First, because whatever pertains to the essence of substance is substance, and whatever pertains to the essence of quantity is quantity; therefore, if such relations are given as pertain to the essence of all absolute things, they will be absolute things: in substance they will be substances, in quantity quantity, and in quality quality. And if they pertain to the essence of certain things only, as to the essence of habit or power, they will also be powers and habits. But these things are false; therefore it will be false to posit such relations.

It is proved second: because if these relations are admitted within the essence of absolute things, another absurdity will have to be conceded: namely, that such essences are composed of an absolute and a relative entity, diverse not only in species but in genus.

39 Others, finally, besides the accidental relations, or relations according to being, admit transcendental ones within the essence of absolute things, yet not relations according to being said, except in name only. For habit, they say, power, and science are purely absolute, and do not say a real respect to their objects, but an absolute proportion with them; which proportion we cannot understand or explain except through a certain respect which the intellect conceives in them; and therefore it speaks of them as of respective things, although they are not truly respective but absolute, though in the common manner of speaking they are called respective; and for this reason they are called relatives according to being said.

[p. 383]

The last way of speaking grants that, besides relations according to being, there are transcendental relations and relations according to being said, and that both pertain to the essence of absolute things; but it so confounds them as to assert that all are to be called transcendental; and so that created real relation is to be divided into only two members, namely into transcendental and categorial: so that under the first member are comprehended both the respects which belong essentially to all the absolute categories and those which belong to certain ones only; but under the second only the accidental relations, which are called according to being and pertain to this category. Our view is explained in three conclusions.

40 The first is: It is necessary to posit certain real respects pertaining to the essence of absolute accidents, such as the respect which the aptitudinal inherence of these includes to the subject, and of habit and power to the object; and these respects are certain diminished relations completing the essence of absolute things. This conclusion is held by St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, ad 1, and q. 28, a. 1; Cajetan, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, On the Soul 2, text 33, where he teaches that the specific essence of powers is to be taken from their acts and objects: which cannot be true unless they include an essential respect to the object. For it is evident that the specific essence of a power is not to be taken from the object in such a way that the object is of its essence, since it is always a thing diverse from it; therefore it must necessarily be taken from the respect of that same power to the object; and therefore such a respect is essential to it. The consequence is proved: because if neither the object nor the respect to it is of the essence of the powers, their species will in no way be taken from the objects.

41 It is proved next by reason: because accidents are not beings simply, but beings of a being, that is, something of substance, to which they say an intrinsic attribution; but such an attribution can neither exist nor be understood except through some respect to that same substance included in the essence of accidents; therefore these essential respects must necessarily be posited in all absolute accidents.

The second conclusion: Of these respects pertaining to the essence of absolute things, many are transcendental, and many also categorial. The first is proved: because that is called transcendental whose proper ratio transcends all the categories, or at least several; but the aptitudinal respect of inherence to the subject, which an accident includes in its essence, transcends all the categories of accidents, just as accident itself does; therefore it will be a transcendental relation.

[p. 384]

Quodintelligendum eftreductiuètantum,ficutpartes reducunturad prædicamentum,&fpeciem totius, &non per fe,&directe : quia incompletumaliquid funt ,atque diminu-tum,&qui non poffunt perſe efficere ſpeciem, niſi ſumul cum abfoluto , cuius effentiam complent : vt fi folum reſpectum potentiæ, authabitus ad obiectum intelligas , non intelligen-doabfolutam rationem qualitatis, nihil completum, autpræ-dicamentaleintelligis:quia reſpectus iſti, eſſentialiter coniun-guntur cum abfoluta ratione qualitatis , quam complent : & ideo nihil completum fine illaintelliguntur conftituere : vn-denec nominapotentiarum , & habituum imponunturad fi-gnificandoshos reſpectus, ſedprincipalem rationem quali- tatis

The second is proved by the opposite reason: for that is transcendent which is common to many categories; but there are many essential respects in absolute things which cannot pertain to several categories; therefore they will not be transcendental. The minor is proved: because the respects of habits and powers to their objects cannot extend themselves to more than the habits and powers themselves to which they are essential; but habit and power pertain only to the category of quality, indeed only to determinate genera of this category; therefore they neither are nor ought to be called transcendental.

The third conclusion: Of the three genera of relations, namely transcendental, according to being said, and according to being, the transcendental pertain to no category; relations according to being said pertain to the category of the absolute thing whose essence they complete; but relations according to being, or accidental relations, constitute the category of relation.

These three things must be proved. And the first, concerning transcendental respects, is easily proved from transcendence itself: for what is transcendent can pertain to no special category; therefore these transcendental relations are excluded from every category. The antecedent is proved: because the categories contain a determinate mode of being, as substance the mode of being per se, quantity the mode of extension; but the transcendent is not determined to any mode of being, but comprehends many; therefore it cannot pertain to a special category.

43 The second, concerning relations according to being said, I prove thus: the respect which power and habit bear to their objects completes their essence; therefore they pertain to the essences which they complete, as something of them; wherefore they must necessarily be placed in the same category and under the same genus under which such essences are. Which is to be understood only reductively, as parts are reduced to the category and species of the whole, and not per se and directly: because they are something incomplete and diminished, and they cannot of themselves make up a species except together with the absolute thing whose essence they complete: as, if you understand only the respect of a power or habit to its object, without understanding the absolute ratio of quality, you understand nothing complete or categorial; because these respects are essentially conjoined with the absolute ratio of quality, which they complete; and therefore they are not understood to constitute anything complete without it. Hence neither are the names of powers and habits imposed to signify these respects, but the principal ratio of quality,

which they follow, as St. Thomas well says, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, ad 1, and q. 7 On Power, a. 10; and therefore they are not constituted in a category per se, but through the absolute thing. And hence it follows that they do not pertain to the category of relation, nor are they called categorial relations, but relations according to being said, by Aristotle. And the reason for this denomination is that such were so called by the ancients, and were confused with true and categorial relations, although they are not relations according to being, but enjoy only their name.

44 The third, finally, that the relations which are essential to nothing but always belong accidentally make up this category per se, is the common consensus of the whole school. And its reason is gathered from their difference from the transcendental relations and those according to being said: which, since they pertain to the essence of the absolute things which they complete, are certain incomplete respects and something of them; and therefore they cannot constitute a categorial ratio per se, but only together with those same absolute things. But the relations which are outside the essence of all absolute things have, first, the mode of a complete nature: because they are nothing essential of anything, but have per se their own mode of being, toward something, which is an entire and complete categorial ratio, like the other categorial accidents, and consequently their own genera, species, and differences, from which a categorial ordering can be made per se. They have also, second, that they are the whole essential being of relatives, so that these include nothing essentially besides the relations themselves; and therefore they are so defined by Aristotle: Relatives are those whose whole being is to be disposed toward another.

45 These relations, therefore, agree with the transcendental ones in this, that they say nothing absolute, but their whole being is to be rationes of referring to another; yet they differ in two respects. In the first, indeed: because respects according to being said are not the whole ratio, the whole being, or the whole essence of relatives, but a certain complement of them; and therefore the things whose complement they are are not relatives simply but absolute simply, and consequently they are called relatives in a certain way. And from this follows the second difference: that these respects are not toward another as toward a term, but as toward a subject or object, as the nature of the absolute thing which they complete requires; whereas categorial relations not only do not say anything absolute, but are the whole ratio, the whole essence, the whole being of the relatives which they constitute; and therefore the relatives constituted by them say nothing absolute, but their whole being is to be referred to another, not indeed as to an object or subject, but as

toward a pure term: because the relation by which alone they are constituted does not require another thing under some particular ratio, to which it orders the relative which it constitutes, but under the precise ratio of term.

46 To the first argument of the second opinion, contrary to relation according to being said, the antecedent must be distinguished. For that whatever pertains to the essence of substance is substance, and whatever pertains to the essence of quantity is quantity, can be understood in two ways: in recto and in obliquo. In the first way it must be denied, because it is not necessary that a thing be predicated in recto of any mode or complement of it whatever, so that it be called simply substance or quantity; but it may well be in obliquo, so that it be called something of substance or of quantity; and in this way it is true that these respects are absolute things or substances, that is, something of absolute things, or of substance.

To the second: it must be denied that it follows that those absolute things in which these respects are enclosed are composed of an absolute and a respective entity: because they are not included in absolute things by way of genus or of difference, or by way of composition, but both in the genus and in the difference, and in the species itself composed of them, by way of a certain complement, both of the composites and of the components; whence it does not follow that they make any composition with them.

## QUESTION VI

Whether the species of categorial relation is to be taken from the term.

47

The question proceeds only concerning categorial relation, not concerning transcendental relations, nor those according to being said, which we proved in the preceding question do not pertain to this category. But in order that what is to be said about relation may be better understood, it is necessary to adduce certain divisions of relatives. The relative, then, which is the supreme genus of this category, is first divided into three intermediate genera, according to the three foundations on which it is founded, enumerated by Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15. The first genus of relatives is of those which are founded on generic or specific unity or diversity, and it has under it three other genera, or species, according to the diverse foundations in which unity or diversity is found. For if it is found in Substance, it will be a relation of identity or diversity; if in Quality, a relation of similarity or dissimilarity; and if in Quantity, a relation of equality or inequality. The second genus of relatives is of those which are founded

on action and passion: as the relations of paternity and filiation; and it has other genera, or subalternate species, according to the diverse actions, present, past, and future. The third, of those which are founded on measure: as the relations of powers and sciences, under the name of the measurable, to their objects under the name of measure; for the object is called the measure of science and of power, and science and power measurable by the object, from the fact that neither can extend to anything, or be concerned with anything, which is not contained under its proper object.

48 The second division is less universal: by it the relative is divided into Mutual and non-mutual. Mutual relatives are those each of which is called such through a real relation: as father and son. Non-mutual, those of which only one is called such through a real relation, while in the other such a relation does not exist: as the measurable and the measure; for the former is called such through a real relation, but the latter does not have such a relation.

The third division is: some relatives are of Equiparance, others of Disquiparance. Of equiparance are those which are of the same ratio and denomination, as like things and equal things. Those are called of disquiparance which are of diverse ratio and denomination, as father and son. Now each of these genera has its own species, and of all and each the title of the question asks from what they take their specific distinction, whether from the term or from something else.

And the first opinion seems to be that of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 35, a. 5, and Quodlibet 9, a. 4: that relation, or the related, does not take its species from the term, but rather from the cause through which it is produced. Which this argument proves: because if relation took its species from the term, it would follow that in both parents there is the same relation to the son. The consequence is proved: because the son is the single term; therefore the relation of the father and of the mother, terminated at him, will be the same. But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also, that relation takes its species from the term. The minor is proved: because the father is the efficient cause of the son, but the mother only a passive one; therefore they have rationes of causes diverse in species, which a diverse relation in each necessarily follows: of paternity in the father, and of maternity in the mother.

49 It is proved second: because the species must be taken from something intrinsic, which is its essential difference; but the term of a relation is a thing diverse from the relation and extrinsic to it, as the father with respect to filiation; therefore the species cannot be taken from it. If you reply that the species is not taken from the term in such a way that the term itself is the specific difference of the relation, but the ordering to the term: against this is that the relation itself is the ordering to the term; therefore, if it is taken from the order or ordering to the term,

which is its species, it will take its species from itself: which is plainly false.

For this opinion, too, the testimony of Aristotle can be adduced: because he distinguishes the three genera of relations (as we have seen) not by diverse terms but by diverse foundations; therefore he holds that the species of relation is not to be taken from the term.

50 The second opinion is the common and true one: that relation, or the relative, takes its species from the term; so that those relations are of the same species which have a term of the same species, as all paternities, all similarities; but those are distinct in species which have terms distinct in species, as similarity and dissimilarity. It is proved from Aristotle’s definition, which says that relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to another, that is, to the term; therefore the relation will be such as the term is to which it refers; and this is to receive its species from it. And St. Thomas without doubt holds the same opinion, 3 p., q. 32, a. 2, where he says thus: Since the specific ratio of relation consists in this, that it is disposed toward another, it must be said that two relations are not diverse according to species if an opposite relation corresponds to them.

It is proved also by reason: because of the four genera of causes, relation does not have matter and form, which are intrinsic causes from which (at least from the form) it could take its species, because, as we proved above, accidents are not composed of matter and form; therefore it has only the efficient cause, by which it is produced, and the end, or term, to which the relative is ordered; but things do not take their species from the efficient cause, because it is altogether extrinsic; therefore there remains only the final cause, which is the term to which the relative is essentially ordered; wherefore it will take its species from it.

51 But in order that this specification of relation may be better understood, it should be noted that Relation, like the other accidents, does not have a Physical composition from matter and form, but a Metaphysical one from genus and difference. In order, then, that it may be understood from what it takes its species, it must be explained from what its genus and difference are taken, and in what way the quidditative definition of any relation whatever can be assigned. The genus of relation, then, is taken from its whole nature considered under the common concept of referring to a term; but the difference from the same nature conceived under a special concept, ultimately determining the genus: namely, from the fact that it is an ordering to such a term. As the Genus of paternity will be the common concept of real relation, which says being an order or ordering to a term; but the Difference, being an ordering to a son; and therefore the definition of paternity will be such: Paternity is the order, or ordering, of a father to a son; and so of the other

relations. Thus the term of the relation is not the specific difference of the relation, nor is being an ordering to such a term, which is extrinsic to the relation; but being an ordering to it is intrinsic; and because such an ordering is that which is to such a term, therefore relation is said to take its species from the term, through which the relation and the relative are to be known and defined.

52 From this doctrine it is plain that the second argument has been solved:

because relation is not specified by the term as term, so that it would be its essential difference, nor is it specified by itself, but by its proper difference, which is taken from its nature as considered under the determinate and ultimate concept of ordering to such a term, through which concept the common and generic one is contracted.

That the testimony of Aristotle may be explained, it should be noted that foundations are causes of relations: either because relations are in some way produced by them, or, if sometimes they are not produced by them, at least they follow by natural sequel once the foundations are posited; whence from foundations of diverse ratio there always follow relations of diverse species. And so it can be granted that the species of relations, or of relatives, is taken from the foundations as it were causally, but from the terms as it were formally. But between these two ways of taking the species of relations, it is plain that the second is more proper, which Aristotle posited in the definition of relatives; and this is the reason why the common manner of speaking of the school uses it rather than the first. But

Aristotle and St. Thomas distinguish them in those places through the foundations, because these are sometimes better known to us, and because that way of distinguishing does not contradict the proper and formal one, but implies it; whence those who distinguish through it do not deny the proper one, which they almost always use.

Whether to the son there corresponds a twofold relation, one in the father and another in the mother, or the same in both parents.

53

We have put off the solution of the first argument to the last place, because concerning it this doubt (though very briefly) must be disputed: whether in the father and the mother there is a single relation to the son, or a twofold and diverse one, namely of paternity in the father and of maternity in the mother.

And the first opinion is that of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 35, a. 5, which Cajetan follows in the same place, and Ferrara on Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 14: that there is a twofold and diverse relation in the father and the mother; which is founded on this, that

Aristotle, whom St. Thomas follows, asserts that the father and the mother concur in the generation of the son in a diverse way, or in a diverse genus of cause: the father as an efficient cause, but the mother

Noftraautem ſententia eft:probabilem eſſe vtramque opi-pionem,nonfolum propterpatrones doctiffimos, fedpropter probabilia fundamenta; ideolibertum eritcuique hancvelilam pralibitufequi,

as a material one; but the effect depends with a diverse mode and a diverse dependence on diverse genera of causes, and regards them in a diverse way; therefore through diverse relations; and so the father is referred to the son by the relation of efficient cause, which is called paternity, but the mother by the relation of passive principle, signified by the name of maternity. And this opinion consequently posits a twofold relation, diverse at least in ratio, in the son: one through which he is referred to the father, and another through which he is referred to the mother; for since relation takes its species from the term, it is impossible that two relations diverse in species should have the same formal term; whence, since the son terminates diverse relations of each parent, he must terminate them through two other relations, formally diverse, but both are signified by the same name of filiation.

54 The second, opposite opinion holds: that in the father and the mother there is one total and complete relation, but as it were composed of two partial relations, of the same ratio, of the father and of the mother; and that in the son only a single one corresponds to it, through which he is referred to both parents as to an adequate term, and to either one as to an inadequate term. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 5, sect. 3; and it has the opposite foundation, namely that the father and the mother concur in the same genus of efficient cause in the generation of the son, as one total and adequate cause, as it were composed of a twofold partial cause. For so Galen holds, whom all the Physicians follow (to whom great credit is to be given in this matter), and with them Scotus, in 3, d., q. 1. And from this foundation it evidently follows that in the father and the mother there are relations of the same species. The consequence is proved: because if they concur in the same way, and in the same genus of efficient cause, and proximately, in the generation of the son, he will depend on them in the same way; he will also regard them in the same way; wherefore through a relation of the same species, but partially distinct in each: because the partial causes are diverse, and the subjects diverse, in which the same accident in number cannot be found. And we can adduce the example of many men hauling a ship, in whom there are diverse partial and inadequate relations to the same effect, but from all of them one total and adequate relation is integrated.

Our view, however, is that both opinions are probable, not only on account of their most learned patrons but on account of their probable foundations; and therefore each will be free to follow this one or that at his pleasure.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the term of a relation is formally absolute or formally relative.

55

There are three things in a relative: the Subject, the Foundation, and the

Relation. The subject is the thing itself which is denominated by the relation. The Foundation is the ratio or means through which the relation arises in it. And the relation is that through which they are formally called relatives:

as in the father, the man is what is denominated father by the relation; generation, or the power of generating, is that on which the relation is founded; and the Relation is paternity itself. Of these three it is certain that the

Subject is not the term of the relation except a material and as it were remote one, about which the question does not proceed, but about the two others, by reason of which the subject can proximately terminate the relation. And since the foundation is absolute, or has the mode of something absolute, therefore the title of the question asks: whether the term of the relation through which one thing is referred to another is the subject itself by reason of the foundation, which is an absolute thing, or by reason of the relation: for if it is the term by reason of the first, the relation will be terminated formally at something absolute; but if by reason of the relation, it will be terminated formally at a relative.

56 But we can consider two things in a relation. The first, that it is the ratio of referring one thing to another. The second, that it is the ratio of terminating the relation of the other: as in paternity, that it is the ratio of referring the father to the son, and that it is the ratio through which the same father terminates the relation of filiation. And since these rationes are diverse in the same relation, it is certain that through the relation according to the first consideration one relative does not terminate the relation of the other; it can only be doubtful whether it terminates it through the relation considered in the second way.

And in this sense it is asked whether the term of a relation is formally relative, that is, whether it terminates the relation of the other through its own relation, at least considered in the second way.

And concerning the question so explained there are three opinions: two extreme, and a third middle one. The first, extreme opinion asserts that one relative always, and in whatever genus of relations, terminates the relation of the other through its own relation, and never through the foundation or absolute ratio. So

Cajetan, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, whom not a few of the moderns follow.

57 They prove it from a twofold property of relatives approved by

Aristotle and by all, namely, that relatives are simultaneous in nature, and simultaneous in cognition and in definition: so that neither can be prior in nature to the other, nor be known without the cognition of the other

nor be defined unless the other is defined: all of which are manifest in the father and the son; but none of these can belong to them except as relatives; therefore as such they are referred to one another, and one terminates the relation of the other. The minor is proved: because the father, by reason of the foundation, is prior in nature to the son, and the son posterior, since through the power of generating and active generation, which are the foundation of the relation, he is his cause, and a cause is prior in nature to its effect; and for the same reason he can be known and defined without the son; therefore in this way one will not be able to terminate the relation of the other; and therefore they can terminate each other only through the relation.

But since some relations are mutual and others not mutual, which are found only in one extreme, while the other is absolute; and therefore such an extreme does not seem able to terminate the other through a relation, but through an absolute ratio: it is not apparent, therefore, how this opinion can be true in all relations.

Therefore it is defended in two ways, as regards non-mutual relations, by the diverse authors who follow it. First, by Cajetan, who says: In these relations one extreme is formally relative through a relation inhering in it; the other, however, not through a relation inhering in it, but through the relation existing in the other. For example: science, which is called measurable, is referred to the object as to a measure through a relation inhering in it; but the object, which is called the measure, is referred to the science not through a relation inhering in it, but through the same relation existing in the science; and so one relative is intrinsic. It is proved from Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, who expressly asserts: In relatives of the third genus, which are the measure and the measurable, one is referred through the relation which it has in itself, the other through the relation by which the other is referred to it.

In the second way it is defended by other moderns, who assert that the extreme in which there is no real relation terminates the real relation of the other not through that same relation of the other, but through its own relation: not a real one, which we suppose it does not have, but one of reason: because by the very fact that science is referred to the object through the real relation of the measurable, the object acquires a new commensuration and correspondence with it, by reason of which commensuration the relative denomination of measure is due to it; and since it cannot have it as real, because it is an absolute thing, it will have it from a relation of reason; which, although it does not exist before the operation of the intellect, it is enough that it be due to it, and as it were in proximate potency, to give it the denomination of relative, though not of related: for relative says the potency for something to be referred to another, but related the actual exercise of referring.

[p. 393]

This opinion, however, whether it be defended in this way or in that, seems to me improbable: because each way of defending it is evidently shown to be false. And first I attack Cajetan’s way thus: the formal effect of relation is to make a relative, just as the formal effect of whiteness is to make a white thing; but it is repugnant for something to be white except by whiteness inhering in it; therefore it will be repugnant for it to be relative except by a relation inhering in it. It is false, therefore, as Cajetan asserts, that the measure is referred to the measurable through a relation existing in that same measurable.

60 Second: because relation, since it is a relative form, cannot refer to another anything except that which it constitutes a relative; but to constitute something a relative is to confer on it its proper formal effect, just as to constitute whiteness, or a white subject, is to confer on it its proper formal effect; and a form does not confer its formal effect except through information; therefore it is repugnant for something to be constituted a relative, or to be referred to another, through a relation existing in the other and not in itself.

The second way is proved false by this reason: the relative and the related, as we proved above, are not related as potency and act; because, since relation is the actual ordering of one thing to another, by the very fact that it is in a subject it refers that subject in act to the term; and therefore it is impossible for something to have in itself a relation through which it is called relative without also being called related through the same. It is impossible, too, for it to be called relative solely from the fact that it can have a relation, unless it has it in act: for a man, before he has the relation of paternity, is not called relative to a son. And just as these things are true and necessary in real relations, so they are no less necessary in relations of reason: because a relation of reason is conceived by the intellect after the likeness of a real relation. In the same way, then, it will be impossible for the measure to be referred to the measurable through a relation of reason before it has it in act from the intellect knowing it, even if it is due to it: just as it is impossible for something to be called relative by a real relation before it has it in act.

16 The second, extreme opinion holds: that the term, not only in non-mutual relations but also in mutual ones, is formally absolute. So Scotus, in 1, d. 30, q. 1, whom all his disciples follow, and many of the moderns; and Capreolus seems to incline to the same opinion, in 1, d. 30, q. 1, a. 2, ad 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 3, ad 2. And concerning non-mutual relations this opinion presupposes as certain that they are terminated at something absolute.

That it is so in mutual relations too is proved first:
