in past action, as father and son: for the former founds the relation of paternity because he begot, the latter the relation of filiation because he was begotten. Of these, moreover, some are relations according to being said only, or even relations of reason; but Aristotle enumerates them all as it were mixed together, because when all are known together the nature of categorial relations is better known. And of all these relations, everyone receives at least those as categorial which are founded in past action; and about these, and also about the other categorial relations of this second kind, we inquire: Whether they are founded in past, present, or future action, or in the potency from which the action proceeds: as, whether paternity and filiation are founded in the past action and passion which these names, to have begotten and to have been begotten, are wont to signify, or only in the active potency of generating of the father and in the passive potency of the son, through which he is said to be begotten?

110 Now potency can be taken in two ways. First, for the formal aptitude or power of acting, which is a certain accident superadded to corporeal substance for operating. Second, for the substance itself from which such a potency proceeds: and the former is called formal potency, the latter radical, because it is its root: as the formal potency for reasoning is the intellect, but the radical one the soul or rational nature.

These things being set forth, the first opinion holds: Relations of this kind are founded not in action but in formal potency: as paternity in the generative potency. So Scotus, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, and on 4, d. 6, q. 10, and d. 13, q. 1. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where he speaks thus: But of those which are according to potency, some are also said to be relative according to times. In which words he says that potency is the foundation of these relations.

Next, by reason. First: Because what does not exist cannot be the foundation of a real relation; but past action no longer exists; therefore a real relation of this kind cannot be founded in it.

Second: Because it is not repugnant that God separate a relation from its subject; but if it were founded in past action, it would be altogether repugnant; therefore it is not founded in it. The minor is proved: because it is impossible that a past action should not have been; therefore it will also be impossible that he who has already begotten should not have begotten, and consequently that he should not have a relation to the begotten actually existing.

The second opinion is opposed to this one: Relations of this kind are founded not in potency but in action and passion. So Soto, Phys. 5, q. 2, a. 2, concl. 1. This is also proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, speaking thus of the foundation of these relations: For thus the father too is called the father of the son, for the one has done, but the other has suffered something.

111 And also by reason. First: Because that is the foundation of a relation which being posited, even if the other things are not posited, the relation is posited, and which being removed, even if the other things remain, the relation does not arise or does not remain; but such is past action; therefore it is the foundation of the relation. He proves the minor: because by the very fact that it is true that a man has begotten, it is true and necessary that he have the relation of paternity to the son; and as long as generation is not posited, even if there be potency and anything else whatever, the relation does not arise, as is manifest of itself.

Second: The relation of the agent in act and of the patient in act is founded not in potency but in present action; therefore neither will the relation of paternity be founded in potency, but in past action. The consequence is evident, because Aristotle speaks of both relations in the same way, and the ratio is entirely the same. The antecedent is proved: because an agent is not called such from potency, since we see that it is possessed by someone for a long time and he is not called an agent in act until the action proceeds from him; from this, therefore, he is denominated, and in this is founded the relation which he has to the patient, and not in potency.

The third opinion: It says that neither action nor active or passive formal potency is the foundation of these relations, but radical potency, taken for the substantial form or the very essence of the thing, from which the formal potency proceeds. Certain moderns follow this on account of this argument: A relation cannot be given in a subject without its foundation, by which, just as it receives its entity, so it is conserved in it: as without whiteness there cannot be given likeness, or without quantity equality; but if the relation of paternity were founded in the generative potency, it could be given in the subject without it; therefore it would be given without its proper foundation. The minor is proved: because after a man has begotten he can lose the potency of generating, or at least God could take it away from him while the son is living, and then the relation would be given in the subject without its proper foundation; lest, therefore, this inconvenience be admitted, they assert that it is founded in the radical potency of generating, which is the soul or the sensitive nature.

112 The last opinion holds that the foundation of these relations is potency, not bare, but as reduced to act through action: so that the action is only a condition, but the foundation is the potency reduced to act. Soncinas holds this, Metaph. 5, q. 15. And it seems to us more probable and to be held.

We say four things, therefore, in this matter. First, that the proximate foundation of these relations is not the radical potency, for the substantial form, or the essence of the thing. This is proved first, evidently, from the doctrine of Aristotle; for in Metaph. 5, ch. 15, he expressly taught that these relations are founded in

generative potency, active and passive; but by generative potency neither Aristotle nor anyone else ever understood the substantial form or the essence of the thing, which it is established a man has in whom there is no generative potency; therefore that third opinion cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle.

113 And it is proved to be false by this argument: Relations of this second kind belong to that which proceeds from another as from an efficient principle, and to that from which another proceeds; but the proximate potency through which one proceeds from another, as the son from the father, is the formal one, and not the radical, except as remote; therefore, if these relations are founded in potency (as the same opinion admits), it is repugnant that their proximate foundation be the form or essence; but it must necessarily be said that they are proximately founded in formal potency. The minor is proved: because the proximate principle of effecting is the formal potency from which the action of generating proceeds; just as the proximate principle from which the action of understanding proceeds is the intellect, and not the soul, except as remote.

Second, we say: Bare potency, before it is reduced to act, is not a sufficient foundation of the relation. This is proved by this reason: The son proceeds from the father as from the actual principle of his being; but he is not an actual principle through potency alone, except by means of generation, as is known; therefore neither is potency a sufficient foundation unless it is reduced to act by means of generation.

114 Third, we say: Action is not the foundation of these relations. This is proved first, because it is not certain, but placed in opinion, that a relation is distinguished from its foundation from the nature of the thing; but it will be evident that these relations are distinguished if their foundation is action and not potency; therefore it is not to be asserted. The minor is proved: because active generation does not remain in the father but passes into the son, or at least is in the prime matter from which he is generated as in a subject; but the relation of paternity is in the father; therefore it will be evident that it is distinguished really from the action, because it is evident that accidents inhering in adequate and really distinct subjects are distinct from the nature of the thing.

Second: Because the relation of filiation follows upon the man begotten; therefore the principle of both is the same; but generation is not the principle, nor the cause, but the causation or medium by which the begotten proceeds from the principle, and consequently the relation of filiation; therefore it cannot be the foundation of the relation either. This last consequence is proved: because in these relations of the procession of one from another, it is the same to be the principle from which another proceeds and to be the foundation of the relation of the same principle to it.

115 Lastly, we say: The proximate foundation of these relations is potency, as reduced to act through action: so that the action is only a condition, but the potency, as the action proceeds from it, is the foundation. This is the express opinion of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where, assigning their foundation, he says: But the active and the passive, according to the active and passive potency, and the actions of the potencies. In which words he teaches that both pertain to the foundation, namely potency and action: the former as principle, and therefore as foundation; the latter as a necessary condition, without which the former cannot be the foundation.

And it is proved by the reasons of the first and second opinions, to which this is to be added: The son proceeds from the father as from the actual efficient principle of his generation, and is referred to him as such; but he is not constituted in the ratio of actual principle except through potency together with the action of generating, through which the potency is reduced to act and denominates the man generating, or the actual principle of generation; therefore potency, as the action proceeds from it, is the foundation of the relation. The arguments of the first and second opinions in part prove our view; therefore they need no reply.

116 For the solution of the argument of the third opinion, concerning the separability of the foundation from the relation, it must be explained how the foundation is related to the relation, and also in what way the latter depends on the former. And the foundation of a relation is not to be taken so materially as the foundation of a house or a wall, upon which they materially rise; but a thing is called the foundation of a relation in this sense: because by means of it the relation comes to be or is produced in the subject. But the dependence of a relation on its foundation is not the same in all relations, but greater or lesser according to the nature of each relation. And there is a difference between the relations of the second kind on the one side and all the others on the other: that in relations of the first and third kind the foundation has the mode of a form, through which the extremes are constituted in the ratio of extremes: as whiteness, which is the foundation of likeness, is the form of the extremes, because by means of it the relation inheres in the extremes; whence, if it were removed from them, they would not have the capacity of receiving the relation: as, if you remove whiteness from the extremes of likeness, it implies a contradiction that such a relation be in them; whence it follows that these relations depend on their foundations not only in being and in becoming, but also in being conserved, so that they can in no way subsist without them.

But the foundations of relations of the second kind are related in another way:

for they are not forms of the extremes, but powers or media only, by which the relation proceeds effectively, as from an efficient principle, not indeed per se but as it were per accidens, because there is no agent that intends a relation per se.

117 For example: the potency of generating is the power of the efficient cause, through which it produces the effect, and consequently the relation consequent upon it; whence the relation inheres proximately in the substance, although it comes to be by means of the potency and the action; whence it follows that these relations depend on their foundations only in being and in becoming, because by means of them they are made by the efficient cause; yet they do not depend on them in being conserved, because they do not depend on them as on forms of the extremes, as was said of the other relations.

And from these things the reply is made to the form of the argument. For the antecedent must be denied, that relations of this second kind cannot remain in their subjects without their foundations: whence it is not repugnant that, when the generative potency is separated from the man who begot, and the begotten son remains, the relation of paternity and of filiation should remain; indeed, if the extremes remain, it must necessarily remain. And the reason of this is: because they do not depend on their foundations in being conserved, but only in being and becoming, as has been explained.

## QUESTION XIII

Whether relations of the third kind are real and categorial.

118

The third kind of relations is that of the measurable and of the measure, concerning which it is not certain among all whether they are true relations, nor whether they are categorial.

And the first opinion holds: They are not true relations, but are so called in name only; and that this is the reason why they are called by Aristotle relations according to being said, as if he grants them only the title, but in reality they are nothing; wherefore they belong neither to this category nor to any other.

So Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 2, q. 4, whom certain moderns follow; and they prove it by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 15, where he says that the measurable, the knowable, and the intelligible are not relatives because they themselves are referred, but because other things are referred to them; therefore on the side of the measurable no relation is given, and much less on the side of the measure; for the measure is something absolute, wherefore they are called relative in name only, and in reality have no relation;

and this is to be relative according to being said, and to belong to no category.

Others, however, grant that such relatives are true and real, but they call them transcendental, not categorial, because they can belong to many categories, as to quality and quantity; and therefore they are not placed in this category. Wherefore, according to these two opinions, there are only two kinds of categorial relation. The first, that which is founded in unity. The second, in potency and action. But the third is a thing of title only, or a title without a thing.

119 The third opinion is that of Cajetan, whom we cited above, asserting that these relations are not only real and categorial, constituting the third kind of this category, but mutual, that is, real on the side of both extremes: of which one is referred to the other through a true relation existing in itself, namely the measurable to the measure; but the latter is referred to the measurable not through a relation existing in itself, but through the relation of the same measurable to it. And he proves this by the same testimony of Aristotle cited for the first opinion.

The common opinion, however, of almost the whole school is: The relations of the measurable and of the measure are true and real, and constitute the third kind of this category, but are not mutual, because they are real only on the side of the measurable, not on the side of the measure. So St. Thomas expressly, Metaph. 5, lect. 17, and 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, and all the interpreters of Aristotle, not only in the present chapter but on Metaph. 5, ch. 15. Indeed, Aristotle himself also expressly in the same place, after he has laid down the first and second kind of relations, adds a third, in which he placed the measurable, the knowable, and the intelligible.

120 But it should be noted first: St. Thomas explains this third kind of relations and distinguishes it from the first and second in the same places, assigning this difference between it and the others: that relations of the first and second kind are mutual, that is, real on the side of both extremes, so that in the two extremes there are two real relations, each of which denominates its own extreme formally, as is manifest in father and son, in the like and the equal; but in relatives of the third kind only one real relation is found, by which both extremes are denominated: the one by a formal and intrinsic denomination, the other only by an extrinsic denomination; as in science and the knowable only one real relation is found, through which science is formally called measurable, and through the same the object is denominated the measure of the same science; but by a denomination

only extrinsic; and therefore relations of this kind are called not mutual.

121 Second, St. Thomas notes the reason why in these relatives there is only one real relation, by which both extremes are denominated, whereas in the other two kinds the single relations denominate the single extremes, and therefore relatives of this third kind are called not mutual.

And he says the reason of this is that the extremes of these relations are not of the same order, but of different ones; and therefore, although one is ordered to the other really, through an intrinsic relation, yet the other is not ordered to it, but is only called such by the real relation of the other. For example: science and a potency are ordered to their proper objects, which are absolute in themselves and do not belong to the order of the sciences and potencies; wherefore neither are they of themselves ordered to the same sciences and potencies; and therefore they do not have a real intrinsic relation by which they are denominated measures, but are denominated only by the relations of the former: so that by the very fact that science and potency are formally denominated measurable by their objects, through their own real relations, the objects themselves, absolute of themselves, acquire the extrinsic relative denomination of measure from the same relations.

122 And this is the sense of Aristotle (says St. Thomas) when he asserted, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, that relatives of the first and second kind are such because they are referred to another, but relatives of the third kind not because they are referred to others, but because others are referred to them: which he teaches that Aristotle asserted not on account of both extremes, for science and potency are also called such because they are referred to the object, but on account of the other alone, namely on account of the object itself, which is not called knowable except because science is concerned with it: whence this was nothing else than to say that these relations are not mutual, but that one serves for both extremes and denominates both, the one formally and the other extrinsically.

Third, St. Thomas notes that that extreme of these relations in which there is no real relation is called such in two ways.

First, by a real extrinsic denomination, from the real relation existing in the other extreme.

Second, by a quasi-formal and intrinsic denomination, not real but of reason.

For from the fact that the intellect sees the object denominated by the relation of science, and terminating the same relation, it conceives it as if it were truly ordered to science, and attributes to it a relation

[p. 428]

of reason, through which it orders it to the same science. And between the two denominations there is this difference: that the first and real one is a relative denomination, because it is received from a relation; yet through it the knowable is not referred to science, but is said to be relative, that is, is denominated relatively, because another is referred to it; whereas the denomination which the intellect attributes to it, since it is a relation on its side, or conceived in it and attributed to it, not only denominates it relatively but also refers it to another.

123 Lastly, it should be noted that potency, habit, and science have two respects: one, which is included in their absolute ratio and completes it essentially; the other, which is outside the absolute essence, and therefore belongs to it only accidentally. And they include the first respect under the names of potencies, habits, and sciences; and therefore according to it they are not relatives according to being, but according to being said: wherefore neither they themselves nor such a respect of theirs belong to this category, but to the category of quality. But through the second respect they are denominated measurable by their objects, and they include nothing absolute under these names, but only a relation; and therefore they are relatives according to being and constitute this third kind of relations: all of which St. Thomas teaches in the same places, and we have explained it more fully according to his mind in q. 6 of this category.

124 The testimony of Aristotle which the first opinion, that of Henry of Ghent and the moderns, adduces for itself has already been explained by St. Thomas according to its genuine sense, in favor of the common opinion which we follow: for it contains that opinion beyond doubt, but is drawn by the moderns into the opposite sense. For they understand Aristotle to have said of these relatives that neither of their extremes is truly relative, but that they are called such in name only: but this is false and contrary to the words of Aristotle, who said of one extreme of them alone that it is not denominated such through the relation by which it is itself referred to another, but through that by which another is referred to it: which cannot be true unless on the side of the other extreme a true real relation were given: for if it is not given, there will be nothing by which it is denominated. The sense of Aristotle, therefore, is: one extreme is relative because it is referred to another through its own relation; but the other is said to be relative not because it is referred, but because it receives a relative denomination from the relation of the other. From which it is also plain that Cajetan did not understand the same testimony of Aristotle well, gathering from it that both extremes of these relations are referred to another, the one through its own relation, the other through the relation of the other: whereas it is repugnant that anything be referred to another except through

a relation existing in itself. Aristotle, therefore, taught that a relative is denominated by the relation of the other, because a relation cannot attribute anything but the denomination of a relative; but that it is referred through another’s relation he never dreamed.

Q U E S T I O N X I V.

Whether a relation is distinguished from its foundation really, or only by reason.

125

The foundation of a relation of the first kind, we have already said, is substance, quality, and quantity, under the ratio of unity or of diversity, generic or specific. The foundation of a relation of the second kind: potency, active and passive, reduced to act through action and passion. And the adequation or commensuration of one thing with another, as of science with its object, is the foundation of a relation of the third kind. We ask, therefore, now: Whether relations arising in the extremes by means of these foundations are distinguished from the same foundations really, and before the operation of the intellect, or only by reason, through the intellect? As paternity from the generative potency, likeness from whiteness, and equality from quantity.

126 And the first opinion: No relation is distinguished really from its foundation, but only by reasoned reason having a foundation in the thing. So hold the

Nominalists, Ockham, and Major on 1, d. 3, q. 1; Gregory of Rimini, d. 28, q.

2, a. 1; Marsilius on 1, q. 32, a. 1; Hervaeus, d. 3, q. 1; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 22;

Soncinas in the same place, q. 28; Durandus on 1, d. 5, q. 2, no. 17. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. bk. 5, text 11, and Metaph. bk. 11, the penultimate chapter. In which places he asserts that relation does not terminate motion per se, because it is often acquired without change of the subject: one white body is made at Alcalá, and another white is made at Rome; the former acquires a new relation of likeness without any change of itself; indeed, without change of the whiteness existing in it; therefore it does not acquire a new real entity distinct from the whiteness. The consequence is proved: because if the relation were a new real entity distinct from the whiteness, it would acquire a new real form, which cannot be acquired without change of the subject; indeed, such an entity of relation would not even be produced by anything, because there is nothing by which it could be produced except the same agent by which the new white is produced at Rome; but it is repugnant that it be produced by that agent, since it cannot act at so great a distance.

It is proved also by reason. First, because those things which are distinguished

really can be separated from one another, at least by the absolute power of God, or the consequence of one upon the other can be impeded; but once the foundation is posited in both extremes, it is repugnant that the relation not follow; and while both also remain, it is repugnant that the relation not remain: as is manifest in two whites of the same degree, from which it is repugnant that likeness be separated; therefore relation is not a real entity distinct from its foundation.

Second, it is proved: Because entities are not to be multiplied without urgent necessity; but once a real distinction of relation from its foundation is posited, almost infinite entities are multiplied in single relatives, especially if they are referred to distinct terms through distinct relations (as is probable); therefore such a real distinction is not to be posited. The consequence is proved: because no efficacious reason urges by which it could be proved that it must be posited; but since relation is nothing else than a mode of being disposed toward another, we can understand without a new entity that a thing is disposed in another way, that is, is referred to another.

128 The second opinion makes use of a distinction. For it asserts that the relations which can be separated from the extremes, so that the extremes, remaining with their foundations, can be without the relation, are distinguished really from their foundations; but that those which cannot be separated from the same foundations once posited in the extremes are not distinguished from them except by reason. But which they are that can be separated from the extremes, and which cannot, it does not explain; indeed, it does not even bring forward any reason to confirm this: wherefore it speaks quite confusedly, declaring only this, that relations of the second kind, which it thinks are founded in bare potency and not in potency reduced to act, are not distinguished from their foundation. And it adds that relations which are identified with substance, whatever they may be, do not belong to this category, because it is repugnant for an accident to be identified with substance. But other moderns distinguish all relations founded in substance really from their foundation, on account of the same reason.

The third opinion: All real relations are distinguished from their foundations really: which almost all the Thomists follow: Cajetan, 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, and Báñez in the same place; Capreolus on 1, d. 3, q. 1; Ferrara on bk. 4 Against the Gentiles, ch. 14; Soto, q. 2 of this category; Fonseca, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 15, q. 2, sect. 1. And Scotus seems to follow the same, on 2, d. 1, q. 5, and on 3, d. 8, q. 1. And it seems to me more probable and to be held. Only this is to be added: that such a distinction is not so real as is found between two things, but such as is found between a thing and its mode: for since a relation cannot be in the nature of things without a relative (as

will be proved afterwards) it is not related to it as another thing distinct from it, but as its mode; therefore it is not distinguished as one thing from another, but through a distinct entity, indeed real and without dependence on the intellect, yet only modal, and by a distinction not of thing but of mode; and, explained in this way, almost all the moderns now follow it.

129 And it is proved from the doctrine of St. Thomas, who teaches three things about the relations of creatures. First, that they have a being distinct from the being of substance, and inhere in it according to this being. Second, that in created relatives, besides what is signified by the relative name, something else is found which is another thing, different from what is signified by the relative name. Third, that a created relation so inheres in its subject as to make a real composition with it, whereas a divine relation does not make a composition. The first and third he asserts in Against the Gentiles bk. 4, ch. 14; the second in 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, ad 2. From which it evidently follows that relation is distinguished from the nature of the thing, at least from the substance in which it inheres and which it orders to another: because real composition and real inherence presuppose a real distinction of the components, and also of the subject and the inhering form; but it was proved above, from the common opinion, that relations of the first kind are founded proximately in substance; therefore, at least of these relations, it is evident in the doctrine of St. Thomas that they are distinguished from substance from the nature of the thing; and since the ratio is the same for the others, it follows that he holds that all are distinguished from their foundations from the nature of the thing.

The same is proved by reason. First, from the new and real acquisition of a relation, and from its real loss. For while a body was white and was not like, it becomes like anew through the production of a new white; and while this white is corrupted, it ceases to be like. From which I argue thus: The first white was not really like before the second was produced; therefore when it is produced it becomes really and formally like, through a real relation of likeness, which it did not have before, although it had whiteness, which is its foundation; but a real relation is a real relative form; therefore it acquires a real relative form which it did not have; and a real form is a real entity; therefore it acquires a real entity which it did not have, although it had the foundation: the relation, therefore, is a thing distinct from the foundation. And the same follows from the real separation of the same relation from the subject: for when the other white is corrupted, the real likeness in this one is corrupted, therefore a real relative form, and therefore a real entity, while the real entity of the foundation remains; which cannot be true unless they are distinct real entities.

131 The moderns try to solve this argument in two ways. First, asserting that while the new white is produced, the old white acquires nothing new, but only has this new thing from the fact that it has been made like anew: namely, that it connotes a new extreme, which it did not connote before; whence the relation of likeness is nothing else (they say) than whiteness as connoting the term to which it is referred. Yet this solution does not satisfy the argument: because that white is denominated like anew, really and formally, and also accidentally, whereas before it was in no way so denominated; but a real and accidental denomination cannot come about except from a real inhering form; therefore a new denomination cannot come about except from a new real and inhering form. It is false, therefore, that to be like anew is only a new connotation of the term. The consequence is proved: because such a connotation, which presupposes a new real, formal, and accidental denomination, can neither be nor be understood without a new acquisition of a real form.

Wherefore others reply, second: It cannot be denied that the old white acquires something new, yet not distinct from the foundation really, but by reason alone; and, to say it in one word, that it does not acquire a new real entity, but a new formal relative ratio, from which it receives a new real denomination. Yet this solution contains only words and nothing else: wherefore it cannot satisfy the argument either; which I prove thus: Before the operation of the intellect, the old white becomes really, formally, and accidentally like, whereas before it was not like, although it had whiteness; but such a denomination cannot come except from an inhering form newly acquired, since the denomination is new, and it acquires such a new denomination without dependence on the intellect, indeed even though it is never known by it; therefore it acquires a new form, without dependence on or distinction by the intellect, and therefore distinct from the nature of the thing from the foundation which it had before.

132 Second: Concerning relations founded in substance, it is proved specially, because substance is a being per se, inhering in nothing, and a real accident by its proper nature inheres in substance; but relation is a real accident; therefore it inheres really in substance. But it is repugnant that the same real entity be per se and inhere in another, because it would be at once per se and not per se; therefore it is repugnant that relation be the same real entity with substance; wherefore it is necessary that a relation founded in substance be distinguished really from its foundation. Nor is there any force in what is customarily replied, that relation does not inhere in substance except as distinct

by reason from it. For this is openly false, because before the operation of the intellect one substance is referred to another through a real and accidental relation; therefore before the operation of the intellect the relation is in the substance. Then, therefore, it is either a being per se, before the operation of the intellect, or a being in another, not per se: if the former, it will be substance and not an accidental relation; therefore it is a being in another, which cannot be understood except through real inherence; and since the same thing cannot really inhere in itself, it follows that the relation really inhering is an entity distinct from the substance in which it inheres and in which it is founded.

133 To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is made with this distinction: for something to be changed happens in two ways, per se and per accidens. That is changed per se whose change is intended by nature or by some natural agent: as when a stone is changed from a higher place to a lower. But it is changed per accidens if its change happens by chance, or from the change of something else extrinsic. When, therefore, Aristotle says that motion does not terminate at relation per se, because a relation is customarily acquired without change of the subject in which it arises, he is speaking of per se change; but he does not exclude that what has newly received only a relation is changed at least per accidens: nor was this required for his intent, but it is enough that it is not changed per se, for it to be true that there is no motion per se to relation.

134 The second argument must be answered before the first. We reply, therefore, granting the major and the minor, but denying the consequence, that we distinguish the entity of the relation from the entity of the foundation without urgent necessity: for the reasons adduced are urgent enough.

Doubt on the separation of a relation from its foundation.

Concerning the solution of the second argument, it is doubted: Whether, once the foundation of the relation is posited in both extremes, the relation so necessarily arises that such a consequence cannot be impeded even by the absolute power of God; and whether, after it has already been posited in both extremes, it can be separated from them, so that two whites of the same degree of intensity remain without the relation of likeness.

And the first opinion holds: It cannot be impeded from following, nor, after it is already in the extremes, be separated from them: so some of the moderns. And that its consequence cannot be impeded once the foundation is posited in both extremes they prove: because it cannot be understood that one man has begotten another without the former being father and the latter son (if both remain); nor can two whites in the same degree be understood without being understood to be like. Therefore it cannot happen

that the relation does not follow once the foundation is posited in both extremes. And that, after the relation is already in both extremes, it cannot in any way be separated from them, they prove by this argument: Relation is nothing else than that one extreme is so disposed toward the other, the foundation being presupposed; therefore it is a mode of the relatives; but a mode cannot be separated from the thing whose mode it is, otherwise it would no longer be a mode but a thing; therefore neither can the relation be separated from the foundations existing in both extremes.

136 Our view, however, is that, supposing the distinction from the nature of the thing between the relation and the foundation, which we defend, the relation can be separated from it even when it is posited in both extremes: so that God can impede it from following in the extremes, and also, after it is found in them, make it cease to be in them: not indeed so that it exists without them in the nature of things, but so that the extremes exist without it.

The two former points are proved by this argument: Relation is an entity distinct from the nature of the thing from its foundation, and does not belong to its essence, or to that of the extremes in which it is; therefore, even if it naturally follows from it once it is posited in both extremes, it does not imply a contradiction that such a consequence be impeded. The antecedent is manifest from our view, because relation is not only an entity distinct from the foundation, but also has a formal and categorial ratio different from it; therefore there is no repugnance in its consequence from the foundation posited in both extremes being impeded by God: just as it is not repugnant that a proper attribute really distinct from the essence from which it proceeds should not proceed from it, as risibility from the essence of man. And by the same reason it is proved that, after it is found in them, they can remain without it.

137 But since its being separated from them can be understood in two ways: first, so that it remains in the nature of things without them, and the extremes also without it; or second, not so, but so that the relation is destroyed or ceases to be, and the extremes remain without it: we say, therefore, that it can be separated from them in this second way, not in the first. The first is proved: because it is not of the essence of the extremes, and the relation has an entity distinct from them; therefore it is not repugnant that it be destroyed by God while the extremes remain without it. The second is proved: because relation is a mode of the extremes, through which one is so disposed in order to the other; therefore it is intrinsic to it actually to refer one to the other; and therefore it is repugnant that it remain in the nature of things without actually referring: because if it were given separated from them, it would refer nothing to another.

To the first argument of the opposite opinion: The antecedent must be distinguished: because that two whites are like can be understood in two ways, formally or fundamentally; and if the relation were separated from them, they would be understood to be like fundamentally, not formally: in which there is no repugnance; and in the same way the one generating and the one generated would be understood to be father and son as it were in the proximate foundation, not formally.

To the second: The antecedent must be granted, that relation is a mode of the extremes; from which it follows only that it cannot be in the nature of things without the extremes, but not that the extremes cannot be without it.

F I R S T D O U B T.

Whether it belongs to relation to have a contrary.

Two doubts remain concerning two properties of relatives, of which the first is: That contrariety is found in them. For Aristotle seems to be contrary to himself in this property. For in the chapter on quantity he expressly denies that relatives have a contrary; but in the present chapter he attributes it to them as a property, that they have a contrary. And they seem to have one: because like and unlike are contraries, and also equal and unequal, and they are relatives of the first kind.

138 The first opinion is that of Toledo in his exposition of the text, who uses this distinction: Relatives can be considered in two ways. First, formally, as they are relatives. Second, materially, for the foundations of the relations, as two whites are considered inasmuch as they are like, and inasmuch as they are white. And under the first consideration, he says, they do not have a contrary, but by reason of the foundation they can well have one; and when Aristotle denied that they have a contrary, he spoke formally; but when he attributes contrariety to them, he speaks fundamentally: for in this way unlike things are contraries, as white and black.

Our view, however, is: Proper contrariety does not belong to relatives, neither formally nor by reason of the foundation; but improper contrariety, for any kind of opposition whatever, belongs to them even formally. That proper contrariety does not belong to them formally is proved by this reason: Contraries are those which, under the same genus, are most distant, and mutually expel one another from the same subject; therefore contraries, as such, formally and expressly regard the subject around which they expel one another; but relatives, as relatives, do not formally and expressly regard the subject, but the term; therefore, as relatives, they are not properly

contraries. And that they are not so by reason of the foundation either is proved: because, although the foundations of some relatives are contraries, as whiteness and blackness, which are foundations of unlikeness, yet contrariety is related per accidens to the ratio of unlikeness. This is proved evidently: because specific diversity alone, without any contrariety, founds the relation of unlikeness: as whiteness and blackness, or any other contraries which are foundations of unlikeness, would found it in the same way even if they were not contraries, through the specific difference alone; therefore contrariety is also related per accidens to founding the relation, and therefore it does not belong to relation by reason of the foundation considered per se, or as it is a foundation.

To Aristotle, however, I reply that he is not contrary to himself: because in the chapter on quantity he speaks according to his own view, denying that anything is contrary to relatives; but in the present chapter he attributes contrariety to them, not because he thinks it is a true property of theirs, but to show that the definition of the ancients is not good: since from it follows that absolute accidents in which contrariety is found are relatives, and that something is contrary to relatives; and since these things are false, it follows that that definition is not good; nor is it true that something is contrary to true relatives, nor did

Aristotle ever teach this from his own view. Finally, that improper contrariety, for any kind of opposition whatever, belongs to them as relatives is evident, since relation, taken formally, includes relative opposition, which is one kind out of the four oppositions.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

Whether relatives admit of more and less.

140

This doubt proceeds concerning relatives according to being and categorial relatives alone. And the reason for doubting is taken from Aristotle, who asserts: It is proper to relatives to admit of more and less. And lest he should seem to anyone not to be speaking of true relatives and from his own view, but from the view of the ancients and according to their definition, he gives an example of this property in the like and the unlike, which are true and categorial relatives.

The first opinion distinguishes relatives: for some are according to being, which properly belong to this category; others according to being said, which are truly absolute, yet include certain respects according to being said, as an essential complement:

[p. 437]

> &illapriora non fufcipiunt magis & minus: hæc verò fufcipe-repoffunt. Ita Albertus Mag, tract. de prædicamento ad ali-quid,cap 3. Secunda opinio,Diſtinguit relationem, expartefui:aut, ex pariefundamenii ; & ex parte fui, negat veram relationem huius prædicamenti fufcipere magis , & minus : fed ratione fundamenti fufcipere concedit. Ita Caietanus,Sotus,&Tole-zus, cap.præfenti. 141 Quod probatur experientia . Nam dum albedo intendi-tur in extremo,in quo erat remiſſa, confequenter fitmagis fi-mile alteri,in quo eſt intenía:ergo albedo,quæ eſt fundamen-tum fimilitudinis,perſeſuſcipit magis, & minùs, & eius ratio -nefimilitudo; & eodem modo, dum aliquid eſt alteri inæqua-le,quò magis auferturde quantitate eius,magis inæquale effi-citur,&hoc eft,relationem inæqualitatis,minorem fieri, ratio-ne fundamenti. Sed addithæc fententia,non efle neceffarium, vtrelatiofufcipiat magis& ininus ratione fundamenti, quod fundamentum fufcipiat magis &minus:nam quantitas, ratio-ne cuius inæqualitas,maior eſt,vel minor, non fufcipit magis &minus : fed ratione fundamenti dicitur relatio fufcipere in hoc fenfu : quodnon poteſt ſuſcipere , nifi aliqua variatio fiat infundamento , quæcunque illa fit : vnde magis & minus,di-ſtinguenda putat Caietanus : quia vel fumuntur Phyfice : & hocmodonon fiunt,nifi per admixtionem contrarij : aut Lo-gicè,& fic ſumpta , in co tantùm confiftunt , quod eft aliquid prædicari de alio, cum his aduerbiis magis & minus,vndecun-que id proueniat. Et Phyficè quidem fumpta, nonconue-niuntverè relationi: Logicè verò conuenire illi poffunt. Hæc tamen diftincto, confundit potiùs rem, quam cam Le üj

and the former do not admit of more and less, while the latter can admit of them. So Albert the Great, in the treatise on the category of relation, ch. 3. And St. Thomas seems to be of this opinion, c. 12, q. 82, a. 4. Others also follow it, who say that according to the truth no relative admits of more and less, but that according to the opinion of the common people some do admit them: as things are customarily called equal or like which, although they are not truly equal or like, yet are little distant from true equality or likeness; and the less they are distant, the more they are called equal or like. So Canterus in the exposition of this property.

The first is proved: because to admit of more and less comes from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary, as that is called more hot which has less cold admixed, and that less hot which has more cold admixed; but true categorial relatives do not have a contrary, as was proved in the preceding doubt; therefore they do not admit of more and less.

The second opinion distinguishes relation on its own side or on the side of the foundation; and on its own side it denies that a true relation of this category admits of more and less, but grants that it admits of them by reason of the foundation. So Cajetan, Soto, and Toledo, in the present chapter.

141 This is proved by experience. For while whiteness is intensified in an extreme in which it was remiss, consequently it becomes more like the other, in which it is intense; therefore whiteness, which is the foundation of likeness, per se admits of more and less, and by reason of it likeness does; and in the same way, while something is unequal to another, the more is taken away from its quantity, the more unequal it is made; and this is for the relation of inequality to become less by reason of the foundation. But this opinion adds that it is not necessary, for the relation to admit of more and less by reason of the foundation, that the foundation admit of more and less: for quantity, by reason of which inequality is greater or less, does not admit of more and less; but the relation is said to admit of them by reason of the foundation in this sense: that it cannot admit of them unless some variation take place in the foundation, whatever it may be. Whence Cajetan thinks that more and less must be distinguished: because either they are taken Physically, and in this way they come about only through admixture of a contrary; or Logically, and taken so they consist only in this, that something is predicated of another with these adverbs more and less, from wherever that may come. And taken Physically they do not truly belong to relation; but Logically they can belong to it.

This distinction, however, confuses the matter rather than

explains it: because Logical predications must be founded in the thing itself; therefore more and less, taken Logically, can never belong to relation except by reason of a real foundation, and Physically; wherefore, if taken Physically they in no way belong to it, neither will they be able to belong to it Logically.

Our view, therefore, is to be explained presupposing this distinction: More and less are taken in two ways, Commonly and Properly. Commonly, for more or less perfect, more or less near or distant: whence, since greater or lesser perfection comes from the foundation, from it will come more and less in relation, taken improperly. But more and less are taken properly as they proceed from greater or lesser intensity.

And now it is explained by two conclusions. The first is: To categorial relations (of which alone we are speaking) it does not belong by reason of themselves to admit of more or less, either properly or improperly. This conclusion is proved: Because it is established by experience that a relation, by reason of itself, does not change from the state in which it emerges unless the foundation is varied in some way; and if this remains invariable, it never admits of more and less; therefore this does not belong to it by reason of itself.

143 The second conclusion: More and less, taken properly and improperly, belong to certain relations by reason of the foundation, yet not to all. Both are proved in relations of the first kind: for some things are called more and less unequal, more and less like; but this does not belong to them by reason of themselves; therefore by reason of the foundation; and to likeness and unlikeness properly, because the qualities in which they are founded properly admit of more and less, as heat, whiteness, and blackness. And when we say that more and less belong to these relations by reason of the foundation, the sense is that, when some change is made in the foundation, they always belong to them; and this change can be remission in the foundation and intensification in the relation, since the foundation is intensified absolutely, as it is a quality, but the relation only by comparison with another. And that this does not belong except to certain relations of the first kind is manifest, because it belongs only to those whose foundations can be changed.

144 To Aristotle the reply is that, when he attributes to relations the property of admitting of more and less, he is indeed speaking of categorial ones, yet he does not understand that it belongs to them by reason of themselves, but by reason of the foundation, as has been explained; nor does he understand that it belongs to them even in this sense in the fourth mode,

since it is established that it belongs neither to all nor to them alone, because it belongs chiefly to qualities. But the property belonging to categorial relatives in the fourth mode is to be simultaneous by nature and in cognition: so that whoever knows one definitively must necessarily know the other.

But someone will say: To admit of more and less proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary; but it has been said that relatives have a contrary neither by reason of themselves nor by reason of the foundation; therefore to admit of more and less will belong to them neither by reason of themselves nor by reason of the foundation. The reply is that by reason of themselves neither belongs to them; but by reason of the foundation it is not repugnant that the second belong to them, although the first does not belong even by reason of the foundation: because the contrariety of the foundation is related per accidens to those relations in which there could be contrariety, as to likeness and unlikeness

(as was proved in the first doubt); but more and less on the side of the foundation are not related altogether per accidens to the more and less of relations, but follow from it as it were naturally. And from the fact that relatives lack contrariety in all ways, it follows only that they could not admit of more and less by reason of themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII

Containing the category of Quality.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

But I call quality that according to which certain things are said to be qualified, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the nature 1

T          and essence of quality, which he numbers in the fourth place before

the six other categories, because it is an intrinsic accident, formally inhering in substance, and therefore more perfect than the rest, which for the most part consist in certain extrinsic denominations. The chapter is divided into three parts. In the first, he defines quality in the abstract and enumerates its four subaltern species, which he therefore calls genera. In the second part, he defines quality in the concrete, that is, through its order to the subject which it denominates, so that through this it may become more manifest. And in the third, he assigns three properties of it. The definition of quality is this: Quality is that by which we are said to be qualified

as whiteness, by which a man is denominated white, and therefore qualified, because if you ask, What kind is the man? it will be well answered if it is said that he is white.

The first species of quality is Habit and disposition. Habit is defined thus: It is a quality difficult to move from the subject, as the habits of the virtues and sciences. But disposition: A quality easily movable from the subject, as heat, which fire produces in water, is easily removed from it.

2 The second genus of quality is Natural potency and impotency, according to which some have a natural inclination or aptitude to some act or some exercise, as to boxing or to wrestling, and are called boxers. Others are inept or impotent for the same act. And it is called natural because it is had from nature itself and is not acquired through acts: for if it were such, it would rather be a habit or disposition.

The third genus is Passion or passible quality; and this is a quality apt to cause passion in the sense, or which is the effect of a permanent passion; as the tangible qualities, which cause sensation in touch, as heat and cold, and so of the others; and whiteness, which is caused in wax by the excessive heat of the sun, is also called a passible quality, because it is the effect of that impression which the Sun causes in the wax; and permanent, because the whiteness produced in the wax does not pass at once, but remains in it. But a quality is called a passion if it is the effect of a quickly passing passion; as the redness caused in the face by shame; and because a passion is not a permanent quality, it does not denominate the subject such simply, but as having suffered according to it: whence from redness caused by shame a man is not called red, but one who has suffered redness, and so of the other passions.

3 The fourth genus of quality is Form and Figure, as straightness, curvature; a statue or a chair are called forms and figures and species of this genus.

In the second part of the chapter Aristotle defines quality in the concrete in this way: Qualified is that which is denominated according to quality, as white and sweet.

In the third part he enumerates three properties of quality, of which the first is That quality has a contrary: as cold is contrary to heat; yet this property does not belong to all qualities, because there are several that have no contrary, as red, pale, and the other intermediate colors.

The second property is To admit of more and less; which, since it proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary, must necessarily belong to those that properly have a contrary; but neither does it belong to

The third property of quality is that according to it things are called like or unlike: as according to whiteness bodies are called like. And this property belongs to quality in the fourth mode, because it belongs to all qualities, to them alone, and always.

## QUESTION I

Whether quality is the supreme genus of this category, and the diverse qualities enumerated by Aristotle are diverse species of it.

hat the question may be better understood, the different accepta4

T            tions of quality must be explained; of which (omitting others) there

are three, as is gathered from Aristotle in the present chapter and

Metaph. 5, ch. 14. Quality in general signifies a determination or modification of substance; and therefore its first acceptation is for anything whatever that determines or modifies another: which belongs not only to all accidents but also to substances, or to their differences. In the second way it is taken for any accidental form whatever which, according to its own proper mode of being, modifies or determines substance: as quantity, relation, and the other accidents; and this acceptation too is common. But the third is the proper one, for a form which determines the subject not only according to the common accidental ratio, but properly: so that it makes the substance inhering in it be disposed in such a way that through it, as through a form, it is formally denominated not extended, not related to another, but qualified; because to the question put about it through what kind, we properly reply through such a form: as, if it is asked, What kind is the substance? we properly reply that it is white, or hot.

And therefore these accidental forms are properly called qualities. And it is according to this acceptation alone, not according to the other two, that quality is taken by Aristotle in the present chapter and is distinguished from the other categories; and concerning it the title of the question asks: Whether it is the supreme genus of this category, and the particular qualities enumerated by Aristotle are true species of it.

5 The first opinion holds that quality so taken is not a true genus which is divided into those qualities enumerated by Aristotle as into true species, but as an analogous term into its analogates, or as a thing into its different modes. The first is affirmed by Simplicius on the present chapter, and he proves it from the same Aristotle, who, before enumerating those qualities, speaks thus: But

quality is among the things that are said in many ways. The second is held by Scotus on the present chapter, q. 36, and in 4, d. 6, q. 10, § But then there is a doubt; and he too proves it by the testimony of Aristotle, who, after enumerating all these qualities, says: Perhaps indeed some other mode of quality might appear; but those which are most of all spoken of are these.

7 It is proved also by reason: Because to be a natural potency, or an acquired aptitude, to be a cause or an effect of passion, signify different relations of quality to the subject, but accidental ones, and denominating as it were extrinsically: since it is extrinsic to quality to last a short or a long time in the subject, to be a cause or an effect of passion. Hence redness caused by shame and redness caused by some other permanent cause are of the same species; and, what is more, these modes belong to the same quality wholly unchanged: therefore they are not essential differences but accidental ones. This last antecedent is proved: Because the same heat, if it passes quickly, will be a disposition; if it lasts long in the subject, it will be a habit; and as the natural power of fire to heat, it will be a natural potency; and finally, insofar as it causes a passion in the sense of touch, or is produced by the motion of heating, it will be a passible quality: from which considerations it is plain that it does not vary.

To this opinion Boethius and Simplicius, on the present chapter, add that the division of quality into these modes, or into these analogates, is not sufficient: because there are other members of this division passed over by Aristotle. This is proved thus: Beauty and health are qualities, and they do not pertain to any member of these four: since they are neither habits nor dispositions, because they are not acquired but natural; nor potencies or impotencies, because they are not ordered to exercising any acts; nor passions or passible qualities, because they neither are per se effects of passion nor cause it in the sense; nor finally are they form and figure, which is plain of health, and is proved of beauty, which admits of more and less, since some are more beautiful than others; but figure and form do not have this.

The common opinion, to be held by us, asserts two things. First, that quality is a true genus, and the supreme genus of this category, divided into the particular qualities enumerated by Aristotle as into true species: against Simplicius and Scotus. Second, that its division into those four members is sufficient, so that no true quality is given which is not comprehended under them: against the same Simplicius and Boethius.

This is the express opinion of Aristotle, not only in this chapter, sect. 5,

[p. 443]

Metaph. ch. 14, and received by the whole school: which posits a category of quality distinct from the others, with it; but it is impossible to constitute the category of quality out of another genus and in other species; therefore quality in common is to be received as the supreme genus, and those inferior qualities as true species. I prove the minor: because neither by these authors who hold the contrary, nor by anyone else, has any other genus or other species been thought up.

It is proved nonetheless by reason: Because the common concept of quality, abstracted from them, is predicated of each of them quidditatively and univocally; therefore it is a genus or a species with respect to them. A species it cannot be, because it has no other genus above itself; therefore it will be a genus. The antecedent is proved: because it cannot be denied that these predications are quidditative: A habit is a quality, A natural potency is a quality, since the definition of quality given by Aristotle belongs to them, and belongs to them equally, without attribution of one to another; therefore it is a univocal and quidditative predicate. And that those qualities are distinguished in species is no less manifest: because the formal ratio of habit is very different from natural potency, and this from form and figure; but different formal rationes constitute and distinguish different species: therefore those four qualities are distinguished in species under the common genus of quality.

8 It is proved, finally, that the division of quality into these four species is sufficient, so that there are neither more nor fewer, by the argument of St. Thomas which he adduced in 1-2, q. 49, a. 2: The intrinsic and proper ratio of quality is to be a determination of substance according to its accidental qualifying mode; but this qualifying mode of substance can stand in only four ways in relation to substance; therefore only four species can be distinguished under it. The minor is proved: because either quality inheres in substance disposing it so that it is well or ill disposed, as it is first in itself; and since this is the first consideration of substance, this will be the first species of quality, which is habit and disposition, so disposing substance. The second consideration of substance is insofar as it is a principle of operation, since each thing exists for the sake of its operation. And therefore the second mode of quality is to affect substance as a principle of operation, and this is the second species, natural potency.

9 But from substance already having the potency of operating there proceeds at once, third, motion, containing action and passion: because motion, as it proceeds from the agent, is action, and as it is received in the patient, is passion; therefore quality, as acquired through motion, is the third

Scoti:Negandum eſt antecedens, quòd rationes formales diuerfæ harum qualitatum,ſint accidentales, aut ex-trinfecæ:nam fpecialis ratio,quam habet quælibet qualifican-di ſubſtantia,intrinfeca fibieſt,& per quam diftinguitur à cæ teris,tanquam per differentiam effentialem: vt eſſe ex propria natura,facilè autdifficilè mobilemà fubiecto,eſſentialis ratio, habitus, &difpofitionis , eſt valde diuerfa à naturalipotentia,

species, which is called passion and passible quality. For if it has a permanent mode, it is a passible quality as well; but if it passes quickly, it is a passion. The last consideration of substance is as already extended through quantity; and so the quality inhering in it by reason of quantity constitutes the fourth species, which is form and figure: for figure either is the termination of quantity or results from its terms. And to these four modes, constituting four species, all qualities can easily be reduced, as was plain from the solution of the arguments. Only this is to be noted: that this argument takes the sufficiency of these species either from the principal member, to which that special ratio of qualifying substance belongs, or from the first; whence it is not necessary that that ratio be found in all the things which are comprehended under such a ratio. For example: the first species is taken from the mode of affecting substance so that it is well or ill disposed according to its proper nature; which only natural habits or dispositions have, which belong first to corporeal substance, such as health, sickness, and the like; not, however, habits or dispositions freely acquired. But since all agree in the ratio of habit and disposition, insofar as they are easily or not easily removable from the subject, all constitute the same genus of quality, distinct from the others, but taken as it were radically from the natural ones, as from the first.

10 To the first testimony of Aristotle adduced for the first opinion: it is replied that quality is said in many ways, not as an analogous or equivocal term, but on account of differences of unequal perfection by which it is contracted to different species; whose diversity does not take away the univocation of the genus, which can be abstracted from them. Or, second, I reply that Aristotle asserted that quality is said in many ways in order to show that quality is a mode of substance, and that its species are taken from the different modes of affecting substance, as has been explained.

To the second testimony, for the opinion of Scotus, it is replied that Aristotle spoke thus to signify that all other qualities can easily be reduced to these four species, although some appear different from them.

11 To the argument of Scotus: the antecedent must be denied, that the different formal rationes of these qualities are accidental or extrinsic: for the special ratio of qualifying substance which each has is intrinsic to it, and is that through which it is distinguished from the others, as through an essential difference: as to be, by its own nature, easily or not easily removable from the subject, the essential ratio of habit and disposition, is very different from natural potency,

And that all the formal rationes of the species can belong to the same quality, we grant; but we deny what is inferred from this, that they are not true species: because specific distinction is not necessarily real; but the same thing can pertain to different species under the different formal rationes which it has; indeed, to different categories, as is plain of action and passion: which, although they are the same real entity or mode, nevertheless make different categories on account of their different formal rationes.

To the argument of Boethius: the antecedent must be denied, that there are other members passed over by Aristotle besides those four: for he himself placed health in the first species, and beauty pertains to the same; and both are natural habits: because habit, as it is the first genus of quality, is taken universally for any quality not easily removable from the subject, whether it be natural or acquired; although the special and most proper ratio of habit is found only in powers that are in some way free, and therefore only acquired or infused habits are habits in that sense. But intentional species, sensible or intelligible, if they are impressed, pertain to the species of habit, because by their own nature they are permanent; but if they are expressed, they pertain to disposition. And the same is to be understood of the other qualities that are to be reduced to these four species.

## QUESTION II

Whether habit and disposition are distinguished in species.

he first opinion holds that habit and disposition are not distinct species, 12

T           but the same, and differ only accidentally: so Soto, q. 9 on this chapter, §

To the second question; Boethius, Ammonius, Titelmans, Villalpando, the

Louvain commentators, also on the present chapter; and it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, because he says three things in the text about these qualities.

First, that they are one species. Second, that all habits are dispositions, although not all dispositions are habits. Third, that a disposition becomes a habit, as time goes on, if it takes very deep root in the subject. From which it follows, in his mind, that they are not distinct species, but are distinguished only accidentally. The consequence is proved: because if they were distinct species, they would neither be one, nor would one be predicated of the other, nor could one be converted into the other.

13 And it is proved by reason. First, because habit and disposition are distinguished by this, that the former is separated from the subject with difficulty, while the latter is easily removed from it; but these are accidental

differences; therefore they differ only accidentally. The minor is proved: for a quality becomes not easily removable from the subject because it is more deeply rooted in it; but greater rooting proceeds from the multiplication of acts, or from length of time, or from both, as is plain in a fever, which, from the mere fact that it lasts long in the subject, is rooted in it and becomes not easily removable; but to persevere more or less in the subject, or for acts to be multiplied, are accidents of the same quality: therefore this difference of habit and disposition is accidental.

Second: any science and virtue is of the same species, whether acquired through the first or the second act, and, with the passage of time, more deeply rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of acts; but in the beginning it has the ratio of disposition, because it can easily be removed from the subject, and afterwards it becomes a habit, because it is now not easily removable: therefore these differences, to be easily and not easily removable from the subject, are accidental. The major is proved: because the specific distinction of science and of virtue is taken from the object; but science or virtue has the same object at the beginning of its acquisition and when it is already rooted in the subject through many acts: therefore it is of the same species.

14 The second opinion distinguishes habit and disposition as two subalternate species, so that under habit several others, of different habits, are distinguished, and likewise under disposition. This is the opinion of St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 49, a. 2, ad 3; of Javelli, Cajetan, Soto, Toledo, and Canterus on the present chapter; which is followed also by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 1 and 2, and by Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 42, sect. 6, no. 6. And it seems to us more probable, and to be held.

But in order that we may explain and prove it, two things are to be noted. The first is: that a quality’s being easily or not easily removable from the subject comes about in two ways: namely, from the nature of its cause, through which it is produced in the subject and in relation to which it obtains its species; or from other causes or extrinsic reasons. And if it is considered in the first way, it is an essential difference of one quality from another, so that one which is in this way not easily removable from the subject is distinct in species from another which, considered in the same way, is easily removable. But if they are considered in the second way, they are only accidental differences. An example of the first consideration we have in science and opinion: for the former has as its cause demonstration, by which it is produced and in relation to which it is specified; and demonstration is an efficacious cause, since it is an evident and necessary argument; and therefore science acquired through it, even through the first act, is not easily removable from

[p. 447]

> fubiecto. the subject. But opinion has as its cause a probable argument, which is not efficacious, but can easily be destroyed by an opposite demonstration, or by an opposite and more probable argument: therefore opinion is easily removable, from the nature of its cause.

15 Whence it follows that, although they are concerned with the same object, they are nevertheless distinguished in species under this genus of quality, by the essential differences of easily and not easily removable, from the nature of their causes. An example of the second consideration is in feverish heat: which, on account of the weakness of the subject, or its particular complexion, or other accidental extrinsic causes, is wont to be so rooted in the subject that not only is it not easily removable from it, but it is naturally impossible for it to be separated from it; and yet it is of the same species at the beginning and at the end, and is distinguished from itself only accidentally.

The second thing to be noted is: that although to be easily and not easily removed from accidental causes, namely from the frequent repetition of acts or from length of time, are accidental differences of habit and disposition, they are nevertheless as it were accidents congruent with the nature of these qualities: so that, since habit is essentially not easily removable on account of the nature of its cause, it is also an accident conformable to its nature to be not easily removable through rooting in the subject.

16 And since disposition is easily removable on account of the nature of its cause, it is also an accident consonant with its nature not to be rooted in the subject, but to be able to be separated from it easily also on the part of accidental causes. And these accidental differences give them the state of habit and of disposition: so that habit then has the state congruent with its nature when it is rooted in the subject, and disposition when it is not rooted. Whence it can come about that some quality has the essence of habit but the state of disposition; and conversely, the essence of disposition and the state of habit; and then they are distinguished essentially, although the accident of the other belongs to one; and therefore it is true that habit is accidentally disposition, and disposition accidentally habit. Science or virtue acquired through the first act has both: because it is essentially habit and accidentally disposition: it has, that is, the essence of habit and the state of disposition. But opinion, rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of acts, conversely, is essentially disposition and accidentally habit: it has the essence of disposition and the state of habit.

17 From this doctrine the difference between the first and the second opinion is understood: for the first holds that to be easily and not easily removable comes only from the side of the subject, or of accidental causes,
