Whence it does not follow that true nouns and verbs are found wherever a proposition is found, but only that terms are found of which it is composed: which in the mental proposition are the concepts of the extremes and of the copula, and in the written one nouns and verbs depicted; and therefore not such simply, but in a certain respect.

## QUESTION II

Whether the noun is defined through word as through a true genus.

Word can be considered in two ways. First, Materially, as it denotes only an articulate sound made by the human instruments. Second, Formally, as significative, from which it has it that it is a noun or a verb. And considered in the first way, it stands as the subject of that same signification, common to the noun and the verb: just as wood is a common subject with respect to a chair and a door, able to receive the artificial form of both. But if it is considered as significative, it is a true genus with respect to the noun and the verb. The question, then, is whether the noun is defined through word taken materially, as through a subject, as a statue is defined through wood; or rather through word taken formally, as significative, as through a true genus: so that significative word is the genus of this definition, and the remaining particles are differences.

And the first opinion holds that the noun is not defined through word as through a subject, but through significative word, as through a true genus common to the noun and the verb. So Nifo, Lemosius, and Psellus, on the present chapter; and it is proved: Because any thing whatever is to be defined by a quidditative definition, if that can be done, since this is the best mode of defining; but if significative is posited as a true genus, the definition of the noun will be quidditative, whereas if word alone is posited as a subject it will not be quidditative, since the subject is not the genus of an accident but outside its quiddity: therefore the noun as defined by Aristotle ought to be understood in the first way rather than in the second.

The second opinion is that of St. Thomas and Ammonius, on the present chapter: that the noun is not defined by Aristotle through significative word as through a true genus, but through word alone, as through a subject, put in the place of the genus. And this is the more probable; its chief foundation is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 6, where

[p. 507]

he says that the proper mode of defining artificial things is through the subject in place of the genus, and through the artificial form in place of the difference: as, if you wish to define a house, you will say that it is stones and timbers so put together. And

St. Thomas, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 7, says that not only artificial things but also all accidents are better defined through the subject in place of the genus than through a true genus. And the reason for this is manifest: because the essence of an accident and its mode of being are taken from its order to the subject:

therefore both become better known through the subject; and since the definition is handed down for this end, that through it we may know the nature of the definitum, the better mode of defining accidents will be through the subject, put in place of the genus, rather than through the true genus, which becomes known through that same subject. But the noun and the verb are certain artificial accidents, made by the intellect and signified in the concrete: therefore they are better defined through word, as through a subject, than through significative word, as through a true genus; and so they are to be judged to have been defined by

Aristotle.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major is to be distinguished. For if the thing that is defined is a substance, it is to be defined quidditatively through genus and difference, if that can be done; but if it is an accident, especially an artificial one and signified in the concrete, the more natural mode, and that through which its essence will be more clearly explained, will be to define it through the subject in place of the genus: because its true genus and its true difference are to be known through the subject with respect to which they are taken, rather than through themselves; and consequently so are its quiddity and essence, for the knowing of which a definition is per se ordered.

## QUESTION III

Whether the noun truly signifies by convention, as is said in the definition.

10

Concerning the mode of signifying of Words, St. Thomas reports three opinions in the commentary on this chapter. The first was that of those who held that they are natural signs of things, as we say of concepts: which Dexippus, bk.

1 of the Questions on the Categories, ch. 6, attributes to Pythagoras and his disciples; and it seems also to have been that of Heraclitus and Cratylus. And it is proved by this argument: Because to those to whom nature has given a faculty, or power, for exercising some act, it consequently gives natural instruments by which they can exercise it: as it gave man the faculty of walking, and therefore gave him feet so fashioned that he can walk with them; but the faculty of speaking is natural: therefore nature gave man, together with

it, natural instruments through which he might speak; but these instruments are words, not bare ones (otherwise brute animals too could speak), but articulate and significative ones, just as to brute animals nature gave sounds signifying naturally, by which they might manifest their internal affections: therefore significative words were given by nature to men, by which they might manifest to others the internal concepts of the mind. From which it evidently follows that their signification is natural, and not from the imposition of men: because whatever is granted by nature is natural.

The second opinion is diametrically opposed, asserting that the signification of words not only is not from nature, but proceeds from the good pleasure of men in such a way that anyone may at his discretion use these names already imposed, or devise other new ones and impose them for signifying, and use them in speaking as he pleases, and afterward, leaving these, impose other new ones. This seems to have been held by a certain Hermogenes, a Philosopher older than Plato and Aristotle, as Plato himself testifies in the dialogue Cratylus.

The reason for this view is: because, if the signification of words depends on the free will of men, it can be changed at discretion; so that words imposed today for signifying may tomorrow signify nothing any longer, or be changed from their first signification and be imposed anew to signify other different things, and therefore be said to fall away from their signification; from which no inconvenience follows.

The third opinion is midway between these extremes, granting that words do not signify naturally, but from the imposition of men; yet that this imposition is not so free that anyone may at his discretion use these or those words and impose them anew for signifying, but is congruent with the natures of the things they are imposed to signify: so that to each thing, according to its proper nature, such names are accommodated. And so the free imposition of men had a certain discerning consideration accompanying or preceding it, through which the imposer, knowing the natures of things, accommodated to them proper names by which they might be congruently signified; and such an imposition lasts perpetually, and has been so inviolably received by all that no one may change it at his discretion or introduce new impositions of words. This view has been followed by the weightiest Philosophers: Plato in the place cited above; Aristotle in these chapters; Cicero, bk. 1 of the Academic Questions; Quintilian, bk. 8 of the Institutes, ch. 6; St. Thomas; Albert the Great, with the other expositors of this chapter. And this is true and to be held.

11 In order to explain and prove it at the same time, it should be noted that things are of two different kinds. For some are Natural, to which it is certain that names were accommodated, at God’s direction, by our first parent, endowed with divine wisdom, through which he perfectly knew the nature of each thing, as these words of Gen. 2 show: Therefore the Lord God, having formed out of the ground all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them: for whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name. As if God were saying that this universal imposition, made by his commission, is perpetual in such a way that it is never altogether, or anywhere, to be changed by anyone, although names are different according to the diversity of nations and languages; in which also it is evident that no one has ever been permitted to change the imposition at his discretion. Others are Artificial things, to which also names have been accommodated by men endowed with art, who through it perfectly know their condition, names agreeing with that condition: that is, such that their signification is taken either from the way in which they are made, or from some property of theirs, or from the use to which they are ordered by art.

This is to be understood as true for the most part: for it sometimes happens that no such likeness, at least none known to us, is preserved in the imposition of a name. And this doctrine at once explains and proves the truth of the common view, which we follow.

But to the argument of the first opinion: Granting the major, the minor is to be denied, namely that words are the instruments of the natural faculty of speaking; rather, the instruments of this faculty are the tongue, teeth, and palate, by which those same words are formed; and once formed they are imposed for signifying, so that they may be media by which a man may express his own concepts to others. Wherefore, although on the part of the sound words are natural, yet on the part of the signification they come about through art or science: just as a chair is natural on the part of the wood, but artificial on the part of the form, made through art, and therefore is called simply artificial; so too nouns and verbs are to be called artificial.

But the argument of the second opinion is solved by the doctrine handed down: because, although the imposition of words for signifying is free, it is nevertheless conformed to the natures of things, and therefore not made by just anyone, but by wise men who, perfectly knowing their natures, accommodated to them such names as were congruent with them; whence neither can the signification of names be varied at discretion, nor can names fall away from it.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether it is true that the parts of a noun, when separated, are not significative.

Aristotle proved this particle of the definition from a composite noun, whose parts when separated, he says, are not significative as they are its parts, even though they are whole nouns: therefore much less will the parts of a simple noun be significative when separated, since they are not whole nouns but syllables and letters. But this reasoning is worth nothing: therefore it is not proved by it that the parts of a noun when separated are not significative; nor will this be true. The antecedent is proved: Because the parts of a composite noun are whole nouns, or a whole noun and a verb, as is plain in this noun agricola [farmer]; and when separated they retain the same signification through which they composed the noun: therefore the parts of a composite noun when separated are significative even as its parts, or according to the signification of the whole. The minor is proved: for this noun ager [field] and this verb colo [I till] composed the noun agricola through their proper significations, namely, ager signifying a field and colo the action of tilling: whence agricola signifies one tilling a field; and they retain this same signification when separated from the composition, as is well known: therefore they truly signify according to the earlier signification, or as they are its parts. Wherefore neither does Aristotle’s reasoning prove that the parts of a noun do not signify when separated, nor can it be true, at least in a composite noun.

It is proved second: Because if simple nouns fell away from their proper signification and were imposed to signify different things, the composite noun too would fall away from its signification: therefore its signification depends on the proper significations of the parts; but the parts when separated retain their proper significations: therefore when separated they will signify according to the signification of the whole. For the solution of this question it should be noted that a composite noun is composed of whole nouns, or of a noun and a verb, in such a way that from their several and different significations there results a certain third, indivisible signification of that composite noun; which signification cannot be preserved in those same parts once separated. In which respect the composite noun is like a natural living composite made of soul and body, not any body whatever but a heterogeneous one, that is, one having parts of different ratio, as the arm, the head, and the feet: for no noun is composed of many nouns signifying the same thing, as from gladius [sword],

and ensis [sword], but of nouns signifying different things: wherefore from these different significations there results a third signification of the whole, different from the parts. As is plain in the noun respublica [commonwealth], and in the noun equiferus: because neither does respublica signify any thing whatever, or public business, but the gathering of citizens disposed under such laws and in such an order, which is something different from the signification of either part when separated; and equiferus signifies not a fierce horse, which the parts signify when separated, but another, very different animal. Whence, just as the soul does not inform the separated parts of the body, but while they are separated from the whole they acquire another, different form: so the form of the composite noun, which is its signification, does not inform the separated parts, but the parts have other significations proper to themselves and different from the signification of the whole, in which they participated while they composed it.

13 And so, just as each part of a composite noun, taken by itself, has its own one and indivisible signification, which does not belong to the syllables nor remain in them when separated, but ceases to be and is as it were corrupted when the syllables are separated: so also a noun composed of other nouns, or of a noun and a verb, has its own signification, distinct from the signification of the parts, and indivisible indeed, and therefore such that it is not predicated of the parts nor can remain in them when separated. And the reason for this is: because the composite noun is imposed by a distinct imposition to signify the whole, and not to signify the parts, and to signify a thing different from the one which the parts signify, yet in some way similar, and which would not result except from these parts. Whence it follows that different nouns so concur through their proper significations to compose another that, since they concur by means of another imposition and to signify another thing, they lose their proper significations in such a composition and participate in another, different one, although similar to their own; but when they are separated from the composition, they lose again that signification which they had in the whole, and retain their own. And this is what is commonly said: that when separated they do not signify according to the signification of the whole, although they seem to signify on account of the likeness found between the signification of the whole and their own; for the signification of the whole depends on them, but it is distinct, and cannot remain in them.

From this doctrine the question is answered: that what Aristotle asserts in the definition of the noun is true, that its parts, if they are taken as parts, are not significative when they are separated from it;

although when separated they retain their proper significations: because, since the signification of the whole is distinct from the proper significations of the parts, and is as it were the form of a heterogeneous thing, informing parts of different ratio, it is corrupted when the parts are separated; and therefore it cannot remain in them.

To the first argument: The minor is to be distinguished, namely that the parts of a composite noun compose it through their proper significations. For if it is understood in this way, that the signification of the whole is not other than the signification of the parts, it is false, since it is imposed by a distinct imposition and to signify a distinct thing, or at least one having a distinct mode. But if they are understood to concur through their proper significations in such a way that a third signification results, distinct from their own and indivisible, to which there also corresponds in the mind a simple concept, distinct from the concepts of the parts taken by themselves, it is true; but from this it does not follow that the parts when separated retain that same signification of the whole, or the one they participated from it: because this is corrupted at once, as soon as the parts are separated, just as the composite noun itself is corrupted; therefore it cannot remain in them.

Wherefore Aristotle rightly said that they no longer signify anything according to the signification of the whole, or as its parts.

To the second: The first enthymeme is to be granted, but the last consequence is to be denied, namely that the parts when separated signify according to the signification of the whole. For although the signification of the whole depends on the signification of the parts, and ceases to be when the parts fall away from their proper signification, nevertheless, since the signification of the whole is distinct from the proper significations of the parts, and indivisible, it is corrupted when they are separated; whence it cannot remain in them. But although they retain their proper significations, it is true that when separated they signify nothing according to the signification of the whole, because they retain nothing of its signification, although they sometimes seem to retain it, on account of the likeness which their own significations have with the signification of the whole, now corrupted.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether the infinite noun is to be altogether excluded from the definition.

14

Six things are to be explained concerning the infinite noun. First, What it is.

Second, What and how it signifies. Third, Of what things it is said. Fourth, Whether transcendental nouns can be made infinite.

Fifth, Whether the infinite noun is to be counted among absolute or among connotative terms. Last, Whether it is said univocally of beings and non-beings, or analogically.

Concerning the first it should be noted that negation can be taken in two ways. First, negatingly, which is to be taken in the whole force of the negation: in which way, even if it is placed at the beginning of the proposition, it negates the copula of that proposition and the whole proposition itself; and for this reason it has been said of it that it is of a malignant nature, so that whatever it finds after itself it destroys and makes into its opposite. In the second way it is taken not according to the whole force of the negation, but according to a limited force: so that it negates only the significate of the word to which it is most immediately joined, and its force does not pass further. Whence, if it is joined to the subject of the proposition, its force does not pass to the copula, nor does it render the proposition negative; and this is to be taken Infinitizingly: because its effect is only to negate the significate of the noun to which it is joined, and thereby, as it were, to make it infinite: because it signifies all other things except the thing on which it falls: as non-man signifies all other things except man, determining none of them; and therefore it is said to have an infinite signification. The infinite noun, then, includes a negation taken not negatingly, that is, not in the whole force of the negation, but taken infinitizingly, that is, according to a force of negating determined to its proper significate.

From which it is understood that the infinite noun is to be defined in this way: The infinite noun is a noun composed of a simple noun and a negation taken infinitizingly: as non-man, non-lion. And so much for its quiddity.

On the mode of signifying of the infinite noun.

As for what pertains to its mode of signifying, some say that materially it signifies the thing which is negated, but formally all the others: as non-man materially signifies man, but formally the lion and the ox and all other things except man. It is better to say, however, that it does not signify the thing which it negates, but materially the others besides it, and formally the pure negation of it: as non-man materially signifies the lion and the ox with the rest, and formally only the negation of man. This is proved thus: because non-man does not signify the lion or the ox according to their positive natures, but inasmuch as they fall or are contained under the negation of man: therefore according to their positive natures they pertain materially to the signification of the infinite noun; but formally according to the negation of such a nature, included in its own signification.

Concerning its significate, however, all agree that it is so extended that it signifies all other things except the thing which it negates, not only those actually existing but also possible ones, and indeed even impossible ones, such as the Chimera and the Hundred-handed. And the reason for this is manifest from what has been said. For if its formal significate is the negation of that thing to which it is joined, then its material significate will be everything to which such a negation can belong; but this belongs to all other things, existing or possible, and indeed even impossible: therefore all these are comprehended under its material significate, but altogether indeterminately and confusedly, and therefore in an as it were infinite mode: because it does not determine one Being more than another, as is manifest of itself.

From which it follows that the infinite noun has two things in which it falls short of the true ratio of a noun. The first, on the part of the formal significate: that it formally signifies no positive thing, or nature, or ratio, but the pure and sole negation of that thing on which it falls: as non-man signifies only the negation of man. The second, on the part of the material significate: because it signifies nothing determinate, but as much that which is as that which is not, and indeed that which is impossible. And on account of these two things Aristotle excludes the infinite noun from the definition of the noun: because a true noun must have a determinate signification, and must signify some positive nature, or at least a positive ratio of it.

Of what things the infinite noun is said in a proposition. 15

The first opinion asserts that, although the infinite noun signifies as much the things that are as those that are not, and as much possible as impossible things, yet in a proposition it cannot be verified except of existing things alone, not of possible or impossible ones. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 1, fifth notable; which he proves by this argument: The infinite noun cannot be said of non-existing and impossible things except in an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject; but such a proposition is false according to the rules of the Summulae: therefore it will never be verified of these, but of existing things alone. He proves the major: because, for the subject of a proposition to be said to supposit for something, it is required that the thing signified exist in the nature of things at the time signified by the copula:

therefore it can supposit only for existing things, not for possible or impossible ones; wherefore a proposition in which it is said of these will be about a non-suppositing subject. And the minor, that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false, he says is manifest in these propositions: Adam is white, Antichrist

is black: for the consequence is evident from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second, as Peter is white: therefore Peter is; therefore this consequence will be evident: Adam is non-man: therefore Adam is; but the consequent is false: therefore the antecedent is too, which is an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject.

The second opinion affirms that the infinite noun not only signifies existing and possible and impossible things, but can also be verified of all of them in a proposition. So St. Thomas, on the present chapter, with Boethius and Ammonius, whom all the modern interpreters follow; and it is the express view of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says thus: But non-man is not a noun: since it is in anything whatever alike, both what is and what is not. And so it is to be held. It is proved by a twofold argument. First, from the intrinsic condition of the infinite noun, which is such that it posits no form in the subject, indeed not even any positive ratio, but the pure negation of the thing to which it is joined: as non-man posits only the negation of man; but negation alone does not require the existence of the subject, indeed not even its possibility, because the negation of man is verified even of an impossible thing, such as the chimera: therefore the infinite noun can be verified of all these. The consequence is proved: because there is an evident argument from a negative proposition to an affirmative one with an infinite predicate in the same terms, as A lion is not a man: therefore a lion is non-man; but the infinite noun is denied of impossible things, because this is true: A chimera is not a man: therefore it will be affirmed of the same in a proposition with an infinite predicate; and so this too will be true: A chimera is non-man. The consequence is proved again: for the reason a negative proposition about an impossible subject is true is that the negation posits nothing positive in the subject; but the infinite noun posits nothing positive in the subject, but only a negation: therefore according to this it can be verified of the same possible thing in an affirmative proposition.

Second, contradictory predicates have an immediate opposition: therefore of any being or non-being whatever one of them must be verified; but man and non-man are contradictory predicates: therefore one of them must be verified of any thing whatever, possible or impossible; but of an impossible thing, such as the chimera, man is not verified: therefore non-man will be verified; and so of the other infinite nouns, which must be verified even of impossible things.

or it pertains to its essence, or stands toward it as a proper attribute. And if it stands in the first way, it is certain that it is attributed to an actually existing subject: because accidents do not belong to subjects except according to actual inherence in them, which, it is agreed, necessarily presupposes actual existence. But if it stands in the second way, it is certain that it does not belong to it according to actual existence, but according to a natural connection with it; and since this determines no time, but is perpetual, always standing in the same way, the proposition too is of perpetual truth, and the copula (as they say) is absolved from time: that is, it does not join the extremes for any difference of time; whereas in an accidental proposition it joins them for a determinate difference of time, in which the extremes exist.

From which it follows that only in accidental propositions do the extremes supposit, and therefore only in these is the actual existence of the extremes required for the truth of an affirmative proposition. And also that only in these is that rule of the summulists to be understood, that an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject is false; and finally that only in these is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second good. But in necessary propositions the subjects neither supposit, nor are united according to actual existence, nor according to any difference of time, but only according to a natural connection, abstracting from existence and from time: whence in them this rule alone is always true and to be observed, that all affirmative propositions are always true, and all negative ones always false. Wherefore neither is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in these: because in the proposition of the third adjacent the predicate is joined to the subject according to a natural connection with it, but in the proposition of the second it denotes actual existence: as if you say, Man is rational: therefore man is, the antecedent will be true when no man exists, and the consequent false. If we apply this doctrine to the infinite noun, we shall find that it signifies all possible and impossible things in an as it were essential mode, since it signifies them all per se. And from this it follows that it is verified of them in a proposition as it were by way of a natural connection, and not according to actual existence: wherefore all affirmative propositions are true, and all negative ones false, because the extremes do not supposit; nor is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in them.

noun cannot be verified of impossible or non-existing things except in an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject; but the minor is to be distinguished, that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false. For if it is accidental, it is to be granted, because the extremes are united according to actual existence, which they must have at the time signified by the copula; and if they do not have it, the proposition will be false. But in necessary propositions the actual existence of the extremes is not required, because they are united only according to a natural connection; and therefore the affirmative, although it is about a non-suppositing subject, is true. And since affirmative propositions with an infinite predicate have the mode of necessary ones, it is to be denied in them too that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false.

Whether transcendental nouns can be made infinite. 17

The first opinion holds that transcendentals cannot be made infinite if they are taken in their whole universality, as being taken absolutely; but if they are taken with a limitation, as for real being only, or for being of reason, that they can be made infinite. So Albert the Great in the commentary on this book, tract. 2, ch. 5, with Avicenna, whom Toledo and others follow on the present chapter. It is proved from the nature of the infinite noun, which is said as much of beings as of non-beings; but if being taken absolutely were made infinite, it could be said only of beings: therefore it cannot be made infinite.

The second opinion grants that transcendentals can be made infinite even when taken in this way. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 1, notable 6, Suesanus, and the Louvain commentators on the present chapter. They prove it:

Because these predications, A chimera is non-being, Nothing is non-being, have an infinite predicate; and the predicate is being in its universality: therefore transcendentals taken in their universality can be made infinite.

For the solution of the doubt, transcendentals are to be distinguished in this way: some are Most universal, as Being; others less universal, as its attributes, True, Good, and One, which are called less universal because according to their formal ratios they do not include one another: for neither is good formally true, nor is true formally one. And again, the most universal transcendental, such as being, can be taken absolutely, or with some limitation: namely for real being alone, or for substance alone. And of the less universal transcendentals it is evident that they can be made infinite, because non-true or non-good can still be verified of beings and non-beings: for the true is non-good, and the one is formally non-true. It is certain also that being taken with a limitation can be made infinite, for the same reason; but whether it can

be made infinite when taken without limitation: about this alone can there be doubt.

And our view is that it can be made infinite. This is proved from the proper definition of the infinite noun assigned by us at the beginning, according to which it means only that it is composed of a simple noun and a negation joined to it; but non-being is composed of both: therefore it is simply an infinite noun. And the argument of the second opinion also proves this.

But to the argument of the first opinion, the antecedent is to be denied, namely that it belongs to the ratio of the infinite noun to be verified of beings and non-beings; this pertains only to the ratio of the particular infinite noun, of which Aristotle and all speak commonly. But to the ratio of the infinite noun as such it pertains only that it be composed of a simple noun, particular or transcendental, and a negation joined to it.

Whether infinite nouns are to be counted among absolute or among connotative terms.

It is certain that they are neither absolute simply nor connotative, since they are not nouns simply, but only in a certain respect. There can therefore be doubt only whether they are to be reduced to the latter rather than to the former. Toledo, in the commentary on this chapter, asserts that they are counted among absolute terms: because they do not have a material and a formal significate, as connotatives do, but signify only a negation in the concrete.

Our view, however, is that they are rather to be reduced to connotative terms: because formally they denote the negation of the thing to which they are joined, but materially any other thing whatever; therefore they have a likeness to connotatives.

Whether the infinite noun is said univocally of beings and non-beings, or analogically.

The answer is that it is said univocally of all. The reason for this is: because its formal significate is only the negation of the thing to which it is joined; but negation belongs equally to beings and non-beings: therefore it is said equally of all, and so univocally; not indeed by proper univocation, because denominatives are not properly univocal, but by improper univocation, such as is found in denominatives.

It should be noted, finally, concerning the definition of the noun, that those two particles, finite and direct, are not to be added to it in order to exclude

## CHAPTER III

On the Verb.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. The verb, moreover, is that which consignifies time, no part of which signifies anything sep‐

arately; and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of the Verb. The chapter

T          is divided into three parts. In the first, he proposes and explains the defini‐

tion of the verb. In the second, he excludes from the ratio of verb the infinite verb and the cases of the verb: that is, verbs of tenses other than the present. In the third, he gathers that the verb agrees with the noun in two things.

The definition of the verb is this: The verb is that which consignifies time, no part of which signifies anything separately; and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another. In this definition, according to the common exposition of the interpreters, these two particles from the definition of the noun must be understood, significative word by convention: because they are common to the noun and the verb; but because this was well enough known, Aristotle did not wish to repeat them in the definition of the verb, but to take its beginning from the consignification of time, because by this particle the verb already begins to differ from the noun. Now to consignify time is the same as to connote time, or to signify it consequently. And so, because the verb per se signifies action or passion, or something by way of action or passion, and action or passion take place in time, it is said to signify time together with, and consequently upon, the action or passion itself, which is per se and primarily signified. And so to signify time and to consignify it are different things. For to signify time is to signify per se the thing which is time, as any other thing; but to consignify time, or to signify with time, is to signify another thing as done in time: for from this, although time is not signified but another thing, yet it is at the same time denoted and at the same time signified as it were consequently, which is to be consignified; and this belongs to the verb alone, whereas to the noun belongs only to signify time, as day, and

and night signify certain determinate times, yet they do not consignify time.

The other particle, no part of which signifies anything separately, distinguishes the verb from speech, and was sufficiently explained in the definition of the noun. There remains only the last, and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another: as if to say that the verb is a sign of, or signifies, the conjunction of the predicate with the subject, which it brings about. For the noun is predicated or made subject in a proposition, but the verb unites the predicate with the subject and signifies such a union; in which it is also distinguished from the noun and from speech.

In the second part he excludes infinite verbs and the cases of the verb from the definition, for the same reasons for which he excluded the infinite noun and the oblique cases from the definition of the noun. Because the verb must signify a determinate action or passion, and a determinate conjunction of the predicate with the subject; but the infinite verb signifies nothing determinate: therefore it is not a verb simply, but in a certain respect; and for this reason it is to be excluded from the definition of the verb; and so too the cases of the verb, that is, verbs of tenses other than the present. Because the office of the verb belongs to them not by reason of themselves but by reason of the present verb; nor do they signify an action or passion that is such simply, but a past or future one, which, since it is not actually in the nature of things, is such only in a certain respect.

In the third part of the chapter, finally, he gathers two things in which the verb agrees with the noun. The first is that the verb taken by itself, that is, outside a proposition, signifies some thing, as the noun does: as I run signifies running. Second, that just as the noun taken by itself does not signify the true or the false unless a verb is joined to it, so the verb taken by itself, that is, outside a proposition, does not signify the true or the false unless a noun is in some way joined to it. And he assigns the reason for this: because truth and falsity are found only in composition and division; but the verb taken by itself does not signify such a composition, because it cannot be understood without the extremes, that is, without the predicate and the subject: therefore the verb without a noun joined to it cannot signify truth or falsity.

## QUESTION I

Whether it is true that the verb consignifies time.

This particle of the definition does not seem to belong to every verb:

therefore it was not rightly put by Aristotle in the definition,

The antecedent is proved: because if the verb consignifies time, this is chiefly because it signifies action, to which it belongs to be measured by time; but not every verb signifies action, as the substantive verb is proves: therefore neither will every verb consignify time. Which becomes even more manifest: since the same verb is unites the extremes according to their natural connection, which it does whenever the predicate is of the essence of the subject, or its proper attribute; for then it does not unite them with any difference of time, since such propositions are true before all time and after all time, and are therefore said to be of perpetual truth; in them the copula is absolved from time: therefore in them it cannot consignify time.

20 Nor does it belong to the verb alone, but also to the noun: therefore on this score too the same particle was not well placed in the definition. The antecedent is proved: because lunch, dinner, and similar nouns signify the action of eating, connoting that it takes place at such a time: therefore they consignify time. Moreover, the participle, as loving, running, is a true noun, since it is placed as the subject or predicate of a proposition; and yet it consignifies time, since it signifies an action to be exercised in present or future time: therefore it also belongs to nouns to consignify time.

Concerning this particle of the definition, two things must be explained. First, Whether it belongs to the verb alone to consignify time, or also to the participle and to other nouns. Second, Whether it belongs to all verbs, and always. Concerning the first, it must be presupposed what it is to consignify time. For it is nothing other than to signify with time; and each of these is to signify something, namely an action to which it belongs to be measured by time: for from this, together with that thing, time is signified, which is to be consignified; or that thing is noted as measured by time, which is to be signified with time.

This supposed, not all speak in the same way about the participle, but most deny that it consignifies time: because, although it signifies an action measured by time, yet it does so not by way of action but by way of a form inhering in a subject: as running signifies the action of running by way of an inhering form, as whiteness inheres; and therefore it does not signify it as measured by time, nor consequently does it consignify time.

The common opinion, however, holds that the participle consignifies time. And this is true. So St. Thomas on the present chapter, where he asserts: The participle is separated from the verb by the last particle of the definition

Circafecundumverò,An omnibusverbis &femperconueniat: folùm eſt difficultas de verbo ſubſtantiuo,eſt : nam de cæteris fatis eit manifeſtum, quòd fignificentcum tempore. Et ratio,

namely, and it is always a sign of those things that are predicated of another. And it agrees with it in all the others. So too Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 2, and Mercado in the same place; Paul of Venice, tract. 2, on the parts of the proposition, ch. 2; Toledo with the other moderns, on this chapter.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who placed the last particle, which explains the proper office of the verb, in order to exclude the participle, as St. Thomas taught; for nothing else can be excluded by it: therefore he thought that it agrees with the verb in the remaining particles, the first of which is to consignify time.

It is proved also by reason: Because the participle signifies action as it goes out from the agent: as heating signifies heating as going out from itself: therefore it signifies action by way of action. The consequence is proved: because the mode of action is to go out from the agent; but action takes place in time: therefore the participle signifies with time; a clear sign of which is that these adverbs, slowly and quickly, are joined to it, which do not belong except to those words that signify motion, or action as it is action. But the participle is distinguished from the verb by the last particle, as St. Thomas asserts: because, although it signifies with time, yet it does not unite the extremes, in which the proper and ultimate ratio of the verb consists. And from these things we have that to consignify time belongs not to the verb alone but also to the participle, which seems to be a medium between noun and verb.

21 But whether it belongs to pure nouns, as to dinner and lunch and the like: It must be said that it does not belong to them: because they signify action only materially, or as it is a certain thing, not formally and by way of action; hence not by the mode in which it is measured by time either. For example, dinner signifies the action of eating as a certain thing, just as whiteness signifies whiteness; yet it does not signify it on its own part as done at such a time, but it only has being done at such a time from the custom of men, not from the fact that it is signified by such a noun: which is what is necessary for consignifying time. For the verb is said to consignify time from the fact that it signifies action by way of action, and therefore as measured by time. Wherefore it is by force of its signification, and not from custom or some other extrinsic reason, that it is said to signify time together with the action, and consequently to consignify it. And from this it is understood that to consignify time belongs only to the verb and to the participle, not to pure nouns.

But concerning the second, Whether it belongs to all verbs, and always, the only difficulty is about the substantive verb is: for about the others it is manifest enough that they signify with time. And the reason

Primum , Quodeſſen- tialeeftei, nempe confignificare tempus, vuiendo extrema,

for doubting is: because it signifies only existence simply, or the existence of a thing under some accidental form: it has the first in this proposition, Man is; the second in this one, Man is white. It must nevertheless be said, with the common opinion of the interpreters: It does not signify true action, but the existence of a thing by way of action; and this is enough for it to signify with time: because existence signified by way of action is signified as measured by time; for just as action is of itself measured by time, so too is what is signified by way of action; and therefore the verb is, signifying the existence of a thing by way of action, consequently signifies time: which is properly to consignify time, or to signify with time.

But whether it always has this, that is, even in propositions in which it unites the extremes only according to the natural connection of the predicate with the subject, in which it is said to be absolved from time, is the greatest difficulty: because it is not explained by all in the same way what it is for the verb in these propositions to be absolved from time, or in what way it can be absolved from time and at the same time signify with time.

21 Leaving aside, however, the explanations of others, because they do not seem to satisfy the difficulty: It should be noted that the verb has two things, contained in two particles of the definition explained by Aristotle. First, To consignify time. Second, To unite the extremes, which Aristotle explained by the last particle of the definition, And it is always a sign of those things that are predicated of another: that is, of the conjunction of the predicate with the subject, which it effects. Now it unites the extremes according to their nature: so that if the predicate expresses actual existence, or actual inherence in the subject, it unites it with the subject according to actual existence or inherence in it, and in this sense the proposition is to be judged true or false. But if the predicate does not express actual existence or inherence in the subject, but an essential or necessary connection with it, it unites it to the subject according to this and not according to that. We have an example of each in these propositions, Man is white, Man is rational: for in the first the predicate expresses actual inherence in the subject, and according to it is united to it; but in the second it expresses the essential connection of the grade rational with man, abstracting from actual existence: for although no man exists in the nature of things, yet it is true that man is rational.

Concerning the consignification of time also, and the union of the extremes, we consider two things in the verb. First, What is essential to it, namely to consignify time in uniting the extremes.

Second, What is as it were accidental, namely to consignify time and to unite the extremes for the time signified. Thus it is essential to the verb to unite the extremes while consignifying time; but to unite them for a determinate difference of time signified is only accidental; and therefore it must be judged from the nature of the extremes whether the verb effects this in the proposition or not. For if they are apt to be conjoined for that difference, they will be so conjoined; but if they are not apt to be conjoined for it, such a mode of conjunction will be suspended, and they will be united simply, without such determination or restriction. And indeed the extremes of accidental propositions, or of those having an accidental mode, are united not necessarily but contingently, since an accident, or what has the mode of an accident, is able to be united to the subject; wherefore they are not apt to be united except for a determinate difference of time; and therefore in such propositions the verb unites the extremes for a determinate difference of time, which it consignifies, namely for present, past, and future time.

22 But the extremes of necessary propositions express a natural connection, holding always in the same way, with the verb; wherefore they do not demand to be united for a determinate difference of time, but absolutely and simply, abstracting from any difference of time whatever; and therefore they are not united with a limitation or restriction to some difference of time, but according to their natural and necessary connection, which abstracts from it. The verb, therefore, unites the extremes in these propositions, but does not narrow the union to the difference of time which it consignifies; rather it leaves it in its own nature and condition. And this is to be absolved from time, that is, also, that such propositions are of perpetual truth, just as their connection is necessary and perpetual, always holding in the same way, and in no way depending on time. It has therefore been sufficiently explained how to consignify time belongs to every verb, and always belongs to it; and what it is to be absolved from time; and how it is not inconsistent always to consignify time and sometimes to be absolved from time.

And by this doctrine the arguments placed at the beginning are solved. For to the first: The minor must be distinguished, because some verbs signify true action, others something by way of action, as the substantive verbs, namely the existence of a thing; and since existence signified by way of action is consequently signified by way of that which is measured by time, the substantive verbs too consignify time; which they have also in necessary propositions, in which they are said to be absolved from time: because there is nothing inconsistent in signifying

To the second: The antecedent, that dinner and lunch signify action by way of action, must be distinguished: for they signify it only materially, as a certain thing, like the other nouns; and therefore not by connoting that it takes place at such a time; but this, its taking place at such a time, comes from without, from the custom of men, and not from the force of their signification: wherefore it does not suffice for them to be said to signify with time, or to consignify time.

## QUESTION II

Whether the verb is a true part of the proposition.

he first opinion holds that the verb is not a part of the proposition, but

T          as it were the binding of the parts. So Soto in the 1st edition of the

Summulae, and others with him; and it is proved first from the composition of a house, in which the timbers and the stones concur as parts, but the nails by which the timbers are united, and the mortar by which the stones are united, are not parts but the bond of the parts: but the verb stands so in the proposition, since it is the copula through which the parts are united: therefore it is not a part of the proposition.

Second: every thing is composed of the same parts into which it is resolved; but the proposition is resolved only into the extremes, which are the subject and the predicate: therefore it is composed only of the subject and the predicate as of parts: wherefore the verb will not be a part, since it is neither subject nor predicate. The minor is proved from Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, who defines the term thus: A term is the extreme of a proposition, into which the proposition is resolved, as into subject and predicate.

23 The second opinion asserts, at least of the substantive verb is, that it is not a part of the proposition: because it signifies no action that can be predicated of the subject: so Villalpando and Suessanus on the present chapter.

The third opinion holds that the verb has two things. First, that it signifies some thing, in which it agrees with the noun. Second, that it unites the extremes: by reason of the first it is a part of the proposition, but by reason of the second it is not a part but the bond of the parts. So certain moderns hold.

The common and true opinion asserts two things. First, That the verb is a part of the proposition, as it were material, by reason of the thing signified. Second, That it is a formal part, through the proper office of the verb, which is to unite the extremes. So Porphyry, Ammonius, Boethius, Albert

[p. 526]

Itaque curſus, in eadem propofitione eſt, qui compo-nitur cum homine , & prædicaturde illo : ſed verbum curre eſt , quod illum cum homine componit, quod illum deho-mineprædicat : curfus etiam eſt prædicatum , quod, ſed ver-bum curro , eſtquaſiprædicatum,quo: cùm fit ratio , & qua-fi forma enunciandi: & tandem curſus , eſt quaſi materiale prædicatum,verbum verò quaſi formale. Etideo D.Thom . afſſeruit , Verbumnonfolumi rationerei fignificata,ſetenere exparte predicati, cùm defubiecto illa enuncietur,fed etiam utestnota com-pofitionis : cùmhocmodo fit quaſi prædicatum formale : & ita ex vtroque eſt prædicatum propoſitionis : ex primo quidem, quafimateriale,& vtquod : cùm resab eo fignificata fit: quæ prædicatur: ex ſecundo , verò, quafiforma , & vt quo : cùm fitfignumcompoſitionis,& prædicationis eiuſdemprædicati cum fubiecto . Quod patet in propofitionibusde ſecundo adia-cente,vthomo currit: inquibus ſolam actionem ſignificatam componitverbum cum ſubiecto,vel eamde illo prædicat. the Great, St. Thomas, and Toledo on the present chapter.

But in order that we may explain and prove both at once, it should be noted that the verb has two things. First, To signify some thing with time, namely an action, or something by way of action, which it has not only in the proposition but also outside it, as Aristotle expressly taught at the end of the preceding chapter. For I run signifies the action of running with time; and the substantive verb is, the existence of a thing by way of action. It has, second, What is to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another (to use Aristotle’s words), which is nothing other than to be a sign of the composition of the predicate with the subject: for it consignifies with time in such a way as to apply the thing to the subject; whence this second is as it were the proper and ultimate difference of the verb, through which it is constituted in the formal and essential ratio of a verb, which it does not exercise except in the proposition, although it is always apt to exercise such an act. For example, in this proposition, Man runs, it signifies the action of running with time in such a way as to apply it to man. And since this application is the formal composition of the predicate with the subject, it is true that the verb contains and signifies the formal composition of the predicate with the subject. Thus in the same proposition it is running that is composed with man and is predicated of him; but it is the verb runs that composes it with man, that predicates it of man: running is also the predicate which, but the verb I run is as it were the predicate by which, since it is the ratio and as it were the form of enunciating; and finally running is as it were the material predicate, but the verb as it were the formal one. And therefore St. Thomas asserted that the verb, not only by reason of the thing signified, holds itself on the side of the predicate, since that is enunciated of the subject, but also as it is a sign of composition: since in this way it is as it were the formal predicate; and so on both counts it is the predicate of the proposition: on the first, as it were material, and as that which, since the thing signified by it is what is predicated; on the second, as it were the form, and as that by which, since it is the sign of the composition and predication of the same predicate with the subject.

Second, it should be noted that it can happen in two ways that the verb applies to the subject the thing signified by it. In one way, bare or alone, when the proposition has no other predicate besides the verb. Which is plain in propositions of the second adjacent, as Man runs, in which the verb composes only the signified action with the subject, or predicates it of him. In the other way, not bare or alone, but conjoined to another predicate and modified by it, as in propositions of the third adjacent

as Man is white, in which there is enunciated not only being, which is signified by the verb, but being conjoined with whiteness; and so the sense of the same proposition is: man is a being affected with whiteness. And in the first way the total predicate is what is signified by the verb, but in the second way it is as it were a partial one; but in both ways it is the material predicate, and the verb is always the formal one: because it always signifies and makes the composition of the predicate with the subject.

From this doctrine two arguments are gathered, by which those two things which our opinion, and the common one, asserts are efficaciously proved. The first argument proves that the verb, by reason of the thing signified by it, is the material predicate of the proposition, and as that which, and consequently a true part of it; and it is this: The verb signifies an action, or something by way of action; but this is what is predicated of the subject: bare, indeed, in propositions of the second adjacent, or conjoined with another predicate, as in propositions of the third adjacent: therefore the verb, through the thing signified by it, is always the total or the partial predicate of the proposition; and consequently it is always a part of the proposition.

The second argument proves that the verb is always the formal predicate of the proposition, and as that by which, and so its formal part; and it proceeds in this way: The proposition, formally, is the composition of the predicate with the subject; but the verb is the formal sign of this composition, making it: therefore it is its formal ratio, and therefore a formal part: just as the soul is the formal part of the living thing which it composes, giving it being as its true form. For the verb unites with the subject through the thing signified by it, and at the same time it is the formal sign effecting the same union; and therefore it is as it were the form, giving life to the proposition, by that likeness by which the soul gives being and living to the body through informing it. And this truth shows the error of the other opinions, which think that the verb is only the material bond of the proposition, such that it unites the predicate with the subject only materially, as the stones of a house are united by mortar, or timbers by a nail: whereas this is entirely false; for the verb so unites the predicate to the subject that it always unites the thing signified by it, by reason of which it is a true predicate of the proposition and a true part of it; it also unites in such a way that it is the formal sign of the same composition of the predicate with the subject; and a sign not only significative but at the same time formally effective: which is to be the form of the whole proposition, and therefore its formal part.

material parts, and the form of the whole proposition, and of the same material parts, is the verb.

From these things the arguments of the first opinion are easily solved. For to the first, the minor must be denied: that the verb stands in the proposition as the binding of the parts of a house stands: for it does not unite the predicate and the subject materially, but by way of the form of the whole composition, as has been explained.

To the second: the minor too must be denied: that the proposition is resolved only into the subject and the predicate as into parts: for it is resolved into these alone as into its extreme parts, which Aristotle therefore calls its terms: because a term signifies not any part whatever of a thing, but the extreme one; and sometimes not a part but an indivisible extreme, which is not a true part, as is plain in the term of a line. The verb, therefore, is a true formal part of the proposition, although it is not an extreme: which I understand of the formal ratio of the verb: for through the thing signified by it, which it applies to the subject and predicates of it, it is also an extreme part of the proposition, since it is its predicate.

## QUESTION III

Whether the infinite verb can be placed in a proposition.

his question presupposes one thing as certain with Aristotle and with

Tall, namely that there is an infinite verb outside the proposition: which

Aristotle expressly taught in the present chapter, excluding it from the definition of the verb; and with him all the interpreters. But it asks something else: Whether the infinite verb is not only found outside the proposition but can also be placed in the proposition.

And the first opinion, that of the ancient Interpreters, Albert the Great and Boethius, on this chapter, is that it cannot be placed in a proposition. This is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because the verb becomes infinite, like the noun, through a negation taken not as negating but as infinitizing, so that its force does not pass further, but it negates only the noun or verb to which it is joined; but it is inconsistent for a negation to be joined to the verb in a proposition unless it is taken as negating: therefore it is inconsistent for the verb to be infinitized in a proposition. The minor is proved: because it is inconsistent for a negation to be joined to the verb in a proposition without the proposition being negated; but it cannot be a negative proposition unless the negation joined to the verb is taken as negating, as is manifest of itself: therefore it is inconsistent for it to be taken as infinitizing when added to the verb in a proposition; and consequently it is inconsistent for the verb to be infinitized.

Second: a negation taken as infinitizing altogether negates that to which it is joined, although its force does not pass further: therefore, joined to the verb, it negates not only its significate but also the proper office of the verb, which is to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another; but when the office of the verb is negated, the proposition is rendered negative: therefore the verb is not infinitized. The consequence is proved: because a proposition cannot be negative unless its negation is taken as negating; but taken as negating it cannot render the verb infinite, but negative, as is plain in negative propositions.

The second opinion holds that the infinite verb is found not only outside the proposition but also in the proposition: so Ammonius, Suessanus, Toledo on the present chapter, Soto and Mercado, Summulae bk. 1, ch. 1, on the verb, and all the modern interpreters. And it seems to us more probable. It is proved first by two testimonies of Aristotle: for in the present chapter he speaks thus of the infinite verb: But not-is-well and not-is-ill I do not call a verb: for it consignifies time, and is always of something. As if to say, it is always predicated of something; but it cannot be predicated except in a proposition: therefore Aristotle thinks that it can be infinitized in a proposition. The second testimony is found in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 10, where Aristotle sets up this demonstration in the first figure: Things that do not twinkle are near us; the planets do not twinkle: therefore the planets are near us. This syllogism, however, will be faulty if the negation in the minor is taken as negating: for then it will make a negative proposition; but with a negative minor the syllogism in the first figure is faulty: therefore it must be taken by Aristotle as infinitizing, so that the sense is, the planets are non-twinkling; and so it will make an infinite verb in the proposition. It is proved also by reason: because the verb outside the proposition is infinite: therefore the negation joined to it is taken not as negating but as infinitizing: either, then, it negates the whole that the verb has, namely its significate and the office of the copula, or only the significate: if the first is said, it follows that it can be infinite in the proposition, even though the whole that it has is negated; and the same also follows if the second is said: because if only its significate is negated, it will not make a negative proposition, but an affirmative one with an infinite predicate, as happens in the demonstration of Aristotle adduced.

But in order that the truth of this opinion may become manifest, and the arguments of the other be more easily solved, it should be noted that the difference between the two opinions consists only in this: that the first asserts that, of the two things which the verb has, namely to signify a thing with time and to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another, the first alone belongs to it outside the proposition, but the second only in the proposition

is exercised; and therefore that outside the proposition it can be infinitized, because the whole which it has in that state can be negated; but in the proposition it cannot, because a negation cannot be joined to it without both being negated; and when both are negated, the proposition is constituted negative; and therefore the negation is taken as negating and cannot make it infinite.

But the second opinion, which we follow, does not think it necessary that the negation joined to the verb in the proposition negate both; but just as, joined to it outside the proposition, it can negate only the significate, without the mark of composition being negated, so in the proposition it can negate that alone, without the same mark of composition being negated; and so the verb can be infinitized and constitute an affirmative proposition with an infinite predicate. And the reason of this is that those two things are distinct in the verb: therefore the first can be negated without the second being negated. Moreover, in that which is to signify some thing, the verb agrees with the noun; and therefore as to this it can be infinitized through negation, but not as to the mark of composition: because, since this is limited to this predicate and this subject, inasmuch as the verb conjoins them, it is necessary that, when this conjunction or composition is negated, the whole proposition be negated, and therefore that the negation be taken as negating: for there is no medium in the composition itself between negative and affirmative; nor can a proposition be infinite as it is formally a proposition, although it can be infinite on the side of the predicate or on the side of the subject.

28 To the first argument, the minor must be denied: that a negation cannot be joined to the verb in a proposition unless it is taken as negating, or unless by that very fact the proposition becomes negative: for it can negate only the significate of the verb, without its union with the subject being negated, as happens outside the proposition: because each ratio is distinct in the verb; and therefore the negation can fall under the one and not under the other, as has been proved, upon the verb.

To the second: the antecedent must be denied: that it is necessary for a negation joined to something to negate whatever is in it; rather, it can negate in the verb the thing signified, as it negates it in the noun, and in the same verb outside the proposition, without the mark of composition being negated. For what prevents the infinite verb existing outside the proposition from being placed in the proposition, without the force of the negation extending to the mark of composition? Nothing, surely: because a negation taken as infinitizing behaves in the same way in the proposition and outside it: therefore one must confess that the verb, just as outside the proposition, so also in the proposition can be infinitized, as the common and true opinion holds.

## CHAPTER IIII

On the Enunciation.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. But speech is a significant vocal sound, some part of which is significant separately, as a

word: not as an affirmation or a negation, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the nature of the

T           Enunciation. It is divided into three parts. In the first, he defines

speech, which is the genus of the enunciation, and expounds its definition. In the second, he defines the enunciation and divides it by various divisions. In the third, he begins to treat of the opposition of enunciations.

In order to define the enunciation, speech, which is its genus, must first be defined. And it is defined thus: Speech is a significant vocal sound, some part of which is significant separately, as a word: not as an affirmation or a negation. In place of the genus is put vocal sound, through which speech is defined as through its subject, as the other accidents in the concrete are, as we said in the chapter on the noun. By the second particle, vocal sounds signifying nothing are excluded from the definition; and by the third, which is to be understood, namely by convention, vocal sounds signifying naturally are excluded: which Aristotle did not express, because it had been sufficiently expressed and explained in the chapter on the noun. But by the following particles the noun and the verb are excluded, whose parts, separated, either signify nothing, or do not signify according to the signification of the whole; whereas the parts of speech, which are different nouns, or a noun and a verb, do signify when separated, as is plain of the parts of this speech, white man. But Aristotle adds that they do not signify as affirmations or negations, but only as words: because any part of speech, separated, contains nothing of being or not being, unless a verb is joined to it.

Speech, now defined, he says in the 2nd part of the chapter, is twofold. One Enunciative, which contains the true or the false; and such are speeches of the indicative mood, as man walks. The other non-enunciative, which contains nothing true or false, as speeches of the imperative or optative or other moods. He says, therefore, that the enunciation is not any speech whatever, but only that which contains the true or the false; and therefore it is to be defined thus: An enunciation is speech signifying the true or the false, in which definition

the first division of the enunciation is hinted at: into true and false. A true enunciation is that which so enunciates one thing of another as they stand on the side of the thing, as man is an animal; a false one, that which enunciates otherwise than they stand on the side of the thing, as an animal is a stone.

29 The second division is: Of enunciations, one is one, another multiple. One is that which signifies one thing, as man is white; or whose parts are united by a conjunction, as Peter runs, and John speaks. Multiple, that which either does not signify one thing, or consists of equivocal terms; or whose parts are not united by any conjunction, as Peter speaks, John walks.

The third division is: Of enunciations, one is Simple, enunciating one thing of one, as man is white; another Composite, which includes several simple ones united by a conjunction, as Peter disputes, and John walks. The last division is of the simple Enunciation into affirmative and negative, which Aristotle calls its species.

Finally he treats of contradiction, or the opposition found between enunciations, which he defines thus: The opposition of enunciations is the affirmation and negation of the same predicate of the same subject. For such an opposition he teaches that at least one condition is altogether required, namely that each enunciation consist of univocal terms: for if they have some equivocal term, they will indeed be of the same of the same, not in reality but in word alone; and therefore they will be opposed in word alone, and not in reality. As The dog barks, the dog does not bark.

QUESTION I. Whether in the definition of speech, speech is defined in general, so as to include perfect and

imperfect, simple and composite.

he first opinion asserts that speech is not defined in general, but only per‐

T         fect speech, common to speech of the indicative mood and of the others. So

Albert the Great, On Interpretation bk. 1, tract. on Speech, ch. 1, and

Philoponus on the present chapter. They prove it: Because a good definition must be given through the proximate genus; but only perfect speech is the proximate genus of the enunciation, whereas speech common to perfect and imperfect is a remote genus: therefore it is defined through the former and not through the latter.

The second opinion teaches that only simple speech is defined: because it thinks that only the simple enunciation, too, is defined, whose genus, it is plain, is not speech in general but only simple speech. So Porphyry and Aspasius on this chapter. They prove it from

the definition of speech, in which it is said that its parts, separated, are significant per se as words, not as affirmations; but the parts of composite speech signify as affirmations, as is plain in this composite speech, man speaks, and the horse runs, each part of which is an affirmative proposition: therefore composite speech is not included in this definition, but only simple speech is defined.

The third opinion is that of Boethius and St. Thomas in this place, who assert that speech in general was defined by Aristotle, as it includes perfect and imperfect, simple and composite. And this is true and to be held. It is proved first, against the first opinion, that speech is defined as common to perfect and imperfect, from the definition, which belongs entire to imperfect speeches: since each of them is a vocal sound significant by convention, whose parts, separated, are significant per se as words, not as affirmations, as this one shows, white man.

It is proved second, against the second, that speech is defined in general, as common to simple and composite: because Aristotle at once divides speech, once defined, into one by signification and one by conjunction, that is, into simple and composite: therefore the definition includes both.

To the argument of the first opinion: The major must be denied, that a good definition must necessarily be given through the proximate genus; rather, it can be given equally well, or even better, through a remote genus, provided all the differences down to the last are placed with it, as we showed in the Predicables. For man will be well defined if we say that he is a substance, corporeal, living, sentient, and rational.

To the second argument, St. Thomas and Alexander reply that in the definition only those things are placed which belong to the defined as such, not those which can belong to it under another particular ratio: as in the definition of animal only those things are placed which pertain to sentient nature, not others which can belong to animal considered in this or that species by reason of some difference. And so in the definition of speech those things are placed which belong to it in general, namely as speech abstracts from simple and composite; among which one is that its parts are not significant as affirmations, but only as words. But that some speech, namely composite speech, has parts significant as affirmations does not belong to it as it is speech, or from the generic ratio of speech which is defined, but from the specific ratio of composite speech: hence this does not contradict the definition, nor prevent its being included under it.
