## QUESTION II

Whether the enunciation is a real being or a being of reason.

31

Three things are to be considered in the enunciation, or proposition.

First, the vocal sounds themselves, the writings, or the concepts.

Second, their ordering in the proposition according to the ratio of predicate, subject, and copula. Third, the act of the intellect by which they are ordered, and from which, once they are so ordered, the proposition is effected.

Concerning the first and the third it is certain that they are real, and no one has doubted it; but because the formal ratio of the Enunciation does not consist in these, but only the material, while the second pertains to its formal ratio, it will also be certain that the enunciation taken materially, and as it were for its foundation, is a real being. The doubt, then, is whether the enunciation formally is real, or a being of reason.

The first opinion distinguishes between the vocal, the written, and the mental enunciation; and of the first two it asserts that they are formally beings of reason, but of the mental it teaches that it is formally a real being. So certain moderns hold; and they prove both points by this argument: The vocal and the written enunciation are real only on the side of the vocal sounds and the writings, but on the side of signification and of truth they are beings of reason, since their signification depends on the free imposition of men, which posits nothing real in them. Truth too, since it is not in them formally but only as in a sign, therefore has nothing real in them either, but only of reason; but to the formal ratio of the proposition the writings and vocal sounds do not pertain except as significant of things and of the truth existing in the mind: therefore the vocal and the written proposition is a real being only materially, but formally a being of reason. That the mental one is formally a real being they prove: because the concepts of which it is made are not only real, but signification (which is in them by nature) and truth are also found in them formally: therefore, both from the formal signification and truth, in which the formal ratio of the proposition consists, and from the material ratio of the concepts, it will be a real being.

This opinion is true as regards the vocal and the written enunciation, but not as regards the mental, which I prove thus: for although those two real things, namely signification and truth, are in the concepts, yet the ordering after the manner of a composition of predicate, subject, and copula cannot be a real being, because it posits nothing real in them; but just as in vocal sounds and writings to be subject, and predicate, and proposition is only a relation of reason, which follows the real act of the intellect ordering them, so in concepts, however naturally they signify, and

which contain the formal ratio of truth, it is only a relation of reason that they are ordered in the ratio of subject and predicate, and of a mental proposition: wherefore, no less in these than in writings and vocal sounds, the formal ratio of the enunciation is a being of reason. As for what is said about the real truth of concepts, although it is left to choice, it must nevertheless be admitted; but it does not follow from it that the mental enunciation is formally a real being: because, although concepts, by the very fact that they are formed by the intellect, have simple real truth, yet they do not have complex or composite truth except on the supposition of the ordering of the intellect and of their constitution in the ratio of predicate and subject, and of proposition; and since these are only relations of reason, the result is that the mental proposition is formally a being of reason.

Our opinion, therefore, is that not only the vocal and the written enunciation are formally beings of reason, but also the mental one, speaking absolutely.

Because, although it has something real pertaining to the formal ratio of the proposition, namely signification and truth, nevertheless the ultimate thing through which the enunciation is constituted in the formal ratio of an enunciation is a being of reason, namely the ordering of the concepts in the ratio of predicate and subject, and of the composition from these; and therefore it must be pronounced absolutely that the mental enunciation is formally a being of reason, and consequently that each and every enunciation is formally a being of reason. And by these things the argument of the opposite opinion is solved.

## QUESTION III

Whether the enunciation was defined quidditatively by Aristotle through truth and falsity.

32

Aristotle, in the present chapter, defines the enunciation through truth and falsity: and therefore we ask whether truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, and so whether such a definition is essential; or rather whether truth is an accident or proper attribute of it, and so the definition is accidental or descriptive.

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, and that it is therefore essentially defined through them. This is proved by this argument: That is the essential difference of a species by which it is distinguished from the others of the same genus; but

Aristotle distinguishes the enunciation from the other, non-enunciative speeches through the signification of the true and the false: therefore truth and falsity are its essential difference, by which it is separated from the other species of speech.

The second opinion holds that the essence of the enunciation does not consist in the signification of the true or the false, but in this, that it enunciates one thing of another; and that truth or falsity is outside the essence of the enunciation, as an accident, or at most as a proper attribute, through which Aristotle described it. So Alexander, Ammonius, and Nifo on the present chapter, and almost all the moderns; and we too judge this to be true, and very consonant with the doctrine of Aristotle.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the chapter on substance in the Categories, where he teaches that the same enunciation, according to species, receives truth and falsity, and is changed from true to false extrinsically, namely by a change of the thing outside. As this proposition, Peter is sitting, remaining the same in number, is true now while Peter is sitting, but becomes false when he is standing; and this change comes to it from without; and therefore it receives contraries without change of itself. From which I gather this argument: The same proposition remains unchanged under truth and falsity: therefore truth and falsity are not of the essence of the proposition, or of the enunciation. The consequence is proved: because if they were of its essence, it would not remain the same, but the true and the false would be different according to species and number: wherefore, according to the mind of Aristotle, to signify the true or the false does not pertain to the essence of the enunciation.

Moreover, Aristotle, defining the proposition in Prior Analytics bk. 1, ch. 1, says that it is a speech which affirms or denies something of something; and in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2, he asserts that a proposition is one part of an enunciation, in which one thing is enunciated of one, no mention being made of the true or the false: therefore he thinks that its essence consists not in these but in this, that it enunciates one thing of another. It is proved also by reason. First: Because if truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, then the true and the false enunciation are distinguished in species, just as truth itself and falsity are diverse in species; but the essential differences of species do not pertain to the essence of the genus, but are outside it, as we adduced from Aristotle and Porphyry on the third predicable, as the differences rational and irrational do not pertain to the essence of animal: therefore to signify the true and the false must be outside the essence of the enunciation taken in general: wherefore there will be something else of its essence which is contracted through the true and the false to diverse species; and this will be to enunciate one thing of another, which is in one case true, in another false.

33 And if you say: The disjunctive whole, namely true or false, pertains to the essence of the enunciation in general, and either of them per se is the specific difference: this is proved to be

false: because the disjunctive whole is composed of opposite parts: therefore it cannot be of the essence of one and the same thing.

Second, the same opinion is proved: Because the enunciation is a genus with respect to the mental, the vocal, and the written: therefore it will belong to them univocally; but truth and falsity cannot belong to them univocally: therefore neither can they pertain to its essence. The minor is proved: because they are found formally only in the mental enunciation, but in the vocal and the written only as in a sign, and therefore by attribution to the mental: therefore they belong to them analogically.

Third: Because this causal proposition is true: Because the enunciation enunciates one thing of another, it is true or false. And this causal proposition is false: Because the enunciation is true or false, it enunciates one thing of another: therefore it is prior by nature that the enunciation enunciates one thing of another than that it is true or false: therefore its essence consists in the former, upon which the true and the false follow as a proper accident. And certainly it is so: for by the very fact that we understand one thing to be enunciated of another, we understand an enunciative speech, although we understand nothing of the true or the false: therefore the essence of the enunciation consists only in that, while these are outside it.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major must be distinguished: for to be distinguished from the other species of the same genus happens in two ways. First, by a specific distinction; and in this way one thing cannot be distinguished from another except through an essential difference. Second, not by a specific distinction but by an accidental one; and so the true and the false enunciation are distinguished, not essentially. And Aristotle chose in the present chapter to define the enunciation through the true and the false, as through its accidents more known to us, from which the essence of the same enunciation might become known to us, which consists only in this, that one thing is enunciated of another.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the mental enunciation is one simple quality.

We ask about the mental enunciation alone, whether it is one simple quality, or rather composed of many simple ones; not about the vocal and the written, about which it is certain that they are composed of many simple vocal sounds or writings. Concerning the mental, then, it should be noted first that if it is taken for the act of the intellect by which we apprehend things, or judge about things apprehended, it is not something composite but simple. For the judgment of the intellect by which we judge this enunciation to be true, man is white, is a single and simple act of the intellect; nor

[p. 538]

is the mental enunciation properly taken for it; therefore the question does not proceed about this, but about the concepts which the intellect forms of the things themselves; when these are formed, it judges that one agrees with another, and in judging it composes one with the other; and it is about this composition and mental proposition that we inquire: Whether it is one simple quality, or only composed of many.

Second, it should be noted that the intellect behaves thus in forming the mental enunciation: it first apprehends the simple things through several simple concepts; then from these it effects a composition, before it judges of the agreement of the one with respect to the other; or sometimes it has an entire apprehension of the whole enunciation before the judgment: because it apprehends the entire composition before it judges of the agreement of the predicate with the subject: as is plain when we hear this proposition, the stars are even, which we apprehend entire before we judge of its truth or falsity; indeed, though we have its apprehension, we never have a judgment, because no reason appears for judging it true rather than false. Of the mental proposition as apprehended, therefore, it is evident that it is not a simple quality: wherefore the difficulty of the question is reduced to the mental proposition as judged, whether it is a simple quality or composite. For we can understand in two ways that the intellect judges true this apprehended proposition, man is white, composed of three concepts. First, in such a way that it judges that the simple concept of whiteness agrees with the simple concept of man: and then it is evident that the judged mental proposition, which is as it were the term of the judgment, is not a simple quality but composite, like the apprehended mental proposition. In another way the intellect can behave in judgment, not by judging that one simple concept agrees with another, but by forming, from the whole composite apprehension, or from the three simple concepts of predicate, subject, and copula, some other distinct concept through which the significates of the whole composition, namely of predicate, subject, and copula, are represented; so that through that one concept it judges at once of the truth or falsity of the whole composition, in the way in which the imagination, from the twofold species of a mountain and of gold, forms a certain third, simple species representing a golden mountain; and in the same way also as an angel, through one simple concept, understands the entire composition made by us. For if it is done so, the mental enunciation will be a single simple concept, and one simple quality, through which predicate, subject, and copula are represented.

[p. 539]

Secundo: Voces fignificant res med is conceptibus:ergo

And the first opinion holds that it happens so, and that therefore the judged mental enunciation is one simple quality. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 5; Toledo, On the Soul 3, q. 19. And it is proved by this argument: The intellect, since it is a power superior to the imagination, has the same or a greater power of composing than it; but the imagination, from a twofold simple species of diverse things, elicits also one simple species representing whatever was represented by those species of its own: therefore the intellect will have the same power; and so it will be able to judge of the composite apprehension, or of the agreement of one simple concept with another, in such a way that it elicits one concept representing whatever was represented by each concept, or by the whole apprehended composition; and so the enunciation judged and represented through that one concept will be one simple quality.

The second opinion holds: This is impossible; and it is altogether necessary that, just as the intellect apprehends the subject, the predicate, and the copula of the proposition not through one but through several concepts, so it attributes one to the other through judgment; and through this attribution composes the judged enunciation from the same simple concepts formed through apprehension. And thus the judged mental proposition is not one simple concept, nor one simple quality, but composed of many concepts and simple qualities. So Father Gabriel Vázquez, vol. 2 on 1 p., d. 13, ch. 13. And it seems to me the true opinion, and expressed in St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 58, a. 4, ad 1, where he speaks thus of the mental enunciation: Not any multitude whatever of understandings causes composition, but a multitude of those understandings of which one is attributed to another. For by the multitude of understandings he means the multitude of concepts, from which, he says, the intellect composes the judged mental enunciation through the attribution of one to another.

35 It is proved also by reason. First: Because the intellect effects the judged mental enunciation through the attribution of one to another, that is, by affirming one of another, or by denying it of it. But to attribute one thing to another, diverse from it, expresses multiplicity: therefore, since that which is attributed to another in the mental proposition is a concept attributed to another concept, just as in the vocal proposition it is one vocal sound attributed to another, the mental proposition is no less a composite quality than the vocal one.

Second: Vocal sounds signify things by means of concepts: therefore

the vocal proposition is a sign of the mental proposition; but the former is not one simple vocal sound, but composed of many: therefore neither will the mental proposition be one simple concept or quality, but composed of many concepts, of predicate, subject, and copula. Which is especially true and necessary where the predicate and the subject are distinguished by reason alone, as in an identical proposition: which it is impossible for the intellect to effect except by distinguishing those things which are not distinct on the side of the thing; but it cannot distinguish these unless it understands them through several concepts and attributes one of them to the other: therefore it is impossible for such a mental enunciation to be one simple concept, or one simple quality.

To the argument of the other opinion: Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: because to elicit, from a twofold diverse simple concept, a third, also simple, representing the several things that were represented by those, can be understood in two ways. First, by way of simple expression, so that by that one concept is expressed whatever was represented by several. Second, by attribution and composition of one with another. And in the first way it can be done by the imagination and by our intellect; but in the second way it is impossible: because to compose one with another expresses a multiplicity of concepts; and since it must be done so through the judgment by which the mental enunciation is constituted, it cannot be done through one concept, but necessarily through several, of which the mental enunciation is composed; and therefore the mental enunciation cannot be a simple concept or a simple quality, but is composed of several concepts and qualities. In the angels, however, it is a simple concept and a simple quality, because they do not judge by composing one with another, or by attributing one to another, but by expressing both by one simple concept. But this mode is incompatible with the imperfection of our intellect, which does not understand except by composing and dividing.

of the other posteriorly; but enunciation is said priorly of the affirmative and posteriorly of the negative; therefore it is analogous with respect to them, and so the division will be of an analogous term into its analogates. The minor is proved: first, from Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says: But the first one enunciative speech is affirmation; then negation. It is proved also by reason: because affirmation signifies composition, negation division; but composition is prior to division. Moreover, affirmation signifies a positive form, of which negation deprives; but form is prior to privation. And finally, negation falls upon affirmation, since a negative proposition is nothing other than an affirmative one with a negation added: the former, therefore, is prior, the latter posterior.

The second opinion is that of Soto, Summulae bk. 2, who asserts that affirmation and negation are different qualities of the enunciation; and since quality is an accident, enunciation will be divided into affirmative and negative as a subject into different accidents. This is proved by this argument: An accident is that which can be present to and absent from a subject without its corruption; but affirmation and negation are so related to the enunciation; therefore they are its accidents. The minor is proved: because the enunciation, remaining the same according to its essence, passes from affirmative to negative, as this same one, Peter runs, becomes negative when a negation is added: Peter does not run.

The third opinion is the common one: that the division of the enunciation is of a genus into species. So hold Porphyry, Ammonius, Boethius, Simplicius, St. Thomas, the Louvain commentators, Suessanus, Lemos, and Toledo on the present chapter. And this is more probable and is to be held.

It is proved, first: because the essence of the enunciation, as we proved above, consists in attributing one thing to another, or enunciating something of it; but this comes about through affirmation and negation; therefore these are essential differences dividing the enunciation. The division, therefore, will be of a genus into species.

Second: the affirmative and the negative enunciation agree in the common ratio of enunciation, which is predicated of both; for this is true, An affirmative enunciation is an enunciation, A negative enunciation is an enunciation; and they are distinguished in species; therefore enunciation is a genus with respect to both. The minor is proved: because the affirmative signifies the union and composition of the predicate with the subject, but the negative its division and separation from it; and these are modes of enunciating formally and essentially different, as is plain; therefore they constitute enunciations formally and essentially different.

To the argument of the first opinion: the major must be distinguished; for to be said

[p. 542]

Secundò: Significare verum , aut falfum, veleſtde eſſentia enunciationis,velpropriapaffio eius:fed enunciatio fimplex, &compofita, conueniuntvniuocè in eo,quod eſt ſignificare, verum,aut falium:nam enunciatio compofita, fimplicitet

priorly of one and posteriorly of another happens in two ways: either by reason of the superior predicate in which they agree, or by reason of the differences by which they are distinguished; and the first way takes away univocation and produces analogy, but the second in no way, since it is found in all genera, in which there is always one species prior to the others on account of the lesser perfection of their difference; which does not prevent the generic nature, on its own side, from being participated equally and univocally by all the species. And so it happens in the enunciation, whose ratio, on its own side, is participated equally by the affirmative and the negative, and not according to prior and posterior; but the affirmative enunciation, on account of the greater perfection of its difference, is prior to the negative, as Aristotle asserts and the argument proves; this, however, does not take away univocation nor the generic ratio.

To the argument of the second opinion: the minor must be distinguished; for the proposition, remaining the same only materially, that is, according to its material terms, passes from affirmative to negative; but not remaining the same formally and essentially: rather, when the negation is added, it becomes of a different species, on account of the different mode of enunciating, as we proved. Wherefore affirmation and negation are essential differences of the enunciation, and not qualities, except in the way in which essential differences are called essential qualities of the genus; wherefore neither are they in any way its accidents.

QUESTION VI. Whether the division of the enunciation into simple and composite is of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into its analogates.

The first opinion holds that this division is univocal, and therefore of a genus into its species. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 6, and others. They prove it, first: because the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in the genus of speech; therefore also in the genus of enunciation, which is inferior to speech. The consequence is proved: because things that agree univocally under a superior genus must also agree univocally under an inferior genus; as, if two animals agree under the superior genus of living thing, they must also agree univocally under the genus of animal, inferior to living thing.

Second: to signify the true or the false is either of the essence of the enunciation or its proper attribute; but the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in signifying the true or the false; for the composite enunciation, simply

is true or false, just like the simple one; therefore they also agree univocally in the common ratio of enunciation, as species under a genus.

The second opinion, of certain moderns, asserts that this division is of a subject into accidents. This is proved by this argument: the more and the less composite differ by this only accidentally, as the wall from the whole house; and the wholly simple enunciation differs from one which is composed, on the side of the subject, of another simple enunciation, such as this, “Man is white” is a proposition, only accidentally from the former, Man is white, because it is more composite. But the composite enunciation differs from the simple only according to more and less composite: because the simple is composed only of subject, predicate, and copula, whereas the composite is composed of these remotely, but proximately of many simple enunciations; therefore they are distinguished only accidentally.

The third opinion is the common one: that this division is of an analogous term into its analogates. So Boethius, Ammonius, Suessanus, Toledo on the present chapter, St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 6, and many moderns. And it seems to us more probable and more in conformity with the doctrine of Aristotle, who called the simple enunciation one, on account of its one significate, and therefore one simply; but the composite one by conjunction, which is to be one in a qualified sense, and therefore an enunciation in a qualified sense.

This is proved by reason. First: because the formal ratio of the enunciation, as we proved above, consists in enunciating one thing of another; but the composite enunciation does not enunciate one thing of another, because it is not composed proximately of subject and predicate, but is called an enunciation only by reason of the simple ones of which it consists, united by a conjunction, and only by reason of them does it signify truth or falsity; therefore the formal ratio of enunciation belongs per se and primarily to the simple, but to the composite only by participation and attribution to it, which is to belong analogically.

Second: one species is not composed formally of another, although it is not repugnant for it to be composed of it materially; but the composite enunciation is composed of simple ones formally, that is, inasmuch as they enunciate one thing of another and inasmuch as they also have simple truth, since if any one of these is taken from them the composite enunciation does not stand; therefore they cannot be species of the enunciation, but will be its analogates, against the first opinion. It is likewise proved against the second that they do not differ only accidentally: because they differ by a formal and essential mode, since in the simple the mode is enunciative, but in the composite it is not; rather, its form consists in the union

of simple ones, or of enunciative ones; therefore they differ essentially. Wherefore the division cannot be of a subject into accidents, but will be of an analogous term into its analogates, as we proved against the second opinion.

To whose arguments one must reply, and to the first: granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied; and the reason is that the ratio of enunciation is far more perfect than speech, and the composite enunciation cannot attain it per se, but only by participation in the simple, although per se and simply it can attain the ratio of speech. And although a similar example is not easily found among natural beings, because their nature is not so variable, it is nevertheless found in those artificial things that are made by the intellect: for species and individual agree univocally under the genus of relation of reason, as its species; yet under the inferior genus, of the relation of predicability, they agree only analogically, because the individual does not attain its perfection, since it is not predicated except improperly, of itself. So the inferior ratio can be so perfect, and the superior ratio so imperfect, that one member cannot participate the former per se, or not univocally, but only by attribution to the other, more perfect member, with which it agreed univocally in the superior, much more imperfect genus; and this suffices for the consequence of one who argues thus not to be good: These two agree univocally in a superior predicate; therefore also in an inferior predicate.

To the second: the minor must be denied, that the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in signifying the true or the false; for this belongs to the composite only by participation in the simple; wherefore it must also be denied that it is true or false simply.

To the argument of the second opinion, the minor must also be denied, that the simple and the composite enunciation differ only according to more and less composite; for they differ by different formal modes of enunciation: because the simple has the formal mode of enunciating, whereas the composite does not have the mode of enunciating per se, whence neither does it enunciate per se, but only by participation in the simple; per se, however, it has only the mode of a conjunction of enunciatives; and therefore they are essentially different.

## CHAPTER VI

On the Opposition and Truth of Enunciations about the Contingent Future.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

In those things, then, which are and which have been, it is necessary that the affirmation and the negation be true or false, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to show that the 33

T            rule of contradictory propositions, which is this: If one is true, the

other must necessarily be false, is not true in the same way in singular propositions about the contingent future as it is true in propositions of necessary and remote matter, and also in contingent propositions with a universal subject. And it is divided into two parts: for in the first, having proposed and solved the question, he proves his own view by a twofold argument; in the second, he delivers a twofold distinction of the necessary, concerning things and propositions.

Aristotle had treated in the preceding chapter, toward the end, of the nature of contradiction, or opposition, found in propositions; and he had said that it is a necessary condition of contradictory enunciations that, if one is determinately true, the other is determinately false. But in the present chapter he proposes this question, namely: Whether this condition of contradictories is true not only in propositions of necessary and remote matter, but also in contingent matter. He speaks, moreover, not of the rarely contingent, such as that one digging should find a treasure; nor of the frequently contingent, such as that a man should lie down at night; but of the contingent ad utrumlibet, that is, toward either side, which can equally be and not be: as that Peter should sin, or live virtuously.

And he presupposes as certain, first, that the rule is true in all propositions of necessary and remote matter, whether they are universal or singular:

for if it is determinately

true that Peter is a man, it is determinately false that Peter is not a man; and if it is determinately true that every lion is not a stone, it is determinately false that some lion is a stone. Second, he presupposes as certain that the rule is also true in contingent propositions with a universal subject: for if it is determinately true that every man is white, it is determinately false that no man is white. He says that a third thing is also certain: namely, that the same rule is true in contingent propositions with a singular subject, if they are about the present or the past: for if it is determinately true that Peter lives, or has lived, virtuously, it is determinately false that Peter does not live, or has not lived, virtuously. For in these propositions there can be no indetermination; but just as it is determinately true that what has been and is, is so, it will be determinately false that it has not been or is not. He says, therefore, that the question proceeds only about singular propositions about the contingent future: whether one of them is determinately true and the other determinately false. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because a contingent or free cause is not determined to a future effect, but can determine itself and can not determine itself; and therefore, as long as its future determination is enunciated by a singular proposition about the future, so long does it remain as it were suspended; and therefore the truth of that same proposition always seems indeterminate.

Aristotle replies, however, that in these propositions the whole disjunction made up of both contradictories is determinately true, as Peter will sin or will not sin: for to sin or not to sin is as necessary as to be or not to be; therefore it is likewise determinately true. But either contradictory taken by itself is not determinately true or false, as Peter will sin, and also Peter will not sin. This he proves by a twofold argument leading to the impossible. First: because if they were determinately true, nothing in things would be contingent, but all things would come about necessarily; as, if it were determinately true that Peter will do this or that, will be virtuous or vicious, that a battle will take place tomorrow or will not take place, those effects would come about necessarily, and therefore could not fail to come about; wherefore nothing in things would be contingent, which is absurd.

The second reason: because if these singular propositions about the contingent future were determinately true, and all future effects came about necessarily, and no effect were contingent, there would be no need to take counsel about future things, nor to deliberate; wherefore there would be neither counsel nor freedom: for delibe

Ethunc modum neceffitatis , atque etiam fecundum , primæ diſtinctionis , reperiri docetin enunciationibus fingularibus contingentibus de præfenti , præterito , & futuro: nam dum Petrus ambulat , neceſſarium eftex ſuppoſitione , ambulare: & etiam quòd ambulauerit , fuppofito , quòd ambulauit ; & etiam eft neceffaria hæc de futuro , Petrus ambulabit , ex fup-poſitione, quòd ambulabir, Neceflarium quoque eſt diſiun-tum hoc , Petrus ambulabit, velnon ambulabit : fed cum v-traque hac neceffitate totius diſiuncti , & etiam cuiuflibet partis per ſe ſumptæ, ex fuppofitione temporis verum eſt, quamlibetperſe ſumptameſſecontingentem,& indetermina-tè veram. MM        ij

ration and consultation concern only contingent things, which can be and not be; for about things that will necessarily come to be, such as tomorrow’s sunrise, no one in his right mind ever said that one must take counsel. But to take away contingency, counsel, deliberation, nay, even our freedom, is absurd; therefore it must not be said that singular propositions about the contingent future are determinately true or determinately false.

Finally he explains a twofold distinction of the necessity of things and of enunciations. The first is this: Some things are necessary from their own nature, as the heavens; others only from the condition of the time by which they are measured, although from their own nature they are contingent: as it is necessary that Peter walk while he walks, not from his own nature but from the condition of the time by which his walking is measured. And in this way he says it is universally true that every thing, when it is, necessarily is, and every proposition, for the time at which it is true, is necessarily true; but he affirms that the first necessity is such simply, while the second is such only in a qualified sense, that is, extrinsically and from the supposition of the time at which the thing is, or at which the proposition is true.

The second is the distinction of the necessary: Some things are necessary absolutely, that is, without comparison to another, as that man is an animal. Others only from comparison to their opposite, so that what, taken by itself, is contingent, taken together with its opposite is necessary: as this is contingent, Peter will walk; but if it is taken with its opposite, it makes the whole disjunction necessary, as Peter will walk or will not walk. And he says that this mode of necessity too is extrinsic and such in a qualified sense, whereas the first is such simply and intrinsically. And he teaches that this mode of necessity, and also the second of the first distinction, is found in singular contingent enunciations about the present, the past, and the future: for while Peter walks it is necessary, on the supposition, that he walk; and also that he has walked, on the supposition that he did walk; and this one about the future is also necessary, Peter will walk, on the supposition that he will walk. This disjunction too is necessary, Peter will walk or will not walk; but with both of these necessities, of the whole disjunction and also of each part taken by itself from the supposition of time, it is true that each, taken by itself, is contingent and indeterminately true.

SINGLE QUESTION. Whether singular enunciations about the contingent future have determinate truth or falsity.

The question proceeds only about singular and contingent ones: for necessary propositions, and also those consisting of remote matter, are necessarily true or necessarily false, whether they are universal or singular; and therefore their truth or falsity is determinate. Contingent ones with a universal subject are also determinately true or determinately false: as every man will walk, no man will walk; and, man will walk, man will not walk. Because, although a future and contingent effect can, in the singular, be and not be, it is nevertheless universally true that the contingent cause will be determined to operate; nay, its determination is necessary in the vague singular, although it is wholly contingent in any determinate singular. By a moral necessity, that is: because, speaking morally, that is, in the human manner, or as human affairs are wont to turn out, it is necessary that men walk; and therefore this is determinately true, man will walk, and some man will walk; and determinately false, every man will walk, no man will walk. For in this sense is taken that saying of Christ in Matthew: It must needs be that scandals come. It is also certain that singular contingent propositions about the present and the past are determinately true or false; nay, necessary, not indeed intrinsically or simply, but extrinsically and from the supposition of time, as was expounded by us. The question, then, can be only about singular ones about the contingent future: whether they have determinate truth, or indeterminate; because the determination of the future cause, on which their truth depends, is indeterminate as long as it is enunciated as future; and therefore it does not seem able to confer determinate truth on those same propositions.

Therefore the first opinion asserts: that such propositions have no truth or falsity at all, but are neutral, that is, neither true nor false. So Antonio de Córdoba, bk. 1 of his Quaestionarium, q. 55, doubt 2. It is proved: because the truth or falsity of an enunciation is taken from its conformity or disconformity to the thing signified; but the thing signified by this enunciation, Peter will sin, is not in the nature of things as long as it is enunciated as future; therefore the enunciation itself is neither conformed nor disconformed to it; wherefore it will be neither true nor false, but neutral. And certainly, if true or false

is granted, it follows that it is at once true and false, which is repugnant. The consequence is proved: because, since the thing signified is indifferent to being and not being, and not determined to the one more than to the other, there is no greater reason why the enunciation should be true rather than false; wherefore it will have either neither or both; and the latter is impossible; therefore the other is necessary, namely that it is neutral.

The second opinion attributes some truth to these enunciations, not indeed determinate, but confused or indeterminate: so that the whole disjunction composed of both contradictories is determinately true and necessary, as Peter will dispute or will not dispute; but either of them, taken by itself, is indeterminately true or false, which is to say that it is indifferent to truth or falsity, and therefore is neither actually true nor actually false, but as it were in potency, not yet determined. So Albert the Great, On Interpretation bk. 1, tract. on opposition, ch. 4; Catharinus in his opuscule on the truth of enunciations; the Louvain commentators and Toledo on the present chapter. And this seems to be the express view of Aristotle, who proved it by this argument: What is determinately true is judged necessary; therefore, if a singular enunciation about the contingent future is determinately true, it will be necessary. From which it follows that all future things come about necessarily. The consequence is proved: because, if this is necessarily true, Peter will dispute, the disputation of Peter, from which it takes its truth, will be necessarily future and not contingent; wherefore no freedom will be left, nor will counsel or deliberation have any place, because we do not deliberate about things necessarily future; nor are necessary things said to be in our power, but only contingent ones, which can come about and not come about, be done in this way or in another.

It is proved, second: for from the fact that the thing is or is not, an enunciation is called true or false; but the thing signified by a singular enunciation about the contingent future is so determined that, as long as it is future and is enunciated as such, it has no determination; therefore neither will a proposition about the future enunciating it have determinate truth, but it will always be indeterminate and indifferent to truth and falsity.

The third opinion holds that such enunciations have determinate truth or falsity, but contingent. And this is true, and very much in conformity with the Catholic faith; it is held by Scotus on 1, d. 3, q. 1, § to the principal arguments; St. Bonaventure, d. 38, a. 3, q. 1, ad 1; Richard, a. 1, q. 5, ad 1; Gregory, q. 1, a. 2; Ockham, q. 1, to the principal argument; Gabriel, q. 1, a. 1, notable 7; Marsilius, q. 40, ad 3; Holcot on 2, q., a. 7; Soto on ch. 9 of the Epistle to the Romans, p. 5,

But in order that we may at once explain and prove it, it should be noted what determinate truth is: for from this it will be clear whether it is to be attributed to singular enunciations about the contingent future.

Now determinate truth must have two things. First, that it be distinct and not confused: as that truth is confused which is found in equivocal propositions, as in this one, Canis movetur [The dog moves], in which the predicate is not verified of any subject distinctly, but its truth remains confused and as it were suspended. Second, it is required that it be actual, which is taken in relation to an actual significate: for if it is only in indifferent potency, the enunciation will be said to be suspended from truth. Now the actual significate of an enunciation is said to be that which actually is in the nature of things at the time signified by its copula: so that, if the enunciation is about the present, it has actual and determinate truth if the thing signified exists at the present time; and if it is about the past, it will be determinately true if its significate at some time was in the nature of things. But if the enunciation is about the future, it will be determinately true if its significate is at some time to be in the nature of things: as this enunciation, The sun will rise tomorrow, is determinately true today, because its significate will be in the nature of things on the morrow.

Second, it should be noted that a proposition about the future, like one about the past, is twofold: one, which determines some time, as this, Peter will dispute tomorrow; another, which determines none, but signifies the whole future time as it were indefinitely, as Peter will dispute. And for the former to be determinately true, it is necessary that the disputation of Peter be future on the morrow; but for the latter it suffices that at some time it is to have actual being in the nature of things, so that it is then true to enunciate about the present, Peter is disputing.

These things supposed, our view is now proved: that singular propositions about the contingent future are determinately true or false. From the Catholic faith, which teaches that God from eternity evidently knew their truth; from which it follows that they had it from eternity. The consequence is proved: because God does not know things to be future unless they truly are future. For example: God knew from eternity that this singular about the contingent future is true, Antichrist will sin; therefore he knew that

Adarg.primæ opinionis, Diftinguenda eft minor,quòdfi-gnificatum propofitionis , fingularis de futuro contingenti, non fitinrerum natura : quia licèt non fit in differentiatem poris præſentis , eſttamen in differentia temporis futuri , fi-gnificata per copulam, in qua habebit eſse determinatum,& actuale, & in hoc fufficit ,vt determinatè fit vera enunciatio, Mm iiij

it will at some time be true about the present; but a proposition which is at some time true about the present was always true about the future, and determinately true, since at some time it is determinately true about the present; therefore God knew from eternity its determinate truth about the future, which cannot be unless it had it. Otherwise God would have known as future that which is not future.

It is proved also by reason. First: because, if Peter is disputing today, it will be determinately true to enunciate about the present, Peter is disputing; therefore it was also determinately true yesterday to enunciate about the future, Peter will dispute. The consequence is evidently proved: because the truth of an enunciation about the future is measured by its significate, and determinate truth by the determination of that same significate; but the present disputation now has determinate being about the present; therefore yesterday it had determinate being about the future; and therefore the enunciation about the future which enunciated it had determinate truth, which, just as it had it yesterday, it is certain it had a thousand years before.

Second: the determinate truth of an enunciation is taken from its determinate significate; but the significate of this enunciation, Peter will dispute, will at some time have determinate being about the present; therefore it now has determinate being about the future; and therefore the proposition which enunciates it about the future will be determinately true, since its significate is determinately future. The minor is proved: because the disputation of Peter will at some time have actual being, and distinct, outside its causes.

It is proved, finally: because, if these propositions do not have determinate truth, then they are in no way true or false, nor will they be at any time, that is, neither in act nor in potency, which is absurd. The consequence is proved: because a potency is in vain which neither is reduced nor can be reduced to act; but these enunciations will never be true about the future, nay, will not be able to be so, if they are not now determinately true: because, when the effect has become present, they are no longer true about the future, but about the present; therefore they have determinate truth about the future neither in act nor in potency, which is to be in no way at all true about the future.

To the argument of the first opinion: the minor must be distinguished, that the significate of a singular proposition about the contingent future is not in the nature of things; for although it is not in the difference of present time, it is nevertheless in the difference of future time signified by the copula, in which it will have determinate and actual being; and this suffices for the enunciation to be determinately true,

about the future; just as the significate of a proposition about the past is not now in the nature of things either, but because it had actual and determinate being in its own difference of time, this suffices for the enunciation about the past to be determinately true. But the other thing that is inferred, that it is at once true and false if it is granted to be determinately true, must be denied: because it is determinately true for this reason, that its significate will have determinate being at the time signified by the copula; and although this can fail to be, since it is contingent, it nevertheless will be; and therefore the proposition will be true, but not false: because, although it can fail to be, it is nevertheless not true that it will not have being in its own difference of time. And so, since it is enunciated as future, and not only as possible, it is not enough for the proposition to be false that it can fail to be; rather it is required that it be not future at all, which is plainly false; and therefore it is badly inferred that the proposition is at once true and false.

For the solution of the arguments of the second opinion, it should be noted that a future effect is twofold, necessary and contingent. That one is necessarily future which cannot fail to be future, because it is future through a necessary cause: as tomorrow’s sunrise is necessarily future, because it is so through a necessary cause, determined to one. But that one is said to be contingently future which, at a future time, is indeed to have being no less than a necessary effect, yet contingently: so that it can fail to be future, because it is so through a free or contingent cause, which so produces it in the difference of future time that it can not produce it; it will so determine itself to operate that it can not determine itself. And since the truth or falsity of an enunciation is measured by the thing signified, the enunciation about the future is also twofold: one necessary, as The sun will rise tomorrow, and the other contingent, as Peter will dispute; and indeed both determinately true or false, but the former necessarily, because it is so true that it cannot be false, the latter contingently, because it is so true that it can be false. Whence it follows that this is not a good consequence: This enunciation, “Peter will dispute,” is determinately true; therefore it is necessary, or necessarily true; for it is so determinately true as to be contingent and contingently true, because it is so true that it can be false; just as the effect signified by it is so determinately future that it can fail to be future.

By this doctrine the argument of Aristotle is solved. Its antecedent must be denied: because not everything that is future will have being through a necessary cause, since many things will have it through a contingent one; and therefore they are neither necessary nor necessarily future, but contingent and contingently future; and consequently the enunciations

[p. 553]

> tiones,per quas fignificantur,licet fintdeterminate verè , non tamen neceffariæ,fed contingentes:quia fic funt veræ , vtpof-finteffe falſæ. by which they are signified, although they are determinately true, are nevertheless not necessary but contingent, because they are so true that they can be false.

For the solution of the other, another thing should be noted, in which the deception of this opinion consists: namely, that a free or contingent cause is indeterminate and indifferent, because it can determine itself and can not determine itself. Yet it is certain that it will determine itself or will not determine itself; and therefore it is also certain that its effect will be future or will not be future; and if it is future, that it could have failed to be future; and if it is not future, that it could also have been future.

For example: the will of Peter is always indeterminate and indifferent to disputing or not disputing, until it determines itself on the morrow, at such an hour, to dispute; and then its indifference will cease. Wherefore the disputation will be determined at such an hour of tomorrow, yet in such a way that it could have failed to be; but just as it will then be true about the present that it is determined contingently, and that it could have failed to have determinate being at that same hour, because the free cause could have not determined itself, so it is true today that it will have determinate being tomorrow, yet contingently, because it is true that it could have failed to be; and therefore it is true that the disputation will have determinate being. The future enunciation, therefore, Peter will dispute tomorrow at such an hour, is not compared to his will as indeterminate, but as determining itself at such an hour to dispute; nor does it signify the disputation as in potency, or as in the power of the will not yet determined, but as determined and having actual being, not present, but future on the morrow at such an hour; and from this it has determinate truth, no less than the proposition about the present uttered at the same time at which the disputation takes place: Peter is disputing. Because, just as then the disputation has determinate being about the present, so now it has determinate being about the future. And in this consists the deception of the second opinion: because it thinks that the proposition about the future is compared to the cause only as indeterminate; whereas it is not compared to it as now indeterminate (although it truly is now indeterminate), but to that same cause as determining itself at the future time signified by the copula; from which the enunciation has determinate truth, although contingent, because it is compared to the cause as determining itself in the future, yet contingently, according to its own nature, and therefore as able not to determine itself.

To the form of the argument, then: the minor must be distinguished, that the thing signified by an enunciation about the future, as long as it is enunciated

as future, has no determination; for although it has no present determination, it nevertheless has a future determination, which it signifies; and a contingent one indeed, since the disputation is so future and determined that it can fail to be: for this does not take away its future determination, but shows that it is contingent; and therefore it does not take away the determinate truth of the enunciation about the future, but shows that its determinate truth is not necessary but contingent.

But what is to be said to Aristotle, who seems to hold that such enunciations are not determinately true? I reply that several solutions are applied by several authors, which indeed do not seem to be according to his mind; and therefore I do not report them. Others, however, whom the aforesaid solutions do not satisfy, have asserted that Aristotle did hold that such enunciations do not have determinate truth, but that he erred in this, against our faith: which, since it holds that God knows evidently from eternity that some are true and others false, it is necessary to grant that they are determinately true or false; because what God knows to be future is determinately future, although contingent. Wherefore Aristotle is not to be listened to in this part.

I, however, cannot believe that Aristotle erred: because it is certain that he knew the freedom of our will and the contingency of the other causes, which are the two roots of the whole contingency of the future effects that singular enunciations about the contingent future enunciate. And since he knew that those same effects will have actual determination, although contingent, at the future time signified by their copula, it is impossible that he did not understand that such enunciations have determinate truth, although contingent.

He denied determinate truth to them, therefore, in that sense in which he granted it to enunciations of necessary and remote matter, and also to contingent ones with a universal subject; nay, even to singular ones about the present and the past, and also to the whole disjunction made up of the two singular contradictories about the future, such as this, Peter will dispute or will not dispute. Now to all these he granted determinate truth taken for necessary, which he denied to singulars about the contingent future; yet he did not deny them determinate contingent truth. So his sense was that the rule of contradiction, that of two contradictories one is determinately true and the other determinately false, that is, one is necessarily true, the other necessarily false, is in all enunciations of whatever matter

true, except singulars about the contingent future, in which alone it fails: because neither, taken by itself, is determinately true, that is, it is not necessarily true, but they are contingently true or false; and for that reason there is no human science of them. Nevertheless they have this truth, contingently determinate, on account of the contingent determination of the effect at the future time signified by their copula. That this was his sense I show from two things.

First, from the arguments by which he proved it, in which he argues from determinate truth to necessary truth. And from the determinate truth of these enunciations he infers that counsel and deliberation are taken away; but the argument would be frivolous unless he took determination of truth for necessity.

Second, from these words, in which he openly signified the same sense: But in contradiction too the reason is the same: it is altogether necessary to be or not to be, and to be future or not. Yet it is not necessary, dividing, to say that one of the two is necessary. I mean, as it is necessary that there will be a naval battle tomorrow or will not be, yet it is not necessary that a naval battle take place tomorrow, nor that it not take place; but that it take place or not take place is necessary. And in this sense Aristotle is explained by Richard on 1, distinction 38, a. 1, q. 5, ad 1, and Major in the same place, q. 1.

Brief Doubt: whether a contingent effect, when it is, is necessary, or still contingent.

It will help not a little toward better understanding the preceding question to determine this doubt, from which will also be explained that universal proposition of Aristotle frequently repeated in this matter, namely: Everything that is, when it is, necessarily is. If this is true, it follows from it that a future contingent, once it is in the nature of things, is not contingent but necessary. Which I also prove thus: for a free cause, before it determines itself to operate, is indeterminate and contingent; but while it operates in the present, its indetermination now ceases; therefore its contingency ceases; and consequently the contingency of the effect will cease, and it will be necessary.

This doubt is to be solved by this distinction: the necessary is taken in two ways. First, from its own nature; and this is said

[p. 556]

> neceffarium fimpliciter, vtortus ſolis:quia ita eſt,vtnon pof-fit non effe,propter neceffitatem fuæ caufæ Secundò , dicitur aliquid neceffarium, non ex propria natura, ſedAb extrinfeco : vt ex determinatione temporisin quo producitur extra caufas, licèt àcauſa contingente fiat. In ſecundolibro husus operis , folum agit Ariftoteles , de enunciationibus modalibus , & oppofitione earum : de qui-bus copiosè in Summulis diſseritur: & cùm exhoclibro de fumpta fint, quæ à Summuliftis repetuntur , & inculcantur, noniudicamusneceſsarium,eanuncrepetere , nec capitahu-ius libri exponere, cum iamfit tota corum doctrina ab ado-lefcentibus fatis intellecta:ſed ad librosde Priori refolutione procedendum eſse .                             S ۱ Finis huius operis.

necessary simply, as the sunrise: because it is such that it cannot fail to be, on account of the necessity of its cause. Second, something is said to be necessary not from its own nature but extrinsically: as from the determination of the time in which it is produced outside its causes, although it comes about from a contingent cause. This supposed, we say that a contingent effect, once it is, is still contingent simply, but necessary only extrinsically, from the determination of time.

The first part is proved: because a free cause freely determines itself to operate; therefore it so determines itself that it can not determine itself; and consequently it so operates that it can not operate; wherefore, while it operates, it operates not necessarily but freely and contingently; and therefore the operation itself, or the effect, even while it comes to be or is present, proceeds contingently from its cause and has contingent being simply. The second is proved, that it is necessary on a supposition: because, supposing that it already has being, it cannot fail to be; otherwise it could at once be and not be, which is repugnant. And in this sense is understood the proposition of Aristotle, Everything that is, when it is, necessarily is: as if to say, from the supposition of the time in which it is present, it cannot fail to be. And this is all that the argument made proves: because, although through the determination of the free cause to operate its indetermination and indifference cease, yet they cease freely; and therefore the effect is always free and contingent from its own nature, even then when it is present, although from the supposition of presentiality it is necessary extrinsically and from a supposition.

In the second book of this work Aristotle treats only of modal enunciations and their opposition, of which there is copious discussion in the Summulae; and since the things that are repeated and inculcated by the Summulists are taken from this book, we have not judged it necessary to repeat them now, nor to expound the chapters of this book, since their whole doctrine is by now sufficiently understood by the young; but rather that we must proceed to the books of the Prior Analytics.

End of this work.

## COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK

O F A R I S T O T L E O N P R I O R A N A LY S I S , or Resolution.

P RO E M O F T H I S WO R K .

his work is the beginning of the third part of Dialectic, in which

T          Aristotle begins to treat of the third operation of the intellect, to

which the syllogism pertains. And it is entitled On Prior Resolution; and logical or intellectual resolution, of which the title is understood, is not the dissolution of the syllogism, as the material and physical resolution of a thing is its dissolution; but it is as it were an examination of the parts of which the syllogism, which is the instrument of Dialectic, ought to consist. The end of the resolution, too, is the perfection of that same syllogism, which ought to be known from the very mode of the resolution, or examination, composing it, so that it may have power for finding and proving the truth, as we shall explain more copiously in the proem of the books of the Posterior Analytics.

On the title of this work.

But why they are entitled On Prior Resolution is not sufficiently clear.

Indeed, many say that these books are called “prior,” and the following ones “on posterior resolution,” because in these the form of the syllogism is treated, in the following ones its matter. This reason, however, is insufficient: because, although it is true that in these books the syllogism is treated according to its form, it is nevertheless false that in the following ones the same is treated only according to its matter; because, if this were true, demonstration would not be distinguished from the syllogism in common, nor from the topical and sophistical syllogism, except by matter, which is openly false; for from it would follow that demonstration is neither a species of syllogism nor distinguished in species from dialectical and sophistical syllogisms. The consequence is evidently proved: because the essential difference constituting a species and distinguishing it from others is not taken from the matter, but from the form. Therefore it must be said that these books are called “on prior resolution,” and the following “on posterior resolution,” because in these the common and generic form of the syllogism is treated, which

is taken from its disposition in figure and mood, and which is clearly common to all syllogisms. But in the following books the special form is treated, namely the mode of concluding one truth necessarily from another, by which demonstration is constituted in the species of syllogism and distinguished from the others, as is also explained more copiously in the proem of the following work. Now the common and generic form is prior and better known to us; therefore these books are rightly entitled On Prior Resolution.

What the object of this work is.

The first opinion asserts that demonstration is the subject: because from these and the following books one work is made, whose aim is demonstration, as the end to which it is proximately ordered. Whence Aristotle, in ch. 1 of this book, proposing the intent of this work, asserts that it is to dispute about demonstration and demonstrative discipline.

The second opinion distinguishes this work from the following one, and therefore denies that demonstration is the object; but neither does it assert that the syllogism is the adequate object, but rather argumentation in common: because Aristotle treats not of the syllogism alone, but also of other argumentations, such as induction, the enthymeme, and the example; wherefore something common to these must be the object of this work.

Our view, however, and the more common one among the expositors of this place, which, supposing the distinction of this work from the following, must necessarily be admitted, since the things treated in each are different, is that the syllogism in common alone is its adequate object. Because either Aristotle treats nothing of the other argumentations in it, or, if he treats something, it is only inasmuch as they can serve the syllogism. This very thing is proved by reason: because the adequate object of any science is that whose parts the science expressly explains, whose definition it delivers, whose attributes it proves; but in this work the parts of the syllogism are delivered, its definition is assigned, and its attributes are proved, as is manifest in bks. 1 and 2; therefore the syllogism is the adequate object of this part. But what Aristotle says, that his purpose is to treat of demonstration, proves only that the following books are as it were the end to which this work is ordered; of which end it is plain that it is not treated in this work, and therefore it does not pertain to its object either.

Division of the whole work.

3

This work is divided into two books or parts. In the first of them

Aristotle treats of the syllogism and its parts; in the second, of its properties or attributes, which Aristotle calls powers or potencies and impotencies.

This first book, moreover, is divided into three parts. In the first, which has the character of a proem, Aristotle proposes the matter of the whole work, and defines the syllogism and its parts (which are the proposition and the term). In the second he treats of the conversions of propositions. In the third, of the figures and moods of syllogisms, and of the things that pertain to those figures.

## CHAPTER I

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

First, to say about what, and of what, the consideration is: that it is about demonstration.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

his chapter is as it were the proem of the whole work, in 4

T          which Aristotle intends to propose its end, to which it is ordered,

and also the things he is going to treat in it. It is divided into two parts. In the first of them, having proposed the end, he proposes the things to be treated, namely the proposition, the term, the perfect and the imperfect syllogism; and he defines each of these, and likewise divides those that are manifold, namely the proposition and the syllogism.

He asserts that the end of this work is demonstration: which, since it is the most excellent instrument of Dialectic, all things are ordered to it, remotely indeed the simple ones, but proximately propositions and the syllogistic form, of which this work is to treat. The form is ordered, in roughly the way a genus is, to constituting its most excellent species.

He defines, then, first the proposition, because it was better known to us, since he had already treated of it in the book On Interpretation; and its definition is this: A proposition is an expression affirmative or negative of something about something. In which expression is put in place of the genus, which of itself affirms or denies nothing. And it is contracted by affirmation and negation, as by essential differences

as we said in bk. 1 of On Interpretation; and it is defined by these rather than by true or false, because in relation to the syllogism, to which it is proximately ordered, it makes no difference whether it is true or false, since the syllogistic form can consist as much in false as in true propositions; but it is necessary that it be affirmative or negative in order to serve the syllogism.

He divides the same proposition by a twofold division. The first is into universal, particular, and indefinite. The universal is that whose subject is distributed for all the inferiors contained under it, as every man is an animal. The particular, that whose subject is affected by a particular sign, as some man is an animal. The indefinite, that whose subject is a common term affected by no sign, as man is an animal. He makes no mention of the singular proposition, because it does not pertain per se to an art or science, nor to the syllogistic form.

The second division of the proposition is into dialectical and demonstrative. The dialectical is the probable one, from which a probable syllogism is made; but it has the form of an interrogation in the one who asks, while in the one who constructs the syllogism it is only a simple probable proposition: as if you say, Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? it has the mode of an interrogation. But if you take away the interrogation, it has the mode of a simple proposition, from which a syllogism is made. The other is the demonstrative proposition, which must be true and necessary; and from either a syllogism can be made; and therefore the syllogistic proposition is common to both.

Next he defines the term by this definition: I call a term that into which a proposition is resolved, as into the predicate and that of which it is predicated: as man and animal.

Finally he defines the syllogism by this definition: A syllogism is an expression in which, certain things being posited, something other than the things posited necessarily follows, by the fact that these are. In which definition expression is put in place of the genus, because it is common to all argumentations, with which the syllogism agrees in it. In which, certain things being posited, that is, two premises disposed in mood and figure, so that it may be distinguished from the example, which from one singular only gathers another; from the enthymeme, which proceeds from one only, as it were suppressing the other; and also from induction, which, although it gathers a universal from many singulars, does so not from singulars disposed in mood and figure, but only enumerated. And he adds, by the fact that these are, to explain that the conclusion of the syllogism follows by virtue of the premises so disposed, without any extrinsic addition.

He divides the syllogism into perfect and imperfect. Perfect, he says, is the one that needs nothing in order to appear necessary; and such are the syllogisms of the first figure. Imperfect, however, is the one that needs some reduction to a perfect one in order to appear necessary.

Finally, he teaches that the principles known per se on which the whole syllogistic art rests are two, namely: Said of all, on which affirmative syllogisms rest, and Said of none, on which negative ones rest. And said of all he explains thus: when nothing can be taken under the subject of which the predicate is not said. But the minor proposition is taken under the major, because its subject is contained under the subject of that same major: therefore it is evident that if the predicate of the major is said of the subject, it will also be said of everything contained under it; which is gathered in the conclusion, as this syllogism shows: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. In its conclusion the predicate of the major, which is called the major extreme, is predicated of the subject of the minor, which is called the minor extreme and is contained under the subject of that same minor. Said of none, moreover, is this: If the predicate of the major is denied of the subject of the minor, it will also be denied of anything whatever contained under it; and this takes place in the conclusion, as if we say: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. For it is evident that if stone is denied of every animal in the major, it is also denied, in the conclusion, of every man, who was assumed under it in the minor. Now a perfect syllogism does not need these two principles, Said of all and Said of none, in order to appear necessary, but in order that it may appear on what its efficacy rests; and therefore it is necessary that we know how to prove it through them, in order to be certain of it. For if someone does not know how to prove it, that is, to reduce the syllogistic form to its indemonstrable principles, he does not have science of its efficacy. And therefore these principles are called Said of all and Said of none prioristically: because in the Posterior Analytics they are taken according to the truth and necessity of the propositions; and they are called posterioristically the principles on which the whole demonstrative art rests.

## CHAPTER II

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

But since every proposition is either of inherence, or of inhering necessarily, or of inhering contingently.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the mode in which 7

T          propositions de inesse are converted. And it is divided into two

parts. In the first he divides the proposition into the one he calls de inesse and another, which is called Modal. In the second he teaches in what way propositions de inesse are converted; for he treats of the conversion of modals in the following chapter.

The division is this: one proposition is that in which one thing is simply predicated of another, or denied of it, without any mode of necessity or contingency adjoined; and this is called a proposition de inesse, because the predicate is said of the subject according to the being it has in it, not according to this or that mode in which it belongs to it, namely according to the mode of necessity or of contingency: as man is an animal. Another is the modal proposition, in which the predicate is said or denied of the subject with some mode of necessity or contingency adjoined: as man is necessarily an animal; the wall is contingently white. Aristotle, therefore, being about to treat of the conversion of propositions, first treats of the conversion of the proposition de inesse before that of the modal, because the proposition de inesse is prior to the modal and as it were its foundation.

8 The proposition de inesse is fourfold: Universal negative, Universal affirmative, Particular affirmative, and Particular negative. He divides it in this way because affirmatives and negatives have a different mode of conversion; but the Indefinite has the same mode of conversion as the particular.

He assigns, therefore, four rules for the conversion of these four propositions. The first, for the conversion of the Universal negative, which he says is converted into itself: as No man is an animal into this, No animal is a man.

The second, for the Universal affirmative, which he says is not converted into itself, that is, not into another universal, but into part, that is, into a particular: as Every man is an animal into this, Some animal is a man. The third, for the Particular affirmative, which he says is converted into itself

Note on the Letter.

9

Certain things should be noted concerning this chapter, so that the doctrine of Aristotle may be better understood. First, what conversion is.

And although it is defined by many thus: The conversion of a proposition is the transposition of the predicate into the subject, this definition is nevertheless insufficient: because conversion is a certain argumentation from one proposition to another through the transposition of the extremes; and that conversion ought to be called good which is a good consequence, because in it it is impossible for the antecedent to be true and the consequent false; and bad, that in which this can be the case. It must therefore be defined thus: The conversion of a proposition is an argumentation in which, through the transposition of the predicate into the subject, we gather one proposition from another: as if we say thus, No man is an animal; therefore no animal is a man. Moreover, the transposition of the extremes in conversion ought to be made in such a way that not only the terms are not varied, but neither their signification, nor their supposition, nor their distribution.

Second Note.

10

Second, it should be noted that conversion is twofold: one, which takes place through the simple transposition of the extremes; the other, which takes place through their contraposition. And the first is sufficiently manifest of itself. The second takes place through the transposition of the extremes indeed, but with two infinitizing negations added to them; and this conversion has no use except in affirmative propositions, because negations cannot be added on top of other negations without great confusion. The universal affirmative, therefore, can be converted into itself by contraposition in this way: Every man is an animal; therefore every non-animal is a non-man. And also the particular affirmative, as: Some man is an animal; therefore some non-animal is a non-man. But Aristotle made no mention of this conversion, because it is not properly conversion: for since negations are added to the extremes, they do not seem to remain the same but to be varied; which, however, we said is necessary for true conversion. Whence it is not
