## CHAPTER II

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

We think, moreover, that we know each thing simply, and not in the sophistical manner, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

n the preceding chapter Aristotle taught that science exists, and is acquired 1

I        anew through demonstration, from preexisting cognition of the principles. In this

second chapter, however, he intends to teach what science is and what demonstration is. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he hands down one definition of science and a twofold one of demonstration. In the second he defines principle, and divides it by a twofold division. And in the third he teaches and proves that the principles, or premises, are better known than the conclusion.

He defines to know, that is, science in the concrete, in many words, from which these few are to be taken, by which a brief definition is assigned: To know is to cognize the cause of the thing, and that it is the cause of that, and that it cannot be otherwise. By which Aristotle defines only the most perfect science, which he calls science Propter quid (for he promises to treat of science Quia, which is less perfect, in ch. 10 of this book), for having which he affirms that a threefold condition is required. The first is that we cognize the cause of the conclusion. The second, that we cognize such a cause to be the cause not only according to our cognition but also according to the thing: for when we prove that man is rational because he is risible, risible is prior in our intellect, and therefore it is the cause of cognizing rational, but it is not the cause of its being; rather it is its effect. And therefore we do not have science Propter quid of rational, but only Quia. The third condition is that we cognize it to be not only a cause of being, but a necessary cause, so that, it being posited, the effect necessarily follows: for this is signified by those words, And that it cannot be otherwise. Aristotle explains the whole definition most briefly, saying: To know is to understand through demonstration; because, if the demonstration is truly

Propter quid, those three conditions are found in the premises with respect to the conclusion.

2 Next he defines demonstration by a twofold definition, the first of which runs thus: Demonstration is a scientific syllogism, or a syllogism producing knowledge; and it is a final definition, because the end of demonstration is to generate science; and this science generated through demonstration is the assent to its conclusion, generated from the premises.

[p. 623]

3 The second definition is material. For just as from the end for the sake of which a house is made, namely that it may defend us from rains and other injuries of the weather, we gather of what material parts it ought to consist, namely of timbers, stones, and other parts disposed in such a way: so Aristotle, from the end of demonstration, gathers of what parts, disposed and ordered, demonstration ought to consist, as if arguing thus: Demonstration is ordered to generating science as to its end; therefore it ought to be such that it proceeds from things true, first, immediate, better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. He proves the single parts of the definition; and first, that demonstration proceeds from things true, in this way: The object of science ought to have being; therefore what is not is not known; but the false is nothing; therefore there cannot be science of it. Therefore the conclusion of a demonstration, whose assent is science, must be true; therefore it ought to proceed from true premises as from a cause. The consequence is proved: because the false, since it is nothing, cannot be the cause of the true. That demonstration proceeds from first things he proves second: because unless the premises are principles evident per se formally, that is, such that, once the signification of the terms is cognized, the intellect at once assents to them, or at least virtually, if he who makes the demonstration knows how to reduce them to principles known per se through other demonstrations, he will not have science of the conclusion, nor consequently a true demonstration, but only a Dialectical syllogism and an assent of opinion concerning the conclusion. He proves finally, third, that it proceeds from things better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. Because to know is to cognize a thing through its cause; therefore the premises ought to be the true cause of the conclusion; but a cause is prior to and better known than its effect; therefore they ought to be prior and better known: not only as regards us, in which way that is prior which is better known to us, although according to nature it is posterior, as an effect is better known to us than the cause, and therefore prior as regards our cognition; but the premises ought to be prior to and better known than the conclusion from the nature of the thing, which they will be if according to the thing they are its causes, as has been explained.

4 In the second part of ch. 2: Because he had said that demonstration ought to proceed from first things, that is, from premises which are indemonstrable principles, he defines indemonstrable principle in this way: A principle is an immediate proposition of demonstration. And he explains what it is to be a proposition of demonstration, or demonstrative, and what it is to be immediate. A proposition, he says, is one part of an enunciation, stating one thing. For an enunciation is divided into affirmative and negative. Therefore to be a proposition

of demonstration is the same as to be an affirmative or negative enunciation which is posited in the demonstration as a premise, for inferring the conclusion; and therefore it ought to be true and necessary, so that it may be distinguished from a Dialectical proposition, which is only probable and therefore can be false. But an immediate proposition is one to which there is no other prior; that is, which does not have another through which it could be demonstrated, but to which the intellect assents from the cognition of the terms alone.

5 Next he divides principle into two members, namely into dignity and position. A dignity, or ἀξίωμα, is an immediate and indemonstrable proposition so universal and manifest that its truth is plain to all; and perhaps it is called a dignity for this reason, because it is worthy that all should assent to it. And for this cause also Aristotle says that all who wish to acquire any science ought to cognize the dignities before they approach to learning it. Such are: Anything whatever is or is not; The whole is greater than its part; and the like. But a position, or θέσις, is a proposition known per se and indemonstrable, but neither so universal as an ἀξίωμα, nor one whose truth is manifest to all; and therefore it is not necessary that he who begins to learn some science should cognize it beforehand, but he can then receive it by himself or from a master. And such are all the principles of the particular sciences, such as definitions. And there is another difference between dignity and position: that dignities scarcely or never enter a demonstration, but are presupposed by all sciences, whereas positions are the premises of a demonstration; and therefore they are called positions, because they are posited in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion.

He divides position again into that which contains the true or the false; and this is the proposition which they call a supposition, because it is posited under such a disposition in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion. And into that which contains neither the true nor the false, but from which a supposition can be made; and he says it is a definition: as rational animal is a principle which is called a definition, from which another principle can be made which is a supposition: as if we say, Man is a rational animal, it is a supposition, because it contains the true or the false.

6 In the third part he teaches that the principles, or premises of a demonstration, ought to be more evident and more certain than the conclusion of the same demonstration. Which he proves from that common axiom: That on account of which each thing is such is itself more so. As, if I love Peter on account of John, I love John more than Peter. ## QUESTION I

Whether the second definition of demonstration is good.

This question is proposed not so much to discuss the difficulty of the matter as to elucidate Aristotle’s definition and to show that it is exact. In order that this may be done, we shall propose two arguments against it, from the solution of which this will become manifest. The first is: Because a definition ought to be given through genus and difference, or through something which is posited in place of the genus or difference; but nothing is posited for the genus in this definition, as its words show, by which it is distinguished from other argumentations, while in none of them does it agree with them; therefore it altogether lacks a genus, and therefore it is not entire or complete.

9 The second: Because a good definition ought not to have even one superfluous word; but this one has many such; therefore it is not good. The minor is proved: because for demonstration to proceed from first things and from prior things is the same, for first and prior signify altogether the same thing; therefore one of them is redundant. Moreover, a cause is prior to and better known than its effect; therefore he who says that demonstration proceeds from causes says that it ought to proceed from things prior and better known; it would therefore suffice to posit in the definition the phrase from causes, and thus the two others, namely from things prior and better known, seem superfluous and make the whole definition faulty. And finally, that it proceeds from first things and from immediate or indemonstrable things is the same, since it is the same for the principles of a demonstration to be first and to be immediate or indemonstrable; therefore some one of these words is superfluous.

Nevertheless I prove that this definition is good thus: A definition is good through which the nature of the definitum is sufficiently explained and distinguished from the rest; but this definition of demonstration performs these two things, explaining the nature of demonstration and distinguishing it from the other argumentations; therefore it is to be judged exact. The minor is proved: because this definition explains the parts of which demonstration ought to consist, namely true and necessary premises, which are true and per se causes of the conclusion, and which are so disposed that the conclusion is evidently inferred from them. And a demonstration constituted of these is essentially distinguished from the other species of argumentation, with which it agrees in the remote genus of argumentation, and with the dialectical syllogism in the genus

Vnum tamen eft notandum : quòddum diciturde- monftrationem procedere ex cauflis:percauſas,non ſolùm in- telliguntur illæ , ex quibus realiter procediteffectus,fed qux

proximate genus of syllogism. Which genus is without doubt understood by Aristotle, nor was it necessary to posit it expressly in the definition: because in the books of the Prior Analytics, immediately preceding, he had defined the syllogism; and in the first definition of the same demonstration, handed down in the present chapter, he expressly posited the same syllogism as the genus, saying: Demonstration is a scientific syllogism, or one producing knowledge. Wherefore the second definition ought to be assigned in these words: Demonstration is a syllogism proceeding from things true, first, immediate, better known, and prior, and causes of the conclusion: so that through syllogism it agrees in the immediate genus with the dialectical syllogism; and through the same particle the other argumentations are judged separated from it, and also the sophistical syllogism, which, since it sins in form, is not a syllogism simply but in a certain respect, and therefore does not agree with demonstration in syllogism as in a genus, but only analogically; and for that reason it is thus judged separated. But by the other particles of the definition demonstration is distinguished from the Dialectical syllogism, which proceeds from very different things, as will be said in the Topics. And from these things the definition of demonstration remains explained, and the first argument solved.

9 To the second: The minor is to be denied, namely that in this definition some word is superfluous: because, although certain of them signify the same thing, yet each signifies a different ratio of the same thing, which is enough for none to be superfluous. Thus, for the principles to be first and to be immediate or indemonstrable denote different rationes of the principles. For a principle is called first in order to the conclusion, which is not first, but derived from the first; but immediate or indemonstrable with respect to another prior middle through which it could be demonstrated, which it lacks. The principles are also called first on account of their dignity, and prior on account of their causality. Finally, a cause has a twofold dignity with respect to its effect: both that it is prior by nature to it, and that it is better known; and although the one follows from the other, they are nevertheless distinguished in ratio. Wherefore there is no word in the definition which does not signify some ratio or dignity of the principles distinct from that which another signifies, which is enough for none to be superfluous. Indeed, it was necessary to posit all those words in the definition, so that all the rationes of the principles might be expressed, and the ratio and dignity of demonstration might be handed down more explicitly. One thing, however, is to be noted: that when demonstration is said to proceed from causes, by causes are understood not only those from which the effect really proceeds, but those which

rationes are prior to others. For of being its properties or attributes are demonstrated in Metaphysics, as that it is one, true, and good; and of God we demonstrate that he is eternal because he is immutable, and this through true demonstrations; and yet there cannot be true causality between the one and the other, since there is not even a distinction from the nature of the thing; but the priority of reason which our intellect posits between them suffices for a true demonstration.

QUESTION II. In how many ways a proposition is known per se, and whether every immediate proposition is to be called known per se.

Concerning the definition and division of a proposition known per se, St.

Thomas and Soto do not seem to think in the same way, and consequently neither do the followers of each. For St. Thomas, On Truth q. 10, a. 12, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 10 and 11, and 1 p., q. 2, a. 1, thus defines a proposition known per se: A proposition known per se is one whose predicate is included in the intrinsic ratio of the subject: as Man is an animal. Next he first divides the proposition known per se into that which is known per se according to its own nature, and not as regards us; and into that which is known per se also as regards us.

10 Known per se by its nature and not as regards us is that whose predicate is truly intrinsic with respect to the subject, but we are ignorant of it; and such will be that in which a definition unknown to us is predicated of its definitum. But known per se by its nature and as regards us will be that whose predicate is truly intrinsic to the subject and is cognized by us: as Man is a rational animal.

Second, he divides the proposition known per se by its nature and as regards us into one whose terms are plain to all. And such are the most universal principles, as Anything whatever is or is not, and The whole is greater than its part. And into another whose terms are not manifest to all, but only to the wise; and such is this: Spiritual things are not in place circumscriptively. This definition of a proposition known per se, together with each division, is embraced by almost all: Richard of Middleton, In 1, d. 3, a. 1, q. 2; Durandus, ibid., q. 5; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 10; Capreolus, In 1, d. 2, a. 1 and 2; Cajetan, 1 p., q. 2, a. 1, and on the present chapter; Soto, on the present chapter, q. 2, ad 9; and many others.

The second opinion, that of Scotus, is opposed, because neither does the definition please him nor does he accept the divisions, but he himself assigns another definition, prolix enough and obscure, in these words: A proposition known per se is one which, from its proper terms, which are something of it, as they are of it,

And he says that every proposition known per se is such, and that therefore it is not to be divided by the divisions handed down by St. Thomas.

11 From which definition he gathers that the proposition in which the first attribute is predicated of the definition, as A rational animal is capable of learning, is distinct from that in which it is predicated of the definitum, as Man is capable of learning; which he proves by many arguments, thinking perhaps that the contrary of this is the view of St. Thomas. But these arguments are to be omitted, because St. Thomas does not deny it, as we shall see. Scotus is followed by Auriol and Gregory (of Rimini), whom Capreolus cites, In 1, d. 2, q. 2, a. 2, who argue thus against the definition of St. Thomas.

First: There are many propositions known per se in the Mathematical sciences in which the predicate is not of the intrinsic ratio of the subject: as The whole is greater than its part; and From any point to any point we can draw a line. And in natural Philosophy, That motion exists, and also That nature exists; indeed, this too is known per se: A rational animal is capable of learning; Snow is white; The raven is black. And on the other side, there are others in which the predicate is of the intrinsic ratio of the subject, as Man is a substance, An animal is a body; and yet they are not immediate, because between the predicate and the subject other middle predicates are given, as is plain. Therefore the definition of St. Thomas is proved insufficient on both sides.

12 Second, they argue against the division: because for a proposition to be known per se does not consist in its terms being cognized by us, but only in its having evident truth of itself; and much less does it consist in its terms being cognized by the wise alone or by all, but only in their being cognizable per se. Therefore the divisions into known per se by its nature and as regards us, and into known per se to the wise or to the unwise, are outside the ratio of a proposition known per se, and therefore ought not to be admitted.

Third: Because a proposition known per se is that which is such from its proper concepts, formed by any intellect whatever; therefore every proposition known per se will also be known per se to us; and therefore it is badly divided into known per se by its nature and as regards us. They prove the antecedent: because either we form its proper concepts or other, different ones; if its proper ones, it will be known per se to us; if different ones, it will not be the same proposition, but another, different one; therefore a proposition known per se of itself will be known per se to any intellect whatever: none

therefore will be given known per se by its nature which is not also known per se as regards us.

On this matter our view is that a proposition known per se is to be defined and divided as Aristotle defined and divided it in the present chapter; and that the view of St. Thomas, which is the common one, is more conformable to his definition and divisions than the view of Scotus.

13 Aristotle’s words run thus: A principle of demonstration is an immediate proposition; and an immediate one is that to which there is no other prior. By which, by a principle of demonstration he understands a proposition known per se: for this alone can be called a principle; for that which is mediate is called not a principle but a conclusion. Thus, therefore, the proposition known per se is to be defined according to Aristotle, so that the definition may be brief, clear, and universal: A proposition known per se is one between whose predicate and subject no middle is given through which it could be demonstrated a priori. In which definition only the proposition known per se of demonstration, or demonstrative, that is, necessary, is defined, which Aristotle openly signified, saying: A principle of demonstration is an immediate proposition; which we say in order to exclude certain propositions which, since they are truly accidental and contingent and not demonstrative, are called by some known per se and immediate: as Snow is white, The surface is colored, and the like.

14 But from the definition so understood it is gathered, first, that a proposition known per se and an immediate and indemonstrable one are altogether convertible: because of each it is true that it has no middle through which it could be demonstrated a priori. And we say a priori because nothing prevents a proposition from being known per se and being demonstrated through an effect: as Man is a rational animal is demonstrated through this, Man is risible, and nevertheless it is known per se, because it is not demonstrated a priori but a posteriori. And so much for the definition of a proposition known per se.

Aristotle divided it by four divisions, of which he posited three in the present chapter, but the fourth in the following chapter. The first is into dignity and position. He called a dignity the most universal one, which scarcely enters a science or demonstration, but is as it were the foundation of many or of all sciences and demonstrations: as Anything whatever is or is not; The whole is greater than its part; which he therefore said must necessarily be cognized by those who begin to learn some science. But a position is a proposition known per se, yet not universal, nor even one that he who wishes to learn some science ought to cognize, but particular and proper to some science, from which demonstrations are made in it, and which is handed down in that very science. And such

are all definitions and all the proper principles of the particular sciences. And this division is the same as the second, which St. Thomas hands down, saying that one proposition known per se is that whose terms are plain to all: such are the most universal ones, which Aristotle called dignities. And another, whose terms are manifest not to all but only to the wise; and these are the ones which Aristotle calls positions.

By the second division he divided it into position and supposition, about which the following question will be concerned.

51 The third division he insinuated clearly enough when he divided things better known into those which are better known by nature and as regards us. For from this division it follows that one thing known per se is so by its nature and not as regards us, and another by its nature and as regards us; and consequently that the proposition known per se is divided by Aristotle in the same ways. And this is proved by this argument: Every definition constitutes a proposition known per se with its definitum; but many definitions are unknown to us; therefore the propositions which they can constitute with their definita will be known per se by their nature, yet not as regards us; indeed, they could be demonstrated, as regards us, a posteriori, through some effect.

Finally, he posited the fourth division in the following chapter: into known per se positively, whose positive predicate belongs to the subject without a demonstrative middle, and into known per se negatively, whose negative predicate belongs to the subject without a middle. Such are propositions in which one predicate is denied of another: as Substance is not quantity. Not, however, those in which a particular genus of one category, or one species, is denied of another, or of the supreme genus of another category: as Whiteness is not quantity, A line is not color, A habit is not number; because these can be demonstrated through the supreme genus of the other category, denied: as Whiteness is not quantity, because it is quality, and quality is not quantity; and A line is not color, because it is not quality. And one species or one genus is denied of another: as Substance is not quantity and Man is not a horse. For these negations are essential, and therefore constitute necessary, demonstrative, and per se known propositions. Aristotle’s words are: Just as certain principles are indemonstrable, that this is that, and that this is in that, so also that this will not be that, nor that this is in that; wherefore some will be principles that something is, and others that something is not.

But that the two divisions assigned by St. Thomas are consonant with the first and third divisions designated by Aristotle, or

rather, that they are the same, we have already proved. It remains, therefore, to show that his definition is conformable to the definition of Aristotle, taken by us from his words.

Which can be proved thus: The definition of St. Thomas is: A proposition known per se is that whose predicate is included in the intrinsic ratio of the subject. But such a proposition does not have a middle through which it could be demonstrated a priori, as will be proved from the solutions of the arguments of Scotus and the others; therefore it is consonant with the definition of Aristotle. But the definition of Scotus we do not reject on the ground that it cannot be reduced to the same, but because it is prolix enough and obscure, as its words show.

For the solution of the first argument: The intrinsic predicate is to be distinguished by a twofold distinction. First, indeed, in recto or in obliquo. Next, according to being or according to causality. And in recto no part is an intrinsic predicate with respect to the whole, although according to being it is intrinsic to it; but in obliquo it is intrinsic; and in this way this proposition is known per se: The whole is greater than its part. Moreover, a per se and immediate effect is not intrinsic to its cause; but the order of causality between the proximate and per se cause and its effect is intrinsic; and consequently the effect itself is in a certain way an intrinsic predicate with respect to the cause, by reason of the same intrinsic order. And when St. Thomas defines a proposition known per se as one whose predicate is intrinsic to the subject, he understands that it ought to be intrinsic by any ratio whatever: that is, either according to being or according to the intrinsic order of proximate causality.

18 From these things the reply is made to the argument, by denying the antecedent, namely that there is any proposition known per se whose predicate is not intrinsic to the subject either according to being or according to the intrinsic order of proximate causality; in recto or in obliquo; according to itself or according to the intrinsic order of one to the other. And since the order of causality between the effect and the proximate and per se cause is intrinsic, it constitutes a proposition known per se when it is predicated of the cause, since it is a predicate intrinsic to the cause: if not by reason of itself, yet well by reason of the intrinsic order. And if not in recto, yet well in obliquo. But other, accidental predications, if in some way they are known per se, are not demonstrative propositions, because they are not necessary. St. Thomas, however, defines only the demonstrative proposition known per se; as of Aristotle too it is known that he defined this alone.

Finally, for the other essential and mediate propositions which the same argument adduces, another distinction is to be used,

namely that the middle is twofold, real or of reason, or formal and virtual. A real middle is said to be that which is distinct in reality from the predicate and the subject between which the middle is posited: as capable of wonder is a real middle between man and risible; and this is also called a formal middle. But a middle of reason is that which is distinguished from the subject and the predicate only by our reason; and it is called a virtual middle, because according to the thing or form it is not distinct from the extremes, but according to our intellect, which conceives several concepts of the same thing, contained, however, virtually and as it were fundamentally in the thing itself. And as far as pertains to demonstrative propositions, each middle constitutes a proposition simply mediate and simply demonstrable. This is proved from Aristotle, who grants that a definition is a middle of demonstration; but a definition can only be a middle of reason, and virtual.

Whence it follows that all propositions which can be demonstrated through the definition of the predicate or of the subject are simply mediate: such as are those in which the first attribute is predicated of the definitum, and also of the definition; because the former can be demonstrated through the definition of the subject, but the latter through the definition of the attribute; and also that in which one attribute is predicated of another, as What is capable of wonder is risible; and also those which are assumed in the argument. But they are commonly called immediate, because according to the thing they are such.

19 To the second: The antecedent is to be distinguished. For just as things are called better known or less known both by their nature and also in order to an intellect that cognizes imperfectly, so too is a proposition known per se; and although it is per accidens to the ratio of a proposition known per se, taken according to itself, that it is not known per se as regards us, nevertheless, taken in common, it is divided, as it were analogically, into a proposition known per se by its nature and as regards us.

To the third: The antecedent is to be denied, namely that a proposition known per se is that which is such from its proper concepts formed by any intellect whatever; rather it is that between whose predicate and subject no middle is given through which it is demonstrable a priori. And because this is not always known to us of any proposition whatever, therefore not every proposition known per se by its nature is known per se as regards us. Of such a proposition, however, we do not form proper distinct concepts, but confused ones; and therefore it is not another but the same; yet not known per se to us, because we do not cognize the immediacy of the predicate and the subject.

## QUESTION III

Whether a bare definition is a principle which is called a position.

20

A       definition can be considered in two ways. First, according to the precise ra‐

tio of definition, as it explains the nature of the definitum: as rational animal. Second, as the definition is at the same time joined in a proposition: as when we say, Man is a rational animal. And in the first way it is taken bare, that is, without the definitum; and of it so taken we ask whether it is a principle of demonstration which is called a position. And on the one side Aristotle supplied the reason for doubting, who divided position into that which is a proposition containing the true or the false, and into another which does not contain the true or the false; such as is the definition, taken barely, that is, and not with the definitum: because when it is joined to the definitum it already contains the true or the false, since it makes a proposition with it.

From which the affirmative part is evidently inferred, namely that a bare definition is a principle which is called a position.

21 But the opposite part, that it cannot be a position, seems to be proved evidently by this argument from the superior to the inferior negatively:

Because Aristotle divided principle into dignity and position, and again position into that which contains the true or the false, and into that which says neither of these, such as is the definition. From this, therefore, such an argument is taken: Principle is something superior in ratio to dignity and position, since it is divided into these special principles; therefore such a consequence from the superior to the inferior negatively is evident: A definition is not a principle; therefore it is not a position. The antecedent is proved from the definition of principle handed down by the same Aristotle: A principle, he says, is an immediate proposition; but a bare definition is not a proposition; therefore neither an immediate proposition; and consequently it is not a principle.

Many solutions are applied to this difficulty, which I deliberately pass over, because no one now cares for them. I shall bring forward only the solution of St. Thomas in the Commentary on this chapter, which almost all the moderns follow, and which seems to me necessarily to be admitted: that position is twofold, formal and virtual. The formal is a proposition. But the virtual is the definition, because from it can proximately be made a proposition which is a formal supposition. Aristotle therefore called the definition a position, not because it is a formal position, but because it is a virtual one. And in this way also it is a principle and an immediate proposition.

22 But against this solution there is an argument: Because, if this suffices in order that

the definition be called a position, the definitum too could be called a position.

The consequence is proved: because, just as from the definition joined to the definitum a proposition can proximately be made which is a formal position, so in the same way from the definitum joined to the definition. But the definitum cannot in any way be called a position; otherwise the denomination of the whole could be attributed to any part whatever; therefore neither can the definition be called a position on account of that virtual ratio. The reply is made by denying the consequence: because there is a special ratio in the definition, so that it is called a virtual position, which is not in the definitum, nor in the others. For the definition, of its proper nature, is the ordered middle through which attributes are demonstrated of the subject in a science; whence it is per se and proximately ordered to constituting a necessary and per se known proposition, which it cannot constitute except with the definitum. It is also posited per se in a science as the foundation of all its truths; and this too is a special ratio on account of which it ought to be called a position. And considering these special rationes, which are not found in the definitum, Aristotle deservedly called it a principle and a position. For since the definitum is not a middle ordered to demonstrating attributes, nor is it per se ordered to constituting a proposition known per se rather than to constituting any other whatever, it is not posited as the proximate foundation of all the truths of the same science, but at most as a remote one. Therefore it cannot in any way be called a position.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the principles of demonstration are more true than the conclusion, and universally, whether one proposition can be truer than another.

23

The definition of truth which all accept is to be presupposed: Truth is the adequation of the intellect with the thing, or to the thing. It is called an adequation of the intellect because truth, at least complex truth (which they are accustomed to call formal), is found primarily and formally in the intellect and in the mental proposition through which it enunciates one thing of another; but in the vocal and written proposition it is found only as in a sign. When, therefore, the intellect enunciates through a mental proposition as the thing is in itself, it is called true; but when it enunciates otherwise than the thing is in itself, it is called false.

For, as Aristotle often repeats, from the fact that the thing is or is not, an enunciation is called true or false: as, if of Peter sitting it enunciates that he sits, it is true; but if that he stands, or does not sit,

[p. 635]

it will be false. Truth therefore consists in the adequation of the concept with the thing itself, or in the adequation of the thing, as represented through the concept, with itself as it is in itself. We ask, therefore, whether this complex truth admits of more and less in order to the premises and the conclusion: so that the intellect, when it assents to the premises, is more true than when it assents to the conclusion; and consequently the premises in the intellect, which are mental propositions, are more true than the conclusion, also in the mind, which is a mental proposition deduced from them; and consequently the same principles, as they are vocal or written propositions, are truer than the vocal or written conclusion. And universally, whether the intellect is more true through one mental proposition than through another, and the mental proposition itself is truer, and consequently the vocal and written one.

24 The first opinion denies that the premises are truer than the conclusion, and universally that one proposition is truer than another. So hold some among the moderns. They prove it from the intrinsic ratio of truth. For truth consists in the adequation of the concept with the thing itself represented, so that it is true when it represents the thing as it is in itself, but false when it represents it in another way. But adequation consists in an indivisible, so that a greater or lesser cannot be understood; therefore the truth of a proposition also consists in an indivisible, so that a greater or lesser cannot be understood in different propositions. The minor is proved: because adequation is a certain equality of the representing concept with the thing represented; but equality consists in an indivisible, so that it cannot be greater or lesser. Because if two bodies have equal magnitude, so that neither exceeds the other, then they are called equal; but if one exceeds the other by however small an excess, they will not be equal, but simply unequal. Therefore in the same way: either the concept represents the thing as it is in itself, or it exceeds or falls short by however small an excess. If it is in the first way, it will be true; if in the second, false. And consequently, if a proposition enunciates the thing as it is, it will be true; but if it exceeds or falls short, however little, it will be false. It cannot, therefore, be understood that one is more true than another; but by the very fact that it is thought of as less true, it will be false. For example: it will be no less true that Peter is white, if whiteness inheres in him, than that he is a man: because the one proposition is no less adequated to the thing signified than the other; just as, if two bodies are equal, it will not be possible to think of others more equal.

Others among the moderns hold the second opinion, affirming

that the principles are truer than the conclusion, and universally that one proposition is truer than another. This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 18, where he teaches that something is more true than something else, and likewise more false; which he proves thus: Because he who says that four are five does not lie equally with him who says that four are a thousand; therefore what the latter asserts is more false than what the former asserts; but the false is contrary to truth; therefore in the same way one proposition will be more true than another. The consequence is proved: because the ratio of contraries is the same. Moreover, in the present chapter he teaches expressly that the conclusion is true on account of the premises; therefore the premises will be more true, because that on account of which each thing is such is itself more so.

They prove it next by reason: Because it is denied by no one that the principles are more certain, more evident, and more necessary than the conclusion, since they are certain per se, evident per se, necessary per se, that is, without any middle, but such that the intellect assents to them once the signification of the terms alone is cognized; whereas the conclusion is not certain, evident, or necessary per se, but through another, that is, through the principles, by means of which the intellect assents to it. But what is more certain, more evident, and more necessary is more true; therefore in the same way it will be more true. And certainly, if one proposition were not truer than another, divine faith would not be more true than science, or than any other human cognition whatever. Whence neither would it be more true that God is three and one than that the wall in which whiteness inheres is white; which, however, is false, and against St. Thomas, 2.2, q. 4, a. 8, where he teaches that divine faith, of its proper nature, is more certain than any science of ours.

26 Our view holds the middle between these extremes, and is explained by this distinction: Truth can be considered in two ways. First, formally, on the part of its essence, which consists in the adequation of the intellect, through a concept or judgment, with the thing existing outside, represented through the same concept. Second, on the part of its foundation and its causes. The foundation is the entity and perfection of the things themselves with which it is concerned. For since the true is an attribute of being, the things that are more perfect according to entity are judged also more perfect according to truth. And the causes of truth can be necessity, infallibility, certitude, and evidence; also the weight, or moment, of the reasons by which it is proved.

27 We reply, therefore, with a twofold conclusion. The first: Truth, on the part of the formal and essential ratio of the adequation itself in which it consists, cannot be greater in one proposition than in another. The second: On the part of its foundation and its causes it can be greater; and

therefore one proposition, on this side, is more true than another. Each conclusion, with the distinction adduced, is expressly contained in the doctrine of St. Thomas, On the Virtues q. 2, a. 9, where he says thus: Since truth consists in the adequation of the intellect and the thing, if truth is considered according to the ratio of equality, which does not admit of more and less, then it does not happen that something is more and less true. But if the very being of the thing is considered, which is the ratio of truth, as is said in Metaph. 2, the disposition of things in being and in truth is the same; whence the things that are more beings are more true; and on account of this also in the demonstrative sciences the principles are believed more than the conclusions. And the argument of the first opinion proves our first conclusion; but the arguments of the second opinion prove the second; and therefore it is not necessary to reply to the former or to the latter.

29 It only remains to explain how one is to speak absolutely on this matter: whether it is to be said absolutely that the premises are truer than the conclusion, and one proposition truer than another, or it is to be denied absolutely. I reply: one is to speak in the same way as we speak of substance. Because just as substance does not have a gradual latitude, but its ratio consists in an indivisible, so truth does not have a gradual latitude, but its ratio consists in the indivisible of adequation. But in substances we do not say that one is more a substance than another; rather, we deny this absolutely with Aristotle; but we do say that one substance is better or more perfect than another, either according to a greater specific perfection or a greater individual one. In like manner one is to speak of truths, or true propositions; so that it is to be denied absolutely that one proposition is truer than another; but it is to be granted that it has a more perfect truth, either essentially or individually. And therefore it is to be said that the premises contain a more perfect specific truth than the conclusion, and one conclusion a more perfect individual truth than another, because it is nearer to the principles from which both are derived. And in the same way one is to speak of falsity. Although perfection is not well applied to falsity, which is nothing, yet one is to speak of it according to its nature in the same way as we speak of truth, though in distinct terms or modes of speaking. This particular ratio, however, is found in falsity: that, since it is as it were a recession from truth, besides those causes on account of which one truth is said to be more perfect than another, and one proposition to contain a more perfect truth than another, one falsity is also said to be greater or more enormous than another, and one proposition to contain a greater falsity than another, because it recedes more from truth. In which sense Aristotle said, in the place cited above,

that he lies more who says that four are a thousand than another who should say that four are five: whose sense is that he utters a more enormous lie.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether it is always necessary that each premise of a demonstration be more certain than the conclusion.

30

The premises of a demonstration can be of a twofold kind. For either they are immediate and indemonstrable propositions, or they can be demonstrated. In order that this may be understood, it must be known that all the conclusions of a whole science are contained virtually in the principles of the same science, from which they proceed in their order, so that some are nearer to the principles than others.

Whence some are demonstrated through other, prior ones, which are, however, mediate and still demonstrable, until one arrives at some one derived immediately from the principles. And hence it is that not all demonstrations have immediate or indemonstrable premises, but many have at least one or the other which can be demonstrated. For example: from the essence of man proceed many attributes, such as capacity for learning, wonder, and risibility, in such an order that capacity for learning proceeds immediately, and by means of this, wonder, and by means of wonder, risibility; and according to this order they are demonstrated in the science of man: the first through the essence, the second through the first, and the third through the second. And therefore that demonstration through which the first attribute is demonstrated of the essence has each premise immediate and indemonstrable; but the others, in which the remaining ones are demonstrated, have one premise indeed indemonstrable, and another which can be demonstrated. The first attribute is demonstrated thus: Every rational animal is capable of learning; every man is a rational animal; therefore every man is capable of learning. Each premise of this demonstration is immediate: the major, in which the first attribute is predicated of the essence; the minor, in which the definition is predicated of the definitum. But in the following demonstration the second attribute is demonstrated through the first: Whatever is capable of learning is capable of wonder; every man is capable of learning; therefore every man is capable of wonder. Whose major is an immediate proposition, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another; but the minor can be demonstrated.

31 These things set out, the question presupposes one thing and asks

another. It presupposes, indeed, that the premises are more certain than the conclusion, taken thus in common. Which has been not only asserted by Aristotle but expressly proved: because the certitude of the conclusion is derived from the premises, and therefore they must be more certain. Which is especially true and necessary when the premises are immediate propositions: for they have certitude of themselves and from themselves, but the conclusion not of itself nor from itself, but derived from them; but what has certitude from itself is more certain than what has it from another; therefore immediate premises are more certain than the conclusion. The question, therefore, can only be about demonstrable premises: whether these too ought to be more certain than the conclusion; so that, when a demonstration has one immediate premise and another demonstrable one, it suffices that the conclusion be less certain than the former, and it can be equal in certitude with the other; or whether it is necessary that it also be less certain than the demonstrable premise.

32 And the first opinion holds that this is not necessary, but the conclusion can be equally certain with the demonstrable premise. So hold certain moderns. And they prove it by the testimony of Aristotle at the end of this chapter, where he did not say that it is necessary to believe all the principles more than the conclusion, but either all or some; he thinks, therefore, that the conclusion has equal certitude with some one of them.

They prove it next by reason: Because, if the premises ought always to be more certain than the conclusion, it is most of all on account of Aristotle’s reason, namely, that on account of which each thing is such is itself more so; but this does not prove except in equivocal causes, not in univocal ones; therefore it does not prove of all premises, but only of the immediate ones. The consequence is proved: because only the immediate premises are equivocal causes of the conclusion, because they differ in species from it; but the demonstrable premise, since it is a scientific assent, is of the same species as the conclusion, and therefore cannot be its equivocal cause, but will always be a univocal one. Whence it will not be necessary that it be more certain than the conclusion. And they prove the minor: because the effect of a univocal cause is of equal perfection with it, as is plain in the man generating and the one generated.

Second, it can be proved: Because the conclusions of the same science are derived from the same principles; therefore they have equal certitude derived from them; but it often happens that the conclusion and the demonstrable premise pertain to the same science, as the second demonstration adduced by us at the beginning of this question shows; therefore it will have equal certitude with it. Which can be proved more firmly in

Theological demonstrations, in which the conclusion proceeds from one premise pertaining to divine faith and from another pertaining to natural Philosophy, as is shown in this one: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible. Then, therefore, the conclusion pertains either to divine faith or to the habit of Theological science; and in either way it is more certain than the evident premise. Because divine faith is more certain than science; therefore that too which is derived from divine faith will be more certain. That conclusion, therefore, Christ is risible, in whatever way it is taken, is more certain than the major premise, namely Every man is risible. Wherefore the conclusion can have not only equal certitude with one of the premises, but sometimes greater.

Our view is: Each premise is always and necessarily more certain than the conclusion, so that in no case can it have equal certitude with either of them. And this is the more common view among the moderns.

It is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because in a demonstration propter quid (of which we are speaking) the demonstrable premise acts in virtue of the principles, from which it is derived more proximately than the conclusion, since the latter is derived by means of it; therefore it will have greater certitude. The consequence is evidently proved: because the more proximately an effect is derived from a cause, the more perfectly it participates its virtue, especially in comparison with another effect, by which it is participated only through some medium.

Second: Because the premises, whatever they may be, contain the union of the extremes with the middle; but the conclusion contains the union of the same extremes with each other, by means of their union with the middle, as the formal and total ratio on account of which they are united with each other; therefore the prior union, on which the second totally depends, is stronger, since it is more immediate. But for the union of the extremes with the middle to be stronger is for the premises to be more certain; therefore greater certitude comes to them from the nature of demonstration. Wherefore it is repugnant that the conclusion should have equal certitude with either of them.

To the testimony of Aristotle, St. Thomas replies, in his Commentary on that passage, that he did not say that all the principles are more certain than the conclusion, but at least some: because, although by the force of the demonstration each premise is always more certain, it nevertheless happens sometimes that the conclusion has another certitude, of experience, besides that which it participates from the premises, by reason of which it will have equal certitude with one of the premises: as when we cognize by the experience of the senses that the moon is now eclipsed; and therefore it is not less certain to us than that the earth is interposed between

it and the sun, through which it is demonstrated a priori. Yet this happens per accidens, and therefore it does not prevent each premise from always being, per se and by the force of the demonstration, more certain than the conclusion.

35 The first argument asks for an exposition of that universal axiom, That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more so: so that it may be clear in what sense it is true, and why it was adduced by Aristotle to prove that the premises must be more certain than the conclusion, and whether it is proved efficaciously from it. Many and various expositions of it are brought forward by different interpreters. They also require many and diverse conditions for its truth, which it would be tedious to report. We, then, say that three conditions are required for it to be true. Two of them Aristotle himself laid down in Metaph. 4, text 4, reporting this same axiom in these words: Each thing is most of all such, in preference to the others, to which, as cause, the same thing belongs in name and in ratio: thus fire is hottest, because it is the cause of heat to the others. By which he asserts, first, that the predicate must belong to several formally, and to one of them per se primarily, but to the others through participation in it, and not from elsewhere. Second, that it belongs to the same one first and to the others in name and in ratio, that is, univocally, and therefore essentially. The third condition St. Thomas laid down in 1 p., q. 87, a. 2, ad 3: that they be contained in the same order of causes, that is, in the same genus of efficient or final cause, or any other whatever; so that, if that to which the predicate belongs per se primarily is the end, the others are means ordered to it; and if it is the efficient, the others are as it were effects proceeding from it. When these three conditions concur, then, that axiom is true and necessary: That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more such. Its sense is: If something belongs to many, and to one of them per se primarily (which is therefore said to be most of all such), but to the others on account of it, it must belong more to the first than to the others. Nor can any case be given in which the opposite happens.

From this axiom Aristotle drew an efficacious argument to prove that the premises are more certain, more evident, more necessary, and contain a more perfect truth than the conclusion: because certitude, evidence, necessity, and truth belong formally both to them and to it, and all are contained in the same order of efficient cause; and these belong to the premises per se primarily, but to the conclusion, as the conclusion of a demonstration, only on account of the premises and not from elsewhere. Therefore it is evidently inferred that they belong to the premises more, or more perfectly.

To the form of the argument, too: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the aforesaid axiom holds true only in equivocal causes;

it is to be denied that it proves only of immediate premises and not of demonstrable ones. For although it proves first of the former, it consequently proves of the latter as well: because demonstrable premises are not the cause of the conclusion by their own power, or according to themselves, but by the power of the principles from which they are derived, and as derived from them. Of this there is an evident sign: if the one who constructs a demonstration does not know how to reduce them to the first principles through evident demonstrations, he will not produce a demonstration, nor will he have science of the conclusion, but he will produce a probable argument, generating opinion. Whence it follows that the first principles, virtually and as such, are the cause of the conclusion. And therefore truth, necessity, certitude, and evidence belong to them per se primarily, according to the same virtual ratio, but to the conclusion only on account of them; and for this reason more perfectly to them.

To the second: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the conclusion has equal certitude with the demonstrable premises because all are derived from the same principles; for they are not derived equally proximately. Therefore they do not participate equally in the certitude of the principles, but the premises more perfectly, because they are derived more properly.

37 The last point added in that second argument touches the demonstrations of the science of Theology, which proceed from one premise of divine faith and from another that is evident, and sometimes from both of faith, through an evident consequence. In these we say that Aristotle’s reasoning holds conclusively, namely that both premises are more certain than the conclusion. This is further proved from another common axiom received in the schools: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises. Therefore, if one or both are of divine faith, since divine faith is obscure, the conclusion cannot be evident; indeed, it cannot even have the same certitude as faith, but will be obscure as well. And if both premises are of divine faith, the conclusion will be obscure, and less certain than either premise. The reason for this is that the premises of faith do not concur in a Theological demonstration to infer the conclusion except by means of the demonstration; therefore their certitude is modified by the certitude of the consequence, which can be no other than natural. Whence they cannot produce a conclusion more perfect in certitude than is the perfection of natural certitude. But this is less than the certitude of divine faith; therefore the conclusion will have less certitude than the premises. And if one of the premises is certain with philosophical certitude, the conclusion will have less certitude. And if it should happen that one of the premises were only probable, the conclusion could not

Concedimus ergo : quòd fides diuina fit certiorſcientia : negamustamen, quodconclufio ab ca deriuata, fit etiam certiorſeientia:nam conclufio abea deri-uata, nonhabet maiorem certitudinem, quam fit certitudo confequentiæ , velillationis perquam modificanturpremiffæ adinferendamconclufionem in illationeverò,autfyllogifine, perfectius eſſehabentpræmiſſæ , quamconclufio in certitudi-ne, euidentia,neceffitate, ac veritate,vt probauimus, &ideo, impoſſibile eſt, conclufionem eflexqualem inhis , cumaltera præmiffarum. be certain, but only probable. All these things are proved by those two reasons by which it was proved that the premises must be more perfect than the conclusion in truth, in certitude, necessity, and evidence, and in all other respects. From which this same axiom was deduced: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises; whose sense is that it can have no perfection equal to the premises, but whatever imperfection is in them must be manifested in the conclusion.

38 From these things I infer that the conclusion of a Theological demonstration does not pertain to the habit of divine faith, as some moderns have held, but to the habit of the science of Theology. This I prove by the following reason: The habit of divine faith rests only on testimony, or divine revelation, and rests on it immediately, not on discourse or reasoning or demonstration; but the conclusion of a Theological demonstration rests immediately on discourse or demonstration, through which it is deduced from the premises, and not immediately on testimony or revelation; therefore it does not pertain to the habit of divine faith, but to that of the science of Theology. The minor, though certain enough of itself, I prove: because, if both premises of a syllogism are of divine faith, or one is evident with natural evidence, and the syllogism is only probable, it is certain that the conclusion is only probable, that is, neither science nor divine faith, but opinion; therefore it is not caused by the premises according to themselves, but as modified by the certitude of the demonstration; on this, then, the conclusion rests proximately, and not on testimony or divine revelation.

39 And from these things the reply to the argument is given: the conclusion of a Theological demonstration pertains neither to divine faith nor to natural science, but to the science of Theology, imperfect and obscure; whence it comes about that it is more imperfect and less certain than either premise. We grant, therefore, that divine faith is more certain than science; but we deny that the conclusion derived from it is also more certain than science. For the conclusion derived from it has no greater certitude than is the certitude of the consequence or illation by which the premises are modified for inferring the conclusion; and in the illation or syllogism the premises have being more perfectly than the conclusion in certitude, evidence, necessity, and truth, as we have proved; and therefore it is impossible for the conclusion to be equal in these respects with either of the premises.

C H A P T E R I V.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

But since it is impossible for that of which there is science simply to be otherwise, what is knowable will surely be necessary, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

ristotle’s intent in the present chapter is to teach what kind of 1

A           propositions demonstration ought to be composed of. It is divid‐

ed into two parts. In the first he proposes this universal conclusion, that science, which is generated through demonstration, is of necessary things; and from it he gathers that demonstration must proceed from, or be composed of, necessary propositions. In the second part he lays down three conditions which propositions must have, in order to be necessary in such a way that demonstration can be composed of them. The conclusion he proposes is: Science, which is the conclusion of demonstration, must be of necessary things.

This he proves thus: We know the conclusion of demonstration from principles, which are immediate propositions; therefore it cannot be otherwise; but what cannot be otherwise is necessary; therefore the conclusion of demonstration is necessary. The first consequence is proved, for the rest are plain of themselves. To know scientifically is to cognize a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of it, and that it cannot be otherwise; therefore not only science, but that which is known, namely the object with which it is concerned, cannot be otherwise. And this is to be necessary, since the necessary is defined thus: that which cannot be otherwise.

From this he infers that demonstration must be composed of, or proceed from, necessary propositions. This can be proved thus: The conclusion of demonstration, which is science, is necessary and of necessary things, and proceeds from the premises as from causes; therefore the premises of which demonstration is composed must be not only true but necessary. The consequence is proved: because, although it happens that a true conclusion is gathered from false premises, and a necessary one from non-necessary premises, yet this comes about not as from causes, but by virtue of the syllogistic disposition; otherwise the effect would be nobler than its cause, which is impossible.

2 In the second part he proposes three conditions which propositions must have, in order to be necessary in such a way that demonstration can be composed of them. The first of these is that they be said of every. That is, that

the predicate in them be said of anything whatever contained under the subject, and for any time whatever. For want of the first, this proposition is not said of every: Every man is disputing, because there are many of whom the predicate is not verified. For want of the second, neither is this one said of every: Every man is awake, because, although the predicate is said of anything whatever contained under the subject, yet not for any time whatever, but for a certain fixed and determinate time. But this one, Every man is colored, is said of every, because it has both, as is plain of itself.

The second condition is: That the propositions be per se; therefore, in order to explain it, he divides per se into four modes. The first mode is per se when the predicate belongs to the essence of the subject, because it is either its definition or a part of its definition: whence all these propositions are in the first mode per se: Man is an animal; Man is rational; Man is a rational animal.

The second mode is when, conversely, the subject pertains to the definition of the predicate, as Man is capable of wonder, Man is risible.

3 The third mode is not of predicating but of being; and that is said to be per se in this mode which subsists per se and does not inhere in another as an accident: and this is the mode proper to the category of substance. The fourth mode is per se of causing, when an effect is predicated of its cause per se. That effect is said to be per se which follows from the proper power of the cause, and not from elsewhere, that is, not by chance or fortune: for chance and fortuitous effects, which do not follow from the power of the cause but from some chance concurrence, or per accidens, are not called effects per se but per accidens. Whence this proposition, The one digging the earth found a treasure, is not per se. But these are per se in this fourth mode: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds. Of these four modes per se, then, the first two are per se of predicating, the third per se of being, the fourth per se of causing; and in order that propositions be apt for demonstration, they must be per se in the first, second, or fourth mode.

The third condition, or term, is that it be predicated universally, which Aristotle defines thus: But I call universal that which is both said of every, and per se, and according as it is itself. This definition contains a threefold condition which a proposition must have in order that in it the predicate be said universally of the subject. The first is that it be said of every; and for want of this condition the predicate is not said universally in this one, Man is awake, because it is not said of every. For want of the second condition, neither is the predicate said universally of the subject in this one, Man is colored, because it is not said per se. For want of the third as well, it is not said in

this one universally: Man is sensible, because sensible does not belong to man according as he is himself, that is, inasmuch as he is man, but inasmuch as he is an animal. For a predicate’s belonging to a subject according as it is itself seems to be the same as belonging to it inasmuch as it is such, that is, not according to a common ratio, but according to its proper one.

## QUESTION I

Whether demonstration must proceed from necessary things.

I     shall propose three arguments by which it seems to be proved that not

every demonstration proceeds from necessary things. Let the first be: This is a true demonstration propter quid: Whenever the earth is interposed between the sun and the moon, an eclipse also follows; but when these two heavenly bodies arrive at such a point, the earth is interposed between them; therefore an eclipse follows. But the minor is not necessary but contingent: because whether they arrive at such a point or not is altogether accidental to their nature, since it can be present to them and absent from them without their corruption; therefore not every demonstration consists of necessary propositions.

Second, because this too is a true and proper demonstration: Everything white is disgregative of sight; but a body having whiteness is white; therefore it is disgregative of sight. And yet the minor is not necessary but contingent: because it is contingent that a body have whiteness and that it be white; whence neither is the conclusion necessary, because, just as it is not necessary that a body be white, so neither is it necessary that, since it is white, it be also disgregative of sight; therefore not every demonstration proceeds from necessary things.

Third, because the necessary is that which cannot be otherwise; but in natural and moral Philosophy there are many demonstrative propositions, and many demonstrated conclusions too, which can be otherwise, and sometimes are otherwise: as that there will be rains in winter, and heat will prevail in summer; therefore not all demonstrations must proceed from necessary things.

Nevertheless Aristotle’s view is universally true and to be held, that no demonstration can proceed from contingent or non-necessary propositions. This is evidently proved by the following reason, deduced from his doctrine: The conclusion of any demonstration whatever is science; but science is had through a necessary cause, as is clear from its definition, which is this: To know

scientifically is to cognize a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of it, and that it cannot be otherwise, but that when it is posited the effect follows; therefore it must proceed from necessary things. The consequence is proved: because the premises from which it proceeds are the per se and necessary cause of the conclusion; therefore they must be necessary.

To the first argument the reply is made in different ways. For Paul of Venice, on the present chapter, replies that it is not demonstrated that the moon is eclipsed in act, but in potency or aptitude; that is, it is not demonstrated that it is eclipsed, but that it is eclipsable. And although to be eclipsed in act is not necessary, yet to be eclipsable is necessary; and by like reasoning, although it is not necessary that the moon itself and the sun arrive at such a point, yet that they can arrive there is necessary. Whence the propositions of that demonstration, taken thus, are necessary. This solution, however, is false, for two reasons.

First, because Astrologers demonstrate not only that the moon is eclipsable, but that it is to be eclipsed on such a day, at such an hour, and at such a point; therefore the propositions of that demonstration must be taken according to act. Second, because a per se cause and a per se effect, not only according to aptitude but also according to act, constitute a proposition per se in the fourth mode; therefore according to act they constitute a necessary proposition. The consequence is proved: because every proposition per se is necessary according to Aristotle and according to all.

6 Therefore there is a second solution, of other moderns: that that demonstration does not proceed concerning this moon and this sun as singulars, but according to their common and specific, or generic, ratio, which is certainly common to many possibles: for several suns, and several moons too, can be made by God. Although, then, it is contingent that this Sun and this Moon arrive at such a point, yet that this belongs to the Sun and the Moon as such is not contingent but necessary. But this solution too either says nothing or is no less false than the preceding one. This I prove thus: because to arrive at such a point and to be eclipsed are taken either according to act or according to potency. If according to act, by the very fact that they are accidental and contingent predicates with respect to these individuals, they are evidently proved to be accidental with respect to the species: for if whiteness inheres contingently in Peter, it evidently follows that it inheres contingently in man and in animal; therefore, if those predicates inhere contingently in this sun and this moon, they must also belong contingently to the sun and the moon taken under the common or specific ratio. And moreover, an effect per se is predicated per se and necessarily of its cause not only in common but also in the singular

and taken in act, as these propositions show: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First: that demonstration proceeds per se primarily concerning the sun and the moon according to their common ratio, or rather concerning that common and specific ratio itself; nevertheless also concerning this sun and this moon, by application. Just as an attribute demonstrated of a species can be applied to this or that individual: and if we demonstrate of man that he is risible, we can apply the same demonstration to Peter, taken for the minor extreme, and say: Every rational animal is risible; Peter is a rational animal; therefore Peter is risible. Thus, then, that the sun and the moon arrive at such a point, and that the latter is eclipsed through the interposition of the earth, is demonstrated primarily of their common ratio, but by application of these singulars.

7 Second, we say that the eclipse is demonstrated not according to potency but according to act, through the actual interposition of the earth; and nevertheless that both propositions are per se: not indeed in the first or second mode, but in the fourth. And therefore, just as they are per se with the perseity of causality, so too they are necessary with the necessity of causality. For a predicate can be compared to a subject, or be predicated of it and belong to it, in two ways: either according to the ratio of being, or of inhering, or according to the ratio of causing. And according to the first ratio they are taken in propositions of the first and second mode per se; but according to the second, in propositions of the fourth mode: because the first and second modes are modes per se of predicating, the third per se of being, and the fourth per se of causing, as Aristotle teaches. Whence it is understood that, if propositions of the fourth mode are taken in the ratio of predicating, hardly any will be per se, but all will be per accidens, as is plain in these: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds. For to build in act is plainly accidental to the builder, and is predicated of him with the predication of the fifth predicable, as is clear; but in the ratio of causing they are per se, because an effect per se, even according to act, is predicated per se of its cause actually causing, with the perseity of causing.

8 To the form of the argument, then: the minor is to be distinguished. For that the sun and the moon arrive at such a point, so that the interposition of the earth follows, belongs to them per se with the perseity of causing; and in the same way the eclipse follows per se from the interposition: for it is impossible for the thing to be otherwise, so that it should follow from the motion of these heavenly bodies that they do not arrive at such a point, and that, when they have arrived, an eclipse of the moon does not occur. If, then, in the ratio

of causing they are taken, the propositions are necessary; and so they are taken here. But if in the ratio of being or of predicating, they are not necessary, but accidental and contingent. But they are not taken in this way. For the solution of the other arguments, it should be noted that a necessary proposition is one which enunciates a necessary thing, that is, one which cannot be otherwise. But a thing happens to be necessary in two ways: simply, or on a supposition. Necessary simply is that which is such from its own nature, so that it cannot not be: as that man is an animal, or rational. Necessary on a supposition is that which by its own nature can not be, or not be such: as that a body disgregates sight is not necessary according to the nature of the body, but contingent; but on the supposition that it is white, it is necessary. Moreover, the necessary simply is in turn threefold.

The first, that which can in no way not be, but it implies a contradiction that it not be: as that man is an animal, or rational. The second, that which cannot not be by the natural power of causes, but can well not be by the supernatural power of God: as that fire is hot, or man is risible. For by the supernatural power of God heat can be separated from fire, and risibility from man. The third, that which cannot not be by the natural power of causes for the most part, although rarely it can, by the same power, not be.

9 And according to these four modes of the necessary, four other modes of necessary propositions are to be distinguished; and it must be said that demonstration must proceed from necessary propositions in one mode or another. But it will be more perfect if it proceeds from propositions necessary simply than if it proceeds only from propositions necessary on a supposition; and most perfect if it proceeds from things necessary simply according to the first mode; less perfect if according to the second; but most imperfect if according to the third. And therefore the demonstrations of natural and moral Philosophy, which consist of many propositions that are true only for the most part, are reckoned most imperfect, and these sciences themselves hold the lowest place of certitude among all.

From these things, then, the second and third arguments are solved. For although those demonstrations do not proceed from things necessary simply, yet they proceed from things such on a supposition, like the one adduced in the second argument; or, if from things necessary simply, yet not always occurring, but only for the most part. And it suffices to proceed from necessary things in some one of these modes. And that it suffices to proceed from necessary things that occur for the most part, Aristotle expressly taught in ch. 24 of this first
