book, and all accept this: because all accept both Philosophies as true science, and rightly so; because what occurs for the most part is reckoned necessary, with natural or moral necessity, and therefore it can be the object of science. Nor is there any danger of erring in such a mode of demonstrating: because it is not demonstrated that the effect always occurs, but as it stands under the power or mode of operating of the causes; and this cannot fail; therefore one who proceeds thus does not expose himself to the danger of error either. And that it suffices for the propositions to be necessary on a supposition is proved: because, taken thus, they cannot be otherwise; wherefore, since in such a process of demonstrating they are taken thus, they evidently infer the conclusion, which, as it stands under the premises, cannot be otherwise, and is therefore scientific and necessary.

## QUESTION II

Whether demonstration must consist of propositions said of every, per se, and universally.

11

I    propose three arguments against these three terms, so that on their occa‐

sion each may be explained. The first will be against the first term, “of every.”

Singular propositions, necessary and per se, can compose a demonstration, and yet they are not said of every; therefore not all demonstrative propositions must be said of every. The major is manifest enough of itself, since in

Philosophy it is demonstrated of God that he exists and that he is one; and not only a posteriori, or by a demonstration quia, but also by a demonstration propter quid we can demonstrate of him that he is eternal, because he is immutable. And many things are demonstrated of Christ the Lord in Theology, the principles of faith being supposed; all of which can be demonstrated only through singular propositions. For since God and Christ are singular terms, nothing but singular propositions can be made from them. The minor, that such propositions are not said of every, is evident, since it is repugnant for a proposition to be said of every and not be universal: for how in a singular proposition can the predicate belong to anything whatever contained under the subject, and for any time whatever, when nothing is contained under a singular subject?

The second argument, against the first and second mode per se, by this reasoning: The first mode per se is when the predicate is the definition, or part of the definition, of the subject; therefore this proposition, The risible is man, and the like, will be in the second mode per

se; which is false, because they are indirect, and demonstrations, at least propter quid, cannot be composed of them. Moreover, the second mode per se is when the subject pertains to the definition of the predicate; but all accidents are defined in some way through the subject, since they have an intrinsic order of aptitudinal inherence to it, which cannot be explained unless that same subject is placed in the definition of accidents; therefore all accidents will be predicated of their subjects in the second mode per se. And so this proposition, Body is white, and the like, will be in the second mode, since white is defined through body; which, however, is plainly false, because they are all accidental and contingent, and it is repugnant for demonstration to be composed of them; therefore the second mode per se is false, and inept for demonstration.

The third argument is against the mode “universally,” which Aristotle expounds thus: A predicate is said universally of a subject if it belongs to it according as it is itself: that is, according to its proper ratio, or as it is such; which plainly it does not have unless it is convertible with it. Therefore no proposition with a superior predicate, such as these, Man is an animal, Man is a body, will be universal; but it is certain that these are in the first mode per se, and that a demonstration propter quid can be composed of them; therefore the mode “universally” is defective, not comprehending all the propositions from which the most perfect demonstration can proceed.

12 Concerning the order of these three terms, St. Thomas on the present chapter, and with him Soto, and now almost all the moderns, assert that they stand to one another as superior and inferior predicates, so that universally is inferior to the others, and after it follows per se, and finally of every. Thus they stand in the same way as Man, Animal, and Living. For whatever is said universally is per se and of every; and whatever is per se is also of every; but not everything that is of every is per se, nor is everything per se universally. This is gathered from Aristotle, who defines universally as that which is of every, and per se, and in which the predicate belongs to the subject according as it is itself, or as it is such: by which he signifies quite openly that per se adds something over of every, just as universally adds something over per se and of every: which cannot be true unless they stand to one another as something superior and inferior, in the manner explained. And this is the true view, and to be held.

Although Toledo holds the contrary as regards the mode per se and of every, affirming that many propositions are per se which are not of every: as that man is grammatical is per se in the second mode, and is not of every, since it does not belong

to every man to have grammar in act. For as regards aptitude, it is evident that it belongs to all; and curvature too belongs to the nose per se, yet not to every one. But it is false that these propositions are per se. For neither is grammar defined proximately and per se through man, just as neither are the other sciences or arts; nor is curvature defined adequately and per se through the nose, since it is certain that it can belong to other subjects as well, besides the nose and man. Whence such propositions pertain to the fifth predicable, as purely accidental.

13 Concerning the term of every, it should be noted, with St. Thomas, lect. 9 of these Commentaries, Themistius, ch. 9 of his Paraphrase, and Soto on the present chapter, that being said of every is twofold: Prioristic and Posterioristic. It is called Prioristic in the sense in which it is adduced by Aristotle in the books of the Prior Analytics, and by the Summulists in book 4 of the Summulae; and its signification is that nothing can be taken under the Subject of which the Predicate is not said: not indeed according to the truth of the proposition, but according to the mode of enunciating. For it is irrelevant to the syllogistic form whether the propositions are true or false, and only the universal form or mode of enunciating is required per se: from which it results that, if the predicate is said of a distributed subject, it must be said of anything whatever taken under it, since it is distributed for all. But being said of every is called Posterioristic in the sense in which it is adduced by Aristotle in this work, namely in relation to demonstration: which, since it must consist of true propositions, requires that the Predicate, of every, be said of anything whatever contained under the Subject, not only according to the mode of enunciating but also according to the truth of the proposition. And in the same sense being said of none is to be taken, of which Aristotle made no mention in this chapter, because it can easily be understood that in negative propositions the predicate’s being denied of every subject is the same as its being said of it in affirmative ones. Whence all negative propositions in which the predicate is denied of every subject, and of anything whatever contained under it, and for any time whatever, are also of every in the negative mode.

14 Concerning the term per se: the reason should be noted why it is divided by Aristotle into four modes, so that there are neither more nor fewer; and it is this: The thing of which we demonstrate something can have only four considerations. The first, as it is in itself and per se. The second, in relation to essential predicates. The third, in relation to proper attributes. The fourth, in relation to its proper operation, of which it is the per se cause. And the first consideration constitutes the third mode, which is not of predicating but of being;

[p. 653]

the second consideration constitutes the first, and the third constitutes the second, which are modes of predicating; but the fourth constitutes the fourth, which is neither a mode of being nor of predicating, but per se of causing. Of the term universally we shall speak in the following question.

These things being supposed: Aristotle’s view, which all the expositors follow, is that every demonstration propter quid must consist of propositions of every and per se; but not every one must consist of propositions that are universally, but only the most perfect among them: that one, I mean, which proceeds from an adequate cause convertible with the effect. And both can be proved efficaciously. The first indeed by this argument: Every demonstration must proceed from necessary things, as Aristotle asserted and proved at the beginning of this chapter; but every necessary proposition must in some way be of every, and also per se; therefore every demonstration must consist of propositions of every and per se. But that not every demonstration propter quid must proceed from propositions in which the predicate is said universally of the subject will be manifest in what follows.

15 Concerning the solution of the first argument: different singulars are to be distinguished. For there are some in which the individual difference is not distinguished from the specific, as many hold of angels; or rather, not from the essential predicates, as in God: in whom, just as being and essence are not distinguished, so by the same reason the essential predicates are not distinguished from the individual ones. There are other singulars in which it is certain that the individual difference is distinguished in some way from the specific, since the individuals are multiplied under the same species. Thus, however, it is distinguished also in angels according to others. And in those individuals in which it is not distinguished there are singular propositions which are per se, and from which a demonstration can be composed; and these are equivalent to universals, because they are essential, and if several individuals of that essence were given, they would be of a common predicate. Whence they are at least virtually of every; and this suffices for it to be true that every demonstrative proposition is of every. But in individuals in which the individual difference is distinguished from the specific, no proposition can be given from which a demonstration propter quid could be made: because of these individuals, taken under the ratio of such individuals, as of Peter as he is Peter, no demonstration can be given, nor any science propter quid, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Metaph. 7, ch. 24, and in many other places. And St. Thomas, q. 9 On Power, a. 2, ad 1, and 1 p., q. 29, a. 1, ad 5, denies that singulars can be defined, and consequently that they are the object of science, because the definition is the middle of demonstration

and of science. Whence it follows that in these no proposition is given which is properly per se, nor of every; but when something is demonstrated of them by a demonstration propter quid, only the common attributes of the species are demonstrated, through the essence, likewise common; and this is to demonstrate them of those individuals inasmuch as they participate in the nature of the species, not by reason of the individual difference: and it is as it were an application of the science of the species, and the same science.

16 And in this way the attributes of man are demonstrated of Christ in Theology, and also the divine attributes and properties, inasmuch as he has both natures, the Divine and the Human: as it were by an application of the science of God and of man to that person, and to that individual having both natures. And the demonstrations themselves show that this is true: which is that, certainly, there is no science or demonstration propter quid of a singular of a corruptible nature as such, but as having the specific nature, or also at the same time the divine nature, of which there can be true science, as has been explained.

Of these individuals, however, there can be science a posteriori, which is called science quia, and also demonstration quia, proceeding from effects known through experience; and therefore both the science itself and the demonstration are called experimental. Such would be had of Peter even if we had no science a priori of man: because we know through experience that Peter and John are capable of learning, and consequently, through the same experience, that man is capable of learning, capable of wonder, and risible. We can therefore construct such a demonstration of Peter: Everything that attains the knowledge of some thing is capable of learning; Peter attains the knowledge of this or that thing; therefore he is capable of learning. And also: Whatever wonders is capable of wonder; Peter wonders; therefore he is capable of wonder. And in like manner we can prove that he is risible and rational. But these demonstrations are very imperfect, as Aristotle shows in ch. 10. Wherefore it is not necessary that they consist of propositions per se or of every, but it is enough that they consist of propositions necessary in whatever way. For Aristotle adduced these three terms, of every, per se, and universally, only for perfect demonstrations, which are called propter quid. And from these things it is clear that the first argument has been solved.

17 Concerning the indirect propositions, from which the first part of the second argument proceeds, there are different opinions. The first, of Cajetan on the present chapter, who says that they are per se in the second mode, since the definition belongs to them: for the predicate is of the definition of the subject, as in this one: The risible is man, or The rational is man. deny altogether that any indirect proposition is per se, or that a demonstration propter quid can be made from it. And this seems to me more probable: because indirect propositions lack the natural form and mode of propositions, in which the predicate has the mode of form, but the subject the mode of matter. But in indirect ones we see the opposite, since that which is truly the subject holds the place of the predicate; and therefore they are as it were propositions against nature. Therefore the ratio of per se, or of every, does not belong to them: for these modes, since they were handed down by Aristotle for demonstrations propter quid, belong only to natural propositions having the true form of propositions, from which a demonstration propter quid can be made. Nevertheless they have a certain likeness to propositions per se and of every.

To the form of the argument, then: the consequence is to be denied, because the definitions of these modes presuppose the ratio of direct propositions. Whence their sense is: the first mode per se is when the predicate of a direct proposition pertains to the definition of the subject; and the second, when the subject of a direct proposition pertains to the definition of the predicate.

To the other part of the same argument: the consequence is to be denied, namely that every accident is predicated of its subject in the second mode per se; because the modes per se presuppose a necessary proposition, just as we said a moment ago that they presuppose a direct proposition. Whence the sense of the definition of the second mode per se is: The second mode per se is when the subject pertains to the definition of the predicate, in a necessary proposition. So the expositors commonly hold on the present chapter, especially Soto and Cajetan; and it is gathered from Aristotle, who, before he defined the modes per se, proved that demonstration proceeds from necessary things; and having explained the first and second modes per se, he adds that all the others are accidents, as if presupposing that these modes are found only in necessary propositions. Also in ch. 6 of this book he teaches expressly that the things which belong per se in these modes belong necessarily. False, therefore, and refuted by us above, is what Toledo asserts, that certain accidental propositions are per se in the second mode.

To the form of the argument, then: granting the antecedent, the consequence is to be denied, namely that the accident is predicated of the subject in the second mode. For it is not enough, for it to be predicated per se of the subject, that the subject pertain to the definition of the accident; but it is required that it belong to it necessarily, and not contingently or purely accidentally.

To the third argument: we grant that not every demonstration propter quid consists of propositions in which the predicate is said universally of the subject, but only the most perfect one, which proceeds from adequate causes convertible with their effects, as will be clear in what follows.

## QUESTION III

What is signified by the term “universally,” and whether it belongs to propositions of superior predicates, or only to those which are made in convertible terms.

19

Concerning the first thing which the title of the question asks, it should be noted that the universal is taken in two ways. First, as it is a mode of the subject, by reason of which a universal proposition is constituted: as Every man is an animal. Second, as it is a mode of the predicate, constituting a proposition with a common or universal predicate. Now it is certain that it is not taken in this place by Aristotle as it is a mode of the subject, but of the predicate, since it is taken by comparison with the subject. But further, as it is a mode of the predicate, it is taken in two ways. In a common ratio, for any predicate whatever common to many, in which acceptation it is taken by Porphyry in the Predicables, and is defined by Aristotle as that which is one in many, On Interpretation 2. But in the posterioristic art it is taken more specially, not for any predicate whatever common to many, but only for that which belongs to the subject according as it is itself, or primarily. Such is the predicate of this proposition: Man is rational. And in this acceptation it is taken by Aristotle in the present chapter, and in the title of the question.

This being supposed, it asks, second: Whether it belongs to propositions with a common predicate pertaining to the essence of the thing, so that all propositions in which the proximate genus is predicated of the species are universally; or only those in which the predicate belongs per se to the subject and is convertible with it.

20 The first opinion asserts that for the predicate to belong to the subject universally is the same as for it to belong to it per se primarily and immediately; and that therefore predications of the genus are such. So Ferrara, on Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 15, and

Soto on the present chapter, sole question. They prove it by the testimony of

Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says thus: Per se and according as it is itself are the same: as the point and the straight belong per se to the line. But a proposition in which the proximate genus is predicated of the species is per se; therefore it will also be according as it is itself. And according

[p. 657]

as it is itself is the same as universally, as the same Aristotle teaches when explaining what universally is; therefore it will also be universally. And St. Thomas asserts the same, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 15, where he teaches that a predicate which belongs per se to something in such a way that it does not belong to it through some cause, but immediately and per se, belongs according as it is itself, and therefore universally. But it is plain that animal belongs to man in this way; therefore St. Thomas holds that it belongs universally.

Next they prove it by reason: because for a predicate to belong to a subject universally is the same as for it to belong to it primarily, or according as it is itself: namely, as such, and not through something else. But the whole definition belongs to the species as such, and not through any other middle, but immediately, which is to belong to it primarily; therefore it belongs to it universally; and consequently any part of the definition will belong universally. But one of them is the genus; therefore, etc.

12 The second opinion is the express one of St. Thomas, who asserts that only that predicate belongs universally which does not exceed the subject, but belongs to it per se and is convertible with it. His words are: It is impossible for one thing to belong to two and to each according as it is itself: for what is said of something according as it is itself does not exceed it; just as to have three angles equal to two right angles does not exceed the triangle of which it is predicated, but is the same with it convertibly, etc. So too Albert the Great, Posterior Analytics 1, tract. 2, ch. 12, Paul of Venice, Cajetan, Toledo, and all the moderns. And this is the true view, and to be held.

22 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who, explaining the term universally, taught expressly that universally adds something over the two other terms, namely of every and per se; therefore he holds that it is not enough, for it to be said universally, that it be a predicate per se in the first or second mode. He asserts further that what it adds over the terms of every and per se is that it belong to the subject according as it is itself, or as it is such. But the proximate genus does not belong to the species as it is such, since it is common to the other species; therefore it will not belong to it according as it is itself, nor universally.

It is proved also by reason: because for a predicate to belong to a subject according as it is itself is to belong to it as it is such, as Aristotle expressly teaches and the adversaries concede; but animal does not belong to man as he is such; therefore neither according as he is himself. The minor is proved: man, as he is such, is distinguished from the horse and the lion and the other species; but through the genus animal he is not distinguished from them, but rather agrees with them; therefore animal is not predicated of man as he is such, and so not according

as he is himself, nor universally. Second: Nothing belongs to something according as it is itself, or as it is such, except what is proper to it and not common to others; what is common belongs to it rather as it shares with them. For example, what belongs to man as he is such, namely as he is man, belongs to him as he is such an animal, and not as he has the sensitive nature common to the other animals; but as he is an animal, he is not such an animal; therefore animal does not belong to him as such, nor according as he is himself, or universally. Thus our view asserts two things. The first is that, in order that a predicate belong to a subject universally, it is not required, nor does it suffice, that it belong to it essentially, or in the first mode per se, or even immediately. For it can well belong in these modes and not belong universally; and conversely, it can well belong in the second mode, and not essentially, nor immediately, and belong universally. Thus substance belongs to man essentially and in the first mode per se, and animal even immediately; and yet neither belongs to him universally. And capacity for learning, or wonder, does not belong to man in these modes; nevertheless they belong to him universally. Second, it asserts: That predicate belongs to the subject universally which belongs to it primarily, and according as it is itself, or as it is such; and to belong in this way is to be its adequate ratio, or to belong to it according to its adequate ratio, and by reason of it to whatever others it is attributed. For example: sensible does not belong to man by reason of himself, because it does not belong to him as he is man, but as he is an animal; nor does it belong to him according to his adequate ratio, but according to an inadequate one. Nor does animal belong to man as he is man, since it is common to him with the other animals; nor is it his adequate ratio. And, to explain this in a word: only that predicate belongs to the subject universally which belongs to it per se and is convertible with it. Such are the propositions in which the whole definition is predicated of the thing defined, or also the difference; such too those in which a proper attribute is predicated of its species or genus, from which it proceeds proximately and adequately. And whenever something belongs to something with a reduplication, it is said to belong to it universally, or according as it is itself.

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is, first, that when he says that universally is the same as per se, the sense is not that it is convertible with it, but that it is the same with it in reality, as an inferior predicate with a superior. Or, second, he asserts that universally is the same as per se convertibly; for what is not

the same simply, is plain from what he teaches immediately afterward: namely, that what it adds over both terms, of every and per se, is that it be according as it is itself.

To the argument: granting the major and the minor, the consequence is denied, namely that any part of the definition, taken by itself, is predicated universally of the thing defined; because not both belong to it as it is such, but the difference alone.

## CHAPTER X

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. But knowing that and knowing why differ, first indeed in the same science, and in this in

two ways.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

ristotle’s intent in this tenth chapter is to distinguish demonstration

A           quia and demonstration propter quid, and to explain the ratio of each.

The chapter is divided into two parts. In the first he teaches that demonstration quia differs from demonstration propter quid in the same science. In the second, that they differ in different sciences.

Knowing quia and knowing propter quid, he says, and consequently the demonstrations themselves, differ in the same science in two ways.

1 For demonstration propter quid proceeds from the proximate and adequate cause; demonstration quia from a remote and inadequate cause, because it does not infer the effect positively, but only by way of negation. And he gives a twofold example. The first, in this demonstration: Whatever breathes is an animal; a wall is not an animal; therefore a wall does not breathe; in which it is plain that to be an animal is not the proximate cause of breathing, but to have lungs; nor is it the adequate cause either, because there are many animals which do not breathe, because they lack lungs. The second example he adduces from the saying of a certain Philosopher, who, being a Scythian and seeing women dancing at Athens, when asked whether there were similar dancing-girls in Scythia, replied that there were no vines, giving the remote and inadequate cause; from which such a demonstration can be constructed: Where there are no vines, there are no dancing-girls; but in Scythia there are no vines; therefore there are no dancing-girls. But the proximate cause would be the absence of wine: for since wine is the cause of merriment, from which dancing comes, its absence would be the cause of the absence of dancing. And because these demonstrations proceed by negation, Aristotle asserts that they are always made in the second figure

A

because their middle too must be predicated. Second, they differ because in the same science demonstration propter quid always proceeds from the cause; and since the cause is prior to the effect, it is called demonstration a priori. But demonstration quia proceeds from the effect, which, because it is posterior, is called demonstration a posteriori. Aristotle adduces two other examples of demonstration quia. The first in the stars, which are of two different kinds: for some are fixed, like those which are in the eighth heaven, which is called the firmament; but others are those which are in the lower heavenly bodies, and these are called Planets. The former, then, because they are far distant from us, seem to have a certain trembling motion, and therefore they seem to twinkle or scintillate, although they have no such motion; but on account of the imperfection of our sight we think the stars have it. But the Planets do not appear with such motion, because they are less distant from us. From this effect, then, such a demonstration quia can be constructed: Stars that do not twinkle are near us; the Planets do not twinkle; therefore they are near us. He adduces another example in the Moon, of which we can prove that it is circular, or round, from this effect: that it receives the increase of its light in a circular manner. And the proof will be this: Whatever is illuminated circularly is round; but the Moon is illuminated circularly by the Sun; therefore it is round.

But he distinguishes a twofold effect: adequate, because it is convertible with the cause; and inadequate, which is not convertible with it. And he says that, if the effect is adequate, from a demonstration quia proceeding from it a demonstration propter quid can be made; and conversely, from a demonstration propter quid a demonstration quia: as is plain in rationality and risibility. For we can prove the former through the latter, and it will be a demonstration quia; and again the latter through the former, and it will be a demonstration propter quid. But if the effect is inadequate, a demonstration quia can be made from it, by which we prove the cause, but not a demonstration propter quid, by which we prove the effect from the cause. And the reason for this difference is that the adequate effect is convertible with its cause, but the inadequate one is not convertible; and therefore in the former both demonstrations can be made, but in the latter only demonstration quia. For an inadequate cause does not necessarily infer the effect. Thus, if we say, Whatever moves with progressive motion is an animal; man moves with progressive motion; therefore he is an animal, it will not be possible to construct a demonstration propter quid proceeding from the cause, because it is not true to say that whatever is an animal moves with progressive motion: for there are certain animals to which such motion does not belong.

2 In the second part Aristotle teaches that demonstration propter quid differs from demonstration quia in diverse sciences. But that sciences are diverse happens in two ways: either they are subordinated, so that one is placed under the other; and such are Geometry and Perspective: the former deals with the line, and the latter with the visual line; and therefore the former is called subalternating, the latter subalternated. And in the same way Arithmetic, dealing with Number, is called subalternating, while Music, dealing with sonorous number, is subalternated to it. Other sciences are diverse but not subalternated, as Geometry and

Medicine. Aristotle asserts, then, that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in subalternated sciences: because demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, which, since it is superior, gives the cause of the principles of the subalternated science and proves them a priori; but demonstration quia pertains to the subalternated science, proceeding from the effect.

They also differ in diverse sciences that are not subalternated: because it sometimes happens that some proposition is evident in one science which nevertheless does not give its cause, but it pertains to another science to give such a cause through demonstration propter quid; and therefore it pertains to the former science to demonstrate such a proposition through demonstration quia, but to the latter through demonstration propter quid. As in Medicine or Surgery this proposition is evident: A circular wound heals with more difficulty than an oblong one.

Yet this science does not give its cause, but Geometry does: because the sides of a circle are farther apart, and therefore are joined with more difficulty. In these diverse sciences, then, demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished.

## QUESTION I

Whether demonstration proceeding from a remote cause is quia or propter quid.

3

A      remote cause is twofold, Adequate and Inadequate. Adequate is that which is

convertible with the effect: as rationality is the remote cause of risibility, convertible with it. An inadequate remote cause is one that is not convertible with the effect: as sensitive nature is the remote cause of respiration, which is not convertible with the effect, since it is established that not every animal breathes. And concerning the adequate remote cause it is certain that it does not constitute demonstration quia, but propter quid. The question therefore proceeds concerning the inadequate remote cause: whether demonstration proceeding from it is demonstration quia or propter quid.

4 And that it is not demonstration quia but propter quid is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, ch. 2 of this book, where, treating of demonstration propter quid, he asserts that it proceeds from first things, or from things that are reduced to first things; and since principles are the cause of the conclusion, it is the same as if he said that it proceeds from a proximate cause, or from a remote one that can be reduced to the proximate; but a remote cause, even an inadequate one, can be reduced to the proximate, since it is called remote with respect to it; therefore demonstration proceeding from it will be propter quid.

It is proved also by reason. First: because demonstration propter quid is demonstration a priori, and demonstration quia a posteriori, for no other reason than that the former proceeds from the cause, which is prior to the effect, and the latter from the effect, which is posterior to the cause; but a remote cause is a true cause, and prior to the effect; therefore demonstration proceeding from it is a priori and gives the cause of the conclusion; therefore it is demonstration propter quid.

Second: Every demonstration proceeding from an effect, proximate or remote, adequate or inadequate, is demonstration quia; therefore every demonstration proceeding from a cause, proximate or remote, adequate or inadequate, will be demonstration propter quid. The consequence is proved: because as the effect stands to demonstration quia, so the cause stands to demonstration propter quid.

For the solution of this question it should be noted that the remote and inadequate cause about which the question is asked is twofold, Superior and inferior. The superior is that from which the effect indeed proceeds by means of the proximate cause, yet it does not proceed from every instance of it, but from some. As being an animal is the remote and inadequate cause of respiration, because respiration proceeds from it by means of the proximate cause, which is having lungs and warm blood; but it does not proceed from every animal, since there are many that lack these; and therefore sensitive nature in them is not the cause of respiration. The other is the remote and inadequate inferior cause, from which the effect indeed always proceeds, and from every instance of it, but not from it alone, since it can also proceed from another: as is plain in the example of dancing adduced by Aristotle, whose remote and inadequate cause is vines and wine; yet it does not proceed from these alone, but also from other causes of gladness, which is the proximate cause of dancing.

Now this is the difference between the two causes: that the inferior infers the effect. For it follows well: from vines and wine, some dancing; but it is not inferred from the effect, since it does not follow: if there is some dancing, there are wine and vines; for dancing can come from another cause, even if neither of these exists. The negation of the effect, however, does infer the negation of the cause. Whence it

is that Anacharsis, the famous Scythian Philosopher, replied, when he was asked why there were no dancing-girls and flute-players in Scythia: he replied that there are none because there are no vines, giving an inadequate cause by way of negation.

5 Second, it should be noted that when Aristotle asserts that demonstration proceeding from a remote cause [is quia], he is speaking not only not of the adequate cause, but not of the inadequate inferior one either, and therefore only of the inadequate superior one. This is gathered evidently from his words: for after he had proposed his own view and confirmed it with examples, he added these words: Such causes are like those that are said according to excess; that is, superior predicates, which are said to exceed the inferiors; therefore he speaks only of superior causes. From these alone the effect can be inferred by way of negation.

6 It should likewise be noted, third, that even so the effect is not inferred from these by way of negation as from causes formally, but just as from the negation of a superior predicate the negation of the inferior is inferred, and from the negation of the genus the negation of the difference, and conversely, from the negation of the difference the negation of the genus, without any proper causality. This can be proved effectively by these examples: Whatever is a man is living; but a wall is not living; therefore a wall is not a man. Whatever is rational is an animal; a stone is not an animal; therefore it is not rational. But in these it is not inferred as from causes, but as from pure negations of the superior predicate; therefore neither in the case of those remote causes is it inferred by reason of any causality, but only by reason of the negation of the superior predicate. The consequence is proved: because just as we prove of a wall that it does not breathe because it is not an animal, we can equally prove that it is not rational because it is not an animal, in this way: Whatever is rational is an animal; a wall is not an animal; therefore it is not rational. Indeed, [we can prove] that it does not breathe from the negation of risibility alone, saying: Whatever is risible breathes; a wall is not risible; therefore it does not breathe. Where no ratio of causality intervenes, but from the negation of the genus alone the negation of the difference follows, or from the negation of the property the negation of that same respiration. From which it follows that, just as through demonstrations proceeding from effects the cause of the conclusion is not given, nor its propter quid, but it is only proved that this or that is so (as that man is rational, through risibility), and therefore they are called by Aristotle demonstrations That this is, so through the negation of a remote superior cause it is only proved that its effect is not in something, without the propter quid of such a negation being posited,

and without any causality; just as from the negation of one predicate the negation of another is proved, even without causality. Wherefore the ratio of cause is found in these only materially; and therefore these demonstrations, proceeding from a remote and inadequate cause by way of negation, are very similar to demonstrations Quia, or That this is. And for this reason Aristotle reduced them to demonstrations quia rather than to demonstrations propter quid.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First, that every demonstration proceeding from a cause as it is a cause, whether it be proximate or remote, whether adequate or inadequate, is propter quid, or διότι. This is evidently proved by the testimony of

Aristotle and the reasons adduced for this side.

7 Second: Demonstrations proceeding from a remote, inadequate and superior cause by way of negation, of which alone Aristotle speaks in the present chapter, were deservedly numbered by him among demonstrations Quia, or ὅτι, rather than among demonstrations Propter quid. The reason for this is that they do not proceed from the negation of such a cause by way of causality, but only by way of the negation of a superior predicate, just as in a similar form the negations of certain predicates are proved through the negations of others; indeed even the negation of the same effect of a remote cause [is proved] through the negation of another, without any causality; therefore the negation of the cause concurs only materially. Wherefore through such demonstrations the propter quid is not stated, but it is only proved that the negation of the effect of such a cause belongs to something, just as it is proved from the effect, and through demonstration quia, that man is an animal, or rational. Wherefore the arguments need not be answered, since they effectively prove what they intend.

## QUESTION II

Whether the division of demonstration into demonstration quia and propter quid is a division of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into its analogates.

he title of the question presupposes as certain that this division is 8

T        sufficient, which all admit. And it can be proved by this reason:

that division is sufficient whose members contain everything that is comprised under the thing divided; but the members of this division comprise any demonstration whatever; therefore they contain whatever is contained under demonstration in general, which is the thing divided of this same division. The minor is proved: for besides demonstration proceeding from the cause and from the effect, Aristotle in what follows enumerates demonstration to the impossible, through which it is proved that one is the other

or is not, by leading to the impossible. Others also add demonstration from a sign, through which, from a sign evidently known to us, we prove that a thing is so: as that the Moon is eclipsed, because we see it lose its light. But both of these demonstrations are comprised under demonstration ὅτι or διότι, and also any other that can be thought up, as Soto and Toledo rightly teach in the present chapter; therefore this division comprises all demonstrations. I prove the minor again: because demonstrations to the impossible always proceed by way of the cause or of the effect, and therefore are reduced to demonstration quia or propter quid, as the two following show. If man were not risible, he would not be rational; but the consequent is impossible; therefore the antecedent also. Whose sense is: if man were not risible, he would not be rational; but it is true that he is rational; therefore it is true that he is risible. And this other: If man were not rational, he would not be capable of wonder; but the consequent is impossible; therefore the antecedent. For the former proceeds from the cause, but the latter from the effect, as is plain.

9 Demonstration from a sign, however, always proceeds from the effect, because a sign known to us through experience is always an effect, as the example of the eclipse of the moon adduced above shows. But the two members of this division, namely demonstration quia and propter quid, are common, and under them are comprised the diverse demonstrations proceeding from causes or from effects. Whence Cajetan wrongly said that another member of demonstration propter quid must be distinguished; for whatever it may be, it is comprised under one member of this division, as a species under a genus. Supposing that the division is sufficient, we ask whether it is univocal, so that demonstration is divided into these two members as a genus into its species; or whether it is analogous, so that [it is divided] rather as an analogous term into its analogates.

And the first opinion asserts that the division is analogous, and not univocal. So Themistius in his paraphrase on bk. 1 of the Posterior Analytics, ch., and Paul of Venice in the present chapter. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who, defining demonstration in ch. 2 of this book, explained only demonstration propter quid by a twofold definition, which definition cannot in any way belong to demonstration quia. Indeed, Aristotle himself in the same chapter asserted as it were with a condition, speaking of demonstration quia: If there is another mode of knowing, we shall say later; referring, no doubt, to this tenth chapter, according to the common view of the expositors.

10 From which it is inferred that demonstration is not univocal, nor a genus to both. For if it were univocal, it would have to be defined as common to both, and not for one of its species only;

since, then, only demonstration propter quid was defined, Aristotle regards this alone as demonstration simply; but demonstration quia only in a certain respect, and by attribution to the former as to the principal analogate. A sign of this is also that Aristotle never defined it, thinking it enough to have defined the chief one, from whose likeness and attribution the other is easily understood.

Finally it is proved by reason. First: because demonstration is the instrument for acquiring science; but science acquired through demonstration quia cannot be such simply, but only in a certain respect; therefore neither will demonstration quia be demonstration simply, but in a certain respect. The minor is proved from two things. From the first indeed: because we do not know simply something whose nature and essence we are ignorant of; but when demonstration quia has been had, we are ignorant of the nature and essence of the thing, and only know that it is such from some extrinsic effect, from which demonstration quia proceeds: as when we demonstrate that man is rational from the effect of laughing, which we experience; therefore it cannot be demonstration simply. From the second: because of first principles there is no science simply, since they are known from their terms; but there is no principle, however immediate, that cannot be proved in some way through demonstration quia; therefore this does not generate science simply, but a certain other cognition of the conclusion, inferior to science; and therefore it will not be demonstration simply, but in a certain respect.

11 Second: If demonstration is a genus to demonstration quia and propter quid, then science also will be a genus to that which is generated through each; and both actual science quia and propter quid, which are the assents of each demonstration, and habitual science, generated through each assent, will be distinguished in species. But the consequent is false; therefore also the antecedent. The minor is proved: because both demonstrations are often had concerning the same object, as concerning man or any other; but sciences are distinguished in species by their objects; therefore neither the actual nor the habitual sciences generated through these demonstrations can be distinguished in species; and so neither can the demonstrations themselves, but only as certain analogates of demonstration in general, which is divided into them.

The second opinion holds that demonstration was divided by Aristotle into demonstration quia and propter quid as a univocal term, and as a true genus into its species. So Ammonius seems to hold, on On the Soul bk. 1, texts 21 and 34, and Dominic of Flanders, ibid., q. 29, a. 3. But expressly Soto and Toledo

[p. 667]

> letus, cap. præſenti, & omnes moderni interpretes : & vide-tur mihi vera, & tenenda. Prob. primò: Quia demonftratio, quia,procedit ex principiis certis, &euidentibus , & per con-ſequentiam cuidentem in modo &figura conſtitutam : ergo eſtſyllogifmus neceffarius,& euidens, ſpecie diſtinctus àpro-babili,& fophiftico,Quod eft,eſſeſpeciemfyllogifmidemon- Aratiui,diftinctamab eaquam conftituit demöftratio,propter quid,vtraque ergo ſpecie fyllogifmi demonftratiui , abſtrahi poteſt ratiocommunisfyllogifmi demoſtratiui vniuoca,atque generica,fub quadiſtinguenturſpecie. 12 Quodprobatur ſecudò:Ex principiisvtriufque,&affen-fibusconclufionum,per vtramquegenitis. in the present chapter, and all the modern interpreters; and it seems to me true and to be held. It is proved, first: because demonstration quia proceeds from certain and evident principles, and through an evident consequence constituted in mood and figure; therefore it is a necessary and evident syllogism, distinct in species from the probable and the sophistical. That is, it is a species of demonstrative syllogism distinct from that which demonstration propter quid constitutes. From both species of demonstrative syllogism, therefore, a common ratio of demonstrative syllogism, univocal and generic, can be abstracted, under which they will be distinguished in species.

12 This is proved, second, from the principles of each, and from the assents to the conclusions generated through each. For demonstrations are distinguished by the principles from which they proceed and by the assents to the conclusions which they generate, since principles are the formal rationes of assenting to the conclusions, and conclusions are the proper effects of principles and demonstrations; but the principles of demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished essentially, because the latter contain the cause of the conclusion and give its propter quid, but the former the effect, and therefore they only prove the conclusion a posteriori. And also the assents to the conclusions are distinguished essentially through these same diverse principles, as through diverse rationes of assenting, which are as it were their formal objects; therefore on both sides demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished in species, and therefore demonstration in general will be divided into them as a genus.

13 Now, in order that the testimony of Aristotle may be explained and the first argument answered, it should be noted that although a genus on its own part is participated equally by its species, nevertheless, on the part of the differences of unequal perfection through which it descends to them, it constitutes those same species unequal in perfection, as is established in the genus animal. In this way, then, demonstration in general, abstracted from both, is participated equally by them on its own part, but the differences of the two are of diverse perfection: because it is far more perfect to give the cause of the conclusion, and therefore its propter quid, than only to prove it from the effect. Therefore demonstration propter quid is a far more perfect species of demonstration than demonstration quia, not by reason of the genus, but by reason of its most perfect difference, as man among the species of animal. And just as this greater perfection of the human species does not take away the univocal ratio of animal, in the same way neither does the greater perfection of demonstration propter quid take away the univocal or generic ratio with respect to each demonstration.

[p. 668]

Primum:An affenfus demonstratio- nis,quia,&propterquid, qui dicuntur fcientiæ actuales , diflin-guantur, fpecie. Secundum:Anperaffenfus generentur habitus Scientia,ſpeciediftincti. Circa primum, eſt primafententia Soti, q1.huius cap.qui licèt teneatdemonftrationesipfas diftingui

Aristotle, then, defined only the chief species of demonstration in the second chapter, because it is the foremost instrument of the demonstrative art for generating science, intending to explain the other, imperfect species in the present chapter; which he also did, saying that it is such as proceeds from the effect, not giving the propter quid of the conclusion but showing that it is so. We deny, therefore, that Aristotle holds that only demonstration propter quid is demonstration simply, and demonstration quia only in a certain respect; although he holds that the former is the most perfect species of demonstration and the latter the most imperfect, by reason of the differences.

To the first argument, the minor must be denied, namely that the assent of demonstration Quia is not science simply. And when it is said, first, that through it we do not know the nature and essence of the thing, I reply that the essence of the thing is not known even through demonstration propter quid, but is presupposed as known through the habit of principles, since the definition is a principle indemonstrable of itself and not knowable through science propter quid in its own genus, but from the cognition of the terms alone. Whence it is not a defect of demonstration quia that the essence of the thing is not known through it; but the office of each demonstration is to deliver the cognition of the object from some property of it. This demonstration propter quid does by proving the properties of the subject a priori and from the cause. But the office of demonstration quia is to deliver the cognition of the same subject from the property itself, known through experience, giving no cause, but only proving from that property that it is of such a nature. It must be denied, then, that science generated through demonstration quia is not such simply, although we grant that it is very imperfect. As to what is said second, that of principles science is not had, a distinction must be made: because perfect science, and a priori, cannot be had of them, since they are known per se and indemonstrable a priori. But being known per se does not prevent their being demonstrable a posteriori through demonstration quia, through which science of them will be had: imperfect indeed, yet univocally such with science a priori and propter quid; wherefore the demonstrations themselves also will have a univocal and generic agreement.

The second argument asks two things. First: whether the assents of demonstration quia and propter quid, which are called actual sciences, are distinguished in species. Second: whether through these assents habitual sciences distinct in species are generated. On the first, there is the first view of Soto, q. 1 of this chapter, who, although he holds that the demonstrations themselves are distinguished

[p. 669]

in species, nevertheless denies that the assents are distinguished in species, and holds that they are of the same species. This he proves by this argument: The principles of a demonstration are an equivocal cause of the conclusion, since they are distinguished in species from it, as the sun is an equivocal cause of heat; but the same effect according to species can proceed from equivocal causes of diverse species, as the same heat from the sun and from fire; therefore the same assent to the conclusion [can] proceed from principles and demonstrations diverse according to species. Although, then, the demonstrations are distinct in species, it does not follow that the assents to the conclusion of each are distinguished in species. This he thinks must necessarily be granted of the eclipse of the moon demonstrated through demonstration propter quid from the cause, and through demonstration quia from the effect: for we do not have from this assents diverse in species, but the same according to species, and distinguished only by a certain accidental and extrinsic ratio, as it proceeds through one demonstration and the other.

15 This view, however, is false, which I prove thus: The assent to a conclusion takes its species from the principles from which it proceeds as from the formal medium of assenting, as all grant and evident reason proves. For the assent to this conclusion, The earth is round, generated from philosophical principles, that is, from those of motion and the physical, and from mathematical principles, is distinguished in species, even if it is of the same proposition and is had by the same intellect; but the media of assenting to the conclusion of demonstration quia and propter quid (which are the principles containing its cause, or proving it from the effect) are established to be distinguished in species, as was proved of demonstrations quia and propter quid; therefore the assent to the conclusions of each demonstration, even if it is had concerning the same thing, will be distinct in species, because it is had through diverse formal media.

16 Our view, therefore, is that the assents of each demonstration are distinguished in species. This is evidently proved, supposing the specific distinction of the demonstrations, which Soto admits. For it is repugnant that through diverse media of assenting, which are the formal objects of those same assents, diverse assents according to species should not be generated.

Nor does Soto’s argument prove the opposite. But the minor must be distinguished, namely that from equivocal causes diverse in species the same effect according to species can proceed: for if they are inadequate, it can; but if they are adequate, it is repugnant. And the reason for this distinction is that from inadequate causes the same effect proceeds indifferently, but from adequate causes determinately and necessarily. Because the adequate cause is convertible with its effect; therefore

it is repugnant that the same effect according to species should proceed from adequate causes of diverse species. But fire and the sun are equivocal causes of heat, of diverse species, but inadequate; and therefore heat can proceed indifferently from either, and from both the same heat according to species. But the assent to a conclusion proceeds from the demonstration and its principles as from an adequate cause; and therefore it is repugnant that the same assent according to species should proceed from both, supposing their specific distinction, proved by us and granted by the same Soto.

The second thing which the same argument asked is whether through these demonstrations there are generated not only diverse assents, which are called diverse actual sciences, but also diverse habits, which are called absolutely diverse sciences. On which there is the first opinion of many of those who hold with us that the assents of each demonstration are diverse, asserting that they do not generate a habit of science diverse according to species, if such demonstrations are concerned with the same thing, as with man, or with natural being, which is the object of natural Philosophy; but that the assent of each demonstration is inadequate with respect to the same habit, and differs from the other only by a partial and as it were inadequate species, and therefore can proceed from the same habit of science according to species. Because habits are distinguished in species only by adequate acts, just as also by adequate objects, and not by inadequate ones.

17 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in the present chapter teaches that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in the same science and in diverse ones. Which cannot be true unless they sometimes pertain to the same science; but the same science is the same habit; therefore neither can it be true unless they pertain to the same habit. Wherefore it cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle that through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing diverse habits of science are generated; otherwise one will have several sciences of the same man, and several philosophies of the same natural being, if he knows their nature and properties through demonstrations quia and propter quid: which is unheard of in the schools.

They prove it next by reason: because just as a power has a greater extension than a habit, and therefore one and the same according to species can, within the latitude of its object, have several habits distinct in species, which are as it were inadequate with respect to it, in the same way a habit has a greater extension than an act, since we see the same habit of science have many and diverse demonstrations; and therefore several

[p. 671]

Sed vtteftimonium Arift.explicemus &argu.foluere poffi-mus, notandum eſt, Vtrumque genus demonstrations,quia, propterquid, verfarialiquando airca eandem rem, aliquando circa

diverse assents, which are several acts, even if they proceed only from the cause or only from the effect; therefore it will be able to have several acts or assents, of which some proceed from the cause through demonstration propter quid, and others from the effect through demonstration quia.

18 And just as the demonstrations, so the assents will be inadequate with respect to the same habit. It is not necessary, then, to multiply several habits concerning the same object on account of demonstrations quia and propter quid and their assents distinct in species; but the same habit will be able to extend itself to them as to diverse but inadequate ones.

Our view is that through these demonstrations not only diverse assents according to species are generated, but also diverse habits of science. This, given the specific distinction of the assents or acts (which the opposing view admits), I prove thus: Habits are generated from acts, and take their specific unity and distinction from them; but the assents to the conclusions of each demonstration, which are the proper acts from which the habits are generated, are distinguished in species; therefore they generate distinct habits. And if you say that they are partial and inadequate acts: from this, first of all, it evidently follows that they generate habits distinct by a partial species; whence you are now bound to grant several habits and several partial sciences concerning the same object, which we proved false in the proemial questions. I prove besides that the assents are distinguished not only by a partial species, but also by a total one.

Because things that are distinguished partially must be parts of some whole; therefore if the assents are distinguished partially and inadequately, since they must be distinguished by the objective formal ratio, there will be some total and common objective ratio of which they are parts; but this is impossible; therefore it is impossible that they be distinguished by a partial species. The minor is proved: because the principles are the objective ratio of the assents, as they are the ratio of assenting to the conclusions; but the principles that contain the cause and those that contain the effect are as it were opposed and altogether diverse, nor are there any other superior or inferior ones of which they are parts; therefore they cannot be distinguished by a partial species, but must be distinguished by a total one; and consequently they cannot generate habits distinct by a partial species, but by a total one.

But in order that we may explain the testimony of Aristotle and be able to answer the argument, it should be noted that each kind of demonstration, quia and propter quid, is sometimes concerned with the same thing, sometimes with

diverse ones. Now the thing with which a science is concerned is only the material object; the formal object is the principles through which the attributes are demonstrated of it. Whence, although they are sometimes concerned with the same material object, they always have diverse formal objects. Nor does this contain any repugnance, since science and opinion too can be concerned with the same material object through diverse media or principles, which are the rationes of assenting and as it were the formal objects. It is nothing new, then, to posit diverse habits of science concerning the same thing, since science and opinion differ more, and yet are sometimes also of the same thing. These diverse habits, then, generated through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing, are comprised under the name of the same science, on account of the identity of the material object and of the abstraction from matter. And this is what Aristotle meant to signify when he said that knowing quia and propter quid, and consequently the demonstrations, differ in the same science and in diverse ones: by the same science understanding both habits, which are contained within the latitude of the same material object, abstracting from matter in the same way; but by diverse sciences understanding those also which are concerned with diverse things, and abstract from matter in a diverse way, as his examples show. And so his sense is not that knowing quia and propter quid differ within the same habit, but within the scientific cognition of the same thing, with which they are wont to be concerned, and which he understands by the name of the same science. And by the same reasoning both habits are understood under the name of the same Philosophy: for in the common way of speaking we call natural Philosophy the scientific cognition of natural being, whether knowing quia and knowing propter quid are distinguished through several assents or habits or not.

20 To the argument, then: we grant the first thing that is assumed in the antecedent, namely that a power has a greater extension than a habit; but we deny the second, that a habit has a greater extension than an act or assent. And the reason for this is that the habit is proximately specified by the act according to the formal ratio, because through it it attains the object; and since this is limited, the habit does not have a greater extension than the act. But the power is more universal, and attains the object under a more universal ratio; and therefore it happens through acts and habits of diverse species. Whence it follows that it is not superfluous to multiply habits where the acts are distinguished in species, but altogether necessary, as we have already proved.

T R E AT I S E O N T H E S U B A L -ternation of Sciences.

What is understood by the name of subalternating and subalternated science.

n the second part of the chapter Aristotle taught that knowing 21

I        quia and propter quid, and consequently demonstrations, differ in diverse

sciences that are not subordinated, but totally diverse, and as it were disparate; and also that the same happens in diverse sciences that are, however, subordinated, which he calls subalternated, in the same sense in which, in bk. 1 of On Interpretation, he taught that propositions have a certain opposition, as it were Subaltern, when they are made of the same predicate and subject, but one is placed under the other, one being universal and the other particular. He asserts, then, that there are certain sciences of which one is concerned with some universal thing, and another with a particular thing contained under it: as Geometry, which is concerned with the line, and

Perspective, with the visual line; so Arithmetic with number, but Music with sonorous number. And the universal he calls Subalternating, but the particular

Subalternated; or the former containing and the latter contained. Of the nature and ratio of these sciences, then, we must treat (which all the interpreters of

Aristotle treat in the present chapter), in order that we may understand the difference of demonstration quia and propter quid designated in them. For what sciences are totally diverse, and how they differ in them, is well enough known.

Having expounded the names of subalternating and subalternated science, four things must be explained about them. First, what it is for one science to be subalternated to another. Second, whether such subalternation is possible. Third, in what way the subalternated science depends on the subalternating, and whether it can exist without it and have the true ratio of science. Fourth, whether the subalternated science, within its own limits, demonstrates the propter quid of its conclusions.

What the subalternation of sciences is. 22

Concerning the conditions required and sufficient for the subalternation of sciences, authors speak in diverse ways: for some assign more, others fewer; some the same, others diverse ones. But among all, Cajetan seems to have enumerated them best, in his treatise On the Subalternation of Sciences, where he reduced them all to four or five chief ones. The first is that the subject of one be contained under the subject of the other; for lack of which Medicine

is not subalternated to geometry: for curable body is not contained under line, but they are disparate. The second, that the subject of the inferior include the subject of the superior, and add over and above it some accidental difference; for lack of which the science of the species is not subalternated to the science of the genus. For although the species is under the genus, it does not add over and above the genus an accidental condition, but an essential differential one; whence the science of both is nearly always the same. The third condition is that the difference which it adds be not a proper attribute of the same subject: because, although an attribute is in a certain way an accidental difference, it is not purely accidental; and therefore it does not pertain to a distinct and subalternated science, but to the same one in which it is demonstrated of that subject. The fourth condition is that the principles of the inferior science be proved a priori and through the cause by the superior science. Now the principles which the subalternated science assumes for proving its conclusions are of two kinds: for some it takes from the subject of the subalternating science, and others from the matter of another science, to which the accidental condition belongs per se which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating science.

23 And all of the former, and they alone, the subalternating science must prove a priori, and not the others: because, since they pertain to the matter of another science, they cannot be proved by it. For example, Perspective assumes one principle that is as it were geometrical, from the matter of the line, which is the object of geometry, and another that is philosophical, from the matter of the visual: for the visual pertains to natural philosophy.

Geometry, then, to which it is subalternated, must prove only those that are derived from its own matter or object, not those that pertain to natural philosophy. Of these conditions one or another will be found in some way in diverse sciences that are not subalternated, but all together can be found only in subalternated sciences; and therefore all together are required, and sufficient, for true and proper subalternation, so that only those sciences, and all those in which they are found, are truly and properly subalternated. And thus it has been explained what the subalternation of sciences is.

Whether the subalternation of sciences explained above is possible, or devised by the imagination alone. 24

We shall propose three arguments which seem to prove that the subalternation of sciences is not possible; and the first is this: Because if the object of the subalternated science adds an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating science, it follows that the subalternated science is not one science per se. The consequence is proved: because a science takes its

unity per se from its object; but its object is not one per se but per accidens, since it consists of a twofold being in act, as visual line or sonorous number shows; therefore neither will it be one science per se, but per accidens. Second: The subalternating and the subalternated science must be distinct in species; but they cannot be distinguished in species if the same condition is true; therefore neither will subalternation be possible. The minor is proved: because sciences are distinguished in species by their objects; but the object of the subalternated science is distinguished only accidentally from the object of the subalternating science, since it adds over and above it only an accidental difference, as visual line is distinguished only accidentally from line; therefore the subalternated science itself will be distinguished only accidentally from the subalternating science. This also seems to be proved from the last condition of subalternation, that the subalternating science must prove a priori the principles of the subalternated science: for if this is true, the principles of the subalternated science will be conclusions of the subalternating; but conclusions pertain to the same science in which they are proved a priori; therefore the subalternated science will make one and the same science with the subalternating. Third: If the subalternated science adds in its subject an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating, it follows that its object has a twofold part: one will be the object of the subalternating science, but the other the accidental condition added over and above it, and pertaining indeed to another science; which supposed, there will be no greater reason why it should be called subalternated to one rather than to the other; and therefore it will be subalternated neither to one nor to the other, but subalternation itself will be reckoned impossible. For example: the object of perspective, which is the visual line, includes a twofold part, namely line, pertaining to Geometry, and the accidental condition of visual, pertaining to natural Philosophy; therefore there will be no greater reason for which it should be subalternated to one of them rather than to the other, and so it will not be subalternated to either of them.

25 Notwithstanding these things, however, all hold with Aristotle that the subalternation of sciences is possible, and that there are some sciences subalternated to others, in which those four conditions concur, as perspective is subalternated to geometry, and music to arithmetic.

But concerning the solution of the first argument there is the first opinion, of Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9, who asserts that the subalternated science is one per se and distinct from the subalternating: because the difference which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating is not a common accident, but a proper attribute of that same object of the subalternating: as visual, he says, is not a common accident of line, but a proper attribute of it; because line belongs to quantity, and quantity is per se sensible, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul 2; therefore line is per se visible,

so that visibility is its proper attribute; and from a subject and a proper attribute there comes about something one per se and not per accidens, as there does from a subject and a common accident, as from body and whiteness.

26 This view, however, is false, and is refuted as such by Cajetan in the present chapter. It is proved evidently, because the two things it asserts are openly false. The first: that visual is a proper attribute of line as it is the object of geometry. For geometry is a mathematical science, abstracting from sensible matter; therefore it deals with line as it abstracts from sensible matter; but visual is a per se sensible condition, since it implies a relation to sight; therefore it is evident that it does not belong to line as it is the object of geometry. Wherefore it will be false that the condition which perspective adds over and above geometry is a proper attribute of the object of geometry. Indeed, even if we granted that it is its proper attribute, the second thing it asserts is false, that it makes something one per se with line: because a proper attribute is a true accident, and outside the essence of the subject; therefore if a common accident cannot make something one per se with its subject, neither will a proper accident be able to make something one per se with it. For risible no less than white is composed of a twofold being in act, namely of subject and accident. And finally: if the condition added to the object of the subalternated science is a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, it will pertain to the same science with it. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute of the object of any science is proved of it in the science whose object it is.

27 Our view, therefore, asserts first of all that the condition which the object of the subalternated science adds is not a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, but a common accident. The object, however, that includes such a condition, as visual line, can be taken in two ways. One way, as it includes both by way of aggregation. And in this way it is evident that it is one per accidens and cannot be the object of a science: because, as so taken, it does not have one nature or essence, but a twofold essence; nor one definition, nor determinate attributes that could be proved of it. In another way it is taken as it includes one with order to the other, or the one as determined by the other, and the other as determining. And so it is one per se, not in entity but in order; which unity suffices for it to be able to be defined and considered per se by one science, and for determinate attributes to be able to be proved of it in that science. And in this way the object of the subalternated science is considered by it: wherefore as one per se, from which that science will have it that it is one science per se. And therefore on this side the subalternation of sciences will not be impossible.

The second argument is answered by another distinction: for
