whether by reduction to the first indemonstrable principles, or in another way.

33 This distinction supposed, our view is contained in two conclusions. The first is: To the essence of science considered in the first way evidence pertains. This is proved: Because if someone demonstrates a conclusion through a cause or an effect known by the natural light of the intellect, he must have evidence of the premises, since they are manifest to him under the clarity of the natural light; and the consequence also is evident there in the same way; therefore the conclusion deduced from them is also evident. The consequence is proved: because from a per se cause evident in every respect an evident effect too must follow; but from such an evident assent to the conclusion the habit of science is generated; therefore it too will be evident essentially. But although evidence is an essential predicate of science, Aristotle did not express it in the definition, because it was sufficiently manifest that it was contained in the words of that same definition. But if someone wishes to express it, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through its cause. And if he wishes to define all science, both quia and propter quid, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

Second conclusion: To the essence of science taken in that more universal acceptation evidence does not pertain; but it can be defined thus: Science is a certain cognition of a thing through demonstration. This is proved: Because Theology, which is had from the principles of divine faith, is a certain cognition of a thing through true demonstration; therefore in some way it is science. The consequence is proved: because it is not opinion, nor human faith, since it is certain; nor is it divine faith, because faith does not rest on demonstration nor on any other argumentation, but only on divine testimony; whereas a Theological conclusion does not rest immediately on testimony but on demonstration, although one of the premises, or both, rests on divine testimony, and so is an assent of faith.

But neither does the same Theological conclusion pertain to understanding, which is the habit of principles, since it is deduced through demonstration; therefore it pertains to the habit of science. I prove the consequence again: because there is not, nor can there be, any other habit to which it could pertain. If, then, Theology is science, though imperfect because it is not evident, it must agree in some way with science taken in the first way; and therefore some ratio of science common to both can be abstracted, to whose essence evidence does not pertain. And this is the one which, considered under this common ratio, has been defined by us.

Whether there is science of singulars, of contingents, and of beings per accidens.

oncerning these three we shall say very briefly and separately what is to

C           be held. And first, concerning singulars, a distinction must be made: for

some are singulars which are at the same time species, or contain the specific perfection eminently and most perfectly, as God and the angels; and, as many hold, in the angels the specific difference is not distinguished from the individual one. And concerning these singulars it is certain among all that the most perfect science can be had. Others are singulars in which the individual difference is distinguished from the specific one and is outside its ratio, as are corruptible things; and perhaps the angels too have this, for it is very probable that they can be multiplied under the same species; and concerning these there can be a doubt whether they can be objects of science, or whether science can be only of universals.

35 Next, science must be distinguished, because it can be taken in three ways. First, for a certain and evident cognition of a thing, had through discursive reasoning or without it, by simple intuition; and concerning science taken in this way it is certain that it is concerned with any singulars whatever. For God and the angels, through intuitive cognition, without discursive reasoning, know all singulars most perfectly; and such intuitive cognition of theirs has the most perfect ratio of science. We too can have science of God and the angels; and by means of the senses we have intuitive cognition of sensible singulars, which according to this acceptation can be called science. In the second way science is taken for that only which is discursive, had through an evident consequence, whether it be a true demonstration or not. In the third way it is taken for discursive science, but had through a true demonstration. The doubt, then, proceeds concerning science taken in these two ways: whether it can be had of corruptible singulars.

But these singulars are further considered in two ways. First, as they participate in the specific nature in which they agree, namely the human nature or another. Second, as they are distinct through their own individual differences; and this is to consider them as they are singulars formally and reduplicatively. And if they are considered in the first way, it is certain that there can also be science of them in some way. For since there can be science per se, primarily and immediately, of the species, there will also be science of the singulars through participation and application of that same science of the species to them: because, if it is proved of man through demonstration that he is risible, it

can be proved of Peter or John, by applying the same demonstration to him and proving through it that he is risible.

36 And in this way, in the science of Theology, some things are demonstrated of Christ our Lord as man, from principles of faith and propositions that are at the same time evident: for instance, that he is risible because he is a man, through this demonstration applied to him: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible.

The whole difficulty, then, concerns these same singulars as they are singulars and distinct through their own individual differences: whether there can be discursive science of them, taken in the second or the third way. And some say that there can, while others say that it is altogether repugnant. Meanwhile our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Discursive science had through true demonstration cannot in any way be of singulars taken in this way. This is proved evidently: because a true demonstration is a true syllogism, disposed in mood and figure, and proceeding from universal indemonstrable principles, whose middle is a true definition composed of genus and difference; but this cannot be made from singular terms; therefore neither can it be had of singulars.

37 For disposition in mood and figure cannot be found in singular terms except improperly, as in the expository syllogism, which is a syllogism very improperly, through a certain likeness to the one that is made in universal terms.

Second: Because of a singular, as it is singular, nothing can be proved except a singular property, belonging to it alone; but through universal principles nothing can be proved except a universal or common property, since it belongs equally to all the singulars, that is, no more to one than to another; therefore such science cannot in any way be of singulars as they are singulars. And since discursive science is said properly and absolutely only of this kind, it must also be said absolutely that there cannot be discursive science of singulars. Therefore Aristotle, in many places of his doctrine, expressly and without any distinction denies that there can be science of singulars, and the common manner of speaking of the whole School holds the same.

38 Second conclusion: Speaking naturally, there cannot be science of singulars as they are singulars even through an evident consequence which is not a demonstration. This is proved by this argument: To have science of something is to prove some property of it through an evident consequence; but of a singular as such we cannot naturally prove any property through an evident consequence; therefore neither have true science

of it. I prove the minor: because the property of a singular as singular is that which follows from its own individual difference, or from the singular as constituted through it; but we know with certainty no determinate individual difference, nor any such property, nor can it be known with certainty by us naturally, as is manifest to all; therefore neither can we prove it of the singular itself through an evident consequence, nor in this way have science of it, even improper science.

Whether there can be science of being per accidens.

Being per accidens is the name given to that which is composed of several beings in act, as white or musician; concerning which we ask: Whether there can be science of it had through true demonstration?

39 And some distinguish a twofold being per accidens. One, which results from two beings in act concurring by chance or fortuitously, as a musician or a builder, or also the finding of a treasure. And of this they deny that there can be science, because it is not only a being per accidens according to its being, but neither can it fall per se under the consideration of the intellect; but just as the things of which it consists are joined by chance, so they stand altogether per accidens in relation to the consideration of the intellect. The other is the being per accidens which results from two things concurring naturally and united, as White, Quantified, etc.; and of this they say there can be science, because although it is a being per accidens according to its being, yet it can be considered per se by the intellect, be defined per se, and attributes can be demonstrated per se of it. For we define white as that which is disgregative of sight; and quantified, as a body having extended parts.

Our view, however, is that there can be science of no being per accidens as it is a being per accidens; and concerning being per accidens resulting from two things concurring by chance or rarely, Aristotle expressly holds this, Metaph. bk. 6, texts 5, 6, and 7. But in order that we may prove it of any other also, it should be noted that it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is composed of two beings in act by way of aggregation, that is, with no order considered in them: such is a heap, such is white and musician, as we consider in them only one aggregate of many actual things. Second, it can be considered as consisting of two things ordered, namely one as determinable, the other as determining. And considered in the first way it is called one per accidens in every way. Wherefore there cannot be science of it.

40 This is proved: Because it has in no way one nature, nor one ratio; wherefore it cannot be explained by one definition,

nor have determinate attributes which can be demonstrated of it. Therefore

Aristotle’s doctrine, in the place cited, extends to every being per accidens. But if it is considered in the second way, although it is one per accidens in entity, it is nevertheless one per se in order; and therefore it can be defined by one definition, in the way in which white and quantified are defined by those definitions which we adduced. It can also have determinate attributes which are proved of it. And music and perspective treat of sonorous number, taken in this way, and of the visual line, as of their proper objects, as we saw in ch. 10, and these are true sciences.

Whether there is science of things by chance and by fortune. 41

That is called Chance which consists of two things concurring by chance: as that summertime is cold and rainy. But Fortuitous, that which comes about from two things concurring by fortune (as it is said): as the finding of a treasure with the digging of the earth. Now these can be considered in two ways. First, in common, as they are called chance or fortuitous things. In another way, in particular, as it is this one or that. And of them considered in the first way there can be science, because the ratio of the chance or fortuitous, considered in common, is per se one and per se considerable. Therefore Aristotle treats of chance and fortune, so considered, in Phys. bk. 2. But of the same considered in particular no science can be had, because they have no ratio per se considerable, but are utterly contingent and per accidens. Wherefore they can neither be defined per se, nor have any attribute demonstrable of them.

T R E AT I S E I I I .

On Opinion and Human Faith.

What opinion is, and what human faith is.

hree things are to be explained concerning opinion and human faith. 42

T           First: What each is. Second: How they are distinguished. Third: Whether

opinion, and consequently human faith, can exist together with science.

Opinion we can define thus: Opinion is the assent to some non-necessary proposition, through a probable middle, or without one. In assent it agrees with science and the other intellectual cognitions; and by the same particle there is understood to be excluded from the ratio of opinion any thought whatever, or estimation, or suspicion, or doubt, by which the intellect, not determined

to either part of a contradiction, does not assent to it, but either thinks lightly, or as it were hesitates or hangs between the two parts. For assent says its determination to one part or the other, which it reckons true, or at least probable. And it is called Probable in order that it may be distinguished from science and understanding, which are evident assents. But it is distinguished from human faith by those particles, Through a probable middle, or without one: because human faith is not had through a probable middle, nor without one, but through the testimony of one worthy of belief.

Through a probable middle, or without one, is said also so that we may understand that opinion is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, through simple intuition alone of the probable truth itself, which Aristotle defined thus in the present chapter, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. The other is that which is had through a probable middle. For it is gathered either from an immediate opinion, through an evident or a probable consequence; or from an evident proposition, through a merely probable consequence; and in both ways it is said to be had through a probable middle, because it is merely probable either on the part of the proposition from which it is gathered, or on the part of the consequence. Thus, just as certain and evident assent is twofold, namely either evident per se, which the intellect has once the signification of the terms is known, and it is called Understanding; or evident through a demonstrative middle, and it is called Science: in the same way probable assent is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms is known: as when the intellect, having known the signification of the terms of this proposition, Every mother loves her son, at once, awaiting no reason, assents to it probably; and it can be called Understanding of opinion. The other probable assent is the one which is had through a probable middle, as has been set out. And thus opinion is twofold, distinct without doubt in species through the diverse mode of assenting, from the cognition of the terms alone, or through a middle; and the definition assigned comprehends both.

Human faith, on the other hand, can be defined thus: Human faith is a probable assent had on account of the testimony of one worthy of belief. So that through Probable assent it agrees with opinion and is distinguished from the other cognitions or assents of the intellect, as we said of opinion; but through Testimony it is distinguished from opinion. And so much for the first point.

Whether fear is of the intrinsic ratio of opinion and of human faith.

This too pertains to the explanation of the quiddity of opinion and human faith. In order that it may be understood, it must be explained

first of all: What is signified by fear. And it is nothing other than an apprehension lest the part to which the intellect assents be false, or the opposite true. For opinion, as we said, is a probable assent under which it is not repugnant that falsehood lie: that is, it is a certain weak assent, of whose truth one rightly fears, or can fear, because the intellect adheres to it in such a way that the foundation on account of which it adheres to it (which is the truth itself, probable per se, or the reason through which it deduced the conclusion from the premises) is not altogether solid nor firm, but such as can fail by its own nature, and be otherwise. The doubt, then, is whether this fear, which they call apprehension, pertains to the essence of opinion or of human faith.

44 The first opinion distinguishes a twofold opinion, Perfect and Imperfect. It calls perfect opinion the one which rests on the testimony of one worthy of belief; but imperfect, the one which rests on probable reasons. And it asserts that fear in no way pertains to the essence of the former, because it says not only the determinate assent to one part, but a firm and certain one: not on account of the firmness of the testimony, but on account of the efficacious determination of the will, by reason of which the intellect adheres to the same part not only firmly but also tenaciously, as we adduced above from Aristotle. But imperfect opinion has fear essentially annexed, without which it neither is found nor can in any way be found. So Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue; Diego Mas, on the present chapter, who says that Capreolus and Cajetan, whom he himself cites, hold so; and, what is more, St. Thomas in many places of his doctrine, especially 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he says thus: It is of the ratio of opinion that one part is accepted with fear of the other opposite, etc.

It proves it also by reason. For he who opines judges that the opinion which he follows can be false; therefore by the very ratio of opining he fears lest it be false; wherefore this fear or apprehension is intrinsic to opinion.

For the solution of this question a twofold fear must be distinguished. For one is Actual, which is an actual fear; the other Virtual, or radical, which does not consist in any actual fear or doubting, but only in this: that the assent of opinion is such, on the part of the object or of the middle of assenting, that it is not repugnant to it that falsehood lie under it. And from this root there is sometimes born an actual fear or apprehension lest the opposite part be true, or that part false to which the intellect assents; and therefore it is called virtual or radical fear.

45 This distinction supposed, our view is that virtual or radical fear pertains to the essence of opinion, or of human faith

but that actual fear is altogether accidental to it, so that it is often found without it. This is the common opinion of almost all the expositors of Aristotle on the present chapter. And it is proved by the express testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, where he speaks thus of opinion: For whether it be true opinion and not science by which men act incontinently, it makes no difference to the argument, since some of those who opine do not doubt, but think they know with certainty.

And it is proved by evident experience: Because there are many opinions, not only in Dialectic but also in Philosophy and Theology, approved by the common consent of almost the whole School and confirmed by efficacious arguments, which we follow without any actual fear or apprehension. And sometimes we see some men deduce from evident principles some conclusion through a syllogism which they think evident, but which is in truth only probable, and such men judge the conclusion to be certain, although in them it is truly only opinion; therefore it is repugnant that they should at the same time have fear lest it be false, or the opposite true. Wherefore it is evident that actual apprehension is not intrinsic to opinion, since it is often found without it. Virtual or radical fear, however, is intrinsic even to these opinions, since on the part of the middle of assenting it is not repugnant that falsehood lie under them.

The testimony of St. Thomas, moreover, is understood of this virtual fear, not of the actual.

To the argument: granting the antecedent with the consequence, the consequent must be distinguished. For if it is understood of actual fear or apprehension, it is false; but if of virtual or radical fear, true; and therefore the argument proves that only this is intrinsic to opinion, not the other.

Whether opinion can exist together with science concerning the same proposition and in the same intellect.

It is certain that opinion can exist together with science concerning the same thing.

For of the line the Geometer has science, and the Dialectician or Metaphysician has opinion whether it is really distinguished from substance. Nor is it certain only that they can exist at the same time concerning the same thing in diverse men or intellects, but also in the same intellect. For the same geometer has science of the line, and can at the same time have opinion about its distinction from substance. Therefore the title of the question does not ask whether they can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same simple thing, but whether concerning the same proposition. Of which it is certain also that in diverse

intellects there can be science and opinion.

47 For it can happen that someone has the assent to some conclusion through a true demonstration which another deduces from the same or other principles through a probable syllogism, and therefore has only opinion. The difficulty, then, is whether the same man can at the same time have science and opinion concerning the same proposition.

But a further distinction must be made concerning science and opinion, because it can be conceived in four ways that they exist at the same time. First, according to habit: so that the same man has at the same time the habit of science and of opinion concerning the same conclusion. Second, so that he has at the same time the assent of each. Third, that he has at the same time the habit of science and the assent of opinion. Fourth, that he has at the same time the habit of opinion and the assent of science. And the present question seems to proceed according to all the comparisons.

On it the first opinion is the negative one, of Scotus, in 3, d. 24, single q., § Contra haec 1; of Cajetan and Soto on the present chapter; and of Diego Mas, in the same place, q. 5. They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle in this chapter, where he proposed almost the same question, whether the same object can be known and opined by the same man. To which he answered that it cannot. And he proves it by this argument: The knowable is that which cannot be otherwise; but the opinable, that which can be otherwise, as it is opinable. But it is repugnant that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictories; therefore it will be repugnant that something be at the same time knowable and opinable, or known and opined. But these are the proper objects of science and opinion; therefore it will also be repugnant, according to the mind of Aristotle, that both exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition.

48 It is proved next by reason. First, concerning the acts or assents; then concerning the habits. Concerning the acts, indeed: Because it is impossible that the same man judge at the same time that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictory judgments. But the assent of science is an actual judgment concerning the conclusion, that it cannot be otherwise; and the assent of opinion is a judgment concerning the same, that it can be otherwise; therefore they contain an actual repugnance; wherefore they cannot exist at the same time in the same intellect. And, what is more, these assents are repugnant as the evident and the inevident: because evidence is of the intrinsic ratio of the one, while the other is inevident by its own nature, since it is contingent, either on the part of the principle from which it is deduced or on the part of the probable middle through which it is deduced. But the evident and the inevident are opposed privatively, like light and darkness, because evidence is the manifestation of an object under the clarity of a light; therefore it is repugnant that they exist at the same time in the same intellect, just as it is repugnant

that light and darkness exist at the same time in the same part of the air.

49 Concerning the habits, they prove it second: Because acts and habits are concerned with the same object and through the same middle; and a habit is an inclination to an act concerning such an object and through such a middle; therefore they have altogether the same repugnance as the acts; wherefore neither can they exist at the same time.

The second opinion is that of Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue, no. 20, where he distinguishes opinion: for, he says, it can be had in two ways. First, from probable premises, or from evident ones, through a probable middle, and one known as such by the one who opines. Second, from necessary premises, and evident ones, and through a middle that is truly probable, but reckoned evident by the one who opines. And if it is had in the first way, it is repugnant that it exist at the same time with science, both according to act and according to habit, as the first opinion asserts, with which it agrees in this. But if it is had in the second way, they can exist at the same time, both according to the acts and according to the habits; in which it contradicts the same opinion.

Therefore he proves this second point by such an argument. The whole repugnance of the assent of opinion and of science comes from this: that by the one it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, but by the other that it can be otherwise. But when opinion is had through a middle thought to be evident, and from evident premises, it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, just as by the assent of science; therefore there remains in them no repugnance or opposition on account of which they could not exist at the same time. On the contrary, they are altogether in conformity, because by both the conclusion is judged necessary, and therefore such that it cannot be otherwise. But two conformable causes can well concur to the same effect; and if the assents are not repugnant in this way, it will be evident that the habits are not repugnant, which can be repugnant only on account of the assents.

50 The third opinion is that of certain moderns, altogether opposed to these two, because it affirms that science and opinion can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, in the same intellect, both according to act and according to habit, and whether the opinion is had through a probable middle reckoned as such by the one who opines, or reckoned necessary. Only concerning the proposition of which each assent is, does it distinguish in this way: for it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is a certain proposition about which each habit or assent is concerned. Second, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, or of a probable syllogism. And the first consideration, it says, is as it were material, the second as it were formal: because there is one and the same proposition about which they are concerned; but that same proposition is the conclusion of each syllogism, and since these are distinguished in species,

[p. 713]

the same proposition is as it were a twofold conclusion, formally and specifically distinct; whence it comes about that each assent and habit is indeed of the same proposition, but not of the same conclusion, rather of conclusions formally diverse. And they say this is the opinion of Alexander of Hales, 3 p., q. 79, memb. 3; St. Bonaventure, in 3, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3; Durandus, q. 1 of the prologue, and in 3, d. 31, q. 4; William of Auxerre, Summa bk. 3, tit. 3, q. 4 and 5; Richard of Middleton, in 3, d. 15, q. 1; and Villalpando on the present chapter; and also St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he grants that the same proposition can be known through diverse middles, an evident and a probable one, as through a perfect and an imperfect middle, which are not altogether repugnant; which he repeats in 3 p., q. 9, a. 3, ad 2, where Father Francisco Suárez follows the same opinion.

51 They prove it first: Because the whole repugnance on account of which the assents of opinion and science concerning the same proposition cannot exist at the same time is that it is repugnant that it be judged at the same time that it can be otherwise and cannot, since these two judgments are contradictory. But this would be so if each were to be judged through the same middle. But since this is done through diverse middles, it would contain no repugnance or contradiction: because it is in no way repugnant that the intellect judge that a proposition cannot be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, and that it can be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a probable syllogism; nor are these two judgments, compared to diverse middles, opposed contradictorily. Which is especially true since actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, nor is it necessary that the one who opines actually judge that the conclusion can be otherwise; indeed he can judge the contrary, as Durandus noted.

Second: Because together with a demonstration a probable reason can be, and usually is, adduced to prove the same conclusion, just as together with divine faith, for believing the same truth; therefore the intellect assents at the same time on account of both middles; and therefore each will have its own effect, which is the probable and the scientific assent, and they will exist at the same time; otherwise each middle would be adduced in vain.

52 Our view is as it were a middle one, and is explained in one conclusion: Science and opinion according to habit can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition, but not according to assent or act. By the first part the first opinion is excluded, and in part the second. By the second part, the second is also excluded in part, and the third as well. Moreover, those authors whom the last opinion cites for itself hold our view, as will be plain to one who reads them; for he will see (unless I am mistaken

) that they grant concerning the habits alone that they can exist at the same time, not concerning the assents. And this is the sense of St. Thomas, especially in the last place, if his words are attentively considered.

But in order that we may at once explain and prove it, it should be noted that science and opinion, while they affirm the truth of the same proposition, are not opposed contradictorily, nor privatively, indeed not by any kind of opposition: Because things of which each affirms cannot be opposed contradictorily; nor is it necessary that the judgments of the two be opposed contradictorily, so that by the judgment of science it is said that the proposition cannot be otherwise, but by the opinative judgment that it can be otherwise. For, as the second and third opinions prove well, it is not necessary that such a judgment be found in the one who opines; rather it is often not found, and sometimes the contrary is found. Further, neither are they opposed privatively: because the assent of opinion does not lack evidence, nor is it properly deprived of it, but it says a certain negation of it, just as any species says the negation of another; and yet they are not on that account said to be opposed privatively or contradictorily, but to be disparate. And so science and opinion stand.

53 And yet they are not altogether disparate or diverse, but very similar, since they are ordered to the same end, which is to make truth firm in the intellect; except that science effects this altogether, but opinion in some part, not fully or perfectly. Therefore they are distinguished only as the perfect and the imperfect, as St. Thomas says excellently in the last place: because science is as it were a perfect form, but opinion as it were a disposition to it; and they have these rationes of perfect and imperfect from their own nature and essence. But the perfect and the imperfect are repugnant in two ways, or in respect of two things. First, in respect of the same form: because it is repugnant that the same form be by its own nature a habit and a disposition; and thus it is repugnant that the same quality or habit be at the same time science and opinion. Second, it is repugnant in order to the same subject: because it is impossible that the same body be at the same time perfectly and imperfectly hot, or the same part of the air perfectly and imperfectly illuminated. And this repugnance science and opinion without doubt have in respect of the same subject, concerning the same proposition. Because opinion does not altogether, or not fully, determine the intellect to its truth, nor make it firm or stable; but it determines it indeed in a certain infirm and weak manner, and leaves it as it were undetermined in some part; and every opinion whatever has this from its nature and essence,

[p. 715]

however it is had, even through a probable middle reckoned necessary. But science fully, perfectly, and altogether determines the intellect to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and also renders it altogether firm and stable.

54 From which each part of our view can be efficaciously proved. First, indeed, that science and opinion cannot exist at the same time according to the acts or assents, against the second and third opinions, by this argument: It is impossible that something be at the same time fully and altogether determined, and not fully and altogether determined, concerning the same thing, since these are opposed contradictorily. But by the scientific assent the intellect is fully and altogether determined to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and is rendered firm and stable in it; and by the assent of opinion it is neither altogether determined, nor made firm and stable; therefore it is repugnant that these two exist at the same time in the intellect concerning the same truth. But you will say, for the third opinion, that this argument concludes that it is repugnant for the intellect to be in both ways at the same time in respect of the same middle, but not by reason of diverse middles. It is therefore proved efficaciously that it is repugnant even through diverse middles: because for the intellect to be at the same time convinced and not convinced concerning the same truth, from whatever source this comes, whether through the same or a diverse middle, is plainly repugnant, since these are to be and not to be at the same time in respect of the same thing; therefore it does not remove the difficulty of the argument that this happens through diverse middles. And if it can happen through diverse middles, it follows that a scientific assent and an erroneous one can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, so that the intellect judges at the same time that it is true and false: true indeed through demonstration, but false through a probable syllogism. For then the opposition will cease, because it is said to be only in respect of the same middle, not in respect of diverse middles; which things, however, are absurd.

Concerning the habits, however, it can easily be proved, because they do not say an actual determination of the intellect to the truth, but as it were a potential and habitual one. And it is not repugnant that the intellect be imperfectly determined in act and be able to be fully determined, although full actual determination is repugnant to the non-full. Whence that there be in the same intellect at diverse times a full and a non-full determination contains no repugnance; but that this should happen at the same time is supremely repugnant.

55 To the argument of Scotus, by which he proved the repugnance of the habits, the consequence must be denied: because although act and habit are concerned

with the same object and are had through the same middle, they nevertheless have far diverse rationes: because a habit is as it were an inclination, and as it were a potency to the act, whereas the act comes about through an actual attaining of the object. But it is not repugnant that someone have at the same time inclinations to repugnant acts, which he can exercise at diverse times, although it is repugnant to exercise both at the same time. Whence, although it is repugnant that the acts or assents of opinion and of science exist at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that the habits exist at the same time.

56 To the argument of Durandus: granting the major and the minor, the consequence must be denied. Because the repugnance of the assents of opinion and of science does not consist in the opposition of the judgments, of which it is well proved that it is not necessary that they be had at the same time; but in this: that the ratio of opinion is essentially imperfect, not altogether determining the intellect to the truth, nor making it firm in it; whereas the ratio of science is essentially perfect concerning the same thing, since it fully and altogether determines the intellect and makes it firm in the same truth. But for the intellect to be firm and stable in the same truth, and at the same time infirm and weak, is repugnant; and likewise to be at the same time altogether determined and undetermined. And this follows whether it happens through the same or through a diverse middle; and therefore it is repugnant that opinion and science exist at the same time concerning the same proposition in the same intellect. Thus, although actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, and although it can be had through a middle that is truly probable but thought necessary (which things are to be granted), nevertheless the assent of opinion has from its own intrinsic ratio that it does not altogether determine the intellect, nor make it firm in the truth. And therefore it cannot exist at the same time with the assent of science, which fully determines and makes it firm; but when this comes, and with it the full determination of the intellect, the former ceases: because all indetermination ceases, and some indetermination pertains to its essence; and therefore when all ceases, some ceases; and consequently there ceases the assent that is in some part undetermined and infirm: just as weakness of the limbs ceases when strength comes, and sickness ceases when health comes. And from these things it is plain that the arguments of the last opinion are solved. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the work of the Posterior Resolution.

The end of this work.

## SOME SELECTIONS FROM

THE BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S TOPICS,

BY WHICH STUDENTS OF THE LIBERAL

Arts of this most flourishing Academy of Alcalá may satisfy the customary questions of the

Masters in the examination to be undergone for the degree of Bachelor.

On the end and division of these books.

he end which Aristotle intends in these eight books of the Topics 1

T          is to hand down a Method of disputing probably on any theme whatever,

or proposed problem. And since the universal and principal instrument of Topical disputation is Dialectical reasoning, which we call the

Topical syllogism, he does two things in the whole work, so that we may propose its universal division. First, he explains the nature of the dialectical syllogism, and the parts of which it is composed. Second, because this syllogism is called Topical, that is, local, he copiously hands down and explains all the places from which we can draw an abundance of probable arguments, so that the Dialectician, thus instructed, may be able to set up any disputation whatever concerning probable matters. We, therefore, desiring to hand down in a certain brief summary the things which are necessary for understanding the

Topical art and for instructing students of the liberal arts, so that they may satisfy the customary questions of the examination to be undergone, shall carry out two other things in the same order. First, we shall explain what the

Dialectical syllogism is, and what and how many are the parts of which it must be composed, both simple ones, such as the Topical predicates, and also composite ones, such as the Dialectical problem and the Dialectical proposition, of which Aristotle treats through the first eight chapters of book 1. Then we shall summarily collect, enumerate, and explain the places from which probable arguments are to be drawn.

What the object of this work is, and its order with the other parts of Dialectic, is explained. 2

From these things it can easily be understood what the object of this work is. For if all the things which are treated in it are either

parts of the Dialectical syllogism, or places from which an abundance of probable arguments can be drawn, which are also ordered to the composition of the same syllogism, then the aim of the whole work, whose nature and properties Aristotle intends to explain in it, will be that same syllogism, and consequently its proper subject or object. For these are the principal conditions of an object. Nor will it be difficult to understand the order which the books of the Topics keep among the other parts of Logic, and the place due to them among the others; for they follow immediately the books on the

Posterior Resolution recently explained by us. The reason for this is: Because among the species of syllogisms, after demonstration, explained in the books of the Posterior Analytics, the dialectical syllogism is worthier than the others; therefore this treatise, dealing with it as with its proper object, must be placed immediately after those same books.

What a Dialectical predicate is. 3

The simple things of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are proximately composed, and the Dialectical syllogism remotely, are the

Topical or Dialectical predicates (which is the same thing), of which Aristotle treats in ch. 4 of the first book, where he enumerates them and explains each by its proper definition. The Topical predicate we can define in general thus: It is the principal part of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are composed.

We call it the principal part to distinguish it from the subject, of which the same Dialectical proposition is composed. For we do not wish now to call the copula of the proposition a part so much as the connection of each part, by which, when coupled, they compose the proposition.

How manifold the Dialectical predicate is. 4

On the one hand the Dialectical predicates seem to be five, on account of this argument: Because a predicate is distinguished from a predicable as act from potency; but act and potency must be numbered in the same way, because potency takes its unity and distinction from act; therefore there will be as many predicates as predicables. But it is established from Porphyry that the predicables are five; therefore the predicates too must be five.

But on the other hand they seem to be ten, on account of a second argument:

Because a category is nothing other than a series and ordering of predicates; therefore the number of predicates and of categories will be the same. But it is established that there are ten categories

[p. 719]

5 These things notwithstanding, our view is that there are only four Topical predicates, as Aristotle expressly teaches, bk. 1, ch. 4, which are: Definition, Genus, Property, and Accident, so that neither are more to be added nor any of these to be taken away. But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in assigning the reason on account of which Aristotle posited these four predicates. For whose explanation it should be noted that the end of this topical art, as we said, is to hand down a method of disputing probably on any thing proposed. But a disputation consists of three parts, ordered thus. First, of the Question, or interrogation, which we usually call the title of the disputation, saying thus: Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? or something similar. Next, of the Places from which probable arguments are to be drawn, by which means we may render the question doubtful; and in the third place, of the Arguments themselves, which are Dialectical syllogisms composed of Dialectical propositions. Now the Dialectical proposition (as will be said afterward) is one part of the problem. And problems, and consequently Dialectical propositions, are made of predicates: because a problem is nothing other than a question or interrogation whether some predicate belongs to such a subject: as when we say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? it is the same as if we asked whether this predicate, incorruptible, belongs to the heavens, or not. Whence it follows that a topical predicate is nothing other than that which can be asked about some thing. There will therefore be as many predicates as there can be questions made about some thing, and as many questions as predicates. And since a question is the same as a problem, the number of predicates and of problems will be the same. And finally, since a proposition and a problem differ only in the form of the interrogation (because a problem is an interrogation of both parts of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible or not, you make a problem; whereas a proposition is an interrogation of one of the two parts, as Do you think the heavens are incorruptible?), there are as many Dialectical propositions as problems. And thus it is understood that the Dialectical predicate is the first thing from which the number of problems must be taken; then from the number of problems, the number of Dialectical propositions. And thus the number of predicates is taken from the order to the problems and propositions to be constituted. And this discourse is drawn from ch. 4 of bk. 1.

6 This supposed, it is proved by Aristotle by this argument that there are only four predicates. A predicate is that which can be asked about some thing for setting up a Dialectical disputation; but four

only can be asked; therefore there are only four predicates. He proves the minor: For either we ask about something its definition, in order that we may understand its nature; or its genus, in order that we may understand in which category it is; or its properties, or its common accidents. And nothing else can be asked which is not reduced to these; therefore there are four predicates, so that there are neither more nor fewer. And these are definition, genus, property, and accident, which he explains by their definitions thus in ch. 4 of bk. 1. Definition is an expression signifying what it was to be. He says it is an expression because it is not a proposition, since it contains neither truth nor falsehood, as rational animal. He also calls the definition a term, taking the metaphor from the boundaries of fields. For to any field there belongs alone and wholly that which is enclosed within its boundaries, so that nothing of it is outside, but the whole that it has is comprehended within its boundaries. So the definition contains whatever pertains to the essence of the thing, so that nothing of it is outside, nor is there anything of it that is not comprehended within it; and therefore it is called a term by Aristotle. Genus, he says, is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, in quid, as animal. Property, that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, as risible in respect of man. Accident is that which is neither definition, nor genus, nor property, but belongs to the thing; or also: Accident is that which can belong to the same thing, as whiteness in respect of a wall.

7 But if you say: Beyond these four questions, or interrogations, or problems, which seem to be general, many special ones can be asked about a thing: as whether it is a man, whether it is a lion, whether it is a substance, and innumerable others; therefore more than four, indeed innumerable predicates must be granted. And besides, the general predicates are still more: because just as we ask about the genus of some thing, as whether Animal is the genus of man or not, so we can ask about its difference, namely whether Rational is the difference of man; and also about the species, as whether Man is the species of Peter or John, or even whether it is a species of animal; therefore two other general predicates must be added, namely Species and Difference.

8 Concerning the first part of the argument, about the special interrogations, Rudolph Agricola, On Dialectical Invention bk. 1, ch. 3, asserts that Aristotle erred in assigning the number of predicates: because, just as there are many kinds of particular problems, so more predicates than four must be established. But this author seems to me to have erred more in reproving Aristotle, because the true solution is to be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, Topics bk. 1, ch. 4, and bk. 5, last chapter, toward the end. he asserts two things. The first: Since problems are ordered to dialectical disputation, whose end is the determination of the same problem about which the dispute is held, so that, after probable arguments have been set out for each side, it may finally be decided which of them is the more probable, it follows that all problems which are determined by the same arguments and in the same way belong to the same genus of problem; and that all their predicates are comprised under one of the four designated. And therefore in this first place he asserts that difference, if it is general, that is, if it is predicated of several species as a genus is, must be counted together with genus, and that no other predicate is to be added for it. The second is what he teaches in the second place: that a question of accident is settled, or determined, solely from someone’s proving that it belongs to the subject. From this doctrine we deduce that all special problems, whatever they may be, are reduced to the problem of accident, and all their predicates to the predicate of accident. And the reason for this deduction is that in every special problem it is asked: Does this predicate belong to such a subject, or is it in it, or not? which plainly has the mode of interrogation, or of problem, of accident, in which we ask only whether an accident belongs to, or is in, the subject. And they are settled, or determined, by exactly the same arguments: because if you ask whether animal belongs to man or not, or whether man belongs to Peter or not, it is sufficiently determined, and the disputation about it will be finished, if we prove that it is in it in any way whatever, even though it is not proved to be of its essence, or to be convertible with it, or to belong to it in any other special way. Therefore they are reduced to the form of an accidental problem, and their predicates are comprised under the predicate of accident, and there is no need to multiply others.

From the same doctrine we can reply to the other part of the same argument, concerning species and difference: that if the difference is subaltern, it is reduced to the predicate of genus; but if it is lowest, to the predicate of definition. Species, however, is reduced to the predicate of genus. And the reason for all of these is that a question of genus and of subaltern difference is settled by the same arguments, since each is predicated of several things differing in species, in quid. For by the same arguments we prove that animal is the genus of man, and that sensible is its subaltern difference; and also that man is the species of Peter and John, because just as genus is predicated in quid of species, so species is predicated of individuals. By the same arguments we also prove that rational animal is the definition of man, and that rational is its atomic difference. As to what concerns species, a quite probable reply is also given by Albert

that it is not to be enumerated among the predicates: because predicates are taken by relation to a common subject, which species does not regard, but singulars. And the reason for this is that predicates, as we were saying, are ordered by their proper ratio to constituting problems and dialectical propositions, and each of these to constituting the dialectical syllogism, which is not constituted per se out of singular propositions, but out of those consisting of a common subject, in which alone the syllogistic form, consisting of mood and figure, can be found, as is manifest per se.

11 To the first argument, concerning the predicables: the antecedent must be distinguished. For predicate taken universally is distinguished from predicable as act from potency, and therefore it is numbered in the same way as predicable. But predicate taken specially, for the Topical one, does not regard the predicable as a potency, but is taken only for the actual one, and indeed in a special mode, distinct from the general predicate, that is, in order to setting up a question, or problem. Hence predicates are also numbered in another, different way, and are allotted a number different from the predicables, and also from the categories, which belong to the ordering of predicates as they are considered under a general ratio, not under a special and Topical one, ordered also to the special end already explained. Wherefore it does not follow from the fact that the categories are ten that the Topical predicates must be as many. And this is the solution of the second argument.

What a dialectical problem is, and how many kinds there are.

12

Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 3, defines the dialectical problem, saying that it is an interrogation, or question, of either part of a contradiction: as if you say,

Whether walking two-footed animal is the definition of man, or not? And there are four genera of problems, as the same Aristotle asserts in ch. 3 and 4, just as there are four predicates. Thus the Problem of definition, such as the one assigned from the definition of man. The Problem of genus, as if you say, Whether animal is the genus of man, or not? The Problem of property, as when we say,

Whether risible is a property of man, or not? And finally the Problem of accident:

Whether whiteness is an accident of the wall, or not? In ch. 9 of the same book, too, Aristotle divides the dialectical problem universally, saying that one is

Practical: that which pertains to choice or avoidance, or to something to be pursued

[p. 723]

or avoided. For this, he says, is ordered to practice, or operation, and therefore it is called practical. Such is this: Whether pleasure is to be chosen, or not.

Another, however, is Speculative: that which contains nothing about something to be pursued or avoided, nor is ordered to operation, but only to the cognition of truth: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not?

The problem can also be divided by another division, according to the matters of the diverse sciences in which it is found; for which reason we say that one is a Physical problem, as, Whether the principle of motion and rest of that in which it is, is the definition of nature, or not? Another Metaphysical, as if you should say, Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or not?

Nevertheless, the formal consideration of all problems, according to which they are reduced to those four, taken from the diverse predicates, is proper to the dialectician: because it pertains to the dialectician alone to teach all how a disputation is to be set up, and what instruments are to be used in it for attaining cognition of the truth about which the dispute is held.

What a dialectical proposition is, and how many kinds there are; and how it is distinguished from a problem. 14

Three things Aristotle delivers in bk. 1, ch. 3, at the end. In the first place he defines the dialectical proposition as being, as it were, the proposition of the other part of a contradiction: as if you say, Do you think that rational animal is the definition of man? And he says that it differs from the problem not in reality but in mode: because the Proposition, as the etymology of the word shows, proposes something to another, so that he may reply to the thing proposed, explaining what he judges or thinks about it. The Problem, however, has the mode of a question, and proposes both parts to be debated by way of a question: as if you say, Whether rational animal is the definition of man, or not? Thus the dialectical proposition interrogates by way of a simple proposition, not by way of a question, and takes up only one part; whereas the problem takes up both, and interrogates by way of a question. This is customarily put forward in two ways: either by interrogating both parts formally, as in the example assigned; or one formally and the other virtually, as if you should say only,

Whether rational animal is the definition of man? And in this way problems are put forward in the common usage of the schools whenever some question to be disputed is proposed: which is done, no doubt, for the sake of brevity, because the other part too is now understood by all to be interrogated, from the very mode of the problematic interrogation.

15 Here we must notice that Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, did not distinguish the dialectical proposition from the problem, nor indeed from the probable proposition: since he said that it is an interrogation of a contradiction, which is proper to the problem; and again, that the dialectical proposition is, for the one who questions, an interrogation of a contradiction, but for the one who reasons, the taking of something apparent and probable. Therefore he referred the distinction of these three to ch. 3 of Topics 1, which he cited, saying: as was said in the Topics. For there was the proper place to distinguish these things, in the way in which they have been distinguished by us. The dialectical proposition is fourfold, as we said of the problem. Of Definition is this: Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? Of Property: Do you think risible is a proper attribute of man? Of Genus: Do you think animal is the genus of man? Of Accident: Do you think whiteness is an accident of man?

16 But it should be carefully noted in this matter that Proposition, taken under this general ratio, signifies only an enunciation as it is proposed in a syllogism for inferring the conclusion. If it is proposed in the first place, it is called Proposition simply, or Proposition, or major premise, or the First part of the antecedent. If in the second place, it is called Assumption, because it is assumed under the major proposition, under which it is contained; it is also called Minor proposition, or Minor premise, and the Second, or posterior, part of the antecedent. And if it is proposed in a demonstrative syllogism, it is called a Principle; if in a dialectical syllogism, a Probable proposition; and an Apparent proposition, if in a sophistical syllogism. But the dialectical Proposition adds to the enunciation the mode of a proposition, as it were by way of one who doubts; and the problem the mode of one who interrogates, as has been explained.

From which it is understood that the Dialectical proposition, as well as the problem, and also the probable proposition, serve for setting up a disputation, but in a different ratio: for the dialectical problem serves by way of a question proposed for disputing, and therefore it holds the first place and is called, as it were, the head of the whole disputation.

17 The dialectical Proposition, however, serves as it were for an interrogation made to the respondent, so that by means of it the respondent may put forward another, through which he explains what he thinks of the thing proposed; and from the reply given the interrogator may take occasion to dispute for one or the other part of the proposed question. The probable proposition, in turn, serves now for constituting the syllogism by which what is intended may be proved, and the question terminated or settled. Thus the problem and the dialectical proposition, under

their proper formal ratios, pertain to setting up a disputation, yet not to the dialectical syllogism, except only antecedently and as it were presuppositively. The probable proposition alone pertains to the same disputation as a part of the dialectical syllogism. Here we must notice that Aristotle in this place distinguishes the proposition from the problem, saying that the problem interrogates both parts.

What a probable proposition is, and how many kinds there are. 18

Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 1, defines the probable in these words: Probable things are those which seem so to all, or to most, or to the wise; and to these, either to all, or to most, or to the most familiar and approved. Which is understood either on account of the thing itself, which of itself appears true, or on account of some verisimilar reason. Thus the probable is not the same as the true, nor yet as the necessary or certain, but is that which appears true to all, or to most, or to the wise. For propositions are of three different kinds. For some are evidently true, and their truth is evidently known. Others evidently false, and their falsity too is evidently known. Others, however, hold the middle: because they are true or false, but their truth or falsity is not evidently known, because their cause is either unknown or not fully known; and therefore they appear true to many, while to others it happens that they appear false, since there is usually a verisimilar reason for each side. And these are called probable. It is plain, then, how the probable proposition is distinguished from the proposition that is True, Certain, Necessary, and false. For it can happen that in reality it is necessary, having necessary truth, or that in reality it is necessarily false, having a necessary cause of its falsity, and yet it seems probable on account of the verisimilitude, the appearance of truth, which it has, or on account of a verisimilar reason by which it can be proved. So that it may be understood that the formal ratio of the probable proposition consists not so much in the thing itself as in the appearance, or in an apparent reason, with respect to many, or to the wise, as Aristotle taught.

From which it follows that, although it is repugnant that two contradictories be true at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that they be probable at the same time: because it often happens that each has on its side learned men, to whom it appears true, and also verisimilar reasons by which it is proved. But in the thing itself one of them must be false. It is not, however, necessary (as some mistakenly think) that if one proposition is probable, by that very fact its contradictory is also probable, since it is manifest that it can happen

that the one appears true to learned men and has verisimilar reasons on its side, while the other appears true to no one, nor has any verisimilar reason been found by which it may be proved.

The probable proposition is twofold: one per se, the other on account of another, from which it is deduced. That is called per se probable whose probability is evident from the cognition of the terms alone, without any other reasoning by which it is proved, so that the intellect cannot but judge that it is probable. Such is this: Every mother loves her son; or, Every friend is to be loved. And this per se probable proposition Aristotle defined in Posterior Analytics 1, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition, understanding by the name of opinion the assent of such an immediate proposition, that is, of one which is judged probable without a middle, from the cognition of the terms alone. And the assent of this per se probable proposition can be called understanding within the genus of the probable proposition, just as within the genus of the evident the assent of a necessary proposition which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms alone is known, is called understanding. The other is the Proposition not per se probable, but which is gathered from another that is per se probable through an evident or probable consequence, or from another evident one through a consequence that is only probable. And this is similar to a scientific conclusion, which we gather from evident premises and through an evident syllogism. Nevertheless, from either probable proposition a dialectical syllogism can be made, as is manifest per se.

What a Topical or dialectical syllogism is.

Once the single parts of the dialectical syllogism have been explained, it will not be difficult to understand its definition, which Aristotle assigned in Topics 1, ch. 1, in these words: But the dialectical syllogism is one which is gathered from probable things; that is, one which, proceeding from probable propositions, gathers a conclusion that is also probable. This is to be understood thus: that it must proceed from both premises probable, or at least from one of them; for it often happens that it is made from one evident and the other probable. For such is this one: Every animal loves its like; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man loves his like. And it agrees with the demonstrative syllogism in the common and generic ratio of disposition in Mood and figure; but it is distinguished from it in species by the mode of concluding: for demonstration concludes through a necessary middle, that is, through a necessary cause or effect; whereas the probable syllogism concludes through a probable middle, because it neither renders

a necessary cause nor a necessary effect of the conclusion, but only a probable one, that is, such as appear so to many or to the wise, as has been explained. Thus they are not distinguished by matter alone, as we proved in the

Posterior Analytics, but also by a special form, taken from the special mode of concluding, since they agree in the generic form of syllogistic disposition.

From the sophistical syllogism, however, it is distinguished by true or apparent form, and also by probable or apparent propositions. For the dialectical proceeds from the former, but the sophistical from the latter. But to proceed from probable things and from apparent ones is something different: for although a probable proposition is one which appears true, even though perhaps it is not true, yet it does not appear so to anyone whatever, but only to the wise, and this on account of the foundation of a verisimilar reason, or on account of the verisimilitude of that same truth. But the apparent things from which the sophistical syllogism proceeds are not called such with respect to the wise, nor do they appear true with the foundation of a probable reason, or with the verisimilitude of that same truth, but to anyone whatever, and without these foundations. Hence they have only the bare appearance of truth, and are therefore properly called deceptive; and the syllogism itself, proceeding from things so apparent, is also called deceptive.

Enumeration and explanation of the places from which probable arguments are deduced for entering upon a disputation. 22

This alone remained to be explained among the things that pertain to setting up a dialectical disputation: namely the Places from which probable arguments, or syllogisms, are to be taken. For once places of this kind have been explained and known, it will be easy for anyone to find probable arguments which he can use in disputations. And although the use of the places pertains to any science whatever, according to their application to its proper matter, their explanation nevertheless belongs to Dialectic alone, whose proper office is to furnish all the sciences and disciplines with a method for setting up a disputation.

23 The Place, then, from which arguments are drawn out, is divided into the Intrinsic and the Extrinsic. The Intrinsic place is called that which pertains to the substance of the thing, or accompanies its substance. Those that pertain to the substance are these: Definition, Genus, Difference, or some Part of the thing, such as Matter and Form; or the integral Parts, such as the

Head, the Hand, or the Arm. That which accompanies the substance, on the other hand, is either the Whole (which is said to accompany the substance of the thing because it includes the parts),

An dialecticafit neceffaria adaliasſcientiascompa-randas, Subiectumhuiusquæſtionis eſtDialectica, Pradicatum veròneceſſarium: Poffumus ergovti definitione Dialecticæ, fic arguentes: Scientiadocens argumentaconficere,neceflaria eft adalias ſcientias comparandas: fed dialectica eſtſcientia, docensargumenta conficere: ergo neceſariaad alias ſcientias comparandas.Et fecundùm eandem proportionem ,poſſumus vi definitioneneceſſarij,quod eſtprædicatum quæftionis, ar-quecriam definitione,fimul fubiecti,& prædicati .

or the Description of the thing itself, or the Property of the thing, or an

Accident, or its subject. Hence there are only nine intrinsic places: Definition,

Genus, Difference, Parts, Whole, Description, Property, Accident, and

Subject.

The extrinsic place is said to be that which is not in the thing itself, nor proceeds from it, but is taken from something extrinsic. And the extrinsic place is divided into That which has some affinity with the thing itself, and

That which has some repugnance to it. The extrinsic places having affinity are

Conjugates, Similars, extrinsic Causes, namely the Efficient and the Final, extrinsic Effects, the Greater, the Lesser, Authority Divine or human. The repugnant extrinsic places, on the other hand, are Contraries, Disparates, and

Dissimilars. Hence the extrinsic places are eleven; and if we join them with the nine intrinsic ones, we shall find that all the places, intrinsic as well as extrinsic, are only twenty. These we shall explain one by one, though very briefly, so that the ratio of each may be understood and their use made easy.

The first place, from Definition. 24

Frequent is the use of this place from Definition in disputations, because the definition contains the essence and is convertible with it. Hence it happens that several universal propositions can be deduced from it, which are called Maxims, and as it were heads under which several particular ones are taken for setting up dialectical syllogisms. And if the proposed question about which the dispute is held is Absolute, we can take up in the argumentation the definition of the subject, or of the predicate, or of both; from which are deduced Maxims, Affirmative and Negative. The affirmative are:

Whatever belongs to the definition belongs to the defined; and Whatever can belong to the definition can belong to the defined; and others like them. The negative: What does not belong to the definition does not belong to the defined; and What cannot belong to the definition cannot belong to the defined. For example: if the proposed q. to be disputed is, Whether dialectic is necessary for acquiring the other sciences, the

Subject of this question is Dialectic, and the Predicate is necessary. We can therefore use the definition of Dialectic, arguing thus: A science teaching how to construct arguments is necessary for acquiring the other sciences; but dialectic is a science teaching how to construct arguments; therefore it is necessary for acquiring the other sciences. And according to the same proportion we can use the definition of necessary, which is the predicate of the question, and also the definition of subject and predicate together.

[p. 729]

But if the question is Comparative, namely, Whether necessity for acquiring the other sciences belongs more to dialectic than to the other arts, we can use the definition of the subject, and also of the predicate, or of both, deducing from them certain Maxims similar to the ones above, with these adverbs more and less. As if we say: To that to which the definition belongs more, the defined belongs more; and To that to which the definition belongs less, the defined belongs less; and so of the rest.

The second place, from Genus. 25

In almost the same ways we can use the place from genus. For on account of the necessary connection which it has with the species, several Maxims are deduced from this place, from which we can set up arguments: such as these, Whatever belongs essentially to the genus also belongs essentially to the species; and, What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species; and so of the others, according to the modes of arguing explained for definition. And to this place of genus is reduced the place of Species, because it has a similar connection with the individuals; and therefore no other place from species is added, but almost the same Maxims can be deduced as from genus, and they must be applied in the same way to forming arguments from species.

The third place, from Difference.

Very similar to the two preceding places, from definition and from genus, is the place from Difference. For difference is twofold, Subaltern and Atomic. And if it is subaltern, it is predicated of the same species as the genus is, and has the same intrinsic connection with them. Wherefore the same Maxims can be deduced from it as from genus. But if it is Atomic, it agrees with definition in two things. First, in that it is intrinsic to the species. Second, because it is convertible with it. Hence similar Maxims too can be deduced from it as are deduced from definition, and they must be applied in the same ways to constructing dialectical syllogisms.

The fourth place, from the parts.

Parts are of three different kinds: Subjective, as species with respect to genus; Essential, as matter and form, or genus and difference; and

Integral, as head, hand, and arm. And of these, some are necessary for the consistence of the whole, without which it cannot be, such as the head, the heart, and the like. Others are not necessary, but it can be without them, such as the hand, the finger, the foot. And from the first an argument can be deduced; from the second it cannot be deduced, because neither

[p. 730]

do they infer the consistence of the whole, nor do they remove it. From the

parts several Maxims can be deduced, on account of the necessary connection which they have with the whole, and the whole with them: such as these, What necessarily accompanies the part must necessarily also accompany the whole; and, What is repugnant to the part is also repugnant to the whole. And these are taken on the side of the subject of the proposed q. Others, however, can be taken on the side of the predicate, according to proportion.

The fifth place, from the Whole. 27

The Whole is twofold. One is universal, which is a universal predicate with respect to its inferiors, which are its subjective parts: as genus with respect to the species, and a term distributed by a universal sign, as every man, with respect to the particulars which are contained under it. And from this whole to its parts are taken all the arguments that are made from superior to inferior negatively; and these are manifest in the Summulae. The other is the

Essential or integral whole, as man, horse, house. And from this whole several

Maxims can be deduced, and from them several syllogisms constructed: as,

When the whole is posited, all the necessary parts must be posited. Hence the argument holds from the positing of the whole to the positing of any necessary part whatever. And also, When the whole is taken away, some necessary part must be taken away. Hence the argument holds from the negation of the whole to the negation of some necessary part, under a disjunction: as, if the house is lacking, either the foundation does not exist, or the roof does not exist, or some other necessary part does not exist.

The sixth place, from Description. 28

Description is a definition which they usually call descriptive, because it does not explain the essence of the thing, nor is it delivered through genus and difference, but through a proper attribute, which is nevertheless convertible with the thing described: as animal apt to laugh with man. And therefore all the Maxims which are deduced from definition can be deduced from description, and applied in the same way to constituting syllogisms.

And what is said of description ought to be understood of the definition of what the name means, since it too is convertible with the thing; but not of the etymology of the name: because it often happens that that from which the name is imposed and that which it signifies are different; wherefore a firm argument cannot be drawn from the etymology to the thing signified.

The seventh place, from Property.

Property is that which does not indicate what it is to be for the thing, but is in it alone, and is predicated convertibly, as Aristotle defines it, ch. 4, bk. 1: as if
