to say that a proper attribute does not pertain to what the thing is, or to its essence, yet is convertible with it, just as the definition is convertible with the defined. And therefore in almost the same ways almost the same arguments can be deduced from property as from definition: because, To whatever the definition belongs, the proper attribute belongs; and, To whatever the proper attribute does not belong, neither does the definition belong. And just as it is rightly gathered that a thing is more perfect the more perfect the definition it has, so also the more perfect the attribute it has, since the latter proceeds from the essence as from its proper cause.

The 8th place, from Accident. 29

An accident is that which is present to and absent from the subject without its corruption, as Aristotle defines it in the same place. But this definition seems to belong only to truly inhering accidents, which are therefore called intrinsic; nevertheless, the others too, which seem to signify only an extrinsic denomination, ought in this place to be understood under the name of accident: as for a wall to be right or left, or to be seen or understood; because in the mode of denominating they are similar to intrinsic accidents. From accident several Maxims can be deduced, and from these several arguments. As,

If the accidents of the predicate do not belong to the subject, the predicate will not cohere with the subject: which argument blessed Peter seems to have used, Acts 2, proving that the disciples were not drunk because that time, the third hour of the day, was not suited to drunkenness, and therefore not to the disciples either, since drunkenness was imputed to them at that same hour. And it is well proved that someone did not kill another if it is proved that at the time when he was killed he was not in the same place as the killing, but elsewhere.

Place 9, from the Subject.

This place is understood of the subject of inherence, in which accidents inhere, not of the subject of predication, to which a predicate can belong essentially; and therefore it is rightly numbered among the intrinsic places.

From the subject these Maxims and the like can be deduced: To whatever the accidents are repugnant, the subject too is repugnant: as, if intellect is repugnant to something, so also is the soul; and if corporeal accidents are repugnant to it, the body too will be repugnant to it. Where the subject is, there the accidents must be; and Where the accidents are not, neither is the subject; and All things move with our motion that are in us, that is, the accidents. And from these and other

Maxims many arguments can be made from the place of the subject. And these are all the intrinsic places. The extrinsic ones follow.

The tenth place, and the first among the Extrinsic ones, from Conjugates.

30

Conjugates are said to be words which under different endings signify and participate in the same form; and for this reason they seem as it were to draw the same yoke, as just, justice, and justly; and all the cases by which the same noun and verb are varied. To these are reduced others which signify the same form, although they are altogether different words: as just and virtuous, which are related, as regards the thing signified, as justice and just are. From these are deduced these maxims and the like: What is said of one of the conjugates is said also of the other in its own way, and with due variation: as, if the Philosopher is knowing, Philosophy will be knowledge; and, Of whatever one of the conjugates is said, the other too is said in its own way. And from these and similar propositions many arguments can be made from conjugates.

Place 11, from the Similar.

Similar things are those which participate in the same form: as all white things.

To these are reduced those which have the same proportion: as the charioteer and the general, because the general ought to have in the army a care similar to that which the charioteer has in his chariot. To similars are also reduced equals; and from them several Maxims are deduced for setting up arguments, similar to this: The swan disperses the sight; therefore the white wall does too. But in these the argument must always be made from the formal ratio of similitude, and not from other material features which similar things can have: for it is not a good argument if we say, The swan is a bird; therefore the white wall too is a bird.

Place 12, from Cause. 31

Cause is fourfold: Final, Efficient, Material, and Formal. But this place, since it is extrinsic, embraces only the Final and the Efficient, not the Material and the Formal, which, since they are intrinsic parts of the thing, will rather pertain to the place of the parts. The final cause is that for the sake of which the efficient operates and produces the effect; the efficient cause, that from which the effect proceeds. The Maxims which can be deduced from them are similar to these: When the cause is posited, the effect is necessarily posited, which is understood of an actual and sufficient cause; and When the effect is not posited, the cause is not posited. The things which pertain to the property of these causes are explained by us in Phys. bk. 2.

Place 13, from the Effect.

Very similar to the preceding is this place, because the same Maxims are deduced from cause and from effect: the mode of arguing in them is the same, as from the positing of the effect to the positing of the cause: e.g., If it is day, the sun is in our hemisphere. When the effect is taken away, the cause is taken away: as, It is not day; therefore neither is the sun in our hemisphere. But these and others like them are understood of necessary and sufficient causes.

Place 14, from the Greater, and 15, from the Lesser. 32

Very similar are these two places, from the greater and the lesser, and therefore we must speak of them together. From the greater this Maxim is taken: What can effect the greater can effect the lesser; and from the lesser this one: What cannot effect the lesser cannot effect the greater either. But each must be understood of a greater and a lesser of the same condition. For if they are of a different ratio, the argument will not hold: e.g., An angel can understand, which is greater; therefore he can walk, which is lesser; because understanding and walking are of different conditions. Likewise, He cannot walk; therefore neither can he understand.

Place 16 and 17, from Authority, Divine and human.

The testimony of one worthy of belief, on which faith rests, is very extrinsic to the things testified or believed, as is manifest of itself. Hence the place from the authority of one worthy of belief is supremely extrinsic. But if it is from

Divine authority, it attributes infallible truth to the thing: because, since God is the highest and first truth, he cannot be deceived; and since he is the highest goodness, he cannot deceive. Hence the things which G o d testifies have infallible truth; and such are the things of our faith, which we believe on account of the Divine authority; and Theological arguments are deduced chiefly from this place.

33 From human authority or testimony, however, so firm an argument cannot be deduced. But it is of very great value for explaining the things of divine faith. For although the sacred Doctors were men, nevertheless an exposition of sacred

Scripture which all, or most of them, put forward (even if one, or another, dissents) produces the greatest belief: because it is not to be believed that

God has permitted those to be deceived in this matter to whom it pertains to expound Scripture and to hand it on, expounded, to others. It is also of great value in matters which depend on the free will of men, as for the imposition and signification of names: because names are to be used as most

use them. Moreover, in things which are evidently known through the senses, and also in those which pertain to history, which must rest on some evidence, had for the most part through assents, from which others believe that things happened thus. But it is not of value in those things which are known through discursive reasoning, in which reason holds the chief place, although even in these the common consent of all is still of much value. A probable argument, therefore, is always drawn from human authority; and the more there are who testify to something, the more efficacious the argument that is deduced. Negatively, however, one must not argue from human authority, as if it were proved that a thing is not so because it is related by no one: because it is not necessary that all things have been written.

Place 18 and 19, from Opposites, and from Repugnants or Disparates.

These two places, from Opposites and from Repugnants, or Disparates, do not differ much, because almost the same arguments are deduced from both. Opposition is fourfold, as we said in the Postpredicaments: Contrary, which is between White and Black; Contradictory, between white and Not-white; Privative, between blind and seeing; and Relative, between Father and Son. And in contradictory opposites this Maxim is always true: What belongs to one cannot belong to the other; and, To whatever one does not belong, the other necessarily belongs: because their opposition is immediate. And the same holds in privative opposites, not indeed absolutely, but concerning an apt subject: as, To whatever blindness belongs, sight cannot at the same time belong; nor, To whatever sight belongs can blindness at the same time belong. And if sight does not belong, blindness must belong; and, If blindness does not belong, sight must belong. In contraries, however, the argument holds from the affirmation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is white; therefore it is not black. But it does not hold from the negation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is not white; therefore it is black; because contrary opposition is not immediate. And similar arguments can be deduced from repugnants, or disparates, whose examples are manifest enough.

Place 20, from the Dissimilar.

Those things are called Dissimilar which have a different form or nature: as whiteness and sweetness, white and black, man and lion. To these are reduced those which, although they have the same form, yet have it not in the same degree but in a different one: such as hot as one and hot as eight. And from both, arguments can be taken: because what belongs to one cannot belong to the other. But they must always be taken formally, that

## ON THE SOPHISTICAL SYLLOGISM

hat Aristotle does in the two books of the Sophistical Refutations we 1

W              comprehend, so as to embrace this whole work in a universal divi‐

sion. He explains the nature of the Sophistical syllogism, and of the parts of which it is composed, as of his proper object. Then he enumerates all the places from which fallacious arguments are deduced, or take their occasion: which are the Fallacies both in Speech and outside Speech. We, however, referring the things that pertain to the fallacies to the Summulae, in which they are copiously explained, shall say something about the nature of the sophistical syllogism; once this is understood, whatever Aristotle delivers about it in the present work can be grasped, at least in some measure.

What a Sophistical syllogism is, and how many kinds there are; and whether it is a true syllogism, or not? 2

The sophistical syllogism, if we follow the etymology of the name, signifies the same as the syllogism of a wise man, since σοφός [sophos] is “wise”; yet by the philosophical usage of the school it has come about that by it is now understood not the syllogism of a wise man, but of one who deceives, or wishes to deceive.

Because by a sophist all now understand not a truly wise man, but one who wishes to seem wise. Aristotle delivers the definition and division of the sophistical syllogism in Topics 1, ch. 1. But in order that the three things which can be considered about it may be explained more conveniently, we must begin from the division.

Aristotle, then, divides the sophistical syllogism into three members, and defines the first thus: But the contentious is a syllogism from things which seem probable but are not. The second in these words: And that which is from probable things, or from things which seem probable, is apparent. And a little below, speaking of each in particular, he asserts that the First is a true syllogism, the Second not true but apparent.

The last member he calls a paralogism; and he says that it is one because it takes up propositions proper to some science, which, as they are taken up by that science, are necessary, but as they are taken up by him, only appear necessary, and are false. And such is this syllogism: Lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal; the chord and the arc are drawn from the same point; therefore they are equal. This syllogism is constituted in matter

of geometry, but geometry takes the major proposition thus: All straight lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal. And thus it is true and necessary; but since it is taken in that syllogism without the word straight, it appears indeed necessary, because it appears the same, but it is false and very different, as is evident; and therefore it proceeds from propositions of that science which appear necessary, yet are not truly necessary, but false.

3 Of these three syllogisms, then, the first, which is called Contentious, and the third, which is called Paralogism, agree in this, that each preserves the syllogistic form, since it is constituted in Figure and Mood; hence on this side it does not sin; but they differ in the things from which they proceed. For the former proceeds from things which appear probable but are not probable; whereas the paralogism proceeds from things necessary and proper to some science, but which are neither necessary nor pertain to that science, but are false. The second, however, which is also called contentious, differs from the other two in both respects. For in the first place it does not preserve the form of the syllogism, but sins in it; and therefore Aristotle said of it that it is a contentious syllogism, but not truly a syllogism, that is, that it does not have the true form of a syllogism, but only an apparent one.

And from these things it is understood, first, that the First and the third have the true form of a syllogism, and are therefore true syllogisms. For to proceed from apparent, or even from false, things does not take away the true form of a syllogism. But the Second is not a true syllogism, but an apparent one; and such are all those which do not preserve the rules of syllogisms, but proceed either from an equivocal middle, or from one not distributed, or from negative premises, or suffer other defects concerning form.

4 It is understood, second, that these three syllogisms are essentially diverse: because they differ either by reason of the syllogistic form or on the side of the premises. On the side of form, the second differs from the first and the third; and since a difference on the side of form is essential, it is evident that it differs essentially from them. Finally, the first and the third, although they agree in the syllogistic and as it were generic form, nevertheless differ in the special form, taken from the mode of concluding.

For the first proceeds and concludes from things which only appear probable; the third, however, from things which appear necessary. Therefore the first and the third differ as true species of syllogism. The second, however, does not differ from them as a true species, because, since it does not have the true form of a syllogism, neither can it be a true species of it, but only according to appearance. Hence

those two are syllogisms simply, but this one is not, except in a certain respect: because it has only the appearance of a syllogism, in the way in which a painted man has only the appearance of a man. It differs from them, therefore, analogically.

Wherefore it is understood, third, that the division of the sophistical syllogism into these three members is a division of an analogous term into its Analogates; but with respect to two members, namely the first and the third, it is a division of a genus into its species. And therefore Aristotle did not define them all by one definition, but by different ones, at once dividing the sophistical syllogism into these three members and defining each by its proper definitions.

It is understood, fourth, that the general division of the syllogism into Demonstrative, Dialectical, and Sophistical is a division of a genus into its species, if sophistical is taken only for that which does not sin in form, in which way it comprehends only the first and the third. For taken in this way alone it is a true species of syllogism, though a subaltern one, since it is divided into two other species. The second syllogism, however, is not a true species of syllogism, since it lacks the form, but only according to appearance. Hence, if sophistical is taken as it comprehends all three, the same general division will, on its side, be analogous, since it comprehends one member which is not a syllogism except in a certain respect.

6 Besides this division of the syllogism into those three members, which is essential, it is divided by an accidental division into members according to the two different effects, or ends, which the sophist can intend through it. The first end is to display knowledge and to hunt for glory; and then it is called a sophistical syllogism only, or contentious: because through it the sophist intends not so much to set up a disputation as a quarrel or strife, and to overcome the respondent with fallacious words, and thus to be held wise in the opinion of the crowd. The second end is to make trial, or to take a test, of the knowledge of another; and then it is called a Tentative syllogism.

Next it is also divided accidentally into five other members, according to the five absurdities to which the sophist intends to lead the respondent. And these absurdities are customarily called goals, or terms: because it is as it were to them, as to the goal, mark, or end of his disputation, that he intends to lead the other. The first is the goal of Refutation: when the respondent is compelled, by the force of an apparent syllogism, to deny what he had previously granted, or to grant what he had denied.

7 The second is the goal of the false: when he is compelled to grant something openly false, as that he himself is not a man, by this syllogism: What I am, you are not; I am a man; therefore, You are not

a man. The third is the goal of the unbelievable, or Paradox: when he is compelled to grant something unbelievable to the wise, or unheard of in the opinion of the crowd, although perhaps it is not false. The fourth, the goal of Solecism: when he is compelled to grant some incongruous expression. The fifth is called the goal of Babbling: when he is compelled to a useless and less ornate expression, by which he seems to babble. As if he is compelled to say that a nose is a curved or snub nose. And let it suffice to have noted these things on the sophistical syllogism: from which we shall know its nature, and also how many species and members it has, and how many of its members are true syllogisms, and how many not true, but only apparent. All the fallacies, however, which are as it were the places from which various fallacious syllogisms can be deduced, have been sufficiently explained in the Summulae; and therefore we do not think that the enumeration and explanation of each is to be repeated in this part.

These things, finally, we have noted in our Commentaries concerning the whole Logic of Aristotle, rendering it, I think, clear enough and brief, so that it may easily, and in a short time, be explained to the students of the liberal Arts of this most flourishing Academy by their Masters in the Schools, and be grasped by them. May G o d , Best and Greatest, grant that this labor of ours, undertaken for their sake, may redound to his glory and that of the most holy Mother of God, and of St. Thomas, and to the greatest benefit of those same students (as we hope). THE END OF THE WHOLE LOGIC.
